Aiṃ, obeisance to Śrī; Oṃ, obeisance to Prīti; Auṃ, obeisance to Aṅgadā.

Having worshipped the *kalās* with "Oṃ *Pūrṇāyai* namaḥ" and "Aḥ *Pūrṇāmṛtāyai* namaḥ," and having added fragrant substances such as cardamom, cloves, and camphor, one should draw the yantra on the material as before; then,
having written "aṃ 16 kaṃ 16 khaṃ 16" along the lines of the triangle, [one writes] in the center.
Having written "haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ" and worshipped it with the three root-mantra sections, [one recites]:
"O Gaṅgā, O Yamunā, O Godāvarī, O Sarasvatī!"

"O Sun, take up residence in these waters of the Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī! O Lord Divākara, by the truth that the sacred fords within the belly of the universe have been touched by Your rays, grant me a sacred ford!
With these and other such verses, having invoked the sacred fords with the *aṅkuśa-mudrā* (the hook-gesture), [one offers] a flower with "vauṣaṭ" and [an oblation] with "vaṣaṭ."

Having thus demonstrated the Gālinī mudrā—wherein the little finger and the thumb of the two hands are joined with one another—the Gālinī mudrā is as follows: "The little finger and the thumbs of the two hands are joined with one another."

With the fingers— the index, middle, and ring fingers— held together, unbent, and not separated, one should consecrate [the offering] with nectar by means of the *dhenumudrā* (cow-seal). Then, having meditated upon the chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*),
worshipped them, performed the *saṅkalīkaraṇa*, and displayed the *śaṅkhamudrā* (conch-seal), one should worship the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) within the hexagon.
In the east: *glūṃ* obeisance to the jewels of the sky; in the south: *slūṃ* obeisance to the jewels of heaven; in the west:
*plūṃ* obeisance to the jewels of the underworld; in the north: *mlūṃ* obeisance to the jewels of humans; and in the center: *nūṃ* obeisance to the jewels of the nāgas.

Having worshipped [the deity], one should recite the root mantra *aiṃ* three times, followed by: *amṛte amṛtodbhave amṛteśvari amṛtavarṣiṇi amṛtaṃ srāvaya sāṃ jūṃ jūṃ amṛteśvaryai svāhā*. Then, one should recite either the *traiyambaka* mantra or the *gāyatrī*.
Reciting "Śāṃ śīṃ śūṃ śaiṃ śauṃ śaḥ, svāhā to her who is liberated from the curse of Śukra," and thus remembering Amṛteśī:
"O you who bestow unbroken, singular, supreme bliss, whose nature is the highest nectar..."
Place here your own spontaneous vibration, which takes the form of nectar.
Resembling ten million suns and as cool as ten million moons,
the god has eighteen arms, five faces, and three eyes;
he stands upon a Brahma-lotus situated in the midst of an ocean of nectar.
Mounted upon a bull, blue-throated, adorned with all ornaments,
holding a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff, and sounding a bell and a ḍamaru drum.
The god who holds a noose and a goad, who bears a mace and a club, and who carries a sword,
a shield, a sharp-edged spear, a mallet, a trident, and a lance.

The best of practitioners should meditate upon the Lord of the Gods, who is red in color, adorned with a garland of various weapons and severed heads, and granting the boons of generosity and fearlessness.
And one should meditate upon the goddesses, possessing the radiance of ten million times ten thousand moons,
white as snow, jasmine, and the moon, five-faced, and three-eyed.

"Endowed with eighteen arms, intent on bestowing all bliss, laughing, large-eyed, and facing the God of gods"— with this mantra, having taken up the substance with the left thumb and middle finger, [one offers it] to Ānandabhairava.
Having worshipped and offered libations there to the pair [of deities] *Va* and *Mithuna*, and having recollected *Amṛteśī*:

"O *Klīṃ*, who abides in the *Kula*, whose form is nectar, O supreme bestower of the knowledge of *siddhi*; O you whose nature is moist (*klinna*), place the state of immortality (*amṛtatva*) here in this object! *Haṃsaḥ*, I offer libations; *namaḥ*. Thus, one should offer libations as before.
Having recollected Amṛteśī and having bestowed the name "having the single flavor of that form" (tadrūpaikarasā), she indeed becomes one whose very nature is this.

"O Mother, having assumed the form of the nectar of the Kula, perform your vibration. Having thus offered libations as before with "Haṃsaḥ," having recited the root mantra seven times, veiled it with the Kavaca (armor) mantra, protected it with the Astra (weapon) mantra, and covered it with the Matsya-mudrā (fish-gesture), one should display the Yoni-mudrā and the Dhenu-mudrā.
Thus ends the procedure for the installation of the vessel (*pātrasthāpanavidhi*). One should perform the installation of the *arghya* water on the right. As follows:

having drawn a triangle, a circle, a hexagon, and a square enclosure, one should worship with the mantra "Oṃ, obeisance to Ādhāraśakti. Then, having positioned the tip of the triangle facing upward, one should display the conch-gesture (*śaṅkhamudrā*).
The conch mudrā is as follows: having placed the thumb inside the left fist with the fingers straight, one should touch [the thumb] with the left thumb of the right hand.

"This is declared by those who know the mantras to be the unsurpassed Śaṅkha-mudrā. Having thus worshipped the six limbs with flowers and unbroken rice-grains in the directions of Agni, Īśa, Asura, Vāyu, and in the center, one should place the washed support (ādhāra) while reciting "Phaṭ," and having worshipped the fire-mandala therein, [one should proceed] with that...

Having washed the conch with the previously mentioned seed-syllable and placed [the water] therein, one should worship the solar disc (*sūryamaṇḍala*) there with the previously mentioned mantra; having offered *jāla* (water) with the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*), one should worship the lunar disc (*candramaṇḍala*) with the previously mentioned mantra, beginning with "O Gaṅgā... and so forth.
Having invoked the *tīrtha*, joined [it] with the syllable "vauṣaṭ," and worshipped it, and having worshipped the *tīrtha-śakti* as well,

having placed flowers with the syllable "vaṣaṭ" and displayed the *gālinī-mudrā*, having rendered [the water] nectarine by means of the *dhenu-mudrā* and the *svadhā-bīja* "ram," having meditated upon the chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) and performed the ritual of integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*), [one should assign] the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*).
Having renounced [the offering], protected it with the Astra-mantra, worshipped it, consecrated it eight times with the root mantra,
covered it with the Matsya-mudrā, and scattered kusha grass tips, unbroken rice, sesame, paddy, barley, clarified butter, white mustard seeds, and flowers;

Having displayed the *yonimudrā*, one should pour a little water from the *śrīpātra* [into the vessel]; this is the procedure for the establishment of the *arghya*. To its left, having worshipped the *ādhāraśakti* within a triangle, circle, and square, [one places] the *pādya* vessel.
Having established the common vessel and filled it with water using the root mantra "Namaḥ," one should cast a flower with "Vaṣaṭ" and perfume with "Namaḥ," and then add uśīra, rocanā,
and either śyāmāka, viṣṇukrāntā, akṣatā, and dūrvā; or—

Having condensed [the mantra] and consecrated it eight times with the Astra-mantra, one should consecrate it with the Mūla-mantra and display the Dhenu and Yoni mudrās. Thus, having worshipped Ādhāra-śakti within a square drawn three times on its side for the vessel of water for sipping (ācamanīya-pātra), and having placed the vessel upon its support, [one says] "Namaḥ."

Having filled [the vessel] either with the root mantra or with water, having cast a flower with "Vaṣaṭ" and perfume with "Namaḥ," and having thrown in the powder of jasmine, camphor, kaṅkola, cloves, tamālaka, and so forth, [he should recite] the Astra-mantra eight times.
Having consecrated it with the root mantra and shaken it, one should show the *yonimudrā*. To its right,
having worshipped the *ādhāra-śakti* upon a vessel that is triangular, circular, and square, one should place the vessel together with its base, filled with honey, ghee, sugar, curd, and milk.

Having stabilized it with the Astra-mantra and consecrated it eight times with the Mūla-mantra, one should display the Dhenu and Yoni mudrās. To its right, having worshipped Ādhāra-śakti within a triangle, circle, and square,
and having placed the vessel upon its support, one should fill it with water while reciting "Namaḥ" or the Mūla-mantra.

Having filled [the vessel], one should cast in a flower with "Vaṣaṭ" and perfume with "Namaḥ"; then, having briefly added uśīra and rocanā, one should consecrate it eight times with the Astra-mantra, consecrate it again with the Mūla-mantra, and display the Dhenu and Yoni mudrās.

One should show [the deity]. Right there, one should place the sacred sandalwood paste, flowers, incense, garments, ornaments, and so forth; having consecrated them with either the water from the general *arghya* vessel or the special water, one should empower them eight times with the root mantra.

One should display the *dhenu-yoni-mudrā* while reciting the mantra *antrya*. In this way, for the purification of all things, one should satisfy the two Bhairavas upon one's own head with special water. One should satisfy the Goddess in the heart three times with the nectar from the *śrīpātra* or with the special *arghya* vessel. And this is the ritual of satisfaction (*tarpaṇa*).

By means of the *tattvamudrā*. That [mudrā] is to be understood through the joining of the ring finger and the thumb. In this context, the purification of the principles (*tattvaśuddhi*) and other rites should also be performed by the Kaulas. Regarding this, there is a scriptural authority (*śruti*):
May my prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna breaths be purified; may I become light, stainless, and free from evil—svāhā! Om, may my earth, water, fire, air, and ether be purified, and so forth;
Om, may my nature (prakṛti), ego (ahaṅkāra), intellect (buddhi), mind (manas), and ears be purified... [and so on].

May they be purified; may I become light, stainless, and free from evil, svāhā! Om! May touch, form, taste, smell, and space be purified for me; may I become light, stainless, and free from evil, svāhā! Om! May wind, fire, water, earth, and the self be purified for me...
"May I become pure, luminous, free from passion, and free from evil—svāhā! Thus, while touching all his limbs seven times, [he recites]: "Oṃ! May my skin, eyes, tongue, nose, and speech be purified;
may I become luminous, free from passion, and free from evil—svāhā. Oṃ."
May my hands, feet, anus, and genitals be purified; may I become light, stainless, and free from evil. Svāhā! Thus ends the purification of the principles (tattvaśuddhi).
Having prepared mandalas in the northeast, southeast, southwest, and northwest corners, and having worshipped Baṭuka, the Yoginīs, Gaṇeśa, Kṣetrapāla, and the Bhūtas,
one should offer the bali-oblation of *vaṭaka* cakes and other items. Having honored the mandala, one should place the substances such as *vaṭaka* cakes and so forth [within it].
Oṃ, come, come, O Goddess, O Jvālāmukha, radiant with the mass of matted hair of a young ascetic;
destroy, destroy all obstacles! Accept, accept this bali-offering together with all ritual attendants!
Svāhā! With this mantra, using the union of the thumb and ring finger, one should offer the bali to Baṭuka in the northeast.
Whether above the cosmic egg, or in the celestial realms, the netherworlds, the surface of the earth, or in the formless void;
whether in the subterranean regions, in fire, in water, or in air; wherever they may be situated, or having established their firm footing in sacred fields, seats, and secondary seats.

"May the goddesses, who are like the lords of the gods, being pleased by flowers, incense, and the like, and by the rite of auspicious offerings, come as constant givers of boons. With the mantra "yāṃ yīṃ yūṃ yaiṃ yauṃ yaḥ yoginībhyaḥ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā," one should offer the bali in the southeast corner using the union of the little finger and the thumb.
"KṢĀṂ KṢĪṂ KṢŪṂ KṢAIṂ KṢAUṂ KṢAḤ, accept, accept the bali offering together with incense, lamps, and so forth, svāhā!"—
with the thumb and index finger, one should offer the bali in the northwest corner (Vāyukoṇa).

"Gāṃ gīṃ gūṃ varavarada sarvajanaṃ me vaśamānaya baliṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa svāhā. Having formed the fingers in the shape of a staff with the middle of the fist, one should offer the *bali* in the southwest (Nairṛta).

Having drawn a mandala on the left side, having placed a vessel with its support, having offered the sacrificial substances (bali) therein, and having performed the consecration (seka) and other rites, [one should recite] with this: "Oṃ hrīṃ, to all obstructors, to all spirits, hūṃ phaṭ svāhā."

One should offer the *bali* to the spirits with the *tattvamudrā*. This offering of *bali*, however, should actually be performed only during the *puraścaraṇa* rite. [It should be drawn] on gold, crystal, or similar materials, using substances such as saffron, musk, sandalwood from Malaya, red sandalwood, and so forth.
And with the mantra "Āsurekhavajrarekhā hūṃ phaṭ svāhā," one should draw the yantra consisting of a hexagon, three inner triangles, an eight-petaled lotus, and a square enclosure. Therein,
having washed [the yantra] with the five products of the cow and the five nectars, [one should perform the rite] with the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra.
Having performed the installation of the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) one hundred and eight times, the mantra is as follows:
"Āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ hoṃ oṃ kṣaṃ saṃ haṃ saḥ hrīṃ oṃ haṃsaḥ."

"Oṃ, may the vital breaths of speech, mind, sight, hearing, smell, and life-force of the glorious Dakṣiṇakālikā—residing within this Yantra consisting of a hexagon, three inner triangles, an eight-petaled lotus, and a square enclosure—come here and remain happily for a long time, Svāhā! Then: "Oṃ, let us know the King of Yantras..."

Having recited "We meditate upon the Great Yantra; may that Yantra impel us" ten times, and having offered ten handfuls of flowers, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa). During the fire sacrifice, one should cast the remnants of the oblation into that [yantra]. Therein, one should perform the worship of Ādhāraśakti and the others. It is as follows:
Having worshipped with "Hrīṃ, salutation to the Ādhāraśaktis," one then places a heap of red sandalwood paste, flowers, and unbroken rice grains, and [worships] with: "Oṃ, salutation to Jayā;
Oṃ, salutation to Vijayā; Oṃ, salutation to Ajitā; Oṃ, salutation to Aparājitā."

Having worshipped the seat-powers (pīṭhaśakti) with "Oṃ nityāyai namaḥ," "Oṃ vilāsinyai namaḥ," "Oṃ dogdhyai namaḥ," "Oṃ aghorāyai namaḥ," and "Oṃ maṅgalāyai namaḥ," [one should worship] with "Hrīṃ kālikāyogapīṭhātmane namaḥ."
Having worshipped with "Hsauṃ Sadāśiva-mahāpreta-padmāsanāya namaḥ," one should then worship the Goddess. Placing a cluster of flowers and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) in the hands,
and having formed the tortoise gesture (*kūrmamudrā*), one should bring Kulakuṇḍalinī to the region of the heart and [place her] at her mouth.
Having cast that [nectar] into the Supreme Brahman and merged it there,

one should place it within the two petals as it becomes liquefied with the nectar inside the lunar orb; then, drawing it out through the left nostril with the syllable "Yam," one should meditate upon the previously mentioned Kāmakalā.
"The face has the form of a drop (bindu), below that the pair of breasts, and below that the rest of the body, together with the adorned maṇḍala.
Then, one should cast flowers and other offerings upon the cakra. Having meditated upon the Goddess, one should invoke her. And the meditation is as follows:
[One should meditate upon] Kālikā, the divine southern [form], who has a terrifying face, is fierce, has loose hair, possesses four arms, and is adorned with a garland of severed heads. || 1 ||
Her left upper and lower lotus-hands hold a sword with its blade recently severed,
while her right upper and lower hands display the gestures of fearlessness and the granting of boons.
She possesses the luster of a great cloud, is dark-complexioned, and likewise naked;
she is smeared with blood dripping from a garland of severed heads hanging around her neck.
She was terrifying with a pair of corpses used as ear-ornaments;
her face was made formidable by fierce fangs, and she possessed full, elevated breasts.
She wears a girdle formed from a multitude of corpses in the form of sprouts; her face is smiling, and her countenance is made radiant by streams of blood trickling from both corners of her mouth.
She has the form of a cow, is exceedingly fierce, dwells in cremation grounds,
has protruding teeth, extends to the south, and has loose, hanging masses of hair.
She is seated upon the heart of Mahādeva in the form of a Śava,
surrounded on the four sides by Śivās of terrible appearance.
Seated together with Mahākāla, she was intent on amorous play;
her face was serene with happiness, and her lotus-like countenance was smiling.
Thus one should contemplate the Goddess who dwells in the cremation ground;
or else, one should perform the meditation as described in the Haṃsatantra, as follows:
"I bow to Dakṣiṇāmūrti, to Kālikā, the supreme Bhairavī."
Resembling a heap of crushed collyrium, it lay amidst the corpses of great heroes.
With streams of blood from her goring, she whose lotus-face was smiling, whose pair of breasts were full and elevated, and who possessed a broad chest and shapely hips; || 2 ||
Facing south, with her hair loosened, she delights in being naked; she rests upon the corpse of Mahākāla, seated atop a smile of bliss. || 3 ||
Her face was gladdened by the fragrance of a dense smile, she was intoxicated with passion,
and she shone with a multitude of eyes that were deep red at the corners.
(36) She has two corpses forming her head-ornament, is radiant with a tilaka of vermilion, and is crimson with the blood of a garland composed of fifty severed heads. (5)
Richly adorned with the splendor of various jewels and beautified by diverse ornaments,
she is decorated with bracelets and conch-shell bangles fashioned from human bones.
Mounted upon the chest of a corpse, she licks a corpse here and there; having made a morsel of the corpse's flesh, she laughs aloud again and again.
She holds a sword and a severed head; her left and right hands bestow the gestures of fearlessness and the boon.
She is jagged-toothed, exceedingly fierce, with a violent roar, and most terrifying. (8)
Surrounded by auspicious yet terrible forms, she is the destroyer of fear;
do not fear, do not fear—she speaks thus to her own devotees with her formidable roars.
"Tell me, what do you desire? I shall give it," thus she speaks—thus one should meditate. And the invocation: "I invoke You, the unborn, pure Supreme Goddess, who abides within my own self."
Reciting the root mantra, "I invoke the sacrificial oblation as if from the forest into embodied form," and saying,
"O Blessed Dakṣiṇakālikā, come here!
one should perform the invocation by placing the two thumbs upon the root joints of the extended and joined fingers.
Then [he recites]: "Oṃ! O Goddess, easily accessible through devotion, accompanied by your retinue! As long as I worship you, may you remain perfectly steady. This is your majestic form;
within it, O Lord, I establish you—who pervade all things—drawn by the oil of devotion like a lamp."

Having recited the root mantra (*mūla*) thus, one should establish [the seat] with the previously mentioned downward-facing mudrā. Reciting the root mantra and the following: "Oṃ, O Goddess, inner controller of all, auspicious one consisting of all seeds, I prepare this supreme, pure seat for you who abide within my own self," using the lotus mudrā (*padmamudrā*).

One should offer a seat of flowers and other materials. Then, reciting the root mantra and the verse: "O Goddess, who are of the nature of the Imperishable, may you be firmly established upon this excellent seat; O Supreme Sovereign, be gracious," one should perform the ritual of installation with the previously mentioned mudrā, saying: "Be established here."

One should establish [the deity] with the following: "O Lord of Gods, O Master, this power of form (mūrti-śakti) is non-different from You; grant Your presence therein, You who are intent on bestowing grace upon Your devotees. Reciting the root mantra and saying "Be present here," one performs the gesture of invoking presence (sannidhāpana-mudrā) by joining the fists with the thumbs raised.

One should perform the act of confinement (*sannidhāna*). Reciting the root mantra: "Oṃ, by Your command, O Goddess of gods, O ocean of mercy, O ocean of virtues, with my own self as the sole witness, I confine You here, O Maheśvarī," and while reciting this, one should say, "Be confined here," using the *muṣṭyātmikā* mudrā, which consists of the fist with the thumb inserted within.

One should perform its cessation [with the mantra]: "Whether due to ignorance, dejection, or the deficiency of the practitioner, if my ritual action should be incomplete, even then, be present before me. Reciting the root mantra, one says:
"Be present here before me."

Thus, one should perform the act of summoning by means of the two hands joined in the form of open fists facing each other. Then, with the mantra "AḤ HŪM," one should perform the veiling (*avaguna*) by rotating around [the object] the left hand in the form of a fist with the index finger extended and pointing downward.

One should resolve thus: "Oṃ! May she who showers ten-fold nectar fill the sacrificial seat (yajñaviṣṭara). O Maheśvarī, be firm in the [deity’s] form, or for the completion of the sacrifice. One should perform the ritual of Sakalīkaraṇa, consisting of the Nyāsa of the six limbs upon the body of the deity. It is as follows:
*Krāṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*; *krīṃ* to the head, *svāhā*; *krūṃ* to the tuft of hair, *vaṣaṭ*; *kraiṃ* to the armor, *hūṃ*; *krauṃ* to the three eyes, *vauṣaṭ*; *kraḥ* to the weapon, *phaṭ*. Then:
"O You who abide at a distance from the speech, mind, eyes, and ears of Your devotees! O Self-effulgence!"

"Be quickly enveloped on all sides by the cage. The consecration as nectar (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) is performed with the seed-syllable *svadhā* and the cow-seal (*dhenumudrā*). Then, the supreme consecration (*paramīkaraṇa*) is performed with the great seal (*mahāmudrā*). As for the great seal:
"With the thumbs interlaced and the other fingers extended, this is declared to be the great seal."

"O beloved one, for the sake of making [the deity] supreme. Likewise: "Oṃ, she whose very sight the gods desire for the attainment of their own cherished goals—to her, the Supreme Sovereign, [I offer] welcome and a hearty greeting to you who have arrived.
Reciting this root mantra, [one should address the deity] as being complete with limbs, weapons, vehicles, and retinues.

"O Śrī Dakṣiṇakālī, welcome to you!"—thus one should offer a welcome with both hands, palms facing downward, with the fingers extended. "Oṃ, I am fulfilled and graced; my life has become fruitful, O Goddess of the lords of gods, for you have arrived."
Reciting "susvāgatamidam punaḥ" (welcome once again) while facing upwards with the previously mentioned mudrā, he should offer a welcome.

One should perform the stabilization of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) by means of the *lelihāna-mudrā* according to the method previously described. As for the *lelihāna-mudrā*: "One should join the index, middle, and ring fingers facing downwards; having straightened the little finger, one should bend the ring finger."
This is the *lelihāna-ātma-mudrā*, proclaimed for the rite of *jīvanīyāsa* (the infusion of life).
The method for the previously mentioned installation of the vital breath (*prāṇasthāpana*) is as follows:
*āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ hoṃ oṃ kṣaṃ saṃ haṃ saḥ*.

Hrīṃ oṃ haṃsaḥ! The vital breaths (prāṇas) of the illustrious Dakṣiṇakālikā are here, the vital breaths. Āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ hoṃ oṃ kṣaṃ saṃ haṃsaḥ hrīṃ oṃ saḥ! The life-soul (jīva) of the illustrious Dakṣiṇakālikā is established here. Āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ...
Yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ hoṃ oṃ kṣaṃ saṃ haṃsaḥ hrīṃ oṃ haṃsaḥ. All the sense-faculties (*sarvendriyāṇi*) of the illustrious Dakṣiṇakālikā are stationed here.
Āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ hoṃ saḥ.

Oṃ kṣaṃ saṃ haṃ saḥ! O glorious Dakṣiṇakālikā, may [your] speech, mind, skin, eyes, ears, tongue, nose, and vital breaths come here and remain happily for a long time; svāhā! Then, with the root mantra, [one should offer] water for the arghya.
There should be sprinkling three times; however, there is neither invocation nor dismissal in the case of a Śālagrāma stone, a gem, or a yantra.

And one should not perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breath). Having formed the *yonimudrā* and the *mahāyoni-mudrā*, one should display the *khaḍga*, *muṇḍa*, *abhaya*, and *vara* mudrās. As for the *mahāyoni-mudrā*: "One should join the index, ring, middle, and little fingers of both hands in their respective order."

"By separating the base of the little finger and placing the tip of the thumb [therein], it is proclaimed as the Mahāyoni. Having turned this [mudrā] face downwards, one should display it preceded by the seed-syllable. The seed-syllable is *aiṃ*. In the case of the Yonimudrā, however, one should not place the tip of the thumb [therein]."

The mudrās for the sword and so forth are indeed clear. Then one should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*). In that regard, [the first] on the foot, the second on the knee, the third on the navel, the fourth on the heart, and the fifth on the head.
Then one should offer the water for the feet (*pādya*) and the other articles. For example:
"I offer this water for the feet (*pādya*) to those pure lotus-feet, by contact with a mere fragment of whose devotion the arising of supreme bliss occurs," while reciting the root mantra.
Saying, "I offer this water for the feet to Dakṣiṇakālikā;

obeisance," one should offer water mixed with the previously mentioned flowers, sandalwood, uśīra, yellow pigment (rocanā), śyāmāka grain, viṣṇukrāntā, lotus, and dūrvā grass, using the union of the ring finger and the thumb.

One should offer [water] at the feet while reciting: "Oṃ, to the Veda of even the Vedas, to the Self of the deities of the gods, I offer water for sipping (ācamana) to the Lord, the cause of purity for those who are pure," and while reciting the root mantra: "I present this water for sipping to Dakṣiṇakālikā."
Thus, with the *ācamana-mudrā*— formed by the four fingers joined together except for the little finger which is lowered while the others are raised—

one should offer water mixed with the powder of sandalwood, *jātī* flowers, camphor, *kaṅkola*, cloves, *tamālaka*, and so forth, into the mouth, reciting: "Oṃ, to her who is free from all impurity, whose nature is perfect bliss..."

"O Goddess, I offer this madhuparka; be gracious to me. Reciting this root-mantra, he should place the madhuparka—which consists of a combination of honey, ghee, sugar, curd, and milk—into his mouth using his thumb touched by the ring finger, which is joined with the downward-pointing [mudrā]. *Oṃ*.
"Even one who is defiled by remnants of food or is impure attains purity merely by remembering her; to her, therefore, [is offered] this water for sipping. Thus is the root text.

Reciting as before, one should offer water for sipping (ācamanīya) into the mouth, while reciting the root mantra: "Oṃ, I prepare this arghya for you—divine, the remover of the three-fold suffering, characterized by supreme bliss, and itself liberated from the three-fold suffering. Thus he should recite.
Reciting this— "I offer this *arghya* to Dakṣiṇakālikā; this *arghya*, svāhā to the illustrious Dakṣiṇakālikā"—
one should first present the water consisting of a mixture of the tips of *kuśa* grass, unbroken rice, sesame, *vrīhi* rice, barley, clarified butter, white mustard seeds, and flowers.
One should apply [the ointment] by rubbing it over all the limbs. Then, one should apply substances for massage such as turmeric and oil.

Reciting the root mantra: "Oṃ, O Mother of the World, O Great Abode, accept this unguent with your essence; O Pure-Souled One among all worlds, I offer this supreme unguent. While reciting this, one should apply the root mantra.

Having said "Namas," one should offer these substances, such as turmeric, and the oil to Dakṣiṇakālikā and perform the dry massage (*udvartana*). Then, reciting the root mantra: "O Īśvarī, whose own form is immersed in the ocean of supreme bliss and awakening, I prepare this bath for You, together with Your limbs and sub-limbs. One should then bathe [the deity].

Having recited, "I offer this bath-ointment to Dakṣiṇakālikā; salutation to this bath-ointment for Dakṣiṇakālikā," one should present the bath-ointment with the mudrā consisting of a fist formed by the right hand with the little finger tucked in.
Reciting the root mantra one hundred times, one thousand times, or as many times as possible, he should bathe [the deity]. Reciting the root mantra while saying:

"Oṃ, to you whose own secret splendor is veiled by the variegated cloth of Māyā, I offer this garment for the sake of warding off the dwelling of consciousness (vijñāna-vāsa). And reciting the root mantra: "This garment is for Dakṣiṇakālikā."
By means of the aforementioned statement, one should offer a red garment with the thumb of the upturned right hand touching its middle finger, saying:
"Oṃ, to her upon whom Mahādeva, the eternal destroyer of the world, depends; to her [I give this]."

With the mantra "I offer this upper garment to Parameśānī" and "This upper garment to Dakṣiṇakālikā," and so forth, one should offer the upper garment using the previously mentioned mudrā. Then, with the root mantra, one should consecrate the Goddess with scented water either one thousand and eight times, one hundred times, or ten times.

If not, [one should recite]: "Oṃ, to Śivā, whose limbs are beautiful by nature, who rests upon various powers, and who is worshipped by the immortals, I fashion diverse ornaments. These ornaments I offer to Dakṣiṇakālikā;
obeisance."
With the mantra and the mudrā consisting of the thumb and ring finger of the right hand touching each other, one should offer the ornaments.

Reciting each letter of the alphabet (*mātṛkā*) encased within the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the limbs of the deity. Reciting the root mantra: "O Supreme Goddess, O You who completely fill the quarters with supreme bliss and auspiciousness, graciously accept this supreme fragrance. And reciting the root mantra...

With the mantra, "idaṃ candanaṃ śrīdakṣiṇakālikāyai namaḥ," one should offer sandalwood paste mixed with camphor and abundant sandalwood to the limbs of the Goddess using the conjunction of the little finger and the thumb. [Then recite: "Oṃ akṣatān dhavalān devi..."
"O Sovereign of the World, accept these [offerings] made of gold and silver; be gracious, O Supreme Goddess!"

Reciting the root mantra and the words, "I offer salutation to the glorious Dakṣiṇakālī, together with her limbs (Aṅgas), weapons (Āyudhas), forces (Balas), vehicles (Vāhanas), and retinue," one should make the offering using all the fingers. Then:
"Oṃ, [this] produced from the fourth forest, enchanting with its various qualities..."

"Please accept this excellent flower of intense fragrance. Reciting "These flowers for Dakṣiṇakālikā, Vauṣaṭ," and reciting the root mantra, one should offer them using the gesture of the index finger and thumb. One should offer a flower that is naturally produced, not stale, flawless, fresh, and auspicious.
In the offering of the *añjali*, having the face turned downwards is not a fault;
[this applies to] the white and red *japā* flowers, *karavīra*, *tagara*, *jātī*, *sevantī*, *yūthikā*,
*dhattūra*, *aśoka*, *bakula*, white and black *aparājitā*, *bakapuṣpa*, bilva leaves, *campaka*, *nāgakeśara*, *mallikā*, and *jhiṇṭī*.

One should offer any one of the following flowers: *ikā*, *kāñcī*, *barbara*, red lotus (*raktapadma*), *puṣpāmala*, *kokanada*, *bandhūka*, *ketakī*, and so forth. The *arka* and *mandāra* are highly praised, as are *tulasī* and *mallikā*.
One should avoid [other forbidden flowers]. One should not worship with *dūrvā* grass. Having consecrated the incense burner with the syllable "Phaṭ," [one should proceed].

Having worshipped with "Namaḥ," one should dry [the hand] by reciting the seed-syllable of Vāyu twelve times; then, placing the back of the right hand upon the palm of the left hand, one should burn [it] by reciting the seed-syllable "Raṃ" sixteen times; finally, placing the palm of the right hand upon the back of the left hand.
Having consecrated [the offering] with the nectar-gesture (*dhenumudrā*) while reciting "Vam" sixteen times,

and having empowered it eight times with the root mantra, one should worship the bell with the mantra "Jayadhvani mantramātaḥ svāhā," touch it with the left index finger while reciting the root mantra, and [recite]: "Oṃ, endowed with the essence of the forest-king..."
"Rich in fragrance, most enchanting, fit to be smelled by all the gods— may this incense be accepted. Saying,
"This incense is for the venerable Dakṣiṇakālikā, obeisance," one should then pour the water from the conch onto the ground.

Sounding the bell with the left hand and displaying the incense mudrā by joining the right index finger and thumb while praising the qualities of the deity, one should fumigate from the region of the navel. One should offer three handfuls of flowers. Such is the manner of offering the lamp: *Oṃ*.
It is a great lamp, brilliantly illuminating, dispelling the darkness on all sides.

"May this lamp, whose light is both internal and external, be accepted," saying this and reciting the root mantra, he should display the lamp-mudrā by joining the middle finger and the thumb, and show the lamp toward the region of the eyes. A ghee lamp should be offered on the right, and an oil lamp on the left.
Having served food such as milk-rice with ghee and sugar in a vessel made of gold or other materials, and having placed it upon a square [plate],

one should protect it with the *cakramudrā* while reciting the mantra "Phaṭ. Then, having dried it by means of the wind-bīja "Yam" recited twelve times, one should place the palm of the left hand upon the back of the right hand while reciting "Ram."
Having incinerated [the hand] by reciting the fire-seed syllable (*raṃ*) twelve times, having touched it with the tip of the right hand,

having rendered it nectarine by means of the nectar-seed syllable *vaṃ* and the cow-mudrā (*dhenumudrā*), and having touched it with both hands while reciting the root mantra eight times, one should consecrate it.

Having displayed the *dhenumudrā* and worshipped with perfumes and flowers, one should indeed offer the food offering (*naivedya*) to the Goddess with the *tattvākhyamudrā*, reciting: "Oṃ! O Mistress of the Gods, I offer this food prepared in a worthy vessel, containing sacrificial oblations and various kinds of eatables; please accept it out of compassion."

Reciting "tat," he should display the *grāsamudrā* (the food-offering gesture) and present the offering with water from a conch shell (*śaṅkhodaka*). Then, having given water for drinking and water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) while reciting: "Oṃ, O Sovereign of all the gods, supreme cause of the attainment of everything; O you who are filled with unbroken bliss, accept this excellent water."
One should offer the *culuka* according to the prescribed rule. One should display the five mudrās known as prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna. They are as follows:
the prāṇa-mudrā is formed with the little finger and the ring finger.

The breath called apāna is [touched] with the middle and index fingers; the breath called samāna with the ring and middle fingers; the breath called udāna with the ring and index fingers; and the breath called vyāna with all the fingers. Then, one should offer betel with the root mantra.
The practitioner, meditating upon [the deity] endowed with the *mudrās* and accompanied by cardamom, cloves, camphor, nutmeg, and so forth, as well as betel leaves,
camphor, and betel nuts, should sprinkle [the offering] while uttering "Phaṭ" and worship it while uttering "Namaḥ" with the wind-bīja.
Having dried [the hand] by reciting twelve times, one should place the palm of the left hand upon the back of the right hand;
having incinerated it with the seed-syllable "Raṃ," recited twelve times, one should place the palm of the right hand upon the back of the left hand.

Having rendered [the offering] nectar-like by means of the *amṛtabīja* "syām" and the *dhenumudrā*, and having consecrated it eight times with the root mantra, [one recites]: "O Goddess, please accept this betel leaf (*tāmbūla*) accompanied by cardamom, cloves, camphor, and betel vine leaves, prepared with portions of areca nut; obeisance."
Reciting "mūlamantra," one should offer the betel leaf (*tāmbūla*) to the region of the mouth with the *tattvamudrā*, saying: "I offer this betel leaf to Śrī Dakṣiṇakālikā; obeisance.
Then, having taken a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), [one should recite]: "Oṃ, O Sovereign Goddess consisting of all, O Supreme Nectar, O Beloved of the sacrificial pap (*caru*)."
"Grant me permission on the right for the worship of my retinue. Therein, first is the six-limbed worship (*ṣaḍaṅgapūjā*).
One should worship the powers of the six limbs in the southeast, northeast, southwest, northwest, the center, and the cardinal directions. As for their visualization: "Like snow and crystal..."

Having meditated thus: "The women, who are the primary forms, are dark-blue, black, and reddish-brown, and they hold the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness," one should worship with the mantra: "O deity of the heart, come here! Stay here! *Kram*! Salutation to the Heart! I worship the Śrī-pādukā. Thus, having performed the worship.

Then: "O deity of the head, come here, stay here, *krīṃ*! To the head, *svāhā*! I worship the *śrīpādukā*. "O deity of the crest-lock, come here, stay here, *krūṃ*! To the crest-lock, *vaṣaṭ*! I worship the *śrīpādukā*."
O deity of the armor, come here—stay here! *Kraiṃ*, to the armor, *hūṃ*!

"I worship the Śrīpādukā. "O deity of the three eyes, come here, stay here! *Krauṃ*, for the three eyes, *vauṣaṭ*! I worship the Śrīpādukā. "O deity of the weapon (*astra*), come here, stay here! *Kraḥ*, for the weapon, *phaṭ*! I worship the Śrīpādukā. Then...
One should worship the lineage of gurus from the northwest (Vāyavya) to the northeast (Īśāna). Therein, the sequence of gurus is as follows:
"Mahādevī, Mahādeva, and Tripurabhairava—these are declared to be the gurus of the Divine Current (Divyaugha).
Now I shall describe to you the gurus of the Siddha Current (Siddhaugha): Brahmānanda..."
Pūrṇadeva, Calaccitta, Calācala, Kumāra, Krodhana, Varada, and Smaradīpana; Māyā and Māyāvatī—listen, O beloved, to these who deliver the multitudes of men.
Vimala, Kuśala, Śrīmatsena, Sudhākara, Prahlāda, Sanaka,
Vasiṣṭha, Bodha, Mīna, Gorakṣaka, Bhojadeva, and Prajāpati.
Mūladeva, Rantideva, Vighneśvara, and Hutāśana.

"Likewise, Samaya, Ānanda, Santoṣa, Kālikā, and Gurava; those ending with the word Ānandanātha are gurus who bestow all siddhis. Even women, if they possess the form of a guru, are proclaimed as ending in 'Ambā'."

Then, the worship: "O Great Goddess, Mother, come here; stay here, O Great Goddess, Mother; I worship the venerable sandals (śrīpādukā) [of you]. O Mahādevānandanātha, come here; stay here, O Mahādevānandanātha; I worship the venerable sandals (śrīpādukā) [of you]."

O Tripurānandanātha, come here! Stay here! I worship the venerable sandals (śrīpādukā) of Tripurānandanātha. O Bhairavānandanātha, come here! Stay here! I worship the venerable sandals (śrīpādukā) of Bhairavānandanātha.
Now, O Siddha hosts, come here! Stay here!
I worship the venerable sandals of Brahmanandānandanātha.
I worship the venerable sandals of Pūrṇadevānandanātha. [I worship] Calaccittānandanātha...
I worship the venerable sandals. I worship the venerable sandals of Calācalānandanātha.
I worship the venerable sandals of Kumārānandanātha. I worship the venerable sandals of Krodhānandanātha. I worship the venerable sandals of Varadānandanātha.
"I worship the venerable sandals of Smaradīpanānandanātha; I worship the venerable sandals of Māyāmbā;
I worship the venerable sandals of Māyāvatyambā. Thus [ends the section]. Now, the lineage of the human tradition (mānavaugha):
Come here! Stay here! I worship the venerable sandals of Vimalānandanātha;
I worship the venerable sandals of Kuśalānandanātha.
I worship the venerable sandals of Śrīmat Senānandanātha.
I worship the venerable sandals of Sudhākarānandanātha.
I worship the venerable sandals of Prahlādānandanātha. I worship the venerable sandals of Sanakānandanātha.
I worship the venerable sandals of Vasiṣṭhānandanātha. I worship the venerable sandals of Bodhānandanātha. I worship the venerable sandals of Mīnānandanātha.
I worship the venerable sandals of Gorakṣakānandanātha. I worship the venerable sandals of Bhojadevānandanātha. I worship the venerable sandals of Prajāpatyānandanātha.
I worship the venerable sandals of Mūladevānandanātha. I worship the venerable sandals of Rantidevānandanātha. I worship the venerable sandals of Vighneśvarānandanātha.
I worship the śrīpādukā of Hutāśanānandanātha. I worship the śrīpādukā of Samayānandanātha.
I worship the śrīpādukā of Santoṣānandanātha. Then, having visualized one's own guru before oneself...

Having worshipped with the fivefold offerings (pañcopacāra), one should then recite the root mantra: "Oṃ, grant me my desired success, O protectress of those who have come for refuge; with devotion, I offer this worship of the enclosure (āvaraṇārccana) unto you," while pouring water from a conch shell mixed with flowers and sandalwood into the left hand of the Goddess.

One should offer the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇapūjā*), and thereafter worship the deities of the multitude of rays (*raśmivṛnda*). Their visualization (*dhyāna*) is as follows: "All [the goddesses] are dark-complexioned, holding swords in their hands, adorned with garlands of severed heads, and displaying the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*)."
And holding [them] with their left hands, they are smiling.

(p. 44) In the corner facing the outer triangle, one should worship Kālī three times with water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings, reciting: "Oṃ, I worship the *śrīpādukā* of Kālī, obeisance. Likewise, to the left of the Goddess, [one should worship] "Oṃ..."
"Oṃ, I worship the śrīpādukā of Kapālinī; obeisance. On the right:
"Oṃ, I worship the śrīpādukā of Kullā," and so forth. In the triangle at its center, facing forward:
"Oṃ, I worship the śrīpādukā of Kurukullā," and so forth. On the left: "Oṃ..."

"I worship the Śrīpādukā of Virodhinī," and so forth. On the right: "Oṃ, I worship the Śrīpādukā of Vipracittā," and so forth. In the triangle facing inward at its center: "Oṃ, I worship the Śrīpādukā of Ugrā," and so forth. Then on the left: "Oṃ..."

"I worship the sandals of Ugraprabhāśrī," and so forth. On the right: "Oṃ, I worship the sandals of Dīptāśrī," and so forth. Inside that, in the triangle facing [the practitioner], "Oṃ, I worship the sandals of Nīlāśrī," and so forth. On the left:
"I worship the sandals of Ghanāśrī," and so forth. On the right:
"Oṃ, I worship the sandals of Balākāśrī," and so forth. Within that, in the triangle facing [the practitioner]:
"Oṃ, I worship the sandals of Mātrāśrī," and so forth. On the left:
"Oṃ, I worship the śrīpādukā of Mudrā," and so forth. On the right:

"Oṃ, I worship the śrīpādukā of Mitrā," and so forth. One should worship with the previously mentioned mantras and offerings such as water for the feet (pādya). Then, on the right of the Goddess: "Hsrauṃ Mahākālāya hūṃ phaṭ."

One should worship Mahākāla with this mantra. In the *Kulārṇava*, however, the mantra of Mahākāla is: *oṃ hrīṃ kṣmīṃ hūṃ mahākālāya hauṃ mahādevāya krīṃ kālikāyai hauṃ*. As for his meditation (*dhyāna*): [the visualization follows].
"Like Mount Añjana, with tawny hair and two arms."

"I bow to him who is adorned with the ornaments of snakes and nakedness"—having meditated thus, one should worship Mahākāla with either of the two previously mentioned mantras. Then: "Oṃ, grant me the fulfillment of my desires, O protector of those who have come for refuge!"

With the mantra, "I offer this worship of the enclosure (āvaraṇārccana) to you with devotion," one should offer the worship of the enclosure into the left hand of the Goddess using water from a conch shell or similar vessel.

Then, one should worship the eight Śaktis on the eight petals in the order starting from the east. For example, in the east, one should perform the worship three times with the formula "Oṃ Āṃ Brahmāṇī-śrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi namaḥ" and so forth, using the water for the feet (pādya) and other offerings. In the southeast corner, "Oṃ Īṃ... [and so on].

"I worship the venerable sandals of Śrī Nārāyaṇī," and so forth. To the south: "Oṃ Ūṃ, I worship the venerable sandals of Māheśvarī," and so forth (p. 45). To the southwest: "Oṃ Ṛṃ, I worship the venerable sandals of Śrī Cāmuṇḍā."
And so forth; in the west: "Oṃ laṃ, I worship the śrīpādukā of Kaumārī," and so forth. In the northwest:
"Oṃ aiṃ, I worship the śrīpādukā of Aparājitā," and so forth. In the north: "Oṃ auṃ, I worship the śrīpādukā of Vārāhī," and so forth. In the northeast...
"Oṃ Āḥ, I worship the śrī-pādukā of Nārasiṃhī," and so forth. The visualization (dhyāna) of these [deities] must be performed prior to the worship. It is as follows:
"The staff, the water-pot, and behind them the rosary and the great [mudrā of] fear..."
Bearing a golden luster, the goddess Brāhmī shone brightly with her black antelope skin.
Carrying a trident, an axe, small drums, and a human skull, the auspicious Māheśvarī, white as snow, should be meditated upon. (2)
Holding a goad, a staff, a khaṭvāṅga, and a noose in her hands, she resembles the bandhūka flower; she is a maiden who bestows all desires. (3)
Holding a discus, a bell, a skull-bowl, and a conch in her hands,
she is to be meditated upon as dark as the tamāla tree, radiant with the graceful charms of a Vaiṣṇava woman.
Vārāhī, who has the luster of a dark cloud, should be meditated upon as holding a pestle, a sword, a shield, and a plough with her four hands.
Indrāṇī, resembling a sapphire, should be meditated upon as bestowing all prosperity; she holds a goad, a noose, lightning, and a thunderbolt in her hands.
Cāmuṇḍā, whose body is red, should be meditated upon as holding a trident, a sword, and a human head-skull in her hands, and adorned with a garland of severed heads.
"Holding a rosary, a citron, and a skull-cup in her hands, she who resembles gold is proclaimed to be Moha-lakṣmī.
Then: "O protectress of those who have come for refuge, grant me the fulfillment of my desires; I offer [this] with devotion."
Reciting the root mantra, "This worship for the removal of obstacles is for you," he should offer water from a conch shell mixed with flowers and sandalwood paste into the left hand of the Goddess.
Then, one should worship the Bhairavas at the front of the Yantra; there, one should first perform meditation.
Namely: his face is terrifying with three eyes, and he is adorned with a crescent moon.
Adorned with hundreds of ornaments such as crystal bracelets and anklets.
I worship him who is eight years of age and whose locks of hair are radiant.
Having meditated thus—[on the deity] holding a staff and a trident, accompanied by Bhairavī and others—one should perform worship.

The sequence of worship is as follows: "Aiṃ Hrīṃ Aṃ, I worship the venerable sandals of Asitāṅgabhairava; obeisance! Aiṃ Hrīṃ Iṃ, I worship the venerable sandals of Rurubhairava; obeisance! Aiṃ Hrīṃ..."
Uṃ, I worship the śrīpādukā of Uccaṇḍabhairava; obeisance!
Aiṃ Hrīṃ Ṛṃ, I worship the sandals of the venerable Krodhabhairava; obeisance!
Aiṃ Hrīṃ Ḷṃ, I worship the sandals of Unmattabhairava Śrī; obeisance!

Aiṃ Hrīṃ Eṃ, I worship the sandals (śrīpādukā) of Ekapāli Bhairava; salutations! Aiṃ Hrīṃ Oṃ, I worship the sandals of Bhīṣaṇa Bhairava; salutations! Aiṃ Hrīṃ Aṃ, I worship the sandals of Saṃhāra Bhairava; salutations! Thus, in counter-clockwise order (vāmāvartena).

One should worship. Right there, starting from the east and proceeding counter-clockwise, one should worship each of the eight Bhairavīs individually with their respective name-syllables. Regarding the visualization of them therein: "I meditate upon the Great Goddess, whose radiance is equal to ten million moons."
White as snow, jasmine, and the moon, she has five faces and three eyes.
Having meditated thus: "She who is endowed with eighteen arms, intent on bestowing all bliss, smiling, large-eyed, and facing the God of gods," one should worship her. As follows:
"I worship the venerable sandals of Śrī Bhairavī; obeisance!"
I worship the śrīpādukā of Mahābhairavī; obeisance! I worship the śrīpādukā of Siṃhabhairavī; obeisance! I worship the śrīpādukā of Dhūmrabhairavī; obeisance!
I worship the śrīpādukā of Bhīmabhairavī; obeisance! I worship the śrīpādukā of Unmattabhairavī; obeisance! I worship the śrīpādukā of Vaśīkaraṇabhairavī; obeisance!

"I worship the sandals (pādukā) of the venerable Mohanabhairavī; obeisance! Then, with the mantra: "Oṃ! Grant me the attainment of my desired goal, O protectress of those who have come for refuge! With devotion, I offer this worship of the enclosure (āvaraṇārccana) unto you," one should offer the worship of the enclosure into the left hand of the Goddess. Then...

Outside the yantra, one should worship Indra and the others. Their visualization (*dhyāna*) is as follows: "One should visualize Indra as blue in color, riding upon Airāvata, holding a thunderbolt in his hand, wearing a crown, and possessing a thousand eyes. [One should visualize] Vahni (Agni) as red in color..."
One should meditate upon him who holds a spear in his hand, whose eyes are like those of a spider, and whose vehicle is a ram.

One should meditate upon Yama, who has a buffalo as his vehicle and holds a staff and a noose, and is dark-complexioned. One should meditate upon Nirṛti, who is dark-colored, holds a sword in his hand, and has a corpse as his vehicle.
One should meditate upon Varuṇa, who holds a noose in his hand, whose vehicle is a makara, and who is of pure complexion.
One should meditate on Vāyu, who is blue in color, riding upon a deer, and holding a goad in his hand.

One should meditate on Kubera, who has a golden armlet, a human as his vehicle, and a dark complexion. One should meditate on Īśāna, who holds a trident in his hand, has a bull as his vehicle, possesses three eyes, and is fair in complexion.
One should meditate upon Brahmā, mounted on a swan, golden-hued, four-faced, and bearing a triple staff, a rosary, and a water-pot, while wearing a mass of matted hair.
One should meditate upon Viṣṇu, who has a dark-complexioned body, whose vehicle is Garuḍa, who holds the conch, discus, mace, and lotus in his four hands, and who is adorned with various ornaments.
Having thus meditated, one should invoke them with the words: "O Indra and the others, come here; stay here."
One should worship, starting from the east and proceeding counter-clockwise, as much as is appropriate:
"I worship the *śrīpādukā* of Indra; *namaḥ*. *Raṃ*, I worship the *śrīpādukā* of Vahni; *namaḥ*."
Yaṃ, I worship the śrīpādukā of Yama; obeisance! Kṣaṃ, I worship the śrīpādukā of Nirṛti; obeisance! Vaṃ, I worship the śrīpādukā of Varuṇa; obeisance!
Yaṃ, I worship the sandals of Vāyu-Śrī; obeisance! Iṃ, I worship the sandals of Kubera-Śrī; obeisance! Hoṃ, I worship the sandals of Īśāna-Śrī; obeisance!
*Hrīṃ*, I worship the sandals of Brahmā-Śrī; obeisance! Then: *Oṃ*, I worship the sandals of Viṣṇu-Śrī; obeisance!
"Grant me the attainment of my desired goal, O protectress of those who have come for refuge! I offer this with devotion."

With the mantra, "This worship of the enclosure is for you," one should offer the worship of the enclosure into the left hand of the Goddess. Then, proceeding counter-clockwise, one should worship the weapons at their respective locations as follows:
Vam! I worship the vajra-glory sandals; homage!
I worship the venerable sandal of Śaṃśakti; obeisance! I worship the venerable sandal of Daṇḍa; obeisance!
I worship the Śrīpādukā Khaṃkhaḍga; obeisance!
I worship the auspicious sandals of Pampā; obeisance!
Aṃ, I worship the auspicious sandal of Aṅkuśa; obeisance!
I worship the sandals of Gagadāśrī; obeisance!
I worship the auspicious Śrīpādukā of Śaṃśūla; obeisance!
I worship the sandal of Pañcapadmaśrī; obeisance!
I worship the auspicious sandals of Cañcacakra; obeisance!

Then, with the mantra: "O protectress of those who have sought refuge, grant me the fulfillment of my desires; I offer this worship of the enclosure (āvaraṇārccana) to you with devotion," he should offer the worship of the enclosure into the left hand of the Goddess. Then, [he should offer it] into the upper left hand of the Goddess.
I worship the Śrīpādukā Khaṃkhaḍga; obeisance! Below that, I worship the Śrīpādukā Muṃmuṇḍa; obeisance!
On the upper right, I worship the Śrīpādukā Abhaya (Aṃ); obeisance!
Below that, I worship the venerable sandals (pādukā) of Śrī Vamvara;
Oṃ, grant me the attainment of my desired goal, O protectress of those who have come for refuge!

"I offer this worship of the enclosures to you with devotion. With this mantra, one should offer the worship of the enclosures into the left hand of the Goddess. One should then offer three handfuls of flowers at the feet of the Goddess. Thereafter, one should perform the previously mentioned ritual placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) as follows:
*Krāṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*; *krīṃ* to the head, *svāhā*; *krūṃ* to the crest-lock (*śikhā*), *vaṣaṭ*;
*kraiṃ* to the armor (*kavaca*), *huṃ*; *krauṃ* to the three eyes, *vauṣaṭ*; *kraḥ* to the weapon (*astra*), *phaṭ*.

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) in this manner, and having worshipped the Goddess with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), while reciting the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*).

One should perform the libation twelve times with water mixed with honey and camphor, using the mantra: "Obeisance, I satiate the goddess Śrīmaddakṣiṇakālī. Then, sounding the bell, one should perform the recitation (japa) there according to the previously mentioned sequence.

One should perform *prāṇāyāma* and the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*). It is as follows: having performed *prāṇāyāma* three times by means of the seed-syllable *krīṃ*—with sixteen counts for inhalation (*pūraka*), sixty-four for retention (*kumbhaka*), and thirty-two for exhalation (*recaka*)—thereafter follows the placement (*nyāsa*).

*Krāṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*; *Krī* to the head, *svāhā*; *Kru* to the tuft of hair (*śikhā*), *vaṣaṭ*; *Kraiṃ* to the armor (*kavaca*), *hum*; *Krauṃ* to the three eyes, *vauṣaṭ*; *Kraḥ* to the weapon (*astra*), *phaṭ*. Then: *Oṃ māle māle mahāmāle sarvatattvasvarūpiṇī...*

"The fourfold aims have been entrusted to you; therefore, grant me success. Reciting "Oṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to the rosary," he places the rosary in his right hand, brings it to the region of the heart, and, touching each bead with the middle finger while not overstepping the *meru* bead, [performs the recitation].

Having visualized one’s own body as the God of Desire and Time, having meditated on the Guru at the head, and while contemplating the Goddess in the heart, one should visualize the mantra in the form of a lamp upon the tongue;
then, within the circle of its radiance, one should visualize the tongue itself in the form of a lamp, either mentally or in a whisper.

Having recited [the mantra] one thousand and eight or one hundred and eight times— either with a rosary of beads (*varṇamālā*), or with a rosary made of any one of the following: refined *mahāśaṅkha* shell, *rudrākṣa*, crystal, and so forth— neither too fast nor too slow, [one should then place] the rosary...
On the head: "Oṃ, O garland, you are beloved by all beings and esteemed by all the worlds."

"O auspicious one, grant me well-being, fame, and valor at all times. Reciting this, he should place [the mantra] down, worship with "Hrīṃ Siddhyai Namaḥ," and again perform breath control (prāṇāyāma), ritual placement (nyāsa), and so forth;
as follows: with the seed-syllable *krīṃ*, [perform] sixteen [cycles of] inhalation (*pūraka*), sixty-four [cycles of] retention (*kumbhaka*), and thirty-two [cycles of] exhalation (*recaka*).

Having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) three times with exhalations (recakas), then follows the ritual placement (nyāsa): *krāṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*; *krīṃ* to the head, *svāhā*; *krūṃ* to the tuft of hair (*śikhā*), *vaṣaṭ*; *kraiṃ* to the armor (*kavaca*), *hūṃ*; *krauṃ* to the three eyes, *vauṣaṭ*; *kraḥ* to the weapon (*astra*), *phaṭ*. Having thus performed the ritual placement and so forth, [proceed].

Then, having worshipped the deity with flowers, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and other offerings, one should offer water from a conch shell containing flowers, sandalwood paste, and *akṣata* while reciting: "Oṃ! O You who guard that which is most secret, accept this recitation performed by us; may success be mine, O Goddess!"
"O Maheśvarī, by your grace!"— with this mantra, having visualized a mass of light in the left hand of the Goddess, one should offer the recitation (*japa*).

Then, having removed the garland from his head and reciting this mantra—“Oṃ! O garland, you are considered the bestower of all accomplishments for all the gods; by that truth, O Mother, grant me accomplishment; homage be to you!”—and having worshipped it, he should carefully conceal it. Then, [he should offer it] to the Goddess.
Having offered eight handfuls of flowers, one should recite the hymn of praise, the armor-mantra (kavaca), and so forth.

If it should fall from the hand, one should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times for the sake of its pacification. Then, having prepared a square maṇḍala on the left, having placed a small vessel upon it,
and having offered into that [vessel] a bali consisting of any one of the following— meat, black gram, rice, vegetables, clarified butter, milk-rice, or cakes— [one should proceed].

Having sprinkled [it] with "Phaṭ," having worshipped it with "Namaḥ," and having purified it by reciting twelve times the wind-seed-syllable "Yam," one should place the back of the right hand upon the palm of the left hand,
inflame it by reciting sixteen times the fire-seed-syllable "Ram," and [then purify it] with the nectar-seed-syllable "Vam."

Having consecrated [the offering] with the *dhenumudrā* by reciting [the mantra] twenty times, veiling it with "Hūṃ," displaying the *yonimudrā* and the *dhenumudrā*, and showing the *tattvamudrā*, one should offer it in the south-western direction (nairṛtyāṃ diśi) with the words: "Oṃ Krīṃ Śrīṃ Dakṣiṇakālikāyai Svāhā! This is the bali, salutation! and then release it.
One should maintain [this]. This is the mantra for the daily offering (*nityabali*). At night, the optional offering (*kāmyabali*) should be given.
The mantra for that is: "Oṃ, Padma, Padma, Mahāpadma, Padmāvatī, Great Lord of Yakṣas! Accept, accept, cause to be accepted, cause to be accepted this offering brought by me; [grant] my..."
With the mantra "sarvaśāntiṃ kurukuru paravidyāṃ cākṛṣyākṛṣya chindhi hrīṃ hūṃ svāhā," one should perform the previously mentioned purification at a place such as a crossroads,
display the *tattvamudrā*, and offer a bali consisting of meat or any other suitable substance.

When one has obtained superior devotion, extraordinary power, the proper time, and other favorable conditions, one should worship Kālī with flowers and other offerings, using each of the names contained within the *Sahasranāma Stotra* in the dative case.
It is as follows:
Oṃ krīṃ, obeisance to Kālī (1); krūṃ, obeisance to Karālī (2); obeisance to Kalyāṇī (3);
obeisance to Kamalā (4); obeisance to Kalā (5); obeisance to Kalāvatī (6); obeisance to Kalāḍhyā (7); obeisance to Kalāpūjyā (8); obeisance to Kalātmikā (9); obeisance to Kalāhṛṣṭā (10).

Salutation to Kalāpuṣṭā (She who nourishes the arts). Salutation to Kalāmastā (She who is the essence of the arts). Salutation to Kalākarā (She who performs the arts). Salutation to Kalākoṭisamābhāsā (She whose radiance equals ten million arts). Salutation to Kalākoṭiprapūjitā (She who is worshipped by ten million arts).
Salutation to Kalākarmmakalādharā (She who possesses the arts of the performance of arts). Salutation to Kalāparā (She who is supreme among the arts). Salutation to [Her]. 17.
p. 50) Salutation to Kalāgamā (18). Salutation to Kaladhārā (19). Salutation to Kamalinī (20). Salutation to Kakārā (21). Salutation to Karuṇā (22). Salutation to Kavyā (23).
Salutation to her whose every limb is the letter *ka* (24). Salutation to her adorned with ten million digits of beauty (25).
Salutation to her who is multiplied by ten million *kakāra*s; 26. Salutation to her whose ornaments are ten million *kakāra*s;
27. Salutation to her whose heart is the syllable *kakāra*; 28. Salutation to her who is adorned with the *kakāra* mantra;
29. Salutation to her whose abode is the syllable *kakāra*; 30. Salutation to her who is devoted to the sound of the crow (*kāka*). 31.

Salutation to her who has the letter *ka* as her crown; 32. Salutation to her whose ornaments are the letter *ka*; 33. Salutation to her whose form is the letter *ka*; 34. Salutation to her who is devoted to the sound of the crow (*kāka*); 35.
Salutation to her who delights in the striking of the *kakavīra* drum; 36. Salutation to her who is worshipped by the source of lotuses (*kamalākara*). 37.

Salutation to Kamalākaranāthā (38). Salutation to her who assumes the form of Kamalākara (39). Salutation to her who is the abode of the perfection of Kamalākara (40). Salutation to her who bestows the fruit of Kamalākara (41). Salutation to her who dwells in the midst of Kamalākara (42). Salutation to her who is gratified by Kamalākara (43).
Salutations to her who is intent on the discourse "How indeed? (44). Salutations to her who has that as her ultimate goal (45).
Salutations to her who stands at the end of the word "how indeed? (46). Salutations to her who is the ground for the meaning of the word "how indeed?
(47). Salutations to the lotus-eyed one (48). Salutations to the one born from the lotus (49). Salutations to her who is worshipped by the lotus-eyed one (50).

Salutations 50. To her who is intent on the boon granted by Kamalākṣa, salutations 51. To Kakarā, salutations 52. To Karbūrākṣarā, salutations 53. To Karatārā, salutations 54. To Karacchinnā, salutations 55. To Karaśyāmā, salutations 56. To Karārṇavā, salutations 57. To Karapūjyā, salutations.

58. Salutation to Kararatā; 59. Salutation to Karadā; 60. Salutation to Karajitā; 61. Salutation to Karatoyā; 62. Salutation to Karāmarṣā; 63. Salutation to Karmanāśā; 64. Salutation to Karapriyā; 65. Salutation to Karaprāṇā; 66. Salutation to Karakajā; 67.

Salutations to Karakāyā, 68. Salutations to Karakāntarā, 69. Salutations to her whose form is Mount Karakācala, 70. Salutations to her who adorns Mount Karakācala, 71. Salutations to the daughter of Mount Karakācala, 72.
Salutations to her who is gratified by Mount Karakācala, 73. Salutations to her who dwells in the abode of Mount Karakācala, 74.
Salutation to the protectress of the Karakācala mountain. 75 Salutation to her who is honored by the Karakācala mountain.
76 Salutation to the creator of the Karakācala mountain. 77 Salutation to her who is enriched by the rains of the Karakācala mountain.
78 Salutation to her who is delighted by the Karakācala mountain. 79 Salutation to the beloved of the Karakācala mountain. 80

Salutations to her who wears a garland of Karakācala mountains; 81. Salutations to her whose food is the Karakācala mountain; 82. Salutations to her whose form is the Karakācala mountain; 83. Salutations to her who resides like an amalaka fruit in the palm of the hand; 84. Salutations to her who bestows the siddhis that are like an amalaka fruit in the palm of the hand; 85. Salutations to her who is to be fully worshipped like an amalaka fruit in the palm of the hand; 86.
Salutation to Karāmalakatāriṇī (87); salutation to Karāmalakakālī (88);
salutation to Karāmalakarociṇī (89); salutation to Karāmalakamātṛ (90);
salutation to Karāmalakasevinī (91); salutation to Karāmalakavaddhyeyā (92).
Salutation to her who places the *āmalaka* fruit in the hand; 93. Salutation to the lotus-eyed one; 94. Salutation to the mother of the lotus; 95.
Salutation to the one dwelling in the lotus; 96. Salutation to the bearer of the lotus; 97.
Salutation to the one who makes garlands of lotuses dear to her; 98. Salutation to the one whose form is the lotus; 99. Salutation to the one born from the lotus.

Salutations 100 to her who is born from the lotus; salutations 101 to her whose gait is like that of a lotus; salutations 102 to her who is devoted to the lotus-oblation; salutations 103 to her who dwells in the center of the lotus-maṇḍala;
salutations 104 to her who is adorned with lotus-ornaments; salutations 105 to her who delights in honoring the lotus.
106. Salutation to her who is intent on the arising of the lotus. 107. Salutation to her whose form is like a mass of lotuses.
108. Salutation to her who dwells in the forest of lotuses. 109. Salutation to her who resides in the midst of the *karañja* tree.
110. Salutation to her who dwells in the *karañja* tree. 111. Salutation to her who is enriched with ornaments made of *karañja* fruit.

112. Salutation to the one who dwells in the Karañja forest. 113. Salutation to the one whose ornament is a garland of Karañja flowers. 114. Salutation to the one who is devoted to the sword. 115. Salutation to the one whose self rejoices in the sword. 116. Salutation to the one who is the beloved arrival of the sword. 117. Salutation to the one whose throat is dear to the sword. 118. Salutation to the one [who is] the beloved of the sword.
Salutation to her who sports with the sword, 119. Salutation to the mother of the sword, 120. Salutation to Karmā, 121.

Salutation to her who brings joy to the sword, 122. Salutation to her whose ornament is a garland of headless trunks, 123. Salutation to her who dwells in the midst of a multitude of headless trunks, 124.

Salutations to her whose form is shaped like a headless trunk (kabandha), 125. Salutations to her whose ornaments are endless headless trunks, 126. Salutations to her who is satisfied by the sound of headless trunks, 127. Salutations to her who bears a headless trunk as her seat, 128. Salutations to her who dwells in the midst of a house of headless trunks, 129. Salutations to her who resides in the forest of headless trunks.
Salutations to Kabandhakāñcī (130); salutations to Karaṇī (131);
salutations to Kabandharāśibhūṣaṇā (132);
salutations to Kabandhamālājayadā (133); salutations to Kabandhadehavāsinī (135).
Salutation to her who is honored by the Kabandha posture, 136. Salutation to her who wears a garland of skulls, 137.
Salutation to her who resides in the midst of a garland of skulls, 138. Salutation to her who is gratified by the skull-vow (*kapāla-vrata*), 139.
Salutation to her who is satisfied by the lamp of a skull, 140. Salutation to her whose form is the lamp of a skull, 141.
Salutations to the one who grants boons with the skull-lamp, 142. Salutations to the one who resides within the soot of the skull, 143.
Salutations to the one who bestows victory through the garland of skulls, 144. Salutations to the one who is pleased by the water in the skull, 145.
Salutations to the one who rejoices in the accomplishments of the skull, 146. Salutations to the one intent on eating from the skull, 147.
Salutation to her who is established in the *kapāla-vrata* (148). Salutation to her whose abode is the lotus of the skull (149).
Salutation to her who is the essence of the nectar of poetry (150). Salutation to her who is the ocean of the nectar of poetry (151).
Salutation to her who is delighted by the perfection of poetry (152). Salutation to her who bestows the gift of poetry (153).

Salutation to her who is worshiped by poets (Kavipūjyā), 154. Salutation to her who is the goal of poets (Kavigati), 155. Salutation to her whose form is that of a poet (Kavirūpā), 156. Salutation to her who is dear to poets (Kavipriyā), 157. Salutation to her whose nature is the bliss of the poets' Brahman (Kavibrahmānandarūpā), 158.
Salutation to her who is gratified by the vow of poetic composition (Kavitvavratatoṣitā), 159. Salutation to her who abides in the vow of poetic composition (Kavitvavratasaṃsthānā), 160.

Salutations to her who fulfills the desires of poets. 161 Salutations to her who resides upon the throats of poets. 162 Salutations to her who bestows the fulfillment of the *kaṃ-hrīṃ-ka-kaṃ-ka* [mantra] upon poets. 163 Salutations to Kañjalā.
164 Salutations to her whose mind is intent on the gift of collyrium (*kañjala*). 165 Salutations to her who is fond of collyrium. 166
Salutations to her whose form is like collyrium from a skull-bowl (167); salutations to her who is worshipped by the Lord of Collyrium (168);
salutations to her who dwells in the midst of the ocean of collyrium (169); salutations to her whose very nature is non-different from collyrium (170);
salutations to her who is pleased by those dear to collyrium (171); salutations to her who delights in those dear to collyrium (172).
Salutation to her who is adorned with a garland of skulls (173). Salutation to her whose hands are decorated with skulls (174).
