Now, one should worship and feed both a virgin (*kumārī*) and a married woman (*suvāsinī*). The procedure for this is as follows:
having brought the virgin to the house of worship, circumambulated her, and bathed her with unguents and other preparations, [one should proceed].
One should consecrate the body with fragrant oil; having groomed the hair, applied vermilion to the forehead, collyrium to the eyes,
and sandalwood paste to all the limbs, and having adorned [the person] with garments and ornaments, washed the feet, seated them upon a throne, and purified the mouth with betel leaf.

Having performed the self-nyāsa oneself, one should perform the nyāsa upon the six limbs: "Oṃ klāṃ Kulakumārikā, obeisance to the heart (hṛdayāya namaḥ). Oṃ klīṃ Kulakumārikā, svāhā to the head (śirase svāhā). Oṃ klūṃ Kulakumārikā, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock (śikhāyai vaṣaṭ). Oṃ klaiṃ Kulakumārikā, hūṃ to the armor (kavacāya hūṃ)."

Oṃ klauṃ, to the three eyes of Kulamumārikā, vauṣaṭ. Oṃ klaḥ, to the weapon (astra) of Kulakumārikā, phaṭ. Then follow the nyāsas of the Mātṛkās upon the limbs. They are as follows: aṃ namas on the forehead; āṃ namas on the face; iṃ namas on the right eye; īṃ namas on the left eye.
*Uṃ* namaḥ to the right ear; *ūṃ* namaḥ to the left ear; *ṛṃ* namaḥ to the right nostril;
*ṝṃ* namaḥ to the left nostril; *ḷṃ* namaḥ to the right cheek; *ḹṃ* namaḥ to the left cheek; *eṃ* namaḥ to the upper lip;
*aiṃ* namaḥ to the lower lip; *oṃ* namaḥ to the [forehead].
"Oṃ namaḥ to the upper row of teeth; oṃ namaḥ to the lower row of teeth; aṃ namaḥ to the head;
aḥ namaḥ to the mouth. Then one should meditate [on her] as "white as a conch, a kunda flower, and the moon, with two arms, granting boons and fearlessness."
"Resplendent with the graceful gestures (*bhāva* and *hāva*) of a great lotus situated in the center of the moon.

Having meditated thus and worshipped her with mental offerings (*mānasopacāra*), one should meditate again and worship as follows: "This is the water for the feet (*pādya*); *hrīṃ*, salutation to Kulakumārikā. In this manner.

With the mantra: "This is the water for honoring (arghya), this is the water for sipping (ācamanīya), this is the unguent (anulepana), these are the unbroken grains (akṣatāḥ), these are the flowers, this is the incense (dhūpa), this is the lamp (dīpa), this is the food offering (naivedya), and this is the betel-leaf (tāmbūla);
Hrīṃ, obeisance to the Virgin of the Kula (Kulakumārikā)."

One should worship. Therefore, one should worship the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with the six-limbed mantra (*ṣaḍaṅgamantra*). It is as follows: "Oṃ klāṃ Kulakumārikā, obeisance to the heart (*hṛdaya*); Oṃ klīṃ Kulakumārikā, obeisance to the head (*śiras*);
Oṃ klūṃ Kulakumārikā, obeisance to the crest-lock (*śikhā*); Oṃ klaiṃ Kulakumārikā..."

"Oṃ kavacāya namaḥ | Oṃ klauṃ kulakumārike netratrayāya namaḥ | Oṃ klaḥ kulakumārike astrāya namaḥ. Having thus worshipped the limbs, [one should worship] with: "Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ, I worship the śrīpādukā of Kulakumārikā."
Having offered three handfuls of flowers, one should worship Kālī as follows:
"Oṃ Aiṃ, salutation to Sandhyā; Oṃ Aiṃ, salutation to Sarasvatī; Oṃ Aiṃ, salutation to Trimūrti;
Oṃ Aiṃ, salutation to Kālikā; Oṃ Aiṃ, salutation to Subhagā; Oṃ Aiṃ, salutation to Umā."
Salutation! Oṃ Aiṃ, salutation to Mālinī. Oṃ Aiṃ, salutation to Kubjikā. Oṃ Aiṃ, salutation to Kālasaṅkarṣiṇī. Oṃ Aiṃ, salutation to Aparājitā.
Oṃ Aiṃ, salutation to Rudrāṇī. Oṃ Aiṃ, salutation to Bhairavī. Oṃ Aiṃ, salutation to Mahālakṣmī.

*Namaḥ*. *Oṃ aiṃ pīṭhanāyikāyai namaḥ*. *Oṃ aiṃ kṣetrajñāyai namaḥ*. *Oṃ aiṃ carcikāyai namaḥ*. (16) Then, having offered three handfuls of flowers with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*), one should circumambulate and prostrate. The mantra for that is as follows:
Oṃ! O you who are worthy of worship by the world, worthy of veneration by the world, whose very nature is all-pervading power!
Accept this worship, O Daughter of Kumāra, Mother of the World; salutations be unto you! || 1 ||
Tripurā, who consists of the three qualities, the sustainer of the world, and whose very nature is the path of knowledge.
I worship the Goddess, the embodiment of the three forms, who is adored by the three worlds. || 2 ||
She who is the embodiment of time, who fears time, whose heart is compassion, and who is auspicious.
I worship her who is the mother of compassion, eternal, and auspicious.
Endowed with qualities such as atomization (aṇimā) and others, she consists of the vowels beginning with 'a'.
I worship Lakṣmī and Rohiṇī, who consist of the nature of various powers.
I worship Kāminī, who is the support of all arts, whose form is the essence of art, whose nature is that of the fierce Time, who grants all desires, and who is the reservoir of compassion.
She who possesses fierce edges, fierce illusions, and who is the destroyer of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa.
I bow to the Goddess of gods and I worship Caṇḍikā.
She who brings about happiness and bliss, who is peaceful, and who is saluted by all the gods.
I worship the goddess Śaṅkarī, who is the self of all beings. || 7 ||
In places difficult to traverse and hard to cross, she is the destroyer of the threefold suffering.
I always worship Durgā with devotion; O Durgā, I bow down to you.
Sundarī, who possesses a golden complexion and bestows happiness and good fortune.
"I bow down to the goddess Subhadrā, the mother of Subhadra.

(9) Then, having performed the *ārārtika* ceremony with wicks made of camphor and other substances, having given the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), and having prostrated, one should bid her farewell. [The goddesses are] Kaumārī, Tripurā, Kalyāṇī, Rohiṇī, and Kāminī.
Caṇḍikā, Śaṅkarī, Durgā, Subhadrā—these are the names of the Kumārīs.

Then one should offer the sacrifice of a goat and other animals as follows: having adorned the goat with vermilion and other ornaments, one should sprinkle it three times with *arghya* water while reciting "Durge durge rakṣiṇi svāhā," and bathe it with this [mantra]:
"Oṃ Vārāhī, Yamunā, Gaṅgā, Karatoyā, Sarasvatī."
The Kāverī, the Candrabhāgā, the Sindhu, the Bhairava, and the Sāgara;
O Maheśānī, manifest your presence here at this spontaneous bath for the destruction of the bonds of the bound souls, to the one residing on Hemakūṭa,
the Supreme, the Most High, the embodiment of the syllable *Hūṃ*.
Then, having sprinkled [the goat] three times with scented water, one should recite with palms joined in reverence:
"Oṃ! O Goat, you have arrived by virtue of great fortune in the form of a sacrificial offering (bali).
I always bow with devotion to you, who possess form and the very nature of the bali."
Salutations again and again to you, O Bala, who take the form of an offering to Caṇḍikā, who destroys the calamities of the donor who desires to please Caṇḍikā.
"Beasts were created by the Self-Existent One himself for the sake of sacrifice;
therefore, I shall cause you to be slain. Thus, in a sacrifice, killing is not killing."
Then follows the worship of the Śaktis:
*Oṃ jayantyai namaḥ* (3 times); *Oṃ maṅgalāyai namaḥ* (3 times); *Oṃ kālyai namaḥ* (3 times);
*Oṃ bhadrakālyai namaḥ* (3 times); *Oṃ mānastokāyai namaḥ* (3 times); *Oṃ vijayāyai namaḥ* (3 times); *Oṃ—*

"Oṃ, obeisance to Aparājitā" (three times). In the center: "Oṃ, obeisance to Ananta. Then one should worship each limb: on the head, "obeisance to Rudhiravadanā"; on the cheek, "obeisance to Caṇḍikā";
on the two eyes, "obeisance to the Moon and Sun"; on the two ears, "obeisance to Bṛhaspati."
On the nose: *namaḥ sarasvatyai*. On the tongue: *nama ugradantikāyai*. On the neck: *namaḥ mahādantikāyai*. On the belly: *namaḥ pṛthivyai*.
On the four shanks: *namaḥ dharmāya*. Then, having taken water in the hand...

"Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, to the one whose form is presided over by the Varuṇa-maṇḍala, to Caṇḍikā in the form of the sacrificial animal (paśu), I sprinkle this animal; svāhā!"—thus is the sprinkling of the animal.
Then, taking sesame seeds, kuśa grass, and water, [recite] "Oṃ—"
Today, in the month of [name],

in the fortnight of [name], on the lunar day of [name], [name] of [gotra], son of [father’s name], desiring the pleasure of the illustrious Dakṣiṇakālikā for a period of ten years corresponding to the number of goats [offered].
"I shall cause these goats, whose deity is Agni, to be sacrificed for you, O Blessed One, Śrī Dakṣiṇakālikā"; then one should worship the sword with perfumes and other offerings.
"Oṃ! [I bow to] Kṛṣṇa, who holds the Pināka bow in his hand, whose nature is like the Night of Doom (Kālarātri), fierce, with a red face and eyes, and adorned with red garlands and unguents."
"Clad in red garments, holding a noose in his hand, accompanied by his family, drinking blood, and devouring a mass of raw flesh.
Having worshipped three times with the mantra: "Oṃ, salutation to Kālikā, Āli-Vajreśvarī, the Iron Staff-bearer."

Having written the syllable *hrīṃ* with vermilion and other substances, and having worshipped it with the mantra "Obeisance to the Sword" (*khaḍgāya namaḥ*), one should cause the *baligāyatrī* to be heard at the ear of the sacrificial animal: "We know the one whose form is the offering (*bali*); we meditate upon the beloved of the Goddess; may that sacrificial animal (*paśu*) impel us. Then, one should pray to the sword.
Oṃ! You are the edge, the destroyer, the sword, with a sharp blade and difficult to approach;
you are the womb of prosperity and victory itself—homage to you, O Protector of Dharma!
Thus, these eight names of yours were spoken by the Creator himself.
Your lunar mansion is Kṛttikā, and your presiding deity is the lord Maheśvara.
The Rohiṇīs are your body; the god Dhātṛ is Janārdana.
O Father, O Grandfather, O God, protect me always.
Resembling a dark blue cloud, with sharp fangs and a slender belly.
He was pure in character, intolerant of opposition, and possessed of exceeding splendor.
She by whom the earth was supported and the demon Mahiṣāsura was slain.
Homage to you, that sword which is sharp-edged and pure.
With the intention that it be the tongue of Caṇḍikā, one should strike it with a single blow.
Let us know the one who binds the individual souls; let us meditate upon the one whose ears are like those of a Brahmin.
"May the goat impel us away from that.
Having placed the entire blood and the severed head before the Goddess, one should illuminate the supreme mark with equal portions. The lamp near the flesh [is marked] with "Krauṃ Krauṃ".

"Namonamaḥ. With this [mantra], one should offer a lamp at every head and then perform libations with these [mantras]: in the east, "I satiate Cāmuṇḍā, obeisance"; in the south, "I satiate Yoginī, obeisance"; in the west, "I satiate Ḍākinī, obeisance"; in the north, "I satiate Bhairavī, obeisance."
In the southeast: "Vidārikā, I satisfy you; obeisance! In the southwest:
"Pāparākṣasī, I satisfy you; obeisance! In the northwest: "Pūtanā, I satisfy you; obeisance! In the northeast: "Kālikā, I satisfy you; obeisance!"

(71) "Oṃ! Desiring to please the illustrious Dakṣiṇakālikā, whose worship has been uninterrupted for ten years, I now offer this goat together with its head, dedicated to the deity Viṣṇu, unto you, O Blessed Śrī Dakṣiṇakālī. This is the procedure for the offering of the goat.

Then, the *ārārttika* offering: for instance, having ground wheat flour in some vessel made of gold or other precious materials, one should light eleven white wicks mixed with camphor and offer the *ārārttika*,
having performed the sprinkling and other rites according to the procedure prescribed for the offering of incense.

Having sprinkled the vessel for the *ārārttika* lamp with "Phaṭ," worshipped it with "Namaḥ," dried it by reciting twelve times the wind-seed syllable "Yam" over the back of the right hand placed upon the palm of the left hand, and burned it with the seed-syllable "Ram" on the back of the left hand; [one should proceed].

Having placed [the vessel] on the palm of the right hand, having rendered it nectar-like by means of the *dhenumudrā* while reciting the mantra "Avaṃ" sixteen times, and having consecrated it eight times with the root mantra,
one should worship the bell with the mantra "Jayadhvanimantramātaḥ svāhā" using the left index finger.
Having touched the root [mantra] while reciting: "Oṃ, that which is joined with camphor, a wick, and ghee, and united with fire."
"O Goddess of the Universe, accept this divine *ārārttika*.

Reciting the root mantra and saying, "I worship this *ārārttika* to Śrī Dakṣiṇakālī, who is with her limbs (*sāṅgā*), her weapons (*sāyudhā*), her army and vehicles (*sabalavāhanā*), her retinue (*saparivārā*), and her enclosures (*sāvaraṇā*); obeisance," one should offer the waving light (*jāland*).
One should cause [the visualization] to revolve ten times in the region of the eyes. Then, having worshipped three times with three handfuls of flowers, saying:
"I worship the glorious Dakṣiṇakālikā together with Mahākāla, along with his weapons, vehicles, and retinue;
homage! one should satisfy her three times. Then...

One should display the *yonimudrā* and other gestures as before. Then, having displayed the parasol and the fly-whisk (*cāmara*), and taking a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), one should recite four verses. The verses are as follows:
"Buddhi is fashioned upon the bow, and the auspicious mirrors..."
Your manifold mental activity has been fashioned in the form of a dance.
O Lord, by means of the various types of musical instruments and sounds, these lotuses have been fashioned by me as umbrellas for you. (2)
The ego (ahaṅkāra) is represented by the form of the chariot-pole through the *suṣumnā* nerve, and by the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth up to the individual soul (*jīva*).
Egotism is represented as the elephant, and impetus is fashioned as the chariot itself. (3)
The senses are in the form of horses; sound and the other objects are their path;
the mind is in the form of the reins; and the intellect is in the form of the charioteer.
Everything else is fashioned by you as being of the nature of your own instruments.
Thus, one should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) and make a prayer. Thus ends the complete ritual procedure for the worship of Śrī Dakṣiṇakālī.

Then one should perform the perpetual fire-offering (*nityahoma*). It is as follows: having inspected the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) or the pit (*kuṇḍa*) with the root mantra; having performed the sprinkling and striking with the weapon mantra (*astramantra*); having covered it with *kuśa* grass;
having uttered the three *vyāhṛtis*; having brought the fire; and having drawn three lines with the weapon mantra.

In the southwest, having discarded the portions for the flesh-eaters (kravyāda), consecrated [the food] with the *mūla-mantra*, rendered it nectar (*amṛta*) by means of the *dhenu-mudrā* while uttering "vaṃ," protected it with the *astra-mantra*, veiled it with "hūṃ," and while rotating it around three times,
recited the *praṇava* (oṃ) three times.

Having meditated upon Vāgīśvarī— lying on her bed after her ritual bath at the end of her menses, wearing blue lotuses, and being enjoyed by the God— within the maṇḍala of her womb, one should place the fire within the lord’s semen with the thought [of it being so],
reciting "HŪṂ, obeisance to the consciousness of fire" (vahnicaitanyāya namaḥ) and reciting the root mantra. Then...
Having worshipped the fire with flowers, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and so forth, and having invoked and worshipped one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) therein,
one should offer four oblations (*āhuti*) using ghee and other substances with the Great Vyahritis both individually and collectively; then,
[one should offer] twenty-five times with *karavīra* flowers as prescribed in one’s own ritual manual, or with ghee and other such materials.

Having recited the root mantra ending with *svāhā*, and then having recited the name of the deity in the dative case ending with *svāhā*, one should offer the oblation. Having again offered oblations with the *vyāhṛtis* and having established the goddesses within the image, one should dismiss the fire with the *saṃhāramudrā* and offer water for sipping (*ācamana*) and other services to the goddess.
Having displayed the fly-whisk and other articles and offered praise, one should perform three circumambulations while reciting "yāni kāni ca" and so forth. Then, having prostrated like a staff,
performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and other rites, and offered a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali), one should [proceed] with the mantra known as Brahmārpaṇa.

One should offer oneself. For example, the offering mantra is as follows: "Oṃ! Whatever [evil] was thought by me from this point forward, through my intellect, due to my status as a human being or a deity, in the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep—whether by mind, speech, hands, feet, belly, or genitals; whatever was remembered, whatever was spoken..."

"May all that has been done become an offering to Brahman, Svāhā! I offer myself and everything belonging to me to you, O Goddess; Om Tat Sat. Then, having performed *prāṇāyāma* and other rites, and having worshipped with flowers, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and so forth, one should ask for forgiveness. The mantra for asking forgiveness is as follows:
Whatever has been done deficiently or in excess, whether through ignorance, forgetfulness, or fear—
And forgive all that was contrary [to the rules], O Supreme Goddess. || 1 ||
O Sovereign of the Gods, [that which is] deficient in mantra, deficient in ritual action, or deficient in the prescribed rule;
O Goddess, you have been worshipped by me; therefore, be the bestower of boons. || 2 ||
I do not know how to perform the invocation, the worship, the recitation of your majesty, nor the dismissal; O Kālikā, may you forgive me.
Whatever has slipped from the syllables and words, lacking vowels and consonants—all that may you forgive, O Goddess; be gracious, O Supreme Sovereign. (4)
O Supreme Goddess, be gracious! By the remembrance of whom and by the utterance of whose name, whatever is deficient in acts such as austerity and sacrifice attains completeness.
O Kāmeśvarī, Mother of the World, whose form is Being-Consciousness-Bliss!
Accept this entire worship; be gracious, O Supreme Goddess!
With these [verses], one should ask for forgiveness by offering a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*). Then, having formed the *yonimudrā* and prostrated, one should say:
"Oṃ, go, go to the supreme abode, your own place, O Supreme Goddess;
and for the sake of returning again at the time of worship and propitiation."
Reciting the root mantra, the goddess, having dismissed [the visualization] with the saṃhāra-mudrā, should establish it within her own heart.

Then, in the northeastern direction, having worshipped Caṇḍeśvarī with the mantra "Hrīṃ, obeisance to Caṇḍeśvarī," [one should pray]: "O Great Goddess Caṇḍeśvarī, [accept] the remains of offerings such as sandalwood paste,
and the remains of food to be licked, sucked, eaten, and drunk, along with garlands and ointments."
"I offer you the remains of the offering (nirmālya) by the command of Śrī Śiva.

With this mantra, one should give the *nirmālya*. Then, having worshipped Ucchiṣṭacāṇḍālinī right there, one should give the liquor (*āsava*) from the food offering of her remains to Ucchiṣṭacāṇḍālī. Then...
Having fed the Brahmins and the maidens, he himself should partake of the prasāda.

In the *puraścaraṇa*, however, there is this distinction: one must perform a recitation (*japa*) numbering one hundred thousand (*lakṣa*), and a fire-oblation (*homa*) consisting of one-tenth of that number, using the aforementioned substances according to the sequence prescribed in the *puraścaraṇa-paddhati* and following the previously mentioned ritual procedure. From one-tenth of that...
Having recited the root mantra, one should offer libations with water mixed with camphor, water from sacred fords (tīrtha), or honey, while reciting:

"I satisfy Dakṣiṇakālī, svāhā. Having worshipped the deity in a vessel with this, one should perform the libation. Then, having again performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) and the other rites, one should perform the ritual dismissal (visarjana).

One should perform the purification (*mārjana*) by one-tenth of that [number]. For example: having meditated upon oneself with the awareness of being the deity and having performed worship, one should recite the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*);
at its end, one should recite the name of the deity in the accusative case, and at the end of that, [recite] "I consecrate, *namaḥ*."
Thus one should consecrate oneself. There should be a feeding of Brahmins numbering one-tenth of that [total recitation]. At the conclusion of that, one should perform a great worship.
(p. 74) Now, the procedure for the abbreviated worship (*saṃkṣiptapūjāvidhi*):

Having drawn a square there on one's left, and having cast flowers and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) therein while reciting "Oṃ hraḥ, I establish the general offering water (*sāmānyārghya*)," one should worship there with "Oṃ, obeisance to the Support-Energies (*ādhāraśakti*)."

Having placed the *argha* vessel there and filled it with water while reciting "Namaḥ," one should invoke the sacred waters (*tīrthas*) into that water from the solar disc by means of the *aṅkuśa-mudrā*. The mantra for this is: "Oṃ Gaṅge ca Yamune caiva Godāvari Sarasvati..."
O Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī, be present in this water!
"Oṃ! O Sun, the holy fords within the belly of the universe have been touched by your rays;
by that truth, O God, O Maker of Day, grant me the holy ford.
Having thus invoked the holy fords, [one says]: "Oṃ, salutations to all the holy fords beginning with the Gaṅgā."

Having thus worshipped with flowers, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and other offerings, [one should recite]: "Oṃ, salutation to the solar orb (*arka-maṇḍala*) consisting of twelve digits (*kalā*); Oṃ, salutation to the fiery orb (*vahni-maṇḍala*) consisting of ten digits; Oṃ, salutation to the lunar orb (*soma-maṇḍala*) consisting of sixteen digits."
Having thus worshipped the three mandalas of the Sun, Fire, and Moon, and having worshipped the six limbs with "Oṃ,

salutation to the six limbs," one should protect [the object] with the Astra-mantra, veil it with the Kavaca-mantra, transform it into nectar by means of the Dhenu-mudrā while reciting "Vam," cover it with the Matsya-mudrā, and [recite] the Praṇava ten times.
One should recite [the mantra]. Having displayed the conch mudrā, one should display the dhenu mudrā and the yoni mudrā.
This is the procedure for the general installation of the arghya water. Now, as for the worship: having drawn the yantra with saffron, kesara, sandalwood, and other substances.

One should draw [the mandala] consisting of a hexagon within which are three triangles, surrounded by eight enclosures (bhūpura). Then, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the seers and other elements as follows: *Namaḥ* to Bhairava, the Seer, on the head; *namaḥ* to the Uṣṇih meter, on the mouth; *oṃ namaḥ* to Dakṣiṇakālikā, on the heart; [and *namaḥ*] on the secret place.

"Salutation to the seed-syllable *krīṃ*. Salutation to the power (*śakti*) *hūṃ* at the two feet. Salutation to the pin (*kīlaka*) *krīṃ* on all limbs. Now follows the ritual placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*). With the words "Salutation to the heart, *krāṃ*," one should touch the heart with the fingers—the index, middle, and ring fingers—extended.
With "KṚĪṂ ŚIRASE SVĀHĀ," one should touch the head with the index and middle fingers. With "KṚŪṂ ŚIKHĀYAIVAṢAṬ," one should touch the top-knot (śikhā) with the thumb while the fists are clenched.
With the mantra "KRAIṂ KAVACĀYA HŪM," one should touch all the limbs with the hands spread apart.

With the mantra "Kroṃ netratrayāya vauṣaṭ," one should touch the three eyes with the index finger and the ring finger, and the space between the eyebrows with the middle finger; thus one should touch the three eyes.
With the mantra "Kraḥ astrāya phaṭ," one should perform the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) by snapping the fingers.
The ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*) is as follows: *krāṃ* to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*;
*krīṃ* to the two index fingers, *svāhā*; *krūṃ* to the two middle fingers, *vaṣaṭ*; *kraiṃ* to the two ring fingers, *hūm*; *krauṃ* to the two little fingers, *vauṣaṭ*.
Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) with the palms and backs of both hands while uttering *phaṭ*,
one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*) ten times, seven times, or five times.

Then, one should perform three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) known as inhalation (*pūraka*), retention (*kumbhaka*), and exhalation (*recaka*), using the root mantra recited four, sixteen, and eight times respectively.
Then, one should meditate upon Dakṣiṇakālī. Then, one should invoke her, as follows: [with] the *karakacchapikā*...
Having bound flowers [to the sandals] and meditated upon the goddesses in their prescribed forms,

having brought them from the heart to above the nose while reciting the root mantra, and having brought them over the flowers held in the hollowed palms with the words, "Come, come, O Great Goddess, O Abode of Compassion, by means of the two sandals," [one should address her as] "Oṃ, O Sovereign of the Gods."

"O You who are easily accessible through devotion and accompanied by Your retinue, remain perfectly steady for as long as I worship You"—with these words, one should cast [the flower] upon the yantra. Then, having recited the root mantra: "O Dakṣiṇakālikā, together with Your limbs, weapons, vehicle, attendants, and retinue, come here!"

One should invoke with the *āvāhana-mudrā* [saying], "Come here. One should establish [the deity] with the *sthāpana-mudrā* [saying], "Stay here. One should effect the presence with the *sannidhīkaraṇa-mudrā* [saying], "Be present here. One should effect the confinement with the *sannirodhana-mudrā* [saying], "Be confined here."

"Be present here," with this *saṃmukhīkaraṇa-mudrā*, one brings [the deity] face to face. Having protected [it] with the *astra-mantra* and veiled [it] with "Hūṃ," having rendered [it] nectar with the *dhenu-mudrā* and "Vaṃ," one should perform the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) upon the body of the deity and effect the unification (*sakalīkaraṇa*) with the root mantra.

One should perform the recitation (*japa*) twelve times with the mantra "Ā Hrīṃ Krom Svāhā" and, using the *lelihāna* mudrā, perform the installation of the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) of the deity. It is as follows:
"Ā Hrīṃ Krom Śrīṃ [to] Dakṣiṇakālikā..."

Having placed his hand [on the deity], he should recite: "O speech, mind, skin, eyes, ears, nose, and vital breaths, come here and dwell happily for a long time; Svāhā! Therein, he should display the *dhenumudrā*. Then, reciting the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), [he offers]: "This handful of flowers [is offered] to [the deity] together with the limbs, weapons, vehicles, and retinues..."
One should offer five handfuls of flowers while reciting: "Obeisance to the deity Rivāra-dakṣiṇa-kālikā."
In this manner, in all instances, the recitation of the root mantra together with its ancillaries (sāṅga) and so forth should be understood as the application.
"This is for foot-washing; this is for sipping water.

"This is the *arghya* offering; this is the *madhuparka*. "This is again for sipping water. "This is for bathing; salutation to the deity Dakṣiṇakālikā. "This is the anointing with red sandalwood paste."

"These are the unbroken grains; these are the flowers—*oṣaṭ* to such-and-such deity! This is incense; this is the lamp; these are the food offerings—*namaḥ* to the goddess Kālikā! Thus is the abbreviated worship.
Having performed this, one should then bring the rosary and place it in some vessel or in the left hand.
Having sprinkled [the rosary] with water for the *arghya* offering while reciting the root mantra:
"Oṃ, O garland, O garland, O great illusion, whose nature is all powers!
The four aims of life are entrusted to you; therefore, be the bestower of success upon me."

Having placed the rosary in the right hand with the mantra "Oṃ Hrīṃ Siddhyai Namaḥ," and having brought it to the region of the heart, touching each bead with the middle part of the middle finger while not overstepping the *meru* (the fixed bead), one should contemplate the *kāmakalā* within the body, meditate upon the Guru at the head, and [meditate] upon [the deity] in the heart.
Meditating upon the Goddess on the tongue as the form of the mantra-lamp,
and having visualized the tongue itself as the form of a lamp within the mass of its radiance, one should [recite] with the mind, or in a whisper, or with a rosary of beads,
or with a rosary of syllables.

Having recited the root mantra one hundred and eight times— using a rosary made of any one of the following: refined conch shell, rudrākṣa, crystal, or others— at a pace that is neither too fast nor too slow, he should place the rosary upon his head.
Reciting: "Oṃ, O Mālā, you are considered dear to all beings and to all the worlds;
O auspicious one, grant me welfare, fame, and valor at all times," he should place [the rosary] down, worship it with "Hrīṃ Siddhyai Namaḥ," and then proceed as before.

Having performed the breath-control (prāṇāyāma), the ritual placement (nyāsa), and so forth, and having worshipped the deity with flowers, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and other offerings, one should offer water from a conch shell containing flowers, sandalwood paste, and unbroken rice grains, reciting:
"Oṃ! You are the protector of that which is most secret; accept this recitation performed by us."

"O Goddess, O Great Sovereign, may there be accomplishment for me through your grace. With this mantra, having meditated upon water consisting of radiant energy in the left hand of the Goddess, one should offer it.
Then, removing the rosary from one's head...
"Oṃ! O Mālā, you are considered the bestower of all accomplishments (siddhis) for all the gods.
By that truth, O Goddess, grant me accomplishment; salutations be unto you!
Reciting this mantra and having worshipped [the mālā], one should carefully conceal it. If it should fall from the hand...

For the sake of pacifying that [obstacle], one should mutter the root mantra one hundred and eight times; then, having offered eight handfuls of flowers to the Goddess, one should recite the hymn of praise, the armor-mantra (kavaca), and so forth.
(p. 77) Now, the Karpūra-stotra:

"O Mother, Consort of the Destroyer of the Three Cities, those who three times recite this seed-syllable—Karpūra, devoid of the middle and final vowels, joined with the moon and the left eye—at the end of the mantra..."
For those who have attained all perfections, their words— both prose and verse— seem to overflow from the cavity of their mouths, as beautiful as a cloud that dispels darkness at will.
O Great Goddess, if a person of dull intellect should ever, even once, mutter another seed-syllable encircled by Īśāna, the Moon, and the left ear (Śrī), at the end of the pair [of syllables],
having conquered the Lord of Speech and the Giver of Wealth; [then he shall become a great sage].
When the moon-crested Lord, who bears the most terrible-roaring serpent as his crest-ornament, prevails, he long deludes the multitude of lotus-eyed women.

O Kālikā, those who mutter your seed-syllable as a pair—consisting of the Lord (Īśa) situated within Vaiśvānara joined with the left eye of the moon-shining Vāmana—while their hair is disheveled; [they attain liberation].
She slays those who hate her at the end and brings the three worlds into a state of subjection;
she whose face bears two streams of weapons from the corners of her mouth is known as Dakṣiṇakālikā. || 3 ||

In the upper left hand, upon the lotus-palm, is a sword; likewise, below it, is a severed head. In the right hands, O Kālikā, who removes the sins of the three worlds, are the gestures of fearlessness and granting boons.
Having recited these syllables of Your name and contemplating the power of Your mantra, O Three-eyed Lord, the eight siddhis appear before their manifested faces, held in the palms of their hands.

Having joined the first letters of the [three] groups situated in fire (the letter *ra*), the moon (*i*) which is exceedingly charming, the pair of eyebrows (*ṅa* and *kūrcayugma*), the two *la*’s (*la-la*), and then the smiling face (*smi*) with the two *ṭha*’s (*ṭha-ṭha*) below it; |||

Those who mutter this mantra to the Mother, the consort of the Destroyer of Smara (Śiva), and meditate upon her own form—those whose eyes are like lotuses for the playful dance of Lakṣmī—become embodiments of desire. || 5 ||
Whether individually, in pairs, or even all three together, those who possess true realization always recite the supreme seed-syllable— the ultimate secret— conjoining it with their own names.

In their lotus-eyes dwells Kamalā, and in the orb of their moon-bright faces resides Vāgdevī; they are enriched by divine garlands of skulls and by full breasts upon their necks that shine with extraordinary luster.
She whose hips gleam with girdles formed by the multitude of arms of the lifeless, who has the quarters as her garment, who is the creator of the three worlds,
and who is the three-eyed goddess.

O Mother, even one of dull intellect becomes a poet by meditating upon you, who are intent on the great love-play with Mahākāla upon a couch situated in a cremation ground, specifically upon the heart of a corpse.
To the consort of Hara, who was revealed upon a funeral pyre utterly crowded with auspicious yet terrible jackals, heaps of corpses, and collections of skulls and bones;
Those who always meditate upon you—having entered [the heart], being satisfied, situated above in sexual union, and never overly youthful—for them there is no defeat anywhere. 8.
O Mother, we speak to you: we are dull-witted; neither the Creator, nor Īśa, nor even Hari knows your supreme nature.
Nevertheless, O Dark One, our devotion to you makes us speak out; therefore, this must be forgiven, for anger toward a mere beast is surely not appropriate.
If a devotee, at night, while naked, with disheveled hair, and meditating upon you, recites your mantra while attached to a young woman who possesses full, swelling breasts and hips,
then all the hosts of *siddhas* shall come under his control.
A poet lives for a very long time on earth. || 10 ||
Having become composed and at ease, one should mutter [the mantra], while constantly reflecting upon and meditating on you, the supreme Great Kāla in the act of sexual union.
Then, for that wise man wandering upon the surface of the earth, the hosts of supernatural powers— including the wife of the Destroyer of Kama— become submissive at his lotus-like hand.
O Mother, you procreate the world, you protect the entire earth and its elements,
and at the time of dissolution, you withdraw them all.
Therefore, even Dhātṛ, the Lord of the three worlds, Śrīpati, and Maheśa—indeed, almost everyone—praises you; what more can I say of you? 12.
Many hosts of gods, who are superior even to you, serve you; yet they are deluded, O Mother, for they do not know anything of the Supreme.
I have taken refuge at will in the primordial Goddess, who is worshipped by the gods beginning with Hari, Hara,
and Viriñci, and who is ever intent upon the great bliss of the essence of passion.
The earth, the water, the fire, the wind, and the sky— you alone, O auspicious Kālī, beloved of Śiva, are all these.
What praise can be offered to you, O Mother? By your own compassion, be gracious toward me who am helpless;
follow me through existence so that my birth may no longer recur.
Staying in a cremation ground, composed, with matted hair and wearing a garment of directions, one should offer a thousand sun-flower blossoms with one's own discharged semen.
O Mahākālī, even one who is intent on meditating upon you while reciting even a single mantra for each of them becomes, by his own will, a sovereign lord of the earth. || 15 ||
Indeed, on a Tuesday at midday, one should offer flowers whose vitality has faded from being swept up in the house, along with their roots, upon the funeral pyre.
Having recited even this mantra once with love at the proper time, the lord of the earth, that preeminent among good poets, always goes forth mounted upon an elephant. 16.
If a devotee, repeatedly meditating upon the temple of the Flower-Bowed God (Kusumadhanus), which is strewn with its own blossoms, mutters your mantra before it— oh, wonderful!— he attains success.
That lord of the Gandharva lineage, too, who is a river of the nectar of poetry, ultimately becomes absorbed in the supreme state and attains sovereignty. || 17 ||
Upon the five-and-three-spoked seat, in the heart of the corpse-Śiva,
she whose face is smiling is intensely devoted to the beauty and the essence of passion with Mahākāla.

O Mother, even a person who is deeply attached to worldly things at night and himself devoted to the joy of sensual pleasure—if such a one should meditate upon you, he would become a destroyer of Smara (the god of love). 18.
O dark one, even the flesh and bones of a cat are at your disposal.
Or else, [one may eat] a camel, a sheep, a human, a buffalo, or even a goat.
Even for virtuous mortals dwelling on earth who offer worship at Balintha, every step brings about an unprecedented attainment of all perfections. || 19 ||
Self-controlled, devoted to consuming sacrificial food, he recites the mantra one hundred thousand times during the day,
intent on meditating upon the pair of your feet, O Mother.

Moreover, a man who is naked at night and delights in the sport of lovemaking becomes truly equal to the Destroyer of Smara (Śiva) on the surface of the earth, [attaining] a hundred thousand [merits]. 20.
O Mother, this hymn of praise of yours,
known as the "Recitation for the Salvation of Manu," is joined with the ritual procedure for worshipping your pair of lotus feet.
Whether at midnight or during the time of worship, for whoever recites this, even if it be mere idle chatter, the nectar-like essence of poetic composition flows forth.
A multitude of fawn-eyed women, trembling with love, follows him; even the lord of the earth, a representative of Kubera, is under his sway.
An enemy regards him as a prison, yet through the playful sport of that [enemy], he becomes a true devotee who is liberated while living throughout every birth. || 22 ||
Thus ends the *Karpūrastotra* composed by the illustrious Mahākāla.
Now, while still within my former body, I offered this hymn: "Since I did not take refuge at your pair of feet nor worship you,
I am today being tormented by the most powerful fires of hunger and thirst, along with hosts of ill repute."

Having cast us into another birth, where shall our refuge be here again? Wherever there may be service, let my offense be forgiven, O Karālā, who can assume any form at will and whose face is revealed! || 1 ||

In my childhood, my dull intellect was benumbed by the prattle of children, and I was absorbed in childish play; thus, O Mother, I did not know you—the one who bestows liberation through the waters that wash away the impurities of the Kali age.
There is no proper conduct, nor indeed worship, nor talk of sacrifice, nor mindfulness, nor service; [all these] must be forgiven. 2.
If I have reached youth, with my limbs bitten by the senses which are like venomous serpents, my wisdom destroyed, and always filled with longing to seize the wives and wealth of others;
I have never, even for a moment, remembered the pair of your lotus feet with my mind; this must be forgiven. 3.

Mature yet desiring alms, striving for food and other necessities for the sake of his sons, daughters, and wife, his body is submerged in incessant daily anxiety as he wonders, "Where shall I obtain it? Where shall I go?"
Neither meditation, nor reliance [on a teacher], nor the ritual of worship, nor the chanting of names—may these be forgiven. 4.

In old age, one is devoid of intellect, with a wasted and helpless body, afflicted by labored breathing, coughing, and dysentery; unfit for action, with failing eyesight and fallen teeth, one is overwhelmed by hunger and thirst.
Burnt by remorse, he should welcome death alone and nothing else;
having performed his ablutions at the start of the day, he has not offered water anywhere, nor flowers, nor food offerings and the like, nor even devotion or faith.
Neither was an offering made, nor worship, nor was your virtues recounted, nor was any adoration performed; this must be forgiven by you. 6.

I know you, yet I am not [able to fully describe] you— the remover of the fear of worldly existence, the bestower of all perfections, enriched by the arising of eternal bliss, composed of the three qualities, and ever-abounding in the dawn of perpetual purity.
One who is oppressed on all sides day after day by masses of suffering due to the longing for false actions must be patient. || 7 ||
She has the hue of a dark cloud, her limbs are dark-complexioned, her hair is disheveled, and she is beautiful with a severed head adorned by a sword;
she grants protection from fear and bestows desired boons, wearing a garland of heads from a multitude of corpses, and her eyes are long.
One who has cultivated through meditations that which removes the birth of existence—the single essence of saṃsāra—should be patient. 8.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and likewise Īśa always meditate upon the pair of your lotus feet; yet, O Mother of the world, due to a lack of fortune, I do not worship the pair of your feet.
O Eternal One, this lustful man, whose mind has been brought under control by constant greed and seductions, begs you; he should be forgiven. || 9 ||

He is intoxicated by passion and hatred, his body defiled by impurities, greedy for the enjoyment of desires, indifferent to what ought and ought not to be done, devoid of noble-mindedness, and abandoned by the assemblies of the Kaulas.
Where is your meditation? Where is your worship? And where is the recitation of mantras? You have done nothing at all.

This wretched man—sick, suffering, poor, dependent on others, miserable, dusty, evil-minded, addicted to sleep and laziness, distracted by filling his belly, and conceited in his imagined self—is to be pitied.
(81) What is this ritual of worship toward you? Where is your consent, where your affection, and where your regard? It must be forgiven. || 11 ||

For one whose mind is enveloped by false delusions and passions, who is possessed by a multitude of afflictions, who is beset by hunger and the onset of sleep, who is devoid of mindfulness, and who is engaged in evil deeds.
Where is there room for Dharma in poverty, O Mother? Where is there delight, and where is the company of the virtuous?
[May this be] forgiven. 12.

O Mother, born from the body of my father, you remained within my womb; O Janani, you are the one who brings about destruction, the creator through the qualities of the senses, whose very nature is the cause of karma.
The notion of "you," the notion of "I" established in the mind, and this entire state of existence—forgive all of this;
you are to be forgiven. 13.

You are the earth, you are the water, and you are the fire; you are the world in the form of air, you are space, and you are the mind; you are primordial nature (prakṛti), preceded by the great principle (mahat), and all that has come before.
O Mother, you are the Self and you are supreme; there is nothing whatsoever beyond you that must be forgiven.
You are Tvaṅkāli and you are Tārā; you are the beautiful daughter of the mountain, Bhairavī; you are Durgā and you are Chinnamastā; for you are indeed Bhuvanā, Lakṣmī, and Śivā.
You are Dhūmā, Mātaṅginī, and you are Bagalā; O Maṅgalā and others whose names are in this hymn, may [any offense] be forgiven. || 15 ||

The person who, always endowed with devotion, concludes [their practice] with this hymn to the Goddess, crosses over the hundredfold host of obstacles that are difficult to traverse due to evil deeds; all impediments go to their destruction.

If mental anguish or physical disease should ever arise, and if you are at fault in every way, then, O Mother of the three worlds, who can assume any form at will, may you forgive all that with the thought of me as your son.
He becomes a knower, a speaker, a lord of poets, a master of wealth, charitable in nature, compassionate, sinless, stainless, a leader of his lineage, skilled, truthful, and righteous.

Eternal bliss, rich in compassion, turning away from the multitude of worldly beings, and habituated to the conduct of the true path—he easily crosses the ocean of saṃsāra by taking refuge at the pair of feet of the Daughter of the Mountain. 17.
Thus ends the hymn of praise.
Then Bhairavī spoke the armor-mantra (kavaca): "O Lord, the worship of Kālī has been heard; O Master, the various dispositions (bhāvas) have also been heard."
Now I desire to hear the Kavaca that was previously indicated. || 1 ||
You alone are indeed the creator, the protector, and the destroyer;
you alone are my refuge, O Lord—protect me from this calamity of suffering.
Bhairava said:
Listen, O Bhairavī, beloved of my life; I shall declare the secret known as the Śrījaganmaṅgala-kavaca, which is the very embodiment of mantra. (3)
By reciting and retaining it, one may delude the three worlds in an instant;
even Nārāyaṇa, having held this, became a woman and [approached] Maheśvara.
Having seized him who had brought agitation to the yogis, the best of the Raghus,
being fully satisfied, slew Rāvaṇa and the other night-stalkers.
By whose grace I am the Lord, the all-pervading conqueror of the three worlds;
by whose grace even Kubera became the master of wealth, and the Lord of the Gods became the husband of Śacī.
Thus, O beloved, all the gods who are lords of all supernatural powers [are the presiding deities] of this Śrījaganmaṅgala-kavaca; Śiva is its seer (ṛṣi).
The meter is Anuṣṭubh and the deity is Kālikā,
who is said to be on the right [side] for the delusion of the worlds, for victory over the wicked, and for the attainment of enjoyment and liberation.
Its application is proclaimed for the attraction of women.
May Kālikā protect my head—she who is the supreme single-syllabled mantra, the sound "Krīṃ."
KṚĪM KṚĪM KṚĪM—may Kālikā, the bearer of the sword, protect my forehead;
HŪM HŪM—may she protect the pair of my eyes; HRĪM HRĪM—may she protect my ears.
May Kālikā protect [me] on the right; may Maheśvarī protect the pair of nostrils.
May Krīṃ Krīṃ Krīṃ protect the tongue; may Hūṃ Hūṃ protect the cheek. || 11 ||
May she whose nature is *svāhā*, the Great Vidyā consisting of twenty-two syllables who bestows happiness, protect my entire face with *hrīḥ hrīḥ*. (12)
May Kālī, bearing a sword and a severed head, protect me on all sides with her entire body; may Cāmuṇḍā, whose mantra consists of the three syllables KRĪM HRŪM HRĪM, protect my heart.
Aiṃ hūṃ oṃ aiṃ, hrīṃ phaṭ svāhā to the pair of breasts; Kakutsthalā, the eight-syllabled great vidyā together with the hand-weapon, may she protect my two arms. (14)
May the six-syllabled mantra—*krīṃ krīṃ hūṃ hūṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ*—protect me;
may *krīṃ* protect the middle of the navel, and may Kālikā protect the right side.
*Krīṃ svāhā*—may that ten-syllabled *Kālikā* protect my back;
*krīṃ*, may *Kālikā* always protect my private parts; thereafter, *namas tatas*. (16)
The seven-syllabled great vidyā, hidden in all tantras—*hrīṃ hrīṃ dakṣiṇe kālike hūṃ hūṃ*—may it protect both hips. (17)
May the ten-syllable mantra of Kālī, "svāhā māmūruyugmakam," and "oṃ krīṃ krīṃ me svāhā," protect my two thighs forever; may Kālikā protect my knees. (18)
This Vidyā named Kālīhṛd bestows the fruits of the four aims of life;
may she protect the right ankle with the mantra *krīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ*, and may Kālikā protect it.
May the fourteen-syllable mantra *krīṃ hrūṃ hrīṃ svāhā* protect my feet.
Kālī, bearing a sword and a severed head, bestows boons and fearlessness. (20)
May she protect every limb on all sides with all her vidyās:
Kālī, Kapālinī, Kullā, Kurukullā, and Virodhinī. (21)
Vipracittā, as well as Ugrograprabhā, Dīptā, Ghanatviṣā,
Nīlā, Ghanā, Valākā, Mātā, Mudrā, and Mitā— may they protect me.
May all these goddesses—Brahmī and likewise Nārāyaṇī—who bear swords and are adorned with garlands of severed heads, protect me in the cardinal and intermediate directions. (23)
Māheśvarī, Cāmuṇḍā, Kaumārī, Aparājitā, Vārāhī,
and Nārasiṃhī— all of them adorned with immeasurable ornaments.
"May they protect me with their own weapons in the cardinal and intermediate directions—just so!
Thus has this divine, most wonderful kavaca been narrated to you. 25.
O Brahmā, this armor known as Śrījaganmaṅgala, which embodies the flood of great vidyās and effects the attraction of the three worlds, has been uttered from my own mouth. 26.
Having performed the worship of the Guru according to the rules, one should then recite the armor-mantra (kavaca) either three times,
once, or as long as one lives.
By covering this half of a hundred [verses], one becomes a conqueror of the three worlds;
indeed, by the grace of this armor (kavaca), one agitates the three worlds.
One shall become a great poet for a month and a master of all supernatural powers;
one should offer handfuls of flowers to Kālikā once with the root mantra alone.
One shall obtain the fruit of worship performed for a hundred thousand years if one wears this written on birch bark, fixed upon gold. (30)
If one should wear [this] on the right arm or on the neck during the asterism Viśākhā, it shall, through its wrath, delude the three worlds and crush the three worlds in an instant. || 31 ||
He shall possess sons, wealth, and prosperity, and become a treasury of various sciences;
furthermore, weapons such as the Brahmāstra will [become effective] through the mere touch of his body.
Whatever woman meets with destruction—whether she be barren or one whose children have died—she shall surely become the mother of many living offspring; of this there is no doubt. (33)
It must not be given to the disciples of others, especially to those who lack devotion;
it should be given to disciples endowed with devotion, for otherwise one will meet death.
Having cast aside rivalry, Kamalā and Vāgdevī reside with certainty in the temple of happiness, maintaining their steadfastness until the end of her grandsons' lives. || 35 ||
He who should worship the Ghoradākṣiṇā without knowing this armor-mantra (kavaca) [will meet with misfortune].
Even after reciting it one hundred thousand times, his vidyā does not become accomplished.
He suffers a thousand blows and shall soon meet his death. || 36 ||
Thus ends the armor-mantra.
Then the venerable Mahākāla spoke this most excellent heart-mantra, known as the Hṛdaya, which is a hymn of great wonder.
Listen, O beloved, to this great secret of the Gopī, well-guarded by Dakṣiṇā. || 1 ||
Though it is unspeakable, I shall speak it out of affection for you;
keep it secret from others, O Daughter of the Mountain, for this is the truth, the absolute truth.
The Goddess said: In which age did it originate, and by whom was this hymn composed in the past?
O Śambhu, Maheśvara, ocean of compassion, please tell me all of that.
Śrī Mahākāla said: "In former times, I severed the head of Prajāpati;
through the sins committed by that killing of a Brahmin, my state as Bhairava came to be."
O beloved, this hymn has been composed by me for the destruction of the sin of killing a Brahmin;
it is a hymn that destroys malevolent spells and removes the guilt of Brahmin-slaughter.
Oṃ. Of this Heart-Stotra Mantra of the illustrious Dakṣiṇakālī, the seer is the illustrious Mahākāla; the metre is Uṣṇik; the deity is the illustrious Dakṣiṇakālikā; Krīṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja);
Hrīṃ is the power (śakti); Namaḥ is the pin (kīlaka). Its application (viniyoga) is for recitation at all times and in all places.
Oṃ krāṃ, salutation to the heart.
Oṃ krīṃ, svāhā to the head.
Oṃ krūṃ, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock.
Oṃ kraṃ kavacāya hūṃ | Oṃ krauṃ netratrayāya vauṣaṭ | Oṃ kraḥ astrāya phaṭ |
Then one should meditate upon Kālī, the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), who has three eyes and many forms;
she has four arms, a lolling tongue, and a face resembling the full moon. || 1 ||
Resembling the petals of a blue lotus, she shatters the hosts of enemies;
she likewise holds a human skull, a sword, a lotus, and the gesture of granting boons.
She bore blood-red fangs upon her face, possessed a terrifying form,
was constantly intent on loud, boisterous laughter, and was always naked.
Having thus meditated upon the Great Goddess, who is seated upon a corpse-seat and adorned with a garland of skulls, one should then recite the heart-mantra.
Oṃ! Kālikā, who possesses a formidable form and bestows the fruits of all desires—the Goddess praised by all the gods—may she bring about the destruction of my enemies. (5)
O you whose very nature is *hrīṃ-hrīṃ*, most excellent and difficult to find in the three worlds! Out of affection for you, I have told this; it must not be given to just anyone. (6)
Now I shall explain meditation; listen, O Supreme Goddess, by the mere knowledge of which one will become liberated while living. (7)
Having meditated upon her who has a serpent as her sacred thread, who has the crescent moon as her crest-ornament, who wears a mass of matted hair, and who stands near Mahākāla; || 8 ||
O fair-faced one, it is the truth, the absolute truth, that all those men who perform such acts as the nyāsa and others attain liberation.
Listen to the Yantra of the Supreme Goddess, which bestows the accomplishment of all goals;
it is more secret than the secret, a great secret to be guarded even more than the most guarded of secrets.
The Kāliyantra, which bestows excellent accomplishment, consists of a triangle, a pentagon, an octagon, a lotus, a square, a series of skulls, and flames.
O beloved, always maintain the mantra previously spoken;
now listen to the garland of names of the goddess Dakṣiṇakālī.
Kālī and Dakṣiṇakālī, whose form is black and who is the supreme self;
she wears a garland of severed heads, has large eyes, and is the cause of creation and destruction. || 13 ||
Mahāmāyā is the nature of stability, the yogic sleep whose essence is the *bhaga*;
she delights in drinking the clarified butter of the *bhaga*, illuminates the *bhaga*, and is born from the *bhaga*.
The primordial one, ever-new, terrible, of great splendor, Karālikā;
she who carries the spirits, the fortune of success, the unobstructed Sarasvatī. || 15 ||
O Maheśvarī, those who recite these garlands of names day after day—to them I am truly, truly the servant of the servant; this is the truth, the truth.

I worship the Goddess Kālī, who carries the skull-bowl, whose form consists of the seed-syllable *kaṃ* and the skeletal remains, who is in the form of a crow, who transcends the *kala*s, and who is the auspicious Kālikā. 17.
I bow down to the Goddess Kālikā, who delights in the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*, who finds joy in the *svayambhū* flower, who is fond of sexual union, and who is exceedingly fierce.
I bow to the beloved of the messenger, the great messenger, the supreme mistress of the yoga of messengers;
I bow to those who delight in the arising of the yoga of messengers and who possess the form of messengers. 19.
By consecrating water seven times with the *krīṃ* mantra and sprinkling it, all diseases are destroyed; there is no need for hesitation in this matter. (20)
Then, one should consecrate sandalwood with great mantras ending in "krīṃ svāhā";
when a tilaka is made with it by the wise, the world shall always be brought under control.
O Dear One, by reciting the mantra *krīṃ hrūṃ hrīṃ* seven times over unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), the destruction of great fear occurs; of this there is no doubt. (22)
One should consecrate the cremation-ground fire with the mantra *krīṃ hrīṃ hrūḥ svāhā*.
Having cast it into the house of the enemy, the death of the enemy will occur. (23)
For the purpose of eradication (uccāṭana), one should likewise recite *hrū*, *hrīṃ*, and *krīṃ* after purifying the flower seven times;
there is no doubt that it will surely drive away the enemies.
And for the purpose of attraction, O Beloved, having recited "krīṃ krīṃ krīṃ," one should throw unbroken rice grains;
even one situated at a distance of a thousand yojanas will quickly come.
One should recite the mantra seven times: *krīṃ krīṃ krīṃ hrūḥ hrūḥ hrīṃ hrīṃ*, thereby purifying the collyrium; with this *tilaka*, one brings delusion to the world. (26)
O Supreme Goddess, this heart-mantra is the supreme remover of all sins;
it is many millions of times superior to the merit gained from gifts such as the horse-sacrifice. (27)

The fruit of gifts such as the giving away of a maiden is said to be ten million times ten millionfold; the fruit of sacrifices such as the sacrifice to the *dūtī* is likewise remembered as ten million times ten millionfold. (28)
The fruit of all holy fords, such as the Gaṅgā and others, is remembered as being ten million times greater [than that].
"By the mere recitation once, the truth has been spoken as consisting of truth. (29)
Having performed the worship of Kaumārī in her own desired form according to the prescribed rite, O Great Goddess, he who recites this hymn is called one liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 30 ||
Having seen the vulva of a woman in her menses, one who recites [this] with a one-pointed mind attains the supreme station in the world of the Goddess, O fair-faced one. (31)

On a day of great suffering, great disease, or great peril, in times of great fear and great terror, one should recite this most excellent hymn. This is the truth, the truth, and again the truth; one should protect it as one would protect the offspring of one's mother.
Thus the *Hṛdaya* is completed.
Then the Upanishad: Then indeed, one attains her, who is the nature of Brahman, at the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra);
she is the auspicious Aṅka, the Amarepha-Indirā, existing in the form of a collective totality (samaṣṭi) at the beginning.

Immediately following that, the form consisting of the union of the two seed-syllables of the agent (*kartṛ*), the *kūrca* seed-syllable, and the sixth vowel with the bindu for the oblation; thereafter, the form consisting of the union of the two worlds,
the world, space, fire, the moon, and the void, [is] O Kālikā, on the right.

Then, having gone before her and uttered the seven seed-syllables (*bīja*), one should recite [the mantra] for the daughter of the Great Sun (*Bṛhadbhānujā*). This is the most supreme among all mantras; by reciting it even once, one becomes the Lord of the Universe, the Lord of Women, the Lord of the Vedas, and the Teacher of All.
He who bows to all becomes one who is established in all the Vedas; he becomes one who has bathed in all sacred fords (tīrthas);
he becomes one who is initiated into all sacrifices. He himself is Sadāśiva. (p.
87) A triangle, a triangle, a triangle, again a triangle, a triangle, and then an eight-petaled [lotus].
Having drawn the filaments with a half-moon and two [petals], and having combined it with a single outer square (bhūpura),

one should worship it with the Sarvajña mantra; then, having placed [the syllables] upon the lines on that petal of the goddess, she should be meditated upon as having a face like a fresh cloud, thick breasts, curved fangs, and seated upon a corpse.
Kālikā, whose hands are adorned with the boon-granting gesture, the gesture of fearlessness, a sword, and a severed head, is to be meditated upon.
Kālī, Kapālinī, Kullā, Kurukullā, Virodhinī, and Vipracittā reside within the hexagon. Ugrā, Ugraprabhā, Dīptā, Nīlā, Ghanā, Balākā, Mātrā, Mudrā, and Mitā reside within the nonagon.
Thus, there are those situated in the fifteen corners. Brāhmī, Nārāyaṇī, Māheśvarī, Cāmuṇḍā, Kaumārī, Aparājitā, Vārāhī, and Nārasiṃhī are situated on the eight petals.
The four deities situated in the four corners are Mādhava, Rudra, Vināyaka, and Saura.

In the four directions are Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, and Kubera. Having first worshipped the Goddess with all her limbs, one should perform libation with the water of the *bhaga* and worship her with the five *makāras*. What more can be said of this ritual? Even the station of Brahmā and the other gods is easily attained through this, yet it must be abandoned [by those seeking liberation].

The Manus appear in the sequence of one, two, and three; here the characteristics of enemies, friends, and so forth apply. For this reciter of the mantra there is success, but for another here there is no success; for this *manu* there is Tārā, for that *manu* there is Durgā, or for that *manu* there is Siddhi. But now, all these have become like dreams; only the Black One (*Asitā*) remains.

O Ānandā, you who are devoted to the sound "Kaha," tell me:
what is the mother? What dwells within? What is the mantra? And what is the Goddess? (64)

They were devoted to singing of Kṛṣṇa, worshipful to Kṛṣṇa, and intent on meditation upon Kṛṣṇa; they were absorbed in the scriptures of Kṛṣṇa, their talk was of Kṛṣṇa, and they were dedicated to the conduct of Kṛṣṇa. || 65 ||
What is her conduct, what is her gait, and what is she who performs the tāṇḍava dance?
What is her forest, what is her movement, and what is she who is devoted to power (śakti)? || 66 ||
She who is the sovereign of the realm of karma, the witness of karma, the beauty of karma;
she who is the knowledge of karma, the course of karma, and devoted to the system of karma.
She whose measure is action, whose body is action, who is devoted to the dharma of action;
she is the destroyer of the lines of karma and the dispeller of the lines of karma. || 68 ||

She who causes delusion regarding the lines of destiny, who is devoted to the fame of karma, whose knowledge is karma, whose essence is karma, who is the support of karma, and who is the field of karma. (69)
She who performs action, she who removes action, she who is beautiful with the wonder of action;
she who is the Kali of action, she who is the Tārā of action, she who cuts through action, and she who bestows action.
She is the Caṇḍālī of karma, the mother of the Veda of action, and the field of action;
she is infinite, delighting in the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa), and is inferred through the ritual section. || 71 ||
She whose girth is the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa), she who has the form of a tortoise (kamaṭha),
whose heart is worshipped by the Tortoise (Kūrma), and who is as beautiful as the neck of a tortoise.
She is to be served upon the seat of Kamaṭha, she is intent on the deeds of Kamaṭhī,
she is the beloved of Karuṇākara, and she is saluted by Karuṇākara.
She who wears a garland of skulls, she who possesses firm breasts,
she whose hair is matted, she who is free from deceit, she who is hard as a diamond, and she who is adorned with herons.
She whose thighs are like the trunks of elephants, who is firm as an elephant's trunk,
whose face is like an elephant's, whose speech consists of sweet melodies, who is the creative power, and who bestows the Kalpa tree.

Seated upon a lotus, she is a garland of digits, lotus-faced, and possesses shimmering radiance; she is the possessor of the earth, full of compassion, and honored by the discourse of what ought to be done. (76)
Adorned with hair, possessing a body of hair, and bearing the beauty of hair; clinging to the breasts of Kaṭhī, she is resplendent with a waist-string. || 77 ||

She who is fond of eating the ears [of grain], whose movement is through the bulbous roots and stories of bulbs, she who destroys the Kali age, the messenger of the Kali age, and she who is worshipped by the leader of poets. 78.
She is the restrainer of the golden girth, honored by the best of poets;
she is the cutter, adorned with a small knife, the female elephant, and the protector of the enemy of Karṇa.

She is the mistress of the instruments of action, the protector of the instruments, the one whose speech is the arts, the treasury of the arts, the creative impulse, the support of creation, and she whose hands bring about all manifestation.
She is the one whose song is beautiful, she is the sign of Cancer (Karka-rāśi), she is highly honored by the sign of Cancer;
she is the sign of Virgo (Kanyā-rāśi), she is a maiden, and she is one who speaks words dear to maidens.
She is satisfied by the gift of a maiden; she is pleased by the gift of a maiden;
she rejoices in those who perform the gift of a maiden; and she grants the desired fruits to those who accept the gift of a maiden. 82.

She who plows the field of the chest, who burns away the undergrowth of desire, who is seated upon a lotus, who brings joy to those with garlands of hands, and who is nourished by garlands of hands. || 83 ||

She whose joy lies in the rosary of beads, she who is united with the rosary of beads, she who bestows the perfection of the rosary of beads, and she who is dear to the hand that holds the rosary of beads. || 84 ||
She who is fond of hands, who delights in hands, who is devoted to the giving of hands;
she who finds bliss in the arts (kalās), whose gait is like that of a child (kali), who is worshipped by the Kali age, and who is the progenitor of the Kali age. || 85 ||
Established in the resonance of *kalanāda*, bestowing the boon of *kalanāda*, abiding in the assembly of *kalanāda*, she is Kaholā and the giver of Kahola. (86)
She resides in the center of Kahola’s abode, she is the bestower of boons upon Kahola,
she is the fountainhead of Kahola’s poetic genius, and she is honored by the sage Kahola.
She is worshipped by Kahola Mānasāra, she acts according to the words of Kahola;
she is the form of the agent, composed of the agent, the mother of the agent, and the instrument of action.
She is to be worshipped with gold, consisting of the pupil of the eye,
the abode of the bliss of youth, and satisfied by the joy of golden splendor.
She who is the small measure of the tip of a finger, she who creates the ocean of stories,
she who is to be approached by elephants, she whose gait is like an elephant’s, and she who is devoted to him whose banner bears an elephant.
The beloved of the Lord of Elephants, who delights in the throat [of her husband], is satisfied by this narrative;
she is lovely, playful, and adorned with beautiful ornaments.
She dwells in a lovely assembly, she is fond of lovely vows, she is to be propitiated by lovely virtues; she is Kapilā, the sovereign lady of Kapila.
She whose heart is worshipped by Kapila, she who speaks words dear to Kapila,
she whose form consists of the syllables of the mantra of the *ka-ha* wheel, and she who possesses the flowers of the *ka-ha* wheel.
She whose nature is *ka-e-ī-lhrīṃ*, she who bestows boons through *ka-e-ī-lhrīṃ*, she who grants success through *ka-e-ī-lhrīṃ*, and she whose very form is *ka-e-ī-lhrīṃ*. || 94 ||

She whose complexion is the syllables *ka-e-ī-l-hrīṃ*, who is born from the digits *ka-e-ī-l-hrīṃ*, who belongs to the *ka*-group of consonants, who resides in the door-panel, and who is capable of opening the door-panel. (95)
Kaṅkālī, Kapālī, she who speaks fondly of skeletons, she who is worshipped by Kaṅkālabhairava, and she who dwells in the mind of the Skeleton. || 96 ||
Delighting in the delusion of skeletons, she bestows the delusion of skeletons;
she is the destroyer of impurity, the remover of impurity, and the annihilator of the suffering caused by impurity. || 97 ||
She who is the flower of the Kali age, the giver of artistic skill, the food of the body, she who is worshipped by Kaśyapa;
she who belongs to Kaśyapa, she who is to be propitiated by Kaśyapa, and she whose body is filled with the Kali age. 98.
She who creates the body, she whose girdle is the gutturals (ka-varga), and she who is formidable;
she who is worshipped by Karālabhairava and she who is the sovereign lady of Karālabhairava. 99.
Terrible, the support of all mental constructions, the bestower of boons upon Lord Kapardin;
she is the creeper of love for Lord Kapardin and is endowed with a garland of Kapardin. || 100 ||
She is enriched with a rosary of matted locks, she is the giver of karavīra flowers, her life-breath is dear to the one who loves karavīra, and she is worshipped with karavīra. || 101 ||
Resembling the *karṇikāra* flower, she is worshipped with *karṇikāra* blossoms;
she abides in the fire of the *kariṣa* and bestows gold by the measure of a *karṣa*.
She is considered Kalaśā, Kalaśārādhyā, Kaṣāyā, Karigānadā, Kapilā, Kalakaṇṭhī, and Kalikalpalatā. (103)
The wish-fulfilling creeper, the mother of all that is wished for, the maker of all that is wished for, and the source of all that is wished for;
she who is radiant with the fragrance of camphor and who bears the scent of camphor.
She who is adorned with garlands of camphor, who bestows the fulfillment of camphor perfumes, who grants victory through garlands of camphor, and who dwells in the midst of the ocean of camphor. 105.
She is devoted to the satiation with camphor, she wears bracelets and garments, she is to be worshipped by Kapaṭeśvara, and she possesses the form of Kapaṭeśvara. || 106 ||
She is pungent, she is worshipped by the banner of poets, she bears the *kalāpa* flower;
she is radiant with the *kalāpa* flower and is honored by the *kalāpa* flower. || 107 ||
She who is the saw and who is to be meditated upon as the saw—how can we describe her ferocity?
How is Kālī, who is free from the act of "how" (doubt), the black one, the end-maker, and the sacrifice?
She who is the beloved woman, she who is worshipped by beloved women, she who wears the flowers of beloved women;
she whose abode is the flowers of beloved women, she who is the full moon of the flowers of beloved women. || 109 ||

Worthy of worship with the flowers of beautiful women, adorned with the flowers of beautiful women, having a tilaka-mark made of the flowers of beautiful women, she kisses the temples of beautiful women. 110.
She is satisfied by union with the beloved woman; she bestows the enjoyment of union with the beloved woman;
she is immersed in the sacrificial pit of the beloved woman; she dwells in the midst of the sacrificial pit of the beloved woman. || 111 ||
She who is to be propitiated by the minds of passionate women, she who is pleased by the pride of passionate women,
she who moves within the minds of passionate women, Kālikā, the dark one of the dark age.
Kāmā, Kāmadevī, Kāmeśī, Kāmasambhavā, Kāmabhāvā, Kāmaratā, Kāmārttā, and Kāmamañjarī. || 113 ||
She whose anklets jingle at will, she who dwells within the beloved of Kāmadeva;
she who is Kāmakālī, the art of love, Kālikā, and she who is worshipped by Kamalā. 114.
Kādikā, Kamalā, Kālī, she whose splendor is equal to the fire at the end of an aeon; the beloved of the conflagration at the dissolution of the world, she who dwells fondly in the wilderness. 115.
She who is to be worshipped at the [proper] time, she who delights in the [proper] time, the mother of time, and Kālinī;
the hero of time, the terrible one of time, the perfected one of time, and the giver of time. 116.
She who has the appearance of black collyrium, who dwells in Kālañjara;
she who is the black supernatural power, the increase of Time, and the liberator from the prison-house. || 117 ||
She is the Kādividyā, the Mother of Ka, she who dwells in Ka, and the beautiful one beginning with Ka;
she is Kāśī and Kāñcī, the Mistress of Kāñcī, and the bestower of boons upon the Lord of Kāśī. || 118 ||
She whose seed-syllable is *krīm* and whose seed-syllable is *krām* is remembered as the abode of the heart;
she is the desirable one, the goal of all desires, the bestower of the fruits of desire, and the source of all longing.
Kāmākhyā, Kāmarūpā, and she who releases the bow of desire; she whose garden is the essence of the god of love, and she who is the abode of the essence of the god of love. || 120 ||
She is the night of desire, the bestower of desires, dwelling on the mountain in the wilderness;
she is the one whose form is desire, the course of time, and devoted to the yoga of desire.
She delights in the crushing of desires, she who expands the abode of desire;
she is the wife of Kālabhairava and the beloved of Kālabhairava. || 122 ||
Established in the yoga of Kālabhairava, she bestows the enjoyment of Kālabhairava;
she is the wish-fulfilling cow, the milker of desires, the mother of desire, and the giver of splendor.
She who desires, she who is worshipped by those who desire, she who increases the bliss of those who desire;
she who is Kārttavīryā, she who is Kārttikeyā, and she who is worshipped by Kārttikeya. || 124 ||
She is the giver of effects from causes, the performer of actions through other causes;
she is accessible through splendor, composed of splendor, and she is Kātyā as well as Kātyāyanī.
The women of Kāśmīra have desire as their essence; they are devoted to the customs of Kāśmīra, delight in the conduct of Kāmarūpa, and speak with affection for Kāmarūpa.
She is the perfection of the conduct of the desire-realm and the form-realm, consisting of mind and capable of assuming any form at will;
she is the full moon night of Kārttika, worshipped by Kārttikeya, and her source is the Kāñcanāra flower.
She has the luster of the *kāñcanāra* flower, she is worshipped with *kāñcanāra* flowers;
she is golden in form, her ground is gold, and she eats from a bronze vessel. 128.
Consisting of the resonance of bell-metal, beautiful as she desires, kissing at will, resembling the kāśa flower, and meeting with the tree of desire (kāmadruma). || 129 ||

She whose flower is desire, the ground of desire, the one worshipped by desire, and the giver of desire; she whose body is desire, whose home is desire, and who is devoted to the seed of desire. || 130 ||
Mounted upon the banner of desire, established upon the banner of desire;
the daughter of Kaśyapa, worthy of worship by Kaśyapa, she who bestows joy upon Kaśyapa. || 131 ||
She who resembles the waters of the Kālindī, she who is worshipped by the waters of the Kālindī;
she who is intent upon the worship of which deity, and she who bestows the supreme goal of which deity? (132)
She is of the nature of karma, she performs actions according to her will, she is the one who severs the bonds of karma;
she is Kākinī, invoked as the Primordial Cause.
She is the nectar of poetry, she is of Kalinga, she is intent on crushing the Kalingas;
she is enriched with the ornament of black agallochum, and she bestows the glory of black agallochum.
She is fragrant with black aloe-wood, she is nourished by black aloe-wood,
she delights in the waters of the Kāverī, and she dwells on the banks of the Kāverī.
She has the form of the revolving wheel of time (kālacakra), she dwells within the wheel of time;
she is the forest, the support of the forest, the maker, and composed of compassion. (136)
She dwells in Kāmpilya; she is the quarter (Kāṣṭhā), the consort of Kāma, and the ground of desire (Kāmabhū).
She delights in drinking Kādambarī wine, and she is the art of the Kādambarī composition. || 137 ||
She who is to be worshipped by desire, the mistress of desire, she who is fully adored by the King of Desire;
she who is the knowledge (vidyā) of the Queen of the King of Desire, beautiful with the curiosity of passion. 138.
Born in Kāmboja, she is the river Kāñcinadā; she is the creator of bronze and gold, her form is like the mountain of gold, and she bestows the gift of the golden mountain.
She is the glory of desire, the one who dwells in the realm of desire, the authoritative verse, and she who rests upon the beloved;
she is the piercer of desire, the destroyer of the affliction of desire, and the ground of desire. 140.
The destroyer of time, the poetic muse, she who assumes any form at will;
she who resides in the body, the radiant glow of desire, the giver of poetry, and the beauty of time. 141.
The Mistress of Desire, the supreme among causes, intent upon the worship of Kāmeśī,
she is enriched with ornaments of girdles and anklets, and endowed with saffron-colored adornments.
Kālacakrā, Kālagati, Kālacakrāmanobhavā, Kundamadhyā, Kundapuṣpā, Kundapuṣpapriyā, and Kujā. (143)
The mother of Kujā, worshipped by Kujā, bearing the excellent axe;
seated upon an elephant, delighting in *kuśa* grass, with eyes like lotuses. || 144 ||

She was like a mineral ore, like a female osprey, like a low-born woman, like a female deer, and one who took refuge in the *kuṭaja* tree; she was adorned with serpents and intent on slaying serpents.
She who delights the mind of Kumbhakarṇa, the crest-jewel of the Kula, the Kula itself, the daughter of the potter’s house, and the beloved of the crest-jewel of the Kula. 146.
She is the one worshipped by the family, the one adored by the family, and she who is devoted to the worship of the family;
she is the ornament of the family, as well as its womb, and she who is served by flocks of ospreys.
She is the flower of the Kula, devoted to the Kula, intent upon the Kula-flower;
she is clothed in the Kula, worshipped by the Kula, and possesses a splendor equal to the sacrificial pit of the Kula. 148.
She is the radiant manifestation of the lineage-vessel (kulakuṇḍa), devoted to the flower of the vessel;
her face is pleased by the flower of the vessel, and her very self is born from the *kuṇḍa* and *goḷa*. 149.

She is the source from which the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka* arise, she consists of the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*, she is the *kuhū* [new moon], her life-breath is dear to the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*, and she is worshipped by the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*. || 150 ||
She is the delight of the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*, the bestower of strength to the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*;
she is devoted to the deity of the *kuṇḍa*, wrathful, and the supreme bringer of *kula*-attainment. 151.
She has the form of the *kulakuṇḍa*, her ground is equal to the *kulakuṇḍa*;
she is the perfection of the *kuṇḍa*, the supernatural power of the *kuṇḍa*, and is intent upon the worship of the *kumārī*. 152.
Her life-force is the worshipper of the maiden; her abode is the worshipper of the maiden;
she is satisfied by the desire for the maiden; she is eager for the worship of the maiden. (153)
She is satisfied by the vow of the maiden, she assumes the form of a maiden,
she delights in the food of maidens, and she is both the maiden and the giver of maidens.

She is the mother of Kumāra, the lineage-giver, the source of the lineage, the sovereign of the lineage, the emblem of the lineage, the bliss of the lineage, the delight of the lineage, and the upholder of the true doctrine. || 155 ||
Kuntī, Kulakāntā, and she who is devoted to the path of the Kula;
Kullā, Kurukullā, Kullukā, and she who grants the desires of the Kula. (156)

She whose body is like a thunderbolt, Kubjikā, the increaser of the bliss of Kubjikā, she who belongs to the Kula, whose gait is like an elephant's, and who moves with the stride of the lord of elephants. || 157 ||
She is the protector of the family, possessed of noble lineage, and likewise the illuminator of the family;
she is the sovereign mistress of the family-yoga, the sacrificial pit, and her form is as red as saffron. (158)
She who finds joy and satisfaction in saffron, she who dwells in the ocean of saffron;
she who is the flower, who is fond of flowers, the source of the Kula, and the beauty of the Kula. || 159 ||
