She is Kumudvatī, Kumudinī, Kuśalā, and the destroyer of unchaste women; she dwells in the midst of the abodes of unchaste women and is pleased by the company of unchaste women. || 160 ||

She is intent upon the abode of the unchaste women, she is Kuśāvartā, she is the Ocean of Kula (Kulārṇavā), she delights in the conduct of the Ocean of Kula, she is Kuṇḍalī, and she has the form of an earring (Kuṇḍalākṛti). || 161 ||
Kumatī, Kulaśreṣṭhā, Kulacakraparāyaṇā, Kūṭasthā, Kūṭadṛṣṭi, Kuntalā, and Kuntalākṛti. || 162 ||
She is of virtuous form and appearance, bearing the seed-syllable *kūṃ*;
she delights in the sounds *kuṃ kuṃ kuṃ kuṃ*, and is devoted to the supreme *krūṃ krūṃ krūṃ krūṃ*.
She whose abode is the sound "kuṃ-kuṃ-kuṃ," she who dwells in the lair of dogs, she who is joined with the company of dogs, and she whose form is infinite like that of a dog. || 164 ||
She whose beginning is the *kūrca* [mantra], whose seed-syllable is the *kūrca*, who is devoted to the recitation of the *kūrca*;
she who is satisfied by the touch of the breasts and who grants joy through the embrace of the breasts. 165.

She who destroys evil destinies, she who is worshipped by Kubera, she whose birthplace is the breasts, the leader of her clan, she who sings ill, the bearer of breasts, the mother of Kumāra, and she who has teeth like kunda flowers. || 166 ||
Kugeyā, Kuharābhāṣā, Kugeyā, Kughnadārikā, Kīrtti, Kirātinī, Klinnā, Kinnarā, Kinnarī, and Kriyā. || 167 ||

She whose sound is "krīṃ," who is intent on the recitation of "krīṃ," whose form is the mantra "krīṃ hrūṃ strīṃ," whose glances and side-long looks are variegated, who is a young maiden, and who wears a crown.

She is the speech of insects, the womb of insects, the mother of insects, and the giver of insects; she is the *kiṃśuka* tree, the speech of parrots, the essence of action, and the possessor of action. || 169 ||
She whose supreme sound is *kīṃ-kīṃ*, who takes the form of the mantras *klīṃ-klīṃ-klūṃ-klaiṃ-klauṃ*;
she whose essential nature is *kāṃ-kīṃ-kūṃ-kaiṃ*, and who is the very embodiment of the mantra *kaḥ phaṭ*. (170)
She is the bliss of the ketakī ornament, endowed with the ketakī adornment; she is the source of joy, the one with beautiful hair, the hair itself, and she is intent upon the slayer of Keśin. 171.
Keśarūpā, Keśamuktā, Kaikeyī, and likewise Kauśikī; Kairavā, Kairavāhlādā, Keśarā, and Keturūpiṇī. || 172 ||
She whose heart is worshipped by Keśava, whose mind is attached to Keśava;
she who destroys impotence, and who is pleased by the recitation of the *klaiṃ* seed-syllable. || 173 ||
Kauśalyā, Kośalākṣī, Kośā, and likewise Komalā;
she who dwells in Kolāpura and she who is the destroyer of the demon Kola. || 174 ||
She whose form is the limit (koṭi), who delights in the limit, the wrathful one, she whose form is wrath;
she is the cry of the peacock, the cuckoo, the limit itself, and she who is devoted to the mantra of the limit.
Endowed with infinite millions of mantras, formless, and residing in Kerala;
she is skilled in the Keralan way of life and dwells in the home of the Lord of Kerala.
She resides at Kedārāśrama and is worshipped by Kedāreśvara;
she is Krodharūpā, Krodhapadā, Krodhamātā, and Kauśikī. || 177 ||
She who holds a bow, she who is of the Krauñca lineage, she who belongs to the Kauśika clan, she who follows the Kaula path;
she who is of the Kaula tradition, she who is worshipped by the Kaulikas, and she who dwells in the Kaulika temple. || 178 ||
She is curious, the moonlight, of the Kaula lineage, the maiden, worshipped by the Kauravas;
she belongs to Kauṇḍinya, she is of the Kauśika clan, and her form blazes with the fire of wrath.
She has the brilliance of ten million fires of the end of time and the form of ten million suns;
she is Kṛttikā, black in color, a black sorceress (kṛṣṇakṛtyā), and distressed by her own actions—or rather, distressed with compassion.
She is slender-limbed, one who has accomplished her purpose, and whose form consists of *kṛṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
She is the syllables of the mantra *krauṃ krauṃ hūṃ phaṭ*, and she is *krīṃ hrīṃ hūṃ phaṭ namaḥ svadhā*.
She is the embodiment of the mantra *krīṃ krīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ tathā hrūṃ hrūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
Thus ends the thousand [names] called the *Śrī-sarvasāmrājya-medhā*. 182.
The account known as the Bestowal of Power upon Sundarī, which indeed reveals her true nature, has been told regarding Dakṣiṇākālī out of affection for Sundarī. || 1 ||
In the course of granting boons, even the secret has been revealed;
it should always be kept hidden with devotion and recited as that which is higher than the highest.
It should be recited especially at dawn, at midday, at midnight, during the time of sacrifice, and at the conclusion of the recitation of mantras. (3)
The steadfast practitioner who recites this for a year indeed becomes the very form of Kālī;
whether he recites it himself, causes it to be recited, hears it, or causes others to hear it.
Or even one who pleases the reciter shall become the very body of Kālikā;
and that man who recites this, whether with ease or with grace, [shall attain the same].

He is liberated from all suffering, the conqueror of the three worlds, and the wise poet; he is the one who delivers those who have lost their children at death, those whose sons die in infancy, those whose daughters die young, and those who are barren.
A woman barren of flowers or barren of labor pains should listen to this supreme hymn, which bestows all perfections, grants the status of a true poet, and ensures long life. (7)
One obtains scholarship and renown; of this there is no doubt.
Having prepared an offering according to one's desire and meditated upon Kālī, one should recite the hymn.
Having placed that very desire within his lap, the practitioner of mantra becomes [successful]; it is not otherwise.
[This is accomplished] with flowers from the womb, flowers from the linga, and even those produced from the *kuṇḍa* and *gola*.

With the flowers of the nectar of yoga, with the blossoms of the goddess of the cloth, with the flowers of Kālī, with the waters of the sacred seat (pīṭha), and with the waters for washing the womb; || 10 ||
O Goddess, [worship] with musk and saffron, followed by black agallochum from the nails,
and with the eight fragrances, incense, and lamps combined with barley and yava.
With red sandalwood, vermilion, and ornaments such as fish and meat;
with honey, milk-rice, and milk—and even with purified blood.
Having worshipped Mahākālī, who is cherished by Mahākāla, with great services and blood-red food offerings endowed with divine flavors; || 13 ||
O Śivā, having recited the Vidyārājñī and the Kullukā, one who is devoted to Kālī, single-minded, and adorned with a vermilion tilaka, should recite the hymn of praise. (14)
With his mouth filled with betel, his hair disheveled, and naked as the sky,
the hero dwells within the womb of a corpse, engaged in amorous play within the cremation ground.
In an empty dwelling, upon a seat of the *bindu* in a forest of Śiva strewn with flowers, one who sleeps, rises, or eats shall obtain the vision of Kālī. || 16 ||
Whatever action is performed there, its fruit shall be infinite;
in sovereignty she is Kamalā herself, and in spiritual perfection she is the Mother Śrī Kālikā.
In poetry he was equal to Tāriṇī; in beauty, he was like Sundarī;
in action, he was like the stream of the ocean; and likewise in learning, he was a Śrutidhara.
Invincible like the Vajra-weapon, wielding the weapon of victory over the three worlds, a slayer of enemies and a composer of poetry, he shall become equal to Śiva in the Kali age. (19)
The yogin who creates moons in every direction and intermediate quarter, who reverses day and night, and who can, in an instant, support the three worlds, is equal to Mahādeva. (20)
Through song, Tumburu himself becomes equal to Karṇa in generosity;
he is a skillful lord of elephants, horses, chariots, infantry, and weapons.
The *bhuśuṇḍī* [mantra] bestows longevity and destroys old age and grey hair;
by it, O Maheśvarī, one shall remain sixteen years of age at all times. (22)
O Goddess of the gods, within the sphere of the universe, nothing is difficult for him to attain at any time;
everything shall come into his hands—of this there is no doubt.
Having seen Kālī there accompanied by Kulapuṣpā, and having reflected upon it,
one should worship the Queen of Vidyās and recite the *Nāmasahasraka*.
Success consisting of the fulfillment of his desires shall always remain in his hand, provided he embraces the wives of others and worships the Supreme Goddess. || 25 ||
Having performed the yoga of hand-to-hand transmission and having recited [the mantra], one should recite the hymn;
having gazed at the female organs, one should recite the hymn, and one will become superior even to Kubera. 26.

O Maheśānī, one should offer into the fire at night the substances produced from the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*, colored with the prescribed pigments, in the land of the ancestors; then one should wipe away the lines of the ritual diagram.

Having diligently brought a young, beautiful, and charming woman who was proud of her restless limbs, and having purified her through the application of ritual placement (nyāsa), [he should proceed]. || 28 ||
Having established a couch of flowers, one should move about upon the earth,
honoring the root-cakra of the Goddess together with the path of her movement.

Having worshipped, O Supreme Goddess, having made the formal resolve (saṅkalpa), O Maheśvarī, and having recited the mantra and praised the Great Goddess, one should meditate upon the Praṇava, O Śivā. (30)

Having diligently consecrated the vulva with one hundred and eight recitations and kissed it, one should perform the recitation while becoming absorbed in yoga; thus one shall become the sovereign of all vidyās.
In an empty house, in a cremation ground, in a temple of Śiva, likewise in a desolate place, by a pond, within the Ganges, or at a crossroads; || 32 ||

In a cremation ground, on a mountain slope, at a solitary linga, in the mouth of Śiva, in a "womb" (yonimunda), during the menstrual period, after bathing, in one's own home, or likewise in the house of a courtesan; || 33 ||
And within the house of a courtesan, as well as in a plantain grove,
one should recite the hymn known as the *Sahasranāma* for the accomplishment of all goals.
In the forest, in an empty pit, in battle, or when encountering an enemy,
one should then recite the thousand names of Kālī.
Having become intent on the joy of the child, and having recited the hymn of praise to Kālikā,
one should meditate upon Kālī, perform the japa, and recite the Thousand Names.
(106) May he become the lord of all accomplishments; may he become the lord of the accomplishment of his desires.
[This occurs] upon the womb [of the goddess], or on the skin of the *muṇḍa* and *cūḍaka*, or on soft [skin], O Śivā. 37.
On a spread of corpse-cloth, or on a seat of flowers or cloth, with disheveled hair and wearing the quarters as his garment, the practitioner of sexual union remains upon his bed. (38)
Having recited [the mantra], one should recite the hymn to Kālī; thus one becomes a possessor of the siddhi of the Khecarīs.
Having attained the yoga of *cikura* and likewise the emission of semen (*śukrotsāraṇa*), [one attains success]. (39)
Having recited the mantra of Śrī Dakṣiṇāṅkālikā, a hundred descents of power (śaktipāta) shall occur;
likewise, by reciting it while touching a creeper, or while enjoying sexual union, or even while performing worship. || 40 ||
Beholding the supreme power residing in all directions, especially after having praised the venerable Dakṣiṇākālī, one should place the Yoni-mudrā in one's own hand. 41.
Whoever recites the Thousand Names shall become superior even to Śiva;
having praised Kālī, one should chant it amidst the creepers, free from agitation. (42)
O Dear One, within just one month, the practitioner becomes possessed of tenfold concentration during the Kālarātri, the Mahārātri, or even the Vīrarātri.

On the fourteenth or eighth day of the dark fortnight, during the transit of the sun, on the new moon, the full moon, or on Fridays and Tuesdays at the beginning of the night— on these occasions, [one should perform the rite].
On the ninth day, on an auspicious day, as well as on a favorable lunar date (tithi),
one should diligently recite the Thousand Names at a sacred site of the lineage (kulakṣetra).
One shall quickly become possessed of the *saudarśana* [discus] and attain the siddhi of the *kinnarī*. There is an ancient linga facing west, devoid of a bull. (46)
O Śivā, staying there, one should recite the hymn for the attainment of all desires on a Tuesday,
at midnight, or on an auspicious new moon day.
An offering of black-gram porridge, a goat, kṛsarā-rice,
milk-rice, burnt fish, blood, curds, milk, and jaggery mixed with arka-flowers.
Having offered the oblation there, one should recite [the mantra] one thousand and eight times,
[visualizing] the beautiful goddess who is served by hosts of gods, gandharvas, and siddhas.
O Goddess of the Gods, within a month he shall attain the consolidation of his seat;
his height shall be three cubits—of this there is no need for doubt.
O Goddess, that man who praises Kālī with ease, playfulness, and devotion can,
in an instant, paralyze Brahmā and the other gods and delude Māheśī.
One may attract the great vidyās within three watches [of the night];
one should perform the slaying of those created by Viṣṇu, such as Yamādi and others.
A man shall certainly and surely uproot even the very novelty of creation itself by means of [the flesh of] sheep, buffalo, cat, donkey, goat, human, and so forth. (53)
With the flesh of rhinoceroses, boars, pigeons, lapwings, and hares; with blood, bones, and meat; and with kāraṇḍa fish, milk, and milk-rice (pāyasa). (54)
With Kādambarī, Sindhu-madya, Surā, Ariṣṭa, and Āsava liquors;
with water for washing the womb, and also with the nectars of the womb and the phallus. || 55 ||
Having worshipped her with flowers native to her own species, one should satisfy Śivā at the end of the recitation;
then, having praised and bowed according to one's ability with the hymn named "The Universal Sovereignty," [one should proceed].
One who, assuming the form of Kālī, recites the hymn with devotion for three days, Dakṣiṇākālikā dwells in his house; it is not otherwise.
Having gone to the house of the prostitute-latā and being intent on kissing her, one should place one's mouth upon her vulva and recite the mantra while licking that essence. 58.
At the conclusion of that, one devoted to devotion should recite the Thousand Names;
for him, the vision of Kālikā shall surely occur within three nights.
Having gone to the dancing hall, accompanied by the five "ma" syllables,
he should place [the deity] upon a bed of flowers, being fully intent on the ritual deposition of the Śaktis (śaktinyāsa).
Having performed the consecration of the vessels, one should proceed with the rite ending with the garments of the directions;
having honored the cakra at its base, one should recite the mantra there along with its enclosures.

O Maheśvarī, [offer] a hundred [prostrations] upon the forehead, a hundred upon the hair, a hundred upon the circle of vermilion, three hundred upon the pair of breasts, and a hundred upon the navel. 62.
O Great Goddess, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred times during the conjunction with Śayyā, and three hundred times during the conjunction with Śayyā;
O Great Goddess, at the conclusion of that, one should recite the hymn of praise.
Within just one month, O Śivā, the practitioner becomes capable of a hundredfold concentration,
having summoned either Mātaṅginī or Kāpālinī.

A garland of teeth should be used for recitation, and one made from human skulls should be worn around the neck; the *yonicakra* or *śakticakra* should be placed upon the lotus of the eyes and in one's own mouth.
Having performed [this], O Maheśānī, one should recite the mantra and worship the Muṇḍa-yatra;
the hero, seated upon the Muṇḍa-throne, is endowed with the five *makāras*.
Embracing one woman, he should mutter the mantra; kissing another, he should indeed recite it;
he should worship one there, while pressing against another, he should perform the japa.
Having performed the *śivanda* in another womb, one should perform it again as before;
even through thousands of attentions and hundreds of lunar falls.
O Queen of the Gods, by means of this practice for five months, one becomes a king; having brought a Yavana woman who is devoted to the power of song, [one attains this]. (69)
One should cause her vulva to open according to the family tradition;
having placed the tongue there, one should recite the Thousand Names. (70)
Having carefully lit a lamp there in a human skull, one should indeed perform the recitation;
one shall become a supreme great poet—of this there is no doubt to be made. (71)
O Supreme Goddess, having brought one afflicted by desire who possesses power, and having drawn the root-cakra upon the vulva, O Śivā, one should write the mantra there.
The Goddess, who knows the true essence of the meaning of all scriptures, should mutter the *tallīha* mantra;
she will certainly cause one to study even those scriptures not yet heard, beginning with the Vedas.
O beloved, without ritual deposits (nyāsa), without recitations (pāṭha), and without meditations and the like,
one becomes the master of the four Vedas and a knower of the three times within three years.
And the fourfold scholarship comes into his hand instantly;
the offering to Śiva (śivābali) should always be presented in the empty maṇḍala.
Meditation on Kālī, contemplation of the mantra, the very practice of the Nīla-sādhana, the recitation of the Thousand Names, and the proclamation of Kālī’s names. (76)
For a devotee, this much is the duty; others know it as the means for prosperity:
the rite of heroic practice (vīrasādhana), the worship of Śiva, and likewise the offering of oblations (bali). || 77 ||

O Goddess, there was the constant application of vermilion tilaka, incessant conversation with courtesans, frequenting the houses of courtesans, and likewise wandering about at night during the hours of darkness. (78)
A man who performs the worship of Śakti, views [the world] as the Yoni, holds a sword in his hand, is naked, has disheveled hair, wears the garb of a hero, and bears the form of the Kula. || 79 ||
O Goddess, one who is a devotee of Kālī shall not otherwise experience agitation;
he tastes the milk, licks the vulva, and is reeling with the bliss of all the servants.
Through union with the creeper of a courtesan, one becomes oneself a wish-fulfilling vine (kalpalatā) within a month;
through union with the circle of courtesans, one becomes oneself equal to the circle of Kālī.
Through union with the body of a courtesan, he himself becomes identical to the body of Kālī;
when shall I behold a practitioner who has entered into the midst of courtesans? 82.
Thus spoke Kālī; therefore, the prostitute is considered the best.
Likewise, the prostitute’s daughter [is so] by virtue of the lineage and family succession of the Pīṭha-born caste. (83)
Having understood the maiden according to the division of the Akula lineage,
one should worship the maiden with devotion at the end of the recitation in the temple, O Dear One.
He who recites the Thousand Names shall become a partaker of the vision of Kālī,
having worshipped with devotion a young maiden born of the family of a prostitute.
O Śivā, having gratified [the deity] with garments, gold, and other offerings, one should recite the hymn with effort;
thus one shall become a conqueror of the three worlds and shine like the moon by day.
Whatever is given to a maiden shall yield infinite fruit;
I am unable to describe the fruit of worshipping a maiden. (87)
Whatever has been said out of fickleness, may this salutation with joined palms be forgiven;
for if one young girl is honored, it is as if a second were also honored.

The maidens, the powers (śaktis), and indeed all this world of moving and unmoving things—he should bring the Possessor of Power (Śaktimān) near and perform the entire network of ritual placements (nyāsa) upon his body. 89.
And having established [the image] on the left side, one should recite the Thousand Names;
one shall become a master of all supernatural powers—of this there is no doubt to be made.
Established in the cremation ground, remaining composed, with matted hair flowing loose, he should wander naked and gather a thousand sun-flowers.
Having endowed [the mantra] with one's own vigor, one should offer oblations while reciting it for each [deity] individually;
having worshipped and meditated with great devotion, the man who is a protector of men (the king) should recite it. 92.
Having first recited the root mantra, with disheveled hair and wearing the quarters as his garment, he should [discard] whatever nails, hair, and his own semen have fallen onto the broom. 93.
Whoever performs a fire sacrifice at midnight in a cremation ground on a Saturday and recites the Thousand Names, there shall be the attraction of the lords of the earth.
O Goddess, when the vulva is joined with flowers, he who is intent on the bliss of union, having again reached the hair [of the vulva], should mutter the root mantra, O Śivā. (95)
Having carefully cast the seed-essence into the fire of the funeral pyre at midnight,
one should worship Kālikā there and recite the Thousand Names.
One should effect the attraction of the lords of the earth; there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
Having reached a grove of plantain trees, a person should perform one hundred thousand recitations.
Attended by the goddess Madhumatī herself, he was like the god of love;
having spoken thus to the illustrious Madhumatī, as well as to all things mobile and immobile, [he departed].
Having recited "Ākarṣiṇīm," one should then recite "Ṭhaṃ Ṭhaṃ Svāhā.
This vidyā, the Attractor of the Three Worlds, shall always remain in his hand. (99)
It draws toward itself from the ends of the quarters rivers and cities, jewels, gold, women, mountains, and trees, as well as the ocean and Mount Sumeru. 100.
And objects that are unattainable even from afar or from the surface of the earth, as well as the secrets of the abodes of the gods—even those known only to the wise—he perceives. (101)
She tells the kings: "One should command the truth with haste;
by reciting it for a second year, Padmāvatī shall become auspicious. (102)
Oṃ hrīṃ padmāvati, followed by the name of the person in the three worlds, and then "report the news" (vārttāñca kathaya dvandva); this mantra is said to end with svāhā. || 103 ||
Whatever may be the state of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others within the three worlds, the auspicious poet, the lord of gods, knows the three times and speaks of it all. (104)
O Goddess, one who recites this for three years shall obtain a share of Bhogavatī,
even if bitten by Mahākāla or situated in the midst of a funeral pyre.
By the mere sight of her, a man shall become long-lived;
having said "Mṛtasañjīvinī" (the reviver of the dead), raise up two who are dead. 106.
This mantra, ending with *svāhā*, is declared to be the essence of the "Reviver of the Dead.
Whoever recites it for four years shall thereafter attain perfection in dreams.
Oṃ hrīṃ svapnavārāhi, one should recite "tell [the dream] regarding Kali"; "grant such-and-such to so-and-so, krīṃ svāhā"—this is considered the mantra. 108.
The Svapnasiddhā [Vidyā] always resides in his dreams from the age of four;
by reciting it for four years, one becomes the master of the four Vedas. (109)
Through contact with the water from his hand, even a fool composes poetry;
by acquaintance with his speech, even an inanimate form attains the state of being poetry.
Placing his hand upon the head while saying, "Speak,
O Vāṇī," the practitioner may fulfill whatever he desires, and that shall indeed come to pass.
O Goddess, whatever Siddhis exist anywhere upon the surface of the earth within this cosmic egg, they all become as clear as a myrobalan fruit held in the palm of one's hand.
By the mere recollection of the practitioner, whatever siddhis exist come before him of their own accord; what need is there to mention the practice of japa and other rites? 113.
Residing abroad, they behave like servants;
there is the sight of the moon on the new-moon day, as well as a lunar eclipse. (114)
On the eighth day, the Great Goddess indeed makes the moon full and likewise creates eight moons and eight suns in the eight directions.

The power of atomization (aṇimā), the state of moving through the sky (khecara), the ability to travel to the cities of both mobile and immobile beings, as well as the magical sandals, the sword, the vetāla, the yakṣiṇī, the guhyaka, and so forth. || 116 ||
The *tilaka*, invisibility, the narrative of the moving and the unmoving, the accomplishment of the *mṛtasañjīvinī* [the life-restoring spell], the magic pill, and the elixir. || 117 ||
O Goddess of gods, the power of flight and the mastery of the sixty siddhis shall reside in his hand, O Goddess; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (118)
O Goddess, [the image] should be depicted and worshipped with diligence on a ketu, a drum, a cloth, a canopy, a covering, a house, a wall, or a wooden plank. (119)
In the center, one should write the ten-syllable mantra as prescribed, and the name [of the person] all around it;
by wearing this, O Maheśānī, one shall become a conqueror of the three worlds.
O Pārvatī, having alone conquered a hundred thousand [enemies] on the field of battle, he returns again happily to his own home.
For one who, having diligently established himself in well-being, recites the Thousand Names, certainly becomes a beholder of hundreds of worlds. (122)

O Maheśānī, the consecration (seka) should be performed for the warding off of all calamities, [including those caused] by bhūtas, pretas, grahas, and the like, as well as by rākṣasas and brahmarākṣasas. 123.
It destroys Vetālas, Bhairavas, Skanda, Vaināyaka, and the rest in a mere moment; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. 124.
Having consecrated the ashes with mantras, one should smear them upon one seized by a planetary spirit;
by the mere application of the ashes, there is the destruction of all planetary spirits.
O Maheśvarī, having consecrated fresh butter with mantras, one should give it to women;
O Goddess, it bestows sons even upon the barren, there is no need for hesitation in this matter. (126)
By wearing [this] on the neck, the left arm, or the womb, O Śivā, a woman certainly becomes fortunate and possessed of many sons. (127)
A man should wear it on his right limb for the sake of all success;
he becomes powerful, famous, blessed, righteous, a successful practitioner, and accomplished. || 128 ||
O wise one, lord of many sons, master of chariots and elephants, intent on attracting women—O you who possess a throbbing right side! 129.
O Goddess, the reciter of the name should mutter the mantra "krīṃ svāhā" ten thousand times;
he shall effect the summoning of those who move in water, through the air, or on the earth.
One who desires subjugation should recite "hūṃ hūṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ" on the right; then, while muttering the previous seed-syllables as before, one should recite "O Kālikā! (kālike). || 131 ||
One may even bring Urvaśī under one's control; there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
A person should mutter [the mantra] joined with "krīṃ dakṣiṇakālike svāhā. (132)
If one should recite the Thousand Names, one will certainly cause the destruction of the three worlds.
This [mantra], O auspicious Queen of Vidyās, should be bestowed upon a true devotee on an auspicious day. (133)
To him who was well-disciplined, peaceful, self-controlled, and possessed of supreme virtues;
to the devoted eldest son, who was entirely intent on devotion to his guru. || 134 ||
To one who is a Vaiṣṇava, who is pure, who is devoted to the garland of Śiva, who is engaged in the worship of courtesans, and who is a worshiper of virgins; || 135 ||
To the devotee of Durgā, to the fierce one, to the expounder of Mahākāla, to him endowed with the state of non-duality, and to the one devoted to Kālī. || 136 ||
O Pārvatī, a thousand names revealed by Svayaṃkālyā must be given to the Guru, the deity, the mantra, and even to Maheśa.
One should remember the mantra without distinction; he is Śiva, he is the Lord of Gaṇas.
The practitioner who meditates upon the mantra is Śiva himself—of this there is no doubt. (138)
He is indeed a Śākta, a Vaiṣṇava, and a Saura; he alone is fully initiated.
This [knowledge] must not be given to an unworthy person, for it would result in the obstruction of spiritual attainment. || 139 ||

Furthermore, for one who reviles prostitutes and women, or who reviles those who consume liquor, by recollecting the mantra of Surāmukhī, he shall become a practitioner of the wine-rite (surācāra). 140.
For these [mantras], one should utter "Hūṃ" for Ghora and Paraghora;
and for Ghorarūpā, Mahāghorā, Mukhī, and Bhīmapadā, one should likewise utter them. || 141 ||
The word *bhīṣaṇyaṃ* ending in the sixth case (*bhīṣaṇyāya*) is the cause in the auspicious pair of arms;
the weapon-mantra for the pair of Śiva’s fires is *hūṃ hūṃ kavacaṃ*. || 142 ||
Merely by the remembrance of this, the Goddess, the destroyer of the prosperity of the wicked, descends into the mouths of the evil. 143.
To one who is wicked, dependent on others, intent on reviling others, fallen, of evil nature, and devoted to the speech of others; (144)

O Goddess, one should not reveal this hymn to a wicked person who is not a devotee of Śiva and is intent upon the wives of others; [to do so] would result in the sin of killing a female buffalo (śivā). 145.
He whose heart is filled with the bliss of Kālī, whose mind is devoted to Kālī—he indeed becomes a devotee of Kālī; he alone is truly blessed.
In the Kali age, Kālī; in the Kali age, Kālī; in the Kali age, Kālī, the bestower of boons;
in the Kali age, Kālī; in the Kali age, Kālī; in the Kali age, Kālī alone indeed.
One should indeed worship with thousands of bilva leaves and likewise with karavīra flowers, each according to its name; by that means, Kālī becomes the bestower of boons.
O Goddess of the gods, having worshipped the wheel, one should offer a thousand lotuses according to their respective names; thus one shall obtain the boon of Kālī. 149.
O Goddess, one who is afflicted by disturbances should not [use] water contained in a jar;
rather, one should sprinkle [the person] with their name, which brings about the destruction of all disturbances. 150.
Likewise, O Madanakandā, the observer of the vow should perform the recitation of the Thousand Names;
by worshipping with the Thousand Names, he shall obtain the boon of Kālī. 151.
Having drawn the wheel, one whose body is the form of Kālikā should wear it;
O Śivā, whatever has been offered to Kālī, one should consume that as her portion.
Having assumed a divine body, one should become firmly established within the body of Kālī. Upon seeing wicked people who revile the food offering (naivedya), the Bhairavas dance. (153)
And the great heroines, O beloved, intent on drinking blood, are engaged with flesh, bones, and skin; they devour them, there is no doubt. (154)
Therefore, O Goddess, one should not revile [it] in thought, deed, or speech;
for he who acts otherwise shall meet with destruction. 155.
Success comes only for those who possess the sequential initiation (kramadīkṣā), and not otherwise;
otherwise, there will surely be a disturbance of the mantra or a shortening of one's lifespan.

One who possesses the Krama-initiation, O Goddess, will certainly become a stealer of sons, a stealer of women, and a stealer of kingdoms; yet, through the Krama, he shall gradually attain sovereignty.
O Goddess, one who recites it once destroys all sins;
and he who recites it twice constantly obtains his desires. (158)
Whoever recites it three times shall attain equality with the Lord of Speech; O Goddess, whoever recites it four times shall become a sovereign over the four castes. 159.
O Goddess, by reciting it five times, one becomes the lord of the five senses;
O Goddess, by reciting it six times, one becomes the lord of the six sovereign powers. || 160 ||
If one recites it seven times, one shall obtain the seven desired objects that have been thought of; O Goddess, if one recites it on a Thursday, one will certainly become a lord of the quarters.
O Goddess, by reciting it nine times one becomes equal to the Nine Lords;
he who recites it ten times becomes a Daśārha, a lord of the sky-farers.
He who recites it twenty times shall become possessed of all sovereign powers;
by twenty-five recitations, he becomes the destroyer of all anxieties.
By repeating it fifty times, one becomes the lord of the five elements;
he who recites it a hundred times possesses an intellect equal to that of Śatānana.
By reciting it five hundred times, one becomes a sovereign lord of kings;
by reciting it a thousand times, O Goddess, Lakṣmī herself chooses him as her own.
By reciting it three thousand times, one becomes like the Three-eyed One;
by reciting it five thousand times, one deludes ten million goddesses of desire.
By ten thousand recitations, one becomes the Lord of Ten Faces;
by twenty-five thousand, one holds the twenty-four siddhis.
By merely reciting it one hundred thousand times, one will become equal to the Lord of Lakṣmī;
by reciting it three hundred thousand times, O Mahādeva, one shall be victorious.
By reciting five hundred thousand times, one is endowed with the five arts;
however, by reciting ten million times, the supreme attainment of the ten Vidyās is achieved.
By twenty-five hundred thousand [recitations], one becomes a Lord of the Ten Vidyās;
by completing fifty hundred thousand, one becomes equal to Mahākāla. (170)
He who should revolve the mantra ten million times beholds Kālī with his own eyes,
her hands raised ready to grant boons, accompanied by Mahākāla.
One who perceives Śivā directly will certainly attain a divine body;
he shall become a conqueror of Śrīvidyā, Kālikā, Tārā, and Triśakti. (172)
Having wiped away the script of fate and cast off the state of servitude, one attains great sovereignty; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. || 173 ||
O Goddess, the Krama initiation is proclaimed for one whose sphere is the three powers;
O Goddess, one who possesses the Krama initiation certainly becomes a king. (174)
The fruit for one devoid of the Krama initiation has been stated previously here.
O Goddess, one who is endowed with the Krama initiation is Śiva himself and nothing else.
One who is endowed with the Krama initiation shall attain the perfections spoken of by Kālī;
for one devoid of the Krama initiation, there is a loss of perfection at every step.
Oh, among those who possess birth, he who follows the sequence [of this practice] in the Kali age is blessed;
even there, O Goddess of Gods, the reciter of the Thousand Names is most blessed. (177)
O Goddess, one should always recite this hymn during the ritual of Daśakālī;
O Mistress of the Gods, one attains success—there is no need for deliberation on this matter. (178)
Kālī, Kālī is the Great Vidyā; in the Kali age, Kālī grants success. In the Kali age, Kālī is perfected; in the Kali age, Kālī bestows boons. (179)
In the Kali age, Kālī is prepared to grant the grace of the practitioner;
in the Kali age, Kālī alone prevails—no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (180)
In the Kali age, there can be no other knowledge, no other knowledge, no other knowledge; for whoever in the Kali age desires to attain perfection while abandoning Kālī, [he shall fail]. 181.

O Goddess, he who desires the enjoyment of pleasure without Śakti, or O Goddess, whoever desires spiritual accomplishment (siddhi) without Kālī in the Kali age—[such a person is like one who desires fruit without a tree]. 182.
Having abandoned the ultimate means of Nīla, he wanders everywhere;
for in the Kali age, whoever seeks liberation must first abandon Kālī.
If a practitioner desires success while abandoning meditation on the Guru, or if anyone in the Kali age desires sovereignty while forsaking Kālī, [he will fail]. 184.
Having renounced food, he desires the way of life of a mendicant;
he is blessed, he is wise, and he alone is honored by the gods. (185)
He is consecrated, happy, virtuous, truthful, and one who has conquered his senses;
he is an expounder of the Vedas and devoted to sacred study—of this there is no doubt to be made. 186.
Having meditated upon the Guru as the form of Śiva, one should remember the Guru as the form of Śiva;
he himself becomes Sadāśiva—there is no need for deliberation on this point. (187)
Having conceived of Kālī within oneself, one should worship the Mother of the Universe;
one shall become a conqueror of the three worlds—of this there is no doubt. 188.
It must be concealed with great effort—concealed, concealed, and concealed;
it is a secret, a supreme secret, and a most supreme secret. (189)
O Goddess, he who recites even half a verse, or a single quarter-verse, or half a quarter-verse, or even half a name, shall not let any day pass in vain. 190.
One should worship the book with devotion for the swift attainment of results;
there shall be no fear of pestilence there, nor fire arising from wind. 191.
Therein, no fear of spirits or other such things exists; everywhere, happiness increases, as if by the application of saffron, lac, gorocana, and agallochum. (192)
One should write the manuscript on birch bark for the sake of accomplishing all desires and purposes.
If one recites with devotion this entire description of the form and color of Kālikā as it has been told,
one shall become a lord of all supernatural powers (siddhis).
One who desires ever-new bliss becomes delighted by all sciences, possessing all accomplishments and the prosperity of all heroes. || 194 ||
Thus has it been briefly told; what else do you wish to hear? || 195 ||
Thus ends the hymn of a thousand names of Kālī.
Thus ends the Kālītantra within the Śrīśāktapramoda.
Compiled and composed by His Majesty King Śrī Rājādeva Nandana Siṃha Bahādura, the sovereign lord of the capital of Śrī Śivahara.
The second Tārā-tantra within the Śāktapramoda.
This has been edited by the learned Paṇḍita Śrī Raghurāja Dubejī, a descendant of the aforementioned royal preceptor.
Printed and published by Śrī Kṛṣṇadāsātmaja Khemarāja at his own Śrī Veṅkaṭeśvara Press.
*Bombay*, p. 119): *Obeisance to Śrī Gaṇeśa*.
Now begins the *Śāktapramoda*.
Now, the Tārā Tantra:
the meditation on Tārā—
she who stands in the pratyālīḍha posture with her foot placed upon the heart of a corpse, and who is intent on a terrible, loud laugh.
Holding a sword, a blue lotus, a flaying knife, and a skull-cup in her arms, born from the seed-syllable *Huṃ*, short-statured,

with a vast mass of matted hair that is dark blue and tawny, adorned with a single serpent— having cast away dullness, the fierce Tārā herself destroys the worlds with her skull-cup and flaying knife.
(p. 120) Now, as for the construction of the yantra: one should draw an eight-petalled lotus together with its birth-place (yoni) using sandalwood paste.
Having taken a soft seat, one should draw Māyā on the eastern petal.
The seed-syllable is the second; PHAṬ is in the south, while ṬHAM is in the north and the west.
One should write the seed-syllable in the center and then perform the purification of the elements (ātmabhūtaśuddhi).
Now, for the extraction of the mantra:
having first uttered the seed-syllable of Speech (Vāgbīja), one should then recite the syllable Oṃ.
Then one should recite the seed-syllable of Lajjā, followed by the seed-syllable of Tārā, "hūṃ phaṭ."
Now the mantra: Aiṃ Oṃ Hrīṃ Krīṃ Hūṃ Phaṭ.
Then, following the path of the Tārā-pūjā, with kusha grass in hand and observing silence, having sipped water (ācamana) with the root mantra,
and having taken up water with the mantra "Oṃ vajrodake hūṃ phaṭ," [he should recite] "Oṃ hrīṃ svāhā."
Having washed one's feet with this [mantra], and having sipped water (ācamana) with "Oṃ hrīṃ, pacify all sins of my own purified dharma;
remove all conceptual constructions, svāhā," [one should proceed] with "Oṃ..."

Having performed the binding of the topknot with "Maṇidhari vajriṇi śikhariṇi sarvavaśaṅkari hūḥ phaṭ," and having purified the ground with "Oṃ rakṣa rakṣa hūḥ phaṭ svāhā," [one should recite] "Oṃ pavitravajraṃ me hūḥ svāhā."
Having consecrated the ground with the mantra "Oṃ āsureśvari vajrarekhe hūṃ svāhā" while touching the earth,
and having worshipped it with "Namaḥ to the lotus-seat of the foundational power (ādhāraśakti)," one should then [prepare] the seat.
Having touched [the earth], one should recite the mantra beginning with "pṛthvi."
p. 121) Then, having dispelled all obstacles, [he recites]:
"Oṃ, may those beings depart who dwell upon the earth."
With the words, "May those beings who create obstacles perish by the command of Śiva," one should dispel all obstacles by scattering unhusked rice grains (*akṣata*).
Having rubbed one's hands with perfume and flowers, one should cast those flowers toward the northeast using the nārāca-mudrā. The mantra for this is:
"Oṃ! May all those who harm me and all harmful beings go to their destruction!"
May death, disease, fear, and anger fall upon the head of the enemy! HŪM PHAṬ!
Next is the procedure for placing the general *arghya* vessel:
there, having consecrated the *ādhāraśakti* with "Oṃ, obeisance to the *ādhāraśakti*," and having drawn a square upon it, [one places] "Oṃ hraḥ" on top of that.

Having performed the placement of the general *arghya* with the mantra "Sāmānyārghyaṃ sthāpayāmi namaḥ," and having placed water therein with the *praṇava* (Om), [he recites]: "O Gaṅgā and Yamunā, O Godāvarī and Sarasvatī..."

Having invoked the sacred waters there from the solar orb with the *aṅkuśa-mudrā*, saying: "O Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī, be present in these waters," one should then offer flowers and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) while reciting: "Salutation to all the sacred waters, beginning with the Gaṅgā."

Having worshipped with "Oṃ namaḥ to the deities of the six limbs beginning with the heart," and having worshipped with "Oṃ āṃ, obeisance to the solar disc consisting of twelve kalās," and "Oṃ, obeisance to the fire-disc consisting of ten kalās," and "Oṃ..."

Having worshipped the solar, fiery, and lunar mandalas with the mantra: "Obeisance to the one whose self consists of the sixteen digits of the lunar orb," having rendered [the offering] nectarine by means of the *dhenu-mudrā* with the syllable *vaṃ*, and having veiled it with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*) by means of the syllable *hūṃ*.
Having protected [the site] with the weapon-mantra "phaṭ," one should recite the Praṇava ten times there. Thus ends the procedure for the general preparation of the arghya water.

Having sprinkled oneself and the ritual implements with the water contained in the general *arghya* vessel, then follows the procedure for establishing the special *arghya* vessel. As follows: having drawn a mandala with the mantra "Oṃ āsurekhe vajrarekhe hūṃ svāhā," then—
Having swept the ground nine times, one should fashion there a mandala consisting of a triangle, a circle, and an enclosure of earth (bhūgṛha). Having worshipped Ādhāraśakti and Kūrma-Śeṣa therein,
one should place the support (ādhāra) there with the mantra "Hrīṃ Phaṭ."
Having worshipped each respective mandala with the previously mentioned mantra of the fire-mandala (*vahnimaṇḍala*),
one should place a conch shell that has been washed with the mantra "hūṃ phaṭ" therein and worship the conch while reciting the fourfold mantra. It is as follows:
Hrā/hrī/hrū: Homage to Kālīkapāla. Strā/strī/strū: Homage to Tāriṇīkapāla. Hā/hī/hū: Homage to Nīlakapāla. (p. 122)

"Hrāḥ strī hūḥ! Salutation to the skull of heaven, the support of all, the source of all, consisting of all purity, red with the blood of all asuras, the bright vessel of wine, the skull of the Goddess"— this is the fourfold mantra.
Then, having worshipped that maṇḍala with the previously mentioned mantra of the solar orb (*arkamaṇḍala*),
and having placed water in the conch with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) while perceiving it as *svadhā*,
one should cast fragrant paste (*gandha*), flowers (*puṣpa*), and unbroken grains (*akṣata*) therein. Therein...
Having displayed the *trikhaṇḍā* mudrā and worshipped that maṇḍala there with the previously mentioned mantra of the moon-maṇḍala:
*aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hroṃ oṃ hrīṃ trīṃ hūḥ phaṭ hsauḥ hūḥ*.

Having consecrated the water eight times with this [mantra], and having displayed the conch mudrā, the cow mudrā, and the womb mudrā with the mantra *hrīṃ*, one should cover [the water] with the fish mudrā and recite the root mantra ten times. Therein:
Having meditated upon a circle with eight petals and six corners, having visualized the Goddess and worshipped her,
and having gratified her four times with the root mantra, one should gratify her with the mantra: "Aiṃ hrīṃ sauṃ namaḥ, I gratify Ānandabhairava."
With that arghya water, one should sprinkle the articles for the ritual worship.
Thus ends the procedure for placing the special *arghya*.
Having purified the flower with the mantra: *Oṃ yathāgatābhiṣekamamāgnimehū/phaṭ*, one should perform the purification of the mind (*citta-śodhana*) with: *Oṃ ā/hrīṃ svāhā*. Then...
The ritual placement of the sages and so forth (*ṛṣyādinyāsa*). It is as follows: on the head, *namas* to Vasiṣṭha, the sage (*ṛṣi*).
Salutation to the mouth with the Anuṣṭubh metre.
In the heart: salutation to the deity Tryambaka.
Then follows the placement of the heart-mantra and the others.
Hrāṃ, salutation to the heart.
Hrīṃ, svāhā to the head;
hrūṃ, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock;
hraiṃ, huṃ to the armor.
Hraum! To the three eyes, vauṣaṭ.
Hraḥ! To the weapon, phaṭ.
Then follows the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa), as follows:
Hrāṃ, salutation to the two thumbs; hrīṃ, svāhā to the two index fingers;
hrūṃ, vaṣaṭ to the two middle fingers.
Hraiṃ to the two ring fingers, hūṃ; hrauṃ to the two little fingers, vauṣaṭ;
hraḥ to the palms and backs of the hands, phaṭ.

Then, one should perform the threefold pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) with the root mantra. Then, one should perform three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) with either the root mantra or one's own seed-syllable (*bīja*). It is as follows:
inhalation (*pūraka*) by reciting [the mantra] four times, and retention (*kumbhaka*) by reciting it sixteen times.
Exhalation is performed by reciting [the mantra] eight times; the second [type of breath control] is the reverse of that.
The third [type] is the opposite of that. Then,

having drawn the yantra consisting of a hexagon, an eight-petaled lotus, and a protective perimeter (bhūpura), and having written the seed-syllable *hsauṃ* in the center and performed the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the yantra.
Therein, in the center,
Medhā, Prajñā, Vidyā, Dhī, Dhṛti, Smṛti, Buddhi, and Vidyaiśvaryā are to be worshipped. Then, having taken a flower, [one should offer it] with "Hsauṃ Sarasvatī-yogapīṭhāya."
Saying "Namas," one should cast a flower into the center of the yantra; then, one should meditate upon the Goddess.
For example:

"She who dwells upon a white lotus shimmering in the midst of water pervading the universe, holding a knife, a sword, a skull-cup, and a blue lotus in her hands, and possessing the luster of the moon."
Her body was adorned with excellent ornaments that had attained the state of girdles, earrings, necklaces, bracelets, armlets, and anklets; she possessed three eyes that were slightly reddened.

[She is] adorned with a single tawny, fierce matted lock; her face is terrifying with fangs that gleam with natural joy; she wears a tiger-skin and a deerskin, and possesses a white bone-garland. [She is] with Akṣobhya.
"One should meditate upon the Mother of the three worlds, whose head is resplendent, whose eyes are within her smiling lotus-face, who sits upon the heart of Śiva, and whose breasts are firm.
Having thus meditated and bound the *karaka* water-vessel, one should take flowers and unbroken rice (*akṣata*) therein.
Then, having raised Kuṇḍalinī from the Mūlādhāra and having brought forth the second form, one should place the lamp-flame of the "A-So-Ham" mantra— the form of the individual soul— into its mouth.
Having united it with Brahmā seated upon the thousand-petaled lotus,
having gratified him with the nectar situated in the lunar mandala, and having separated the life-form from Kuṇḍalinī,
one should visualize the flowers and unbroken rice grains emerging through the right nostril.

Having placed [the deity] within a yantra consisting of a hexagon, eight petals, and a square enclosure made of those flowers and unbroken rice grains (akṣata), one should invoke the Goddess there. It is as follows:
"O You who dwell within the great lotus forest, whose form is the bliss of the primal cause..."

Having recited, "O Mother, slayer of all beings, come, come, O Supreme Goddess! and while reciting the root mantra, [one says]: "O such-and-such Goddess, come here, stay here, accept my worship; be present here, be firmly established here."
Having displayed the respective mudrās with the words "Be present before me," and having recited the root mantra while saying "This handful of flowers—O Goddess [Name], accept this vajra-flower!
HŪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ. Homage to the Goddess [Name]! while reciting thus.
One should scatter five handfuls of flowers.
Having recited the root mantra, one should say, "This is the water for washing the feet; salutation to [Name] Devī.
Having recited the root mantra and uttered, "This is the water for sipping; salutation to [Name] Devī," one should offer it. This is the honey-mixture (madhuparka); having recited the root mantra...
Having recited "Obeisance to [Name] Devī" (p.
124), one should offer the *madhuparka*.
Having uttered the root mantra and saying "Obeisance to [Name] Devī," one should [offer] this bath-water to the Goddess.

One should bathe [the deity]. In the same way, one should offer garments and ornaments. Having recited the root mantra and uttered, "Vajrapuṣpaṃ pratīccha hūṃ phaṭ svāhā, vauṣaṭ to the goddess [Name]," one should offer the flowers. Then...

Regarding the worship of the deities of the enclosure (*āvaraṇapūjā*): one should first worship Gaṇeśa in the east. As follows—one should worship him with [the mantra] beginning, "O Gaṇeśa, come here, stay here," and so forth. There is a specific mantra for the offering of flowers: "Gaṃ Gaṇeśa..."
One should offer the flower with the mantra "vajrapuṣpaṃ pratīkṣya phaṭ svāhā.
In this manner, one should worship Baṭuka in the south; likewise, one should worship Kṣetrapāla in the west;
and one should worship the Yoginī in the north. Then, [one should worship] upon the head of the Goddess.

One should worship Akṣobhya. One should worship Akṣobhya with the mantra: "Akṣobhya vajrapuṣpaṃ pratīccha svāhā. Then, one should worship the six limbs in the six corners as follows: "Namaḥ ekajaṭāyai" for the heart.

One should worship with "Tāriṇyai namaḥ" on the head; with "Vajrodakāyai namaḥ" on the crest-lock (śikhā); with "Ugratārāyai namaḥ" on the armor (kavaca); with "Mahāpariśarāyai namaḥ" on the eyes; and with "Piṅgograikajaṭāyai namaḥ" in the cardinal directions. Then, [one should worship] in the petals of the directions.
The mantra for the offering of flowers is: "Vairocana, Amitābha, Padmanābha, Śaṅkhapāṇḍura, Vairocanavajrapuṣpa, pratīkṣya svāhā! and so forth.
[O you who are] named Kamma, Akampa, Pāṇḍura, and Antāraka, in the intermediate directions!

One should worship. The mantra for offering flowers is as before. Then, at the four gates of the subterranean chamber (bhūgṛha), starting from the east, one should worship Padmāntaka, Janmāntaka, Vighnāntaka, and Narakāntaka. The mantra for offering flowers is as before.

Then, as before, one should worship the guardians of the directions (dikpālas), beginning with Indra, outside of that. Outside of that, one should worship the [eight] emblems: the thunderbolt (vajra), spear (śakti), staff (daṇḍa), sword (khaḍga), noose (pāśa), goad (aṅkuśa), mace (gadā), trident (triśūla), and discus (cakra). Then, [one offers] incense to [the Goddess] together with her limbs (aṅgas), her weapons (āyudhas), and her retinue (parivāras).
"Salutation to the root deity [Name], together with the vehicle. In this manner, one should offer the lamp.

Then, one should offer the food offering (*naivedya*). For instance, having served the food offering in a vessel made of gold or other materials, one should recite the seed-syllable of Vāyu twelve times.
Having purified the food offering (*naivedya*) with the wind arising from that [mantra],

and having placed the left palm upon the surface of the right hand, one should burn away all defects of the food offering by reciting the fire-seed syllable (*agni-bīja*) twelve times while [visualizing] the fire arising from that [gesture].

Again, placing the right hand upon the back of the left hand and displaying that [mudrā], one should consecrate the food offering by sprinkling it with the stream of nectar arising from the seed-syllable *vaṃ*, while reciting it twelve times.
Having consecrated [the disciple] again with the root mantra and touched him, one should recite the root mantra eight times,
display the *dhenumudrā*, and worship him with perfumes and flowers. Then,
having touched the food-offering vessels with the thumb of the left hand—
Holding the *jāla* with the right hand while reciting the root mantra, one should offer the food offering (*naivedya*) by saying:

"Obeisance to [Name] Devī, together with her limbs (*sāṅgāyai*), her weapons (*sāyudhāyai*), her retinue (*saparivārāyai*), her vehicle (*savāhanāyai*), and her enclosures (*sāvaraṇāyai*). Having thus offered the *naivedya*, [one should proceed].

Having displayed the *naivedya-mudrā* with the thumb and ring finger, while drawing up [the offering] three times with both hands holding flowers, one should display the *grāsa-mudrā* with the left hand. Thereafter, one should display the *prāṇa*-mudrās and so forth. Oṃ.

Reciting "Prāṇāya svāhā," one should display the *prāṇa-mudrā* with the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb. Then, reciting "Oṃ apānāya svāhā," one should display the *apāna-mudrā* with the index finger, the middle finger, and the thumb.
Then, reciting "Oṃ udānāya svāhā," one should display the *udāna* mudrā with the ring finger, middle finger, and thumb.
Then, [reciting] "Oṃ vyānāya svāhā."
Reciting "Paṭha," one should display the Vyāna-mudrā with the index, ring, middle, and thumb fingers.
Then, reciting "Oṃ samānāya svāhā," one should display the Samāna-mudrā with all the fingers. Then [to] the Goddess...
Having visualized her as being satisfied, one should offer water, reciting the root mantra:
"This water is for such-and-such a goddess, *namaḥ*.
This water for sipping is for such-and-such a goddess, *namaḥ*. And this betel leaf."
This is the offering of a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*). Now, the procedure for recitation (*japa-vidhi*):

Having performed, as before, the ritual assignments (*nyāsa*) of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and so forth, the hand-assignments (*karanyāsa*), the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*), and the meditation (*dhyāna*), [one should recite]:
"Hrīṃ! O Garland, O Great Garland, you whose nature is all reality; the four aims [of life] reside in you."

Reciting, "Therefore, placed [upon me], be the giver of success," one should worship the rosary with the root mantra (mūlamantra) and perform the recitation (japa) according to one's capacity. At the conclusion of the recitation,
having again performed the breath-control (prāṇāyāma) and other rites, one should meditate upon the Goddess.
Reciting: "Oṃ! O you who guard that which is more secret than the secret, accept this recitation performed by us.
May success be mine, O Goddess, through your grace, O Great Sovereign," he should offer the recitation into the left hand of the Goddess while meditating on her as consisting of radiant light.

Having offered eight handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), one should recite the hymn of praise (*stotra*), the armor-verse (*kavaca*), and so forth. Then, having circumambulated [the deity] and prostrated like a staff (*daṇḍavatpraṇipatya*), [one should say]: "Oṃ, from this time forward, by virtue of my life-force, my body, and my authority over religious duties (*dharma*),"

Whatever has been remembered, whatever has been spoken, and whatever has been done by the mind, speech, the two hands, the two feet, the stomach, or the generative organ during the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep—all that [is offered]. (p. 126)
"May this be an offering to Brahman, svāhā! And may all that is mine be offered to you, O Goddess.
Then, taking a handful of flowers, [one should pray]:
"O Sovereign of the Gods, [whatever has been performed] deficient in mantra, deficient in ritual action, or deficient in procedure..."
O Goddess, may that which has been worshipped by me be fulfilled for me.
The invocation, the worship, its greatness, and likewise the recitation;
I do not know how to perform the dismissal; O Śrī Devī, may you forgive me.
Whatever has been done deficiently or in excess through ignorance, forgetfulness, or delusion—
"And forgive all of that which was contrary [to the ritual], O Supreme Goddess.

Having thus asked for forgiveness with the mantra "This handful of flowers is offered to [Name] Devī, obeisance," one then recites: "Oṃ, go, go to the supreme abode, your own station, O Supreme Goddess."

And at the time of worship and propitiation, for the sake of her returning again, [the practitioner], having taken a single flower with the *saṃhāramudrā*, should dismiss the Goddess and cast that flower into another vessel in the northeast. And in that vessel, [he should worship] Caṇḍeśvarī.
Having worshipped [her] with "Oṃ Caṇḍeśvari Mahādevi," [he offers] the remains of sandalwood paste and other substances,
as well as the remains of food to be licked, sucked, eaten, and drunk, along with garlands and ointments.

"I give you the offering of remains (nirmālya) by the command of Śrī Śiva. Reciting "This nirmālya, obeisance to Śrī Caṇḍeśvarī," one should cast the remains [into water]. Then, [one should offer] a small portion of the goddess's food offering (naivedya).
Reciting "ucchiṣṭacāṇḍālyai namaḥ," one should offer [the remains] to her. Then, one should eat the *naivedya* oneself.
Now, the hymn to Tārā:
O Mother Nīlasarasvatī, bestower of good fortune and prosperity upon those who bow before you,
you who stand in the pratyālīḍha posture upon the heart of a corpse, with a smiling lotus-face;
O you with eyes like full-blown blue lotuses, O three-eyed one, who holds a curved knife, a skull-cup, a blue lotus, and a sword—You alone are my refuge; I take shelter in You, the Sovereign Lady.
O Mistress of Speech, O wish-fulfilling creeper for Your devotees, O Sovereign of the accomplishment of all aims!
O you who bestow the attainment of all goals through the composition of prose, Prākṛt, and verse;
O you endowed with three eyes like blue lotuses; O ocean of the waters of compassion; through your grace, which increases the nectar of good fortune— (p. 127)
Sprinkle [favor] upon one such as I. || 2 ||

Upon the humpbacked one, whose body is filled with a multitude of prides, resplendent in attire such as that of a serpent, beautiful at the waist with a tiger-skin girdle and marked by swinging bells,
the hair from two freshly severed heads falls mingling with the dust.
O terrifying one, who is beautiful with a garland of human heads and a string of knots, destroy my fear! 3.
O Mother, whose form consists of the transformations of the limbs of Māyā, who are the Lalanā, the Bindu, the Half-moon, and Ambikā;

O you who consist of the syllables *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*, you alone, as the essence of mantra, are the refuge for one such as me. O Mother, your form is fashioned from the three abodes—the gross, the extremely subtle, and the supreme.
I take refuge in her who is praised by the wise as being in no way within the sphere of the Vedas. || 4 ||
By serving your lotus feet, the virtuous attain union with that Śrī Parameśvara, whose nature is equal to the three-eyed Lord and Brahmā;
[union] with the gods headed by Indra, whose bodies are incapable of enduring immersion in the ocean of saṃsāra.
O Mother, what person of dull intellect would serve those who are indeed averse to service at your feet? || 5 ||
O Mother, those gods whose crowns are marked by the seal of the pollen from Your two lotus feet have, in the battle for victory, fearlessly come into Your lap;
yet they are defeated by the pride that carries the thought, "I am a god in this world, and there is no one equal to me."
Those who are like them certainly go to destruction themselves, just as impure things do. || 6 ||
Upon remembering your name,
the hosts of bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, rākṣasas, and yakṣas, as well as the lords of the nāgas,
the foremost of the daityas and dānavas, the sky-dwellers, and creatures such as tigers, become intent on fleeing and are unable even to look at you.
O Mother, on this earth, even the ḍākinīs and the enraged Antaka cannot prevail over a human being for even a moment.

O beautiful woman, [this practice grants] prosperity, the host of supernatural powers (siddhis), the perfected ones beginning with the magical sandals (pāduka), the paralyzing of enemies, the immobilization of herds of elephants, and likewise enchantment (mohana).
Indeed, by serving at the feet of the Mother, those various virtues are accomplished for men;
even a lowly person becomes a Vācaspati (Lord of Speech) when exhausted by the beautiful God of Love. 8.
The man who, endowed with devotion, recites this meritorious *Tārāṣṭaka*, [attains...]
At dawn, at midday, and in the evening, being self-restrained and pure. || 9 ||
One obtains poetic skill and knowledge, becoming a knower of the meaning of all scriptures; having attained imperishable fortune and enjoyed pleasures as desired, [one attains liberation]. || 10 ||
Having attained fame, beauty, and freedom from disease, one shall attain liberation at the end.
Thus ends the hymn to Tārā in the Nīlatantra. (p. 128)
Then Īśvara spoke the Tārākavaca: "This knowledge, which liberates one from extreme fear, is indeed to be kept secret within the Koṭitantras."
Indeed, her armor is divine; listen to how it grants all desires. || 1 ||

For the Tārākavaca, Akṣobhya is the seer (ṛṣi), Triṣṭubh is the meter (chandas), the Blessed Lady Tārā is the deity (devatā), and the application (viniyoga) is for the sake of attaining success in all mantras.
Oṃ: May Praṇava protect my head, the Great Goddess in the form of Brahman;
Hrīṃkāra: may the Great Goddess in the form of the seed-syllable protect my forehead. (2)
May the syllable *strīṃ* protect the face, the Great Goddess in the form of modesty;
may the syllable *hūṃ* protect the heart, assuming the form of the power (*śakti*) of Bhavānī. (3)

May the syllable *phaṭ*, the bestower of the fruit of all accomplishments, protect my entire body. May the Goddess Kharvā, the sovereign of gods who grants all accomplishments, protect me between the eyebrows. (4)
May the blue Goddess of the gods, the dispeller of fear, protect my two cheeks;
may Lambodarī, the dispeller of fear, always protect my two ears.
May the Goddess, beloved of Śiva, whose waist is draped in a tiger skin, protect [me];
may Maheśvarī, with full and elevated breasts, protect me on both sides. (6)
May she with blood-red, round eyes always protect the region of the waist;
may Māmbhuvaneśvarī, with her tongue lolling out, always protect the navel.
May Karālāsyā, the goddess beloved of Hara, always protect [me] at the *liṅga*;
may Piṅgograikajaṭā, the destroyer of obstacles, protect my shanks.
The Great Goddess Maheśvarī, blue in color and holding a sword in her hand, always protects my knees at all times. May she protect them forever. (9)
May she who wears serpent-earrings protect the pair of feet;
may the Goddess who wears a serpent-necklace protect every limb at all times. 10.
May the goddess Gāṅgadharā protect from the land of Pāṇḍava;
may she, the four-armed destroyer of enemies, always protect me while traveling. 11.
May the Great Goddess, sword in hand and bestower of victory, protect me! May the Goddess, clad in blue garments and destroyer of obstacles, protect me! 12.
May she who holds a sword in her hand always protect the performer from enemies in debate;
may the Goddess, assuming the form of Brahmā, always protect him in battle. 13.
May she who wears the serpent-bracelet protect me always during meals;
may the Great Goddess Śavakarṇā protect me always during sleep. 14.
May the Goddess, who maintains the heroic posture (vīrāsana), protect me always during sleep. || 15 ||
May the Goddess, bearing bow and arrow, protect me amidst the multitude of obstacles.
May the Goddess, whose hips are curved like a serpent, protect me in all undertakings. 16.
May the Goddess, bearing severed heads, protect me always in the forest;
may the Goddess, stationed in the midst of the funeral pyre, protect me always during the act of slaying. || 17 ||
May the Goddess, who wears a leopard skin, who bestows sons, wives, wealth, and other blessings, and who is adorned with ornaments—the beloved of Hara—protect me. 18.
Protect, protect! O Great Goddess, whose form is that of the seed-syllable, accompanied by *hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ* in the river-thicket; may you always protect [me] on the mountain. (19)
O Goddess who wears jewels, wielder of the thunderbolt, likewise Mahāpratisarā;
protect, protect me always, hūṃ hūṃ! Oṃ hrīṃ svāhā, O Maheśvarī! 20.
May Puṣpaketu protect the Arhat in the forest at all times;
Oṃ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ phaṭ, may he also protect Pāṇḍava at all times. || 21 ||
In *puṣpe*, *puṣpe*, and *mahāpuṣpe*, may Maheśvarī protect my sons;
joined with *oṃ svāhā* and *śakti*, may she always protect my wife. || 22 ||
Oṃ, O pure vajra-ground, hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!
May the goddess Pūrikā, the destroyer of all obstacles, protect me. 23.
O Goddess drawn from the mind, consisting of the *nāginīs*, accompanied by *āsurekhe*, *vajrarekhe*, *hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*, may you protect me in the netherworld (*pātāla*). 24.
May the Great Goddess Maheśvarī, in the form of Śakti, protect me in the east as Hrīṃkārī;
may the Supreme Goddess, in the form of Strī, protect me in the south as Strīṃkārī.
May Mahāmāyā, whose nature is *hūṃ* and who possesses a wrathful form, protect me;
may Mahāmāyā, whose nature is *ka*, always protect me in the west. (26)

May the Goddess in the form of the syllable *ḍha*, beloved of Hara, protect me in the north; may the Queen of the Gods, the daughter of the Mountain, in the form of the syllable *hūṃ*, protect me in the center. (27)
May she who is blue in color always protect everywhere; may Vāgbhavī, the bestower of all sovereignty, always protect me in my home. || 28 ||
May the Goddess Sarasvatī, who delights in the gift of knowledge, protect my mouth;
[protect me] in the study of scriptures, in debate, in battle, in water, and on treacherous mountains. (29)
May she of terrifying form, who destroys fear in the cremation ground, always protect me; may she protect me in the terrible, inaccessible fortress that is the abode of spirits and ghosts.
May the Great Goddess, the messenger of Śiva, protect [me] eternally everywhere.
No one can describe the majesty of this armor even in hundreds of years.
O Goddess, I am able to tell you what the fruit of that [act] may be for one's sons, wife, kinsmen, and throughout all lands at all times. (32)
No fear exists for him; he shall be honored by kings.
Whether pure or impure, this armor grants all desires. (33)
O Maheśānī, by reciting or remembering this, a mortal becomes free from suffering and grief, and certainly becomes a supreme poet in all scriptures. (34)
Such a mortal becomes a master of all speech, a lord over the world, and a master of wealth;
his victory shall be certain in battle, at dice, and in debate. (35)
Endowed with sons and grandsons, that mortal man becomes an enjoyer of all women;
his enemies fall into servitude, and he is always beloved by everyone.
The proud indeed becomes humble, and the disputant flares up at the mere sight [of her].
Death comes under her control, and even a lord of the earth becomes her servant. (37)
All this has been told as an incidental discourse; it is the armor that grants all desires.
By reciting or remembering it, a mortal becomes capable of both inflicting curses and bestowing favors.
He shall become a sovereign lord of oceans of blissful multitudes, a preeminent poet, a master of all yogis, a mortal friend to the world, and forever happy. (39)
Having obtained the grace of the Guru and acquired the well-guarded lore, even therein, O Goddess, the armor-mantra (kavaca) is difficult to attain within the three worlds. (40)
The Guru is God Hara himself, and his wife is the beloved of Hara;
for him who conquers through non-duality, perfection is not far off.
O Maheśānī, O beloved, the practices of mantra have been described previously;
one should likewise contemplate the light at the navel, the mouth, and the heart. (42)
O Goddess, upon seeing that practitioner, those who bestow sovereignty, poetic skill, and Rudra himself as the granters of success become filled with shame. (43)
In heaven, on earth, and in the netherworld, all those gods who are the best among the asuras always praise that supreme practitioner upon seeing him.
And all those gods who are the lords of obstacles, whether in heaven, on earth, or in the netherworld, always praise that most excellent practitioner upon seeing him. (45)
Thus, O Goddess, I have fully proclaimed to you this which directly bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, being of the very nature of the wish-fulfilling tree.
Having approached and propitiated the Guru today,
who would not be deluded— whether by delusion, pride, or even dullness— with respect to this support of the wish-fulfilling tree?
He who has mastered this reaches the further shore of all sufferings and calamities on earth at the time of death;
O Goddess, the king becomes his friend, and his misfortunes quickly perish.
Upon reaching his body, weapons such as the Brahmāstra and others indeed become fixed upon the earth;
prosperity shall remain permanently in his home, and the goddess of speech shall surely dwell in his mouth.
If a man worships Tārā without knowing this armor-verse (*kavaca*), he will undoubtedly become short-lived, destitute, and foolish. (49)
Whoever, having written it down, should wear it on the neck, on the head, or on the arm,
for him there shall be the accomplishment of all aims, whatever resides in his mind.
O Great Goddess, one should especially write the mantras using gorocanā and saffron, or with red sandalwood paste, or with barley-juice. 51.
O Goddess of the gods, on the eighth day, on an auspicious day, or likewise on the fourteenth, one should write the mantra at twilight with a concentrated mind.
Especially under the asterisms of Maghā, Śravaṇā, or Revatī, when the moon has entered the zodiac sign of Leo and the sun is situated in Cancer. || 53 ||
When Jupiter has entered the sign of Pisces and Saturn is situated in Scorpio,
the practitioner who, with a spirit of devotion, writes this down and wears it [on his person], [attains success].
Before long, his success shall be achieved; there is no need for deliberation on this point. || 54 ||
The disputant becomes mute, the critic offers praise, the king acts as a servant, the proud man is humbled, the all-knowing one becomes dull-witted, and the fire becomes cold.
Through such conduct, another may attain the state of a Siddha; but [to attain it] through you is indeed difficult.
I bow to the beloved of the blue-throated Lord of Mountains, who shatters the fear of worldly existence. || 55 ||
Thus ends the Paramarahasyaka Ugratārā-kavaca in the Nīlatantra.
Now, the Heart of Śrītārā:
Śrī Śiva said, "Listen, O Pārvatī, may you be blessed; this [teaching] brings benefit to the worlds."
The supreme secret within the heart is always being told.
Śrī Pārvatī said: O Lord, how did this hymn originate, and by whom was it composed in the past?
Out of compassion for me, please tell me its entire virtuous history.

The illustrious Śiva said: O beloved, in a former battle between the gods and the asuras, Indra performed this [rite] for the sake of destroying wicked enemies, and for the purpose of increasing his strength and fame.

Om. Of this *Śrīmad-ugratārā-hṛdaya-stotra-mantra*, the Seer (*ṛṣi*) is Śrī Bhairava, the Metre (*chandaḥ*) is Anuṣṭubh, the Deity (*devatā*) is Śrīmad-ugratārā, the Seed-syllable (*bīja*) is *strīṃ*, the Power (*śakti*) is *hūṃ*, and the Nail (*kīlaka*) is *namaḥ*. It is recited for the purpose of destroying all enemies.
The application.
Oṃ strīṃ, salutation to the heart; Oṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to the head; Oṃ hūṃ, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock;
Oṃ trīṃ, hūṃ to the armor.
Oṃ aiṃ netratrayāya vauṣaṭ | Oṃ haṃsaḥ astrāya phaṭ | Now, the meditation:
One should meditate [upon her] as resembling the brilliance of ten million suns, with the crescent moon joined upon her crest.
I bow to the Blessed Lady Tārā, the savior of the world, whose limbs are red, who wears a tongue and crimson garments, whose face is like the orb of the full moon,
who is endowed with four arms holding a noose, a knife, a great goad, and other implements,
and who is adorned with various ornaments.
Having meditated thus, one should recite the heart-mantra from the beginning of the auspicious [syllable] up to the end.
May the Supreme Power (Parāśakti), who is non-different from Rāma, who is established in the reality of Tāriṇī, and who illuminates all principles, grant me the destruction of my enemies.
May Tārā always grant me victory in the face of the fury of my enemies.
The Goddess, whose form is *strī-trīṃ*, is renowned throughout the three worlds; out of affection for you, I have declared it, but let it not be revealed to the uninitiated (*paśus*).
Listen, O Goddess, out of affection for you, I shall describe in truth the names of Tārās— names that are secret and difficult to obtain within the three worlds.
She is the Savior, the Tremulous One, the Star, possessing three forms and the radiance of the sun; she is the embodiment of purity, the great virtuous lady, and the protector of all the righteous.
She is delightful, yet of the nature of passion (rajas), the supreme creator of the world;
she is of the nature of darkness (tamas), the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), possessing a terrible roar and fearsome.
She is the form of Time, known as Kālikā, the destroyer of the world;
she is the supreme bliss of the knowledge of reality and the purifier who bestows the knowledge of reality.
She has red limbs, wears red garments, and is adorned with a red garland;
she is Siddhilakṣmī, Brahmāṇī, Mahākālī, and Mahālayā.
O beloved, for those mortals who always recite these names with one-pointed minds, I shall perform the service of a servant for them.
I worship Ugratārā, the savior from the ocean of worldly existence, the goddess who transcends Tārā, Antārā, and Parā, and who is worshipped by the Lord of Tārakas.
Having consecrated water with the mantra *strīṃ hīṃ hūṃ trīṃ phaṭ*, one should perform the sprinkling;
all diseases perish—this I speak as the truth, the absolute truth.
Then, O beloved, the wise one should consecrate sandalwood with three great mantras ending in *svāhā*; he who applies it as a tilaka mark will bring the world under his control.
One should consecrate cemetery ashes with the mantra *strīṃ hrīṃ trīṃ svāhā* and,
having thrown them into the house of an enemy, the death of that enemy will occur.
Having purified a flower seven times with the mantras ending in *hrīṃ hūṃ strīṃ phaṭ*, [one should cast it].
It swiftly effects the eradication of enemies; of this there is no doubt.
By means of the excellent mantra *strīṃ trīṃ hrīṃ*, unbroken grains (*akṣata*) are consecrated;
by merely casting them [at her], the proud woman quickly returns. (Hamsa: Oṃ)
O Dear One, having purified lampblack with the mantra *hrīṃ strīṃ hūṃ hūṃ saḥ* (p. 133),
one should apply a tilaka of that very substance and effect the enchantment of the world.
O Goddess, the heart-mantra of Tārā destroys all sins;
it is superior by millions upon millions of times the merit of sacrifices such as the Vājapeya.
The fruit of all holy places, such as the Gaṅgā and others,
is said to be ten millionfold when one is in great suffering, great disease, distress, or in danger to life.
In great fear and in great terror, one should recite this most excellent hymn.
Truly, truly, O Pārvatī, beloved as my own life, I have spoken this to you.
This must be guarded with great effort and never revealed anywhere.
Thus ends the *Śrīmad-Ugratārā-hṛdaya* from the *Śrī-Bhairavī-tantra*, in the dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī.
Now begins the Tāropaniṣad: Oṃ tat sat.
That Brahman is that form, beyond primordial nature, like the sky, the supreme among the supreme.

The syllable *Hrīṃ*, which is the Great Truth, is red in color and located at the navel; the syllable *Trīṃ* is tawny in appearance; and the syllable *Hūṃ* is brilliant white, having the form of my heart.
The circle of the earth is my *phaṭ*-sound, smoke-colored; my sword is the blazing form of the syllable *oṃ*; the Vedas are my hands; the moon, sun, and fire are my eyes;
day and night are my feet; the two twilights are my ears; and the year is my [body].
My belly is the month of Māgha; my two rows of teeth are the fortnights;
my two sides are the months and seasons; my fingers are the sciences; my nails are the fires; my mouth is the earth; and my tongue is the ocean.

The sky is my mouth, the atmosphere is my heart, devotion is my skin, the sap is my blood, water is my food, fruits are my garments, the earth is my flesh, the netherworlds and other realms are my marrow, immobile beings are my body hair, and the heavens are my teeth. I am devoid of ego.
My two breasts are the primordial sound (nāda), my navel is knowledge, my mind is the intellect, and forgiveness is my seat; the stars are my ornaments.
This body of mine is the Vairāja, and my water is the quality of goodness (sattva).

Know that the nature of the *bindu* is the nature of the Great Form (*mahākāra*), consisting of light. Know that the head is Ugratārā, Mahogrā, Nīlāṅganā, Ekajaṭā, and Mahāmāyā, who is primordial nature (*prakṛti*). He who, having known this, recites my forms, he who knows my mantra—he [attains success].

The practitioner who recites [the mantra] fashioned in my form and worships the Bhaga remains always free from conceptual construction; he becomes my very form. Having bowed to and praised the Guru, and having offered garments and ornaments, all ritual actions are accomplished and one becomes fearless.
Having attained this Upaniṣadic knowledge, one who recites it becomes liberated while living.
Thus ends the Tāropaniṣad in the Saubhāgyakāṇḍa of the Atharvaveda.
Now begins the hymn of the hundred names of Tārā.
Śrī Śiva said:
She is the savior, tremulous, slender, the star, and a young creeper;
she is the boat in the form of the shore, dark-complexioned, with small and diminished breasts. || 1 ||
She is the fourth state, the tremulous one, she of swift movement, the blue-flowing river;
she is Ugratārā, Jayā, Caṇḍī, and the crest of the glorious Ekajaṭā.
