Aiṃ is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), sauḥ is the power (*śakti*), and klīṃ is the peg (*kīlaka*). The application (*viniyoga*) is for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
Salutation to Ānandabhairava, the Seer (*ṛṣi*), on the head; salutation to the divine Gāyatrī meter (*chandas*), on the mouth;
salutation to the deity Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, on the heart; salutation to the seed-syllable Aiṃ, on the navel.

*Sauḥ*, salutation to Śakti at the Svādhiṣṭhāna; *Klīṃ*, salutation to the Kīlaka at the Mūlādhāra; for the sake of Dharma, Artha, Kāma, and Mokṣa, the application (*viniyoga*) is at the feet. *Aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ*, salutation to the two thumbs (*aṅguṣṭha*); *klīṃ śrīṃ sauḥ aiṃ*, *svāhā* to the two index fingers (*tarjanī*); *sauḥ*.

Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ madhyamābhyāṃ vaṣaṭ; aiṃ ka e lahrīṃ ha sa ka ha lahrīṃ anāmikābhyāṃ hūṃ; klīṃ sa ka lahrīṃ kaniṣṭhikābhyāṃ vauṣaṭ; sauḥ sauḥ aiṃ klīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ karatalapṛṣṭhābhyāṃ phaṭ; aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ aiṃ ka.
And: *Aiṃ hrīṃ sarvajñāyai mahātripurasundaryai hṛdayāya namaḥ*. *Aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ sahakahalhrīṃ nityatṛptāyai mahātripurasundaryai śirase svāhā*.
*Aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ sauḥ sakalahrīṃ anādibodhāyai mahātripurasundaryai*.

To the crest-lock, *vaṣaṭ*: *Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Ka E La Hrīṃ* to Mahātripurasundarī, the Independent One; to the armor, *huṃ*: *Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Klīṃ Ha Sa Ka Ha La Hrīṃ* to Mahātripurasundarī, whose power is eternally undiminished; to the three eyes, *vauṣaṭ*.
*Aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ sauḥ sakala hrīṃ anantāyai mahātripurasundaryai astrāya phaṭ haḥ astrāya phaṭ.* Thus is the binding of the directions (*digbandha*). This concludes the *svatantra-nyāsa*.
[Now follows the *caturdaśāra-cakra-nyāsa*:]* *Aiṃ* on the head; *klīṃ sauḥ* on the eyebrows; *aiṃ* on the forehead.
*Klīṃ sauḥ* on the two ears; *aiṃ* between the eyebrows; *klīṃ sauḥ* on the two eyes; *aiṃ* on the head;

*klīṃ sauḥ* on the two nostrils; *aiṃ* on the chin; *klīṃ sauḥ* on the two lips; *aiṃ* on the nose; *klīṃ sauḥ* on the two cheeks; *aiṃ* on the throat; *klīṃ sauḥ* on the two armpits; *aiṃ* on the neck.

*Klīṃ sauḥ* on the two arms; *aiṃ* on the chin; *klīṃ sauḥ* on the two breasts; *aiṃ* on the heart; *klīṃ sauḥ* on the two sides; *aiṃ* on the navel; *klīṃ sauḥ* on the two breasts; *aiṃ* on the heart; *klīṃ sauḥ* on the two hands; *aiṃ* on the *liṅga*; *klīṃ sauḥ* on the two buttocks; *aiṃ* on the back; *klīṃ sauḥ* on the two hips.

Aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ, and the root mantra, "Obeisance to the support of all" (sarvādhārāya namaḥ) at the *mūlādhāra*. Thus ends the fourteen-syllable placement (*caturdaśāranyāsa*). [Then follows the placement of the deities of the limbs (*aṅgadevatānyāsa*): Aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ ḷṃ ḹṃ eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ aṃ aḥ.

*klīṃ* *rasinī-vāgdevatāyai namaḥ* on the head; *kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ* *klīṃ kāmeśvarī-vāgdevatāyai namaḥ* on the forehead; *caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ śrīṃ odanī-vāgdevatāyai namaḥ* on the mouth; *ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ*.

*Oṃ vimalānanāvāgdevatāyai namaḥ* on the throat; *taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ śrīṃ avyayāvāgdevatāyai namaḥ* on the heart; *paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ śrīṃ jayinīvāgdevatāyai namaḥ* on the navel; *yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ*.

*Kṣmīṃ vāgdevatāyai namaḥ* at the *mūlādhāra*; *śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ saṃ kṣaṃ haṃ kṣmīṃ kaulinīvāgdevatāyai namaḥ* on the two feet. Thus ends the *aṅgadevatā-nyāsa*. [Now the *mantra-nyāsa*: the first seed-syllable...]

The second seed-syllable on the head; the third seed-syllable on the mouth; the third seed-syllable on the heart. Then, one should place the entire root-mantra from the head down to the feet. Having thus performed the placement of the mantras (*mantranyāsa*), one should perform the placement of the seat (*pīṭhanyāsa*). First, [place] *aiṃ* on the heart.
Salutation to the lotus-seat of the foundational power (Ādhāraśakti-kamalāsana). Aiṃ! Salutation to Ananta. Aiṃ! Salutation to the Earth. Aiṃ!
Salutation to the Ocean of Nectar. Aiṃ! Salutation to the Island of Jewels (Ratnadvīpa). Aiṃ! Salutation to the Wish-fulfilling Tree (Kalpavṛkṣa). Aiṃ!
Salutation to the Pavilion of Jewels (Ratnamaṇḍapa). On the right shoulder, salutation to Dharma. On the left shoulder...
Salutation to Jñāna on the right thigh; salutation to Vairāgya on the left thigh; salutation to Aiśvarya on the face; salutation to Adharma on the right side; salutation to Jñāna on the left side;
salutation to Anaiśvarya on the left side; salutation to Avairāgya on the navel.
In the heart: *anantāya namaḥ*, *padmāya namaḥ*, *oṃ arkamaṇḍalāya namaḥ*,
*oṃ somamaṇḍalāya namaḥ*, *ma vahnimaṇḍalāya namaḥ*, *sa sattvāya namaḥ*, *ra rajasena namaḥ*, *ta tamasena namaḥ*, *hai he chīṃ hasauḥ cakrāsanāya namaḥ*.
"Obeisance to the seat of the Sattva-mantra; obeisance to the seat of the Sādhya and Siddha.

Then, having meditated upon the lotus-wheel of the heart, one should visualize a pedestal upon it, adorned with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata), and having formed the *karaka* and *kūrma* mudrās, one should meditate [upon it] with the verse beginning "sakuṅkuma... and so forth.

I take refuge in the Auspicious One (Śivā), who has the luster of the orb of the rising sun, who possesses four arms and three eyes, and who holds a noose, a goad, arrows, and a bow. Having offered a flower upon the head:
*Obeisance to the Gurus; obeisance to the Paramagurus; obeisance to the Parātparagurus*.

Salutations to the supreme preceptor-gurus. Having mentally worshipped the Goddess, having displayed the *āvāhana-mudrā* (invocation gesture) and the *yonimudrā*, one should then perform the placement of the *arghya*. With the mantra *sauḥ astrāya phaṭ*, one should wash the conch and draw a triangular maṇḍala on the ground. Oṃ.

One should worship with "Oṃ namo ādhāraśaktaye," "Oṃ namaḥ kūrma-āya," and "Oṃ namo anantāya. Having placed upon that a tripod (tripadī) washed with water while reciting "namaḥ," and having placed a conch (śaṅkha) upon that, one should fill it three times with the root mantra, cast dūrvā grass, unbroken rice (akṣata), and other offerings, [and then worship] with "Oṃ, obeisance to the self of the sixteen digits (ṣoḍaśakalā)."

Having worshipped the three-line mantra "sūryamaṇḍalāya namaḥ," one should worship in the water with "a/dvādaśakalātmane vahnimaṇḍalāya namaḥ" and "u/somamaṇḍalāya ṣoḍaśakalātmane namaḥ. Then: "Oṃ Gaṅge ca Yamune caiva Godāvari Sarasvati..."
O Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī, be present in these waters!
Having brought the holy water from the solar disc by means of the *aṅkuśa-mudrā*,
having veiled it with the *avaguṇṭhana-mudrā*, having recited the root mantra eight times,
having displayed the *yoni-mudrā*, and having rendered it nectarine with the *dhenu-mudrā*, one should again recite the root mantra eight times.
Having recited [the mantra] and sprinkled with that water, one should install [the deity]. Then follows the installation of the special *arghya* (offering water).

Having sprinkled with the water of the general *arghya* on a spot slightly to one's left, one should draw a mandala consisting of a triangle within a circle, which is itself within a circle, followed by a hexagon, a circle, and a square.
One should worship in the four corners beginning with the southeast: "Oṃ, I worship the śrīpādukā of Uḍḍīyāna, obeisance!
Jāṃ, I worship the śrīpādukā of Jālandhara, obeisance!"
"Pūṃ, I worship the Śrīpādukā of Pūrṇaśaila, obeisance!

Kāṃ, I worship the Śrīpādukā of Kāmarūpa, obeisance! Having worshipped the support (ādhāra) with "Obeisance to the Ādhāra-maṇḍala," while pronouncing the name preceded by the root mantra, [one proceeds]. (p. 166)
Having worshipped the three-footed mantra *sauḥ astrāya phaṭ namaḥ* and placed it within the mandala, one should worship it with:
*maḥ vahnimaṇḍalāya daśakalātmane namaḥ*. Then, having washed the conch with *sauḥ astrāya phaṭ namaḥ* and placed it there, [one worships] *aṃ sūryamaṇḍalāya*.

Having worshipped the conch with the mantra: "Obeisance to the vessel of *arghya* for Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, whose self consists of twelve *kalās*," and having filled it with water while reciting: "Oṃ, obeisance to the nectar-arghya for Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, whose self consists of sixteen *kalās* of the lunar maṇḍala," [one should place] therein that water.

Having offered *dūrvā* grass, unbroken rice, and other items, one should invoke the sacred water (*tīrtha*) from the solar orb with the mantra beginning "Oṃ Gaṅge ca Yamune caiva" while forming the *aṅkuśa-mudrā*; then, having rendered it nectarine with the *dhenu-mudrā*,
displayed the *yoni-mudrā*, and recited the root mantra eight times over it, [one should touch it] with the right thumb.

Having touched water and recited the root mantra, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *arghya* water, beginning from the southeast corner: "Salutation to the heart" (*hṛdayāya namaḥ*), "Svāhā to the head" (*śirase svāhā*), "Vauṣaṭ to the crest-lock" (*śikhāyai vauṣaṭ*), and "Phaṭ to the weapon" (*astrāya phaṭ*).
Having thus placed [the mantras] in the four directions and worshipped them with the mantra "Hrīṃ," one should place the five jewels.

One should place the five jewels—glūṃ ślūṃ plūṃ mlūṃ jlūṃ—which are the jewels for traveling to heaven, the mortal world, and the netherworld; then, one should cover them with the fish-mudrā (matsyamudrā).

Having protected [the object] with the Saṃrakṣaṇa-mudrā, veiled it with the Avaguṇṭhana-mudrā, rendered it nectar with the Amṛtīkaraṇa-mudrā, awakened it with the Prabodhana-mudrā, and having recollected the root mantra: "O supreme one, who dwells in Akula, the mine of nectar, the source of accomplishment and knowledge; O treasury of immortality, in this [place]..."
Having thus consecrated the water— which possesses a moist form—
and having sprinkled oneself and the ritual implements with that water, one should begin the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭha-pūjā*).
Having purified the ground with water and *kuśa* grass while reciting "Aiṃ Hrīṃ Namaḥ," one should place the tripod (*tripadī*) upon it and worship it.

Aiṃ! Salutation to the lotus-seat of the foundational power (Ādhāraśakti); salutation to Kūrma; salutation to Ananta; salutation to Pṛthivī; salutation to the ocean of nectar (Rasāmbudhi); salutation to the Jewel Island (Ratnadvīpa); salutation to the Nandana Garden;
salutation to the Jewel Pavilion (Ratnamaṇḍapa); salutation to the Jewel Altar (Ratnavedikā); salutation to the Jewel Lion-throne (Ratnasiṃhāsana).

Salutations to the Śrīcakra. Then, having purified the copper pedestal with the mantra *hraṃ* and having placed the Śrīyantra upon it, one should worship the four corners of the pedestal starting from the southeast: *namaḥ* to Dharma, *namaḥ* to Jñāna, *namaḥ* to Vairāgya, and *namaḥ* to Aiśvarya. Then...
In the four directions beginning with the east: *namaḥ* to Adharma; *namaḥ* to Ignorance (*ajñāna*);
*namaḥ* to Non-detachment (*avairāgya*);
*namaḥ* to Non-sovereignty (*anaiśvarya*). Upon the pedestal: *namaḥ* to the Root of Bliss (*ānandakanda*).

Salutation to the one whose abode is the pervasive lotus-stalk; salutation to the one who has compassion for all principles (*tattva*). Salutation to the pericarp consisting of the fifty phonemes; salutation to the filaments consisting of the transformations (*vikāra*);
salutation to the petals consisting of primordial nature (*prakṛti*). Salutation to the *maṃ* syllable, the mandala of fire.
Oṃ, homage to the solar disc; homage to the lunar disc; homage to the quality of goodness (sattva);
homage to the quality of passion (rajas); homage to the quality of darkness (tamas); homage to the self (ātman); homage to the inner self (antarātman);
homage to the supreme self (paramātman); homage to the self of knowledge (jñānātman).
Aiṃ, salutation to the seat of Kāmarūpa-pīṭha. Aiṃ, salutation to the seat of Pūrṇagiri-pīṭha.
Aiṃ, salutation to the seat of Jālandhara-pīṭha. Aiṃ, salutation to the seat of Uḍḍīyāna-pīṭha. Having thus worshipped:
Aiṃ, salutation to Tripureśvarī with the two middle fingers. Klīṃ, [salutation to] Tripureśvarī.
To the two ring fingers, *namaḥ*. To the two little fingers, *sauṃ* Tripureśvarī, *namaḥ*.
To the two thumbs, *aiṃ* Tripureśvarī, *namaḥ*. To the two index fingers, *klīṃ* Tripureśvarī, *namaḥ*. To the palms and backs of the hands, *sauḥ* Tripureśvarī, *namaḥ*.

Hrīṃ klīṃ sauḥ, obeisance to the seat of the Goddess; obeisance to the seat of the Cakra; obeisance to the seat of all mantras; obeisance to the seat of the Sādhya and the Siddha. Aiṃ, obeisance to the heart of Tripureśvarī; klīṃ, svāhā to the head of Tripureśvarī; sauḥ, [obeisance] to Tripureśvarī.

*Śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*. *Aiṃ Tripureśvarī kavacāya hūṃ*. *Klīṃ Tripureśvarī netratrayāya vauṣaṭ*. *Sauḥ Tripureśvarī astrāya phaṭ*. Then, having meditated and brought forth the divine splendor with a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), [one should perform the invocation] into the yantra and the conceptualized form (*kalpitamūrti*) by means of the *āvāhana-mudrā*.
Having invoked [the deity] and established her with the *sthāpana-mudrā*, and having bound the *trikhaṇḍa-mudrā*, [one should pray]:

"O Mother, whose form is composed of compassion, who dwells within the great forest of lotuses, who acts for the welfare of all beings, O Supreme Goddess, come, come hither! Then, having displayed the *amṛtīkaraṇa* and *paramīkaraṇa* mudrās, one should recite the root mantra.

May the vital breaths of Śrī Mahātripurasundarī be well-established here. Having recited the root mantra: *pādyaṃ namaḥ* (water for the feet, obeisance); the root mantra: *arghyaṃ namaḥ* (the respectful offering, obeisance); the root mantra: *gandho namaḥ* (scent, obeisance); the root mantra: *puṣpaṃ namaḥ* (flower, obeisance); the root mantra: *dhūpo namaḥ* (incense, obeisance); the root mantra: *dīpo namaḥ* (lamp, obeisance).

Salutations! I offer the root food offering (mūlannaivedya), salutations. Haṃ! I offer the incense (dīpa) consisting of the element of earth, salutations. Āṃ! I offer the flower (puṣpa) consisting of the element of space, salutations. Yaṃ! I offer the incense (dhūpa) consisting of the element of air, salutations.

"I offer the lamp whose nature is *raṃ* and fire; *namaḥ*. I offer the nectar whose nature is *vaṃ* and *aṃ*; *namaḥ*. Having thus presented the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*), [one addresses] Śrī Mahātripurasundarī.
Having received your command, I worship the retinue. Having received the command, one should perform the worship:
in the center—*hrīṃ śrīṃ kāmeśvaryai namaḥ*, *bhagamālinyai namaḥ*, *klinnāyai namaḥ*, *bheruṇḍāyai namaḥ*, *vindhyavāsinyai namaḥ*, *mahāvidyeśvaryai namaḥ*, *śivadūtyai namaḥ*, *tvaritāyai namaḥ*.

Having worshipped with "Obeisance to Nityā, Nīlapatākā, Vijayā, Śrī, Sarvamaṅgalā, Jvālāṃśumālinī, and Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Vicitrā," [one should worship] Gaṇapati at the eastern gate, Baṭuka at the western gate, and [the deity] at the northern gate.
*Hrīṃ durgāyai namaḥ*. At the southern gate: *Kṣaṃ kṣetrapālāya namaḥ*.
On the line outside the outer square, at each of the four gates starting from the west:
*Hrīṃ śrīṃ aṇimādi-siddhi-śrī-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi namaḥ*.
I worship the Siddhi of Laghima; obeisance! I worship the Siddhi of Mahima;

obeisance! I worship the Siddhi of Ishita; obeisance! In the four outer corners, beginning from the east, I worship the venerable Siddhi of Vasitva; obeisance! I worship the venerable Siddhi of Prakashya; obeisance!
I worship Bhaktisiddhiśrī; obeisance! I worship Icchāsiddhiśrī; obeisance! Below, I worship Prāptisiddhiśrī; obeisance! Above, I worship Sarvakāmasiddhi; obeisance! [In] the central square.
In the four gates starting from the west: *hrīṃ śrīṃ āṃ* salutation to Brāhmī; *īṃ* salutation to Māheśvarī; *uṃ* I worship the *śrīpādukā* of Kaumārī, salutation;
*ṛṃ* [I worship] Vaiṣṇavī, *śrī*... in the outer corner of the central square.
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Ḷṃ Vārāhī Śrī; Aiṃ Indrāṇī Śrī; Auṃ Cāmuṇḍā Śrī;
Aḥ Mahālakṣmī Śrī. [These are] at the four gates, beginning with the western one, of the inner square. Trikhaṇḍākṣamudrā Śrī; Hrīṃ Sarvasaṅkṣobhiṇīmudrā Śrī.
Hrīṃ, Śrī of the Sarvavidrāviṇī Mudrā; Klīṃ, Śrī of the Sarvākarṣiṇī Mudrā.
In the four outer corners of the inner square:
Kluṃ, Śrī of the Sarvāveśakarī Mudrā; Śrī of the Sarvonmādakarī Mudrā.

*Krauṃ*—the *Mahāṅkuśā-mudrā*, to the venerable sandals (*śrīpādukā*). *Kluṃ*—the *Khecarī-mudrā*, to the venerable [sandals]. Then, in the triple circle (*trivalaya*), the seed-syllable mudrā (*bījamudrā*), to the venerable [sandals]; the *Yoni-mudrā*, to the venerable [sandals]. Salutation to the Cārvāka system of philosophy. Then, taking the water for the offering (*arghya*) with the hand, [one says]: "In this four-cornered wheel (*caturasracakra*) that fascinates the three worlds (*trailokyamohana*)."
"May these Prakaṭa Yoginīs, beginning with Īśitva, presided over by Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, along with their Śaktis,
Siddhis, weapons, vehicles, and retinues,
be fully worshipped with all ritual offerings"— thus one should offer [the worship] with the root mantra.
Then, on the sixteen petals, beginning from the western petal and proceeding in a clockwise direction around the Goddess, one should worship as follows: *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Aṃ Kāmākarṣiṇī Nityākalā Śrī*;
*Āṃ Buddhyākarṣiṇī Nityākalā Śrī*; *Iṃ Ahaṅkārākarṣiṇī Nityākalā Śrī*.
Īṃ Īśabdākarṣiṇī Nityākalā Śrī; Uṃ Urūpākarṣiṇī Nityākalā Śrī; Ūṃ Usparśākarṣiṇī Nityākalā Śrī; Ṛṃ Urasākarṣiṇī Nityākalā Śrī; Ṛṃ Ugandhākarṣiṇī Nityākalā Śrī; Ḷṃ Ucintākarṣiṇī Nityākalā Śrī.
Ḷṃ Dhairyākarṣiṇī Nityākalā Śrī; Eṃ Smṛtyākarṣiṇī Nityākalā Śrī;
Aiṃ Nāsākarṣiṇī Nityākalā Śrī; Oṃ Bījākarṣiṇī Nityākalā Śrī;
Aṃ Amṛtākarṣiṇī Nityākalā Śrī; Aḥ Śarīrākarṣiṇī Nityākalā Śrī.
On the line: "Oṃ, obeisance to the Buddhist view. Then, taking the water for the *arghya* offering with the hand:

"In this sixteen-petaled wheel (*ṣoḍaśadala-cakra*), which fulfills all desires and is presided over by the venerable Mahātripurasundarī, here are these secret yoginīs, beginning with Kāmākarṣiṇī, together with their *mudrās*, their *siddhis*, and their weapons."

"May [the goddesses], together with their vehicles and retinues, be worshipped with all ritual offerings. Thus one should offer this to the Goddess using the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). Then, on the eight-petaled wheel, in the eastern petals, [one should worship] Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Ka Kha Ga Gha Ṅa—Anaṅgakusumā Devī Śrī...

Ca, cha, ja, jha, ña: [Salutation to] the Goddess Anaṅgamekhalā, Śrī... Ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ḍha, ṇa: [Salutation to] the Goddess Anaṅgamadanā, Śrī... Ta, tha, da, dha, na: [Salutation to] the Goddess Anaṅgamadanāturā, Śrī...
Pa Pha Ba Bha Ma – the goddess Anaṅgarekhā, Śrī; Ya Ra La Va – the goddess Anaṅgaveginī, Śrī; Śa Ṣa Sa Ha – the goddess Anaṅgakuśā, Śrī.

I worship the venerable sandals of the Goddess Anaṅgamālinī; salutations! Here, within this eight-petaled wheel that causes agitation and is presided over by the illustrious Mahātripurasundarī, are these most secret Yoginīs, beginning with Anaṅgakusumā, together with their mudrās and siddhis.

"May they be worshipped with all offerings, together with their weapons, vehicles, and retinues"—with these words, he should offer the arghya water to the Goddess. *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ*, I worship the sandals of the Śrī-pādukā of the power Sarvasaṅkṣobhiṇī-śakti and the power Sarvadrāviṇī-śakti; obeisance!
I worship the śrīpādukā of the power that attracts all; obeisance! [I worship] the śrīpādukā of the power that gladdens all;
the śrīpādukā of the power that deludes all; the śrīpādukā of the power that paralyzes all; the śrīpādukā of the power that causes all to yawn; (p.
170) the śrīpādukā of the power that brings all under control; the śrīpādukā of the power that delights all.
Śrī Sarvonmādinī-śakti; Śrī Sarvārthasādhanī-śakti;
Śrī Sarvāśāparipūraṇī-śakti; Śrī Sarvamantramayī-śakti;
Śrī Sarvadvandvakṣayaṅkarī-śakti—[these are] outside.
Salutations to the systems of Sāṅkhya and Nyāya! Here,

in this fourteenth wheel (cakra) which bestows good fortune and is presided over by the venerable Mahātripurasundarī, reside these powers (śaktis), beginning with Saṅkṣobhiṇī, who are the Yoginīs of the tradition.

"May the oceans, together with the Siddhas, their weapons, their vehicles, and their retinues, be fully honored with all ritual offerings. With these words, he should offer the arghya water to the Root Goddess. Then, on the outer ten-spoked wheel:

One should worship from the west up to the end of the tenth [digit]: Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, the Goddess who bestows all siddhis, Śrī; the Goddess who bestows all prosperity, Śrī; the Goddess who is dear to all and brings peace, Śrī;
the Goddess who causes all auspiciousness, Śrī; the Goddess who bestows all desires, Śrī.
Glorious Goddess Sarvaduḥkhavimocanī; Glorious Goddess Sarvāṅgasundarī; Glorious Goddess Sarvamṛtyuvināśinī; Glorious Goddess Sarvaduḥkhavināśinī;
Glorious Goddess Sarvasaubhāgyadāyinī. Here, in the wheel that fulfills all hopes.
Presided over by Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, these goddesses— beginning with Sarvasiddhipradā—
who are the Kula-Kaulinī Yoginīs,
are worshipped with all ritual offerings, together with their mudrās, siddhis, weapons, vehicles, and retinues.
"Be seated. Having said this, he should offer [the water] with the root mantra using the arghya water to the Goddess.
Then, he should worship starting from the tip of the inner ten-spoked wheel (antardaśāracakra) up to the right side.
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Sarvajñā Devī Śrī... Sarvaśaktimayī Devī Śrī...

The Goddess Śrī who bestows all sovereignty; the Goddess Śrī who consists of all knowledge; the Goddess Śrī who destroys all diseases; the Goddess Śrī who fulfills all hopes; the Goddess Śrī who removes all sins; the Goddess Śrī who consists of all bliss.

O Śrī, Goddess who brings an end to all desires and forms; O Śrī, Goddess who bestows the fruits of all that is desired! Here, in this inner ten-spoked wheel (antardaśāracakra) which is the maker of all protection, presided over by Tripuramālinī and the illustrious Tripurasundarī.

"May these Yoginīs, beginning with Sarvajñā, who are fearless, along with their mudrās, siddhis, weapons, vehicles, and retinues, be fully worshipped with all ritual offerings. Having said this, one should offer the arghya water to the Goddess using the root mantra. Then, on the eight-spoked wheel, starting from the west of the wheel and ending in the south—
One should worship as follows:
(p. 171) *hrīṃ śrīṃ* a ā i ī u ū ṛ ṝ ḷ ḹ e ai o au aḥ — *vaśinīvāgdevatāśrī*; ka kha ga gha ṅa — *kāmeśvarīvāgdevatāśrī*; ca... [and so forth].

Cha, ja, jha, ña: to the venerable Vāgdevatā Modinī. Ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ḍha, ṇa: to the venerable Vāgdevatā Vimalā. Ta, tha, da, dha, na: to the venerable Vāgdevatā Avyayā. Pa, pha, ba, bha, ma: to the venerable Vāgdevatā Jayinī. Ya, ra, la, va: to the venerable Vāgdevatā Sarveśvarī. Śa.

Ṣa Sa Ha Kṣa. To the venerable goddess of speech, Kaulinī. Here, in this eight-spoked wheel (*aṣṭāracakra*) which removes all diseases and is presided over by the illustrious Mahātripurasundarī, these secret yoginīs beginning with Vaśinī—along with their mudrās, siddhis, weapons, vehicles, retinues, and all ritual offerings—are [worshipped].
"May they be fully honored. With these words, he should offer the water of the *arghya* to the Goddess with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*).
He should then present three handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) three times into the three inner corners. In the center of the circle, on the right:
"Salutation to the Supreme Arrow (*uttamabāṇa*). On the left: "Salutation to the Enchanting Bow (*mohadhanus*). Below that—

Salutation to Karkkaśāya. In the south, salutation to Stambhāṅkuśāya. In front, *klīṃ*, salutation to Kāmeśvarī; salutation to Āñcakriṇī; salutation to Aiṃbhagaśālinī. With the root mantra, salutation to Śrī Mahātripurasundarī. Then, in the center of the triangle:
One should meditate on her in the form of the syllable *mī*, which is the essence of the *kāmakaḷā*.

Then, having worshipped with "Obeisance to the five *pretas*—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśāna, and Sadāśiva" and "Obeisance to the nine planets," one should take up the rosary and recite [the mantra] according to one's capacity. Then:

"You are the protector of the most secret of secrets; accept this recitation performed by us. O Goddess, O Great Sovereign, may accomplishment be mine through your grace. With these words, he should offer water into the left hand of the Goddess. While reciting, he should visualize that it has been accepted by the Goddess as consisting of radiant energy (*tejomaya*). [He should then offer] whatever is deficient in ritual, deficient in action, or deficient in devotion.

"O Three-eyed One, may all that [I have offered] become complete through your grace. Having praised thus according to one's ability, having performed three circumambulations and prostrated, one should consider oneself to have achieved one's purpose.
One should display the *yonimudrā* and dismiss [the deity] with the *saṃhāramudrā*. Taking the *nirmālya*, [one should depart].

Having fashioned a triangular maṇḍala in the northeast and worshipped with "Aiṃ Caṇḍeśvaryai Namaḥ," one should place the *nirmālya* upon one's head and move about as one pleases. By the mere knowledge of the Śrīvidyā, all accomplishments (*siddhi*) arise. Therefore, this Vidyā should never be imparted to one who is not a devotee. Thus [it is said].
The Ritual Manual for Worship.

(p. 172) Then, O Mother, was not praise offered at the root of your lotus feet with services that were like auspicious showers filled with nectar, serving as the auspicious lamps for Lakṣmī’s self-choice marriage? Was it not performed in your mind?
Of people possessed of devotion. || 1 ||
O Mother, lotus-eyed one dwelling in the waters, this alone is truly desirable in your adorations:
the presence of your form, which resembles a blossoming red lotus and is drenched with supreme nectar. || 2 ||

How many indeed are there, such as Brahmā and others, whose power is slightly tarnished and who are overwhelmed by dissolution day after day? O Mother, he alone remains possessed of stable perfection who performs even a single prostration at your feet. (3)
O Tripurasundarī, having once obtained your side-glance— the very essence of the splendor of the sprout of compassion—
those who possess devotion to you, made beautiful by the state of passion, bring others into a state of infatuation.
A young woman even within the three worlds. || 4 ||
O Mother Tripurā, dweller in the triangular abode, three-eyed one— those who chant your name as "Hrīṃ" alone,
having abandoned the defeat by the messengers of Yama upon the mere remembrance of you, sport in the Nandana grove together with the guardians of the world.
O Mother, how could the cruel force of poison not have become full-blown in the past, as it flowed from the slayer of Pura,
were it not for this body of yours which is eternally cooled by being drenched in nectar and serves as a source of consolation?
O Goddess, prostration at your two lotus-feet produces omniscience and eloquence in the assembly; moreover,
it bestows a shimmering crown, a radiant parasol, two chowries,
and the great earth.

O Mother, Tripurasundarī, look upon me, the protectorless one who is filled with devotion for You alone and whose gaze is fixed upon You— by Your side-long glances, which are oceans of compassion and which grant all desired objects like wish-fulfilling trees. 8.
Alas, others indeed fix their minds on other deities and carry out devotion toward them;
yet, O Mother, I remember you alone with my mind, I bow to you alone, and you alone are my refuge.
O Tripurasundarī, even though there are hundreds of thousands of glances from your eyes, look upon me somehow!
Surely, a person like me—a sole vessel of compassion—has been born, will be born, or is currently being born;
for what indeed is difficult to obtain here for one who daily mutters your name, "Hrīṃ Hrīṃ"?
In the work titled *Tripurābhidhāna*, on page 173:
"Lakṣmī herself, full of sweetness, serves those who are worthy of honor, adorned with garlands and crowns, and mounted upon elephants in rut. (11)

O lotus-eyed Mother, may your salutations— which bestow prosperity, delight all the senses, are skilled in granting sovereign power, and are intent on uprooting evil— perpetually attend to me alone and no other. 12.

Victorious is that single form of yours, the witness [of all], which is the very embodiment of the supreme Bhairava, the Lord Khaṇḍaparaśu, who performs his cosmic dance at the dissolution of the aeons; [in this form] the noose, the goad, the sugarcane bow, and the flower-arrows are present. 13.
O Mother, may this form of yours— whose supreme splendor is crimson with the paste of abundant saffron,
adorned with a radiant crown and an ornament of the crescent moon— be ever present before me.
The triangle is delighted and anointed with supreme nectar. || 14 ||
O Mother, the knower of mantras who recites this hymn— kindled by the great mantra encapsulated by three *hrīṃ*s—
before you every day, finds that kings remain under his control,
his fortune endures for a long time, and his speech remains awake, filled with the weight of pure and eloquent expressions.
Yyaśaḥ || 15 || Thus ends the *Ṣoḍaśī-kalyāṇī-stotra* composed by Brahmā.
Then the Goddess spoke the armor-mantra:
"O God of gods, O Mahādeva, bestower of joy upon your devotees!"
Reflecting well upon it, tell me the armor (kavaca) of the Great Goddess.
The illustrious Mahādeva said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim this armor (kavaca), which is difficult even for the gods to obtain;
it is not to be revealed, a supreme secret that grants the desired accomplishments of the practitioner.
O Goddess, the seer of the Kavaca is the imperishable Dakṣiṇāmūrti;
the meter is declared to be Paṅkti, and the deity is Tripurasundarī. (3)
O Goddess of the Suras, the application for the attainment of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa consists of the Vāgbhava, Kāmabīja, and Śaktibīja mantras.
May the Vāgbhava [syllable] protect my head, and likewise may the Kāma-bīja protect my heart;
may the Śakti-bīja always protect my navel, as well as my private parts and feet.
May Bālā protect me for the sake of all accomplishments during conversation with the mantra *e klī sauṃ*;
may Bhairavī protect the region of the throat with the mantra *hasauḥ sakalahrīṃ*.
Sundarī is always at the region of the navel, and Kāmakalā is at the head;
Mahātripurasundarī is between the eyebrows and the nose.
May Subhagā protect the forehead; may Bhagā protect the region of the neck; may Bhagodayā protect the heart; and may Bhagasarpiṇī protect the belly. (8)
May Bhagamālā protect [me] at the region of the navel; may Manobhavā protect the penis;
may the Great Goddess Śivā, the Sovereign of the Kings of Kings, protect the private parts. May she protect [me]. 9.
May the Mother of the Universe, whose form is consciousness, protect my feet;
may Nārāyaṇī, who brings auspiciousness to the entire body, protect all my limbs. 10.
May Brahmāṇī protect me in the east, and likewise Vaiṣṇavī in the south;
may Vārāhī protect me in the west, and Maheśvarī in the north. (11)
May Kaumārī protect in the southeast; may Mahālakṣmī protect in the southwest;
may Cāmuṇḍā protect in the northwest; and may Indrāṇī protect in the northeast.
May Mahāmāyā protect me in the water; may Sarvamaṅgalā protect me on the earth;
may Varadā, the sovereign of all the three worlds, protect me in the sky. 13.
But this armor of the Goddess is difficult to obtain even for the gods;
he who, having risen at dawn, being pure and with a restrained mind, should recite it—14.
For him there shall be no mental anxieties, no physical ailments, and no fear anywhere;
nor shall he have fear of pestilence, nor likewise fear of sins.
One shall not fall under the power of poverty, nor shall one remain under the power of death;
one shall go to the eternal city, O Goddess—this I tell you as the truth, the absolute truth. 16.
O Dear One, he who recites the Śrīvidyā without knowing this armor-mantra (kavaca) does not obtain its fruit; rather, he shall suffer the stroke of a weapon.
Thus ends the armor (kavaca) of the venerable Śoḍaśī-vidyā in the Siddhayāmala.
Then, on Mount Kailāsa, Hṛdayā— her mind overcome with compassion and intent on helping others— questioned Maheśvara, the ocean of mercy, who was exceedingly gracious.
Śrī Pārvatī said:
O Brahman, in the coming Kali age, people will be devoid of righteous conduct and ritual action; how will their spiritual welfare be secured?
The illustrious Śiva said: Listen, O Goddess, O Maheśvarī; out of affection for you, I shall proclaim the *Sundarīhṛdayastava*, which is difficult to obtain in the three worlds.
For those men who are tormented by suffering and whose minds are struck down by poverty, their welfare shall be attained merely by the recitation of this very [text]. || 4 ||
Om. Of this *Śrīmahāṣoḍaśī-hṛdaya-stotra-mantra*,
Ānandabhairava is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the divine Gāyatrī is the meter (*chandas*), Śrī Mahātrisundarī is the deity (*devatā*), and Aiṃ is the seed-syllable (*bīja*).
Sauḥ is the Śakti; Klīṃ is the Kīlaka; the application (viniyoga) is for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
Salutation to the sage Ānandabhairava on the head; salutation to the meter Devīgāyatrī on the face;
salutation to the deity Śrī Mahātripurasundarī on the heart; salutation to the seed-syllable Aiṃ at the navel;
salutation to the power Sauḥ at the Svādhiṣṭhāna; salutation to the pin Klīṃ at the Mūlādhāra.
The application of the feet is for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. Now follow the ritual assignments (nyāsa) of the hands and limbs.

Aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ, salutation to the two thumbs (aṅguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ). Klīṃ śrīṃ sauḥ aiṃ, svāhā to the two index fingers (tarjjanībhyāṃ svāhā). Sauḥ oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, vaṣaṭ to the two middle fingers (madhyamābhyāṃ vaṣaṭ). Aiṃ ka-e-īla hrīṃ hasaka-hala hrīṃ, hūṃ to the two ring fingers (anāmikābhyāṃ hūṃ).

*Klīṃ* to both little fingers, *vauṣaṭ*. *Sauḥ sauḥ aiṃ klīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ* to both palms and backs of the hands, *phaṭ*. Thus is the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*). The visualization (*dhyāna*):
[I meditate upon] Bhāratī, who resembles the immeasurable light of the sun at dawn, who bestows auspiciousness, and whose face is slightly blossomed with a smile.

With hands shaped like four lotuses, she holds a noose, the gesture of fearlessness, a goad, and the boon-granting mudrā; she who bestows prosperity, dispels the darkness of worldly existence, and illuminates the quarters with her smiles—I worship the Sixteenth [Kalā] with devotion. 5.

The beautiful one, who removes all impurities, whose splendor is as desired by ten million lotus-lovers, and whose meritorious lotus-feet are to be worshipped by those who have performed virtuous deeds for ten million kalpas. (6)
Her face is as beautiful as the moon, the lord of the night; she is the refuge of the merit of Śrīśa’s power;
her holy feet are to be sought by the virtuous; and she is well-praised by the hosts of gods in times of distress. (7)

I worship her, the unconquered Mother of the World, the Victorious One, who—endowed with speed in the battle between the gods and the asuras—struck down the exceedingly invincible sons of Diti who were engaged in combat; she who is the source of all worlds.
I worship that auspicious Goddess who dwells in the hearts of yogis whose minds are disciplined through yoga and whose selves are restrained;
she who remains awake in this world, whom the twice-born diligently recite within their hearts.

I worship that Kālī, who destroys the impurities of the Kali age, whose lotus feet are cherished by the Kaulikas, and whose power brings benefit to the people of the Kali age, while the creators of the world reckon her as Time itself. 10.
The Goddess, who illuminates the horizons with the rays of her own body like the infinite light of the rising sun;
who blazes intensely, appearing like a great forest fire to the demon-slaying woods;
who has tamed those of fierce minds and crushed the sons of Diti; who is beautiful to behold yet difficult to endure for the wretched—[protect] us from distress.
With a joyful mind, I meditate upon the sixteenth digit within my heart, which is beyond the reach of the ordinary mind.

Wise and fortunate are those whose heads are bowed by their husbands, whose lotus-feet are free from dust, who are bold, and whose beautiful moon-like luster dispels the instability of the earth below the clouds.

I meditate upon Sundarī, who offers the sacrifice of the Dharma; who upholds the gods of the earth; whose form is the object of meditation; who is blessed among the wise; who is exceedingly fortunate; and who is surrounded by the wealth of Kubera. || 12 ||
Victory, victory to the eloquent Yoginī, united with Yoga! Victory, victory to the gentle Saumyā, the beautiful one with a lovely face!
Victory, victory to Padmā, the lotus-like consort of Keśava! Victory, victory to Kālī, the dark goddess, beloved of Kāla! 13.

Victory, victory to the dwarf-like Ṣoḍaśī, who holds the Vedas in her hand! Victory, victory to the Sustainer, the virtuous one, the peace of the Creator! Victory, victory to Vāṇī, who is praised by the Brāhmaṇas and by Brahmā! Victory, victory to Durgā, the destroyer of the enemies of the gods! 14.

O Goddess, at the time of creation, you are the Rajasic one, red in form, borne by the lotus-born Brahmā; at the time of preservation, you are the Sattvic Mother, white in form, held in the heart of Hari; and at the end of existence, you are the Tamasic one, black in form, filled with great wrath and residing in the abode of Bhava—these and all others are indeed you alone.
She is the Earth, honored by men, the beautiful one, the primordial and absolute. || 15 ||

O Goddess, knower of the virtues of the Gopīs, this *Sumālāsumana* hymn— worthy of being grasped through reflection and yoga, destroying the sixteen-fold fetters, possessing a nature like the celestial tree (*suratara*), and highly esteemed— is capable of bestowing grace upon those who recite it, for it is known as the "Heart" (*hṛdaya*). 16.
This most wonderful hymn of the sixteen-syllabled Tripurasundarī—whatever man hears it, he always enjoys happiness. (17)
It must not be given to a Śūdra, nor to a rogue, nor to one whose soul is defiled;
it should be given to one who is self-controlled and devoted, especially to a Brāhmaṇa.
Thus ends the *Ṣoḍaśīhṛdayastotra* in the *Śrītripurasundarītantra*.
Now, the Upanishad: Oṃ. Śakti, who is the supreme cause, by whom is the body formed of nine wheels?
The Śrīcakra consists of the power of the nine wheels. Vārāhī is the form of the ancestors; Kurukullā is the deity of the earth.
The oceans are the purposes of the Mother; the body is the island of the nine jewels; the mudrās are the nine supports;

the powers (śaktis) are endowed with the many sevenfold constituents such as the skin; the volitions are the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpataru); the splendor is the Kalpa-grove; and all this shines forth through the sense of taste.

The six tastes—sweet, sour, bitter, pungent, astringent, and salty—are the seat of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), the *kuṇḍalinī* who is the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*). I am the power of will (*icchāśakti*), the Great Tripurasundarī; I am the knower, the sacrificer, the knowledge, the offering water (*arghya*), and the oblation (*havis*) to be known.
Salutations to the knower, knowledge, and the known; to the contemplation of duality;

to the worship of the Śrīcakra; to the nine aesthetic sentiments beginning with erotic love accompanied by destiny; and to those consisting of desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, envy, merit, and demerit.
The eight powers beginning with Brāhmī; the nine powers of the mudrās as the support;

and the sixteen powers consisting of the transformations of earth, water, fire, air, ether, the ear, the skin, the eye, the tongue, the nose, speech, the hands, the feet, the anus, and the generative organ.
The eight powers, such as Anaṅgakusumā, are the faculties of speech, grasping, movement, excretion, pleasure, taking, receiving, and equanimity;
they correspond to the channels Alambuṣā, Kuhū, Viśvodarī, Varuṇā, Hastijihvā, and Yaśasvinī.
The fourteen channels— Gāndhārī, Pūṣā, Sarasvatī, Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumnā—
are the deities of the fourteen spokes beginning with Sarvasaṅkṣobhiṇī;
[the vital airs] are Prāṇa, Apāna, Vyāna, Udāna, Samāna, Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkala, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya.

The ten Vāyus, beginning with Sarvasiddhiprada, are the deities of the ten outer spokes; this group of ten Vāyus, through the distinctions of their adjuncts (upādhi) in association [with other elements], exists in five forms according to their enumeration as vital breaths (prāṇa): namely, recaka, pūraka, poṣaka, dāhaka, and alpāvaka-amṛta. Furthermore, there is the digestive fire (jāṭharāgni) of human beings, which causes delusion.
It digests the fourfold food consisting of what is chewed, swallowed, licked, and sucked. Then, [the self] becomes possessed of space,
along with all the ten internal deities beginning with omniscience,
as well as the eight powers beginning with Vaśinī, which consist of cold and heat, pleasure and pain, desire, and the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas.

The five subtle elements (tanmātras)—sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—are the five flower-arrows; the bow is the sugar-cane of the mind; passion (rāga) is the arrow, hatred (dveṣa) is the noose, and the goad is the Unmanifest (avyakta), the Great Principle (mahat-tattva), the ego (ahaṃkāra), and Kāmeśvarī.

The deities at the tips of the inner triangle are Vajreśvarī and Bhagamālinī; they are the fifteen Nityās who perceive the transformations of time in the form of the fifteen lunar days (tithis), the pure presiding deities corresponding to their respective forms,
the Kāmeśvarī of all gods free from limiting adjuncts, eternally full of bliss.

Lalitā Kāmeśvarī, whose form is one with my own self, is eternally full of the density of bliss; the deity whose form is one with my own self is indeed Lalitā. Thus, the composition of the literary work is the true essence. Free from the notions of "this must be done" or "this must not be done," there is the sense of "I-ness" (ahantva) regarding the ritual offerings, whether they exist or do not exist.

The dissolution of the conceptualization of "this should be done" and "this should not be done," or "this is to be worshipped" and "this is not to be worshipped," is the *homa*. The capacity of the external and internal organs to perceive forms is the *āvāhana* (invocation) of that [consciousness].
The taking up of objects of a single form by the external and internal organs is the *āsana*;
the unification of the red and white elements is the *pādya*; and the bliss of the bliss of the essence of radiant fragrance is the *arghya*.
The sipping of water (*ācamana*) is the recollection of one's own pure, innate power;

the bath (*snāna*) is the recollection of the power of supreme bliss whose nature is the fire of consciousness (*cidagni*); the garment (*vastra*) consists of the knots of Brahmā, which are composed of will and action, each divided twenty-sevenfold.

The Brahma-thread is the channel of Brahman consisting of the vital breath; its ornamentation is the recollection of being free from the attachment to garments other than the sacred thread; its fragrance is the recollection of being spontaneously fulfilled;
and its flowers are the contemplation of all sense objects through the stability of the mind.

Inhalation at all times is the incense; the upward-flaming light, severed by the breath, is the lamp; the body of space consisting of Being-Consciousness-Bliss is the food offering; and the cessation of all coming and going is the betel leaf.

From the *mūlādhāra* up to the *brahmarandhra*, and from the *brahmarandhra* back down to the *mūlādhāra*, there is the movement in the form of a clockwise circuit; this constitutes the fourth state (*turyāvasthāna*), the immersion into the void of the subtle body (*saṃskāradeha-śūnya-pramāditāvatimajjana*), and the offering of oblations (*baliharaṇa*). This is the reality (*sattva*).

What is to be done and what is not to be done, equanimity, the dissolution of the self, and the fire-oblation (*homa*); the contemplation of the non-difference of the objects of meditation, the libation (*tarpaṇa*), and one’s own immersion into the Guru’s sandals—this is the perfect meditation through the contemplation of the three forms. Thus, by means of the contemplation of the three forms...

One who is thus disciplined becomes liberated; for him, there is the attainment of the identity of the deity and the self. The activities of consciousness are accomplished without effort; he alone is called a Śiva-yogin. Thus ends the Ṣoḍaśy-upaniṣad.
Then Śatanāma Bhṛgu said:
"O Four-faced One, Lord of the World, O Master, recite this hymn for me."
By the mere performance of which a person may attain devotion. || 1 ||
Brahmā said:
Having extracted one hundred and eight names from the Thousand Names,
that which is more secret than the secret has been proclaimed as belonging to Sundarī.

Om. Of this hymn consisting of one hundred and eight names of the venerable Ṣoḍaśī, Śambhu is the seer (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandas), and the venerable Ṣoḍaśī is the deity (devatā). It is employed for the attainment of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
Oṃ! Tripurā is the mother of the sixteen [syllables], the three-syllabled, the triad, and the triple Veda;
she is the beautiful one, the fair-faced, the one to be served, and she who is devoted to the Sāmaveda. || 3 ||
Śāradā is the abode of sound, the ocean and the garment of rivers;
she is the most excellent woman, purest among the pure, and solely devoted to the meditation on Śiva. (4)
She is the Mistress, the Consort of Śambhu, the Daughter of Śambhu, and Sarasvatī;
she churns the ocean, moves with swiftness, and bestows swift accomplishment.
She is to be served by the virtuous, accessible to the virtuous, and her mind is satisfied by the virtuous;
she carries a skull-topped staff, is short of stature, and bears a sword and a begging bowl.
Free from the states of the six groups, she is the attendant of the six groups;
she is the six groups themselves, the six limbs, the sixteenfold, and sixteen years of age.
She is the embodiment of will (*kratu*), possessed of will, the mistress of the *Ṛbhus*, and adorned with will;
she begins with the *ka*-group and ends with the *pa*-group, having the form of the intermediate consonants (*antasthā*) as her inner essence.
Devoid of form and the absence of form, she removes time, death, and old age; she is slender, the sovereign of reality, Tārā, three years of age, and the embodiment of primordial wisdom.
Kālī, Karālī, Kāmeśī, Chāyā, Sañjñā, Arundhatī, Nirvikalpā, Mahāvegā, Mahotsāhā, and Mahodarī. (10)
Meghā, Bālakā, Vimalā, the bestower of stainless knowledge; Gaurī, Vasundharā, Goptrī, she who is served by the Lord of Cows (Indra). || 11 ||
Bhagāṅgā, Bhagarūpā, and she who is devoted to the state of bhakti;
Chinnamastā, Mahādhūmā, and likewise Dhūmravibhūṣaṇā. || 12 ||
She who is devoid of worldly religious rites yet devoted to the supreme dharma;
she who is Sītā, Mātaṅginī, and Medhā; she who is the destroyer of the demon Madhu.
Bhairavī, the mother of the world, the bestower of fearlessness, the beauty of worldly existence; Bhāvukā, Bagalā, Kṛtyā, Bālā, and Tripurasundarī. (14)
She is Rohiṇī, Revatī, the delightful Rambhā, and she who is saluted by Rāvaṇa;
she consists of a hundred sacrifices, she is the essence of being, and she bestows the boons of Śatakratu.
The goddess has a face adorned with a hundred moons, resembling a thousand suns;
her eyes are the moon, the sun, and fire, and she is clothed in a tiger skin.
"O Gopī, I have thus told you the one hundred and eight names of her who bears the crescent moon, who is intoxicated, who is the essence of wine, and whose eyes are like wine. (17)
It is for the beautiful one, granting everything, worthy of service, and the destroyer of great sins;
it must be kept secret, kept secret, kept secret in the Kali age. 18.
Whatever fruit is proclaimed for the recitation of the Thousand Names, ten million times that merit is obtained from the recitation of this hymn. || 19 ||

"The man who, endowed with devotion, should always recite [this] at midnight, or at the break of dawn, or during the evening twilight, or on the ninth day, shall obtain most wonderful and beloved enjoyments. (p. 180) Thus ends the hymn of one hundred and eight names of the Sixteenth [Vidyā] in the Pūrvakhaṇḍa of the Brahmayāmala.
It is finished.
Then, on the beautiful peak of Kailāsa, adorned with various jewels,
situated amidst wish-fulfilling trees, and graced with diverse flowers, [the Thousand Names were recited].
In the center of a jeweled pavilion frequented by sages and gandharvas,
he beheld the Blessed One, the Teacher of the World, seated in supreme bliss.
He holds a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff, has the crescent moon as his crest-ornament,
carries a trident and a ḍamaru drum in his hands, and has the great bull as his vehicle.
O God who wears a mass of matted hair, whose neck is adorned by Vāsuki,
who is decorated with sacred ash, O God who is blue-throated and three-eyed!
Clad in a leopard skin, resembling pure crystal,
he possesses the brilliance of a thousand suns and is adorned by having the daughter of the mountain as half of his body.
Having bowed his head to the Lord, the cause of all and the one whose form is the universe,
Śikhivāhana joined his palms in reverence and spoke to him.
Kārttikeya said:
O God of gods, Lord of the world, whose nature is creation, preservation, and dissolution;
you alone are the Supreme Self, and you are the refuge of all embodied beings.
You alone are the refuge of all the worlds and of the distressed;
you alone are the support of the universe, and you are this cause of the entire world.
You alone are worthy of worship by all; other than you, there is no refuge for me.
What is the supreme secret in this world? What single thing bestows all perfections?
What is that one supreme and most excellent yoga which bestows heaven and liberation,
even without sacred fords, without austerity, without gifts, and without sacrifices?
A person may attain perfection through meditation even without absorption (laya).
From what does creation arise, and in what does dissolution occur?
O Lord, why is one crossed over from the perilous ocean of saṃsāra?
O Maheśvara, I desire to hear that; please tell me.
Īśvara said:
"Excellent, excellent! You have asked well, O delighter of Pārvatī. There is something most secret, my son; I shall tell it to you without doubt."
Sattva, rajas, and tamas, as well as the others beginning with Mahat,
and whatever other numerous beings there are, all of which arise from primordial nature (prakṛti).
She alone is the Goddess, the Supreme Power, Mahātripurasundarī;
she alone gives birth to the universe, and into her alone shall the universe pass away.
She alone withdraws this entire universe, including all that is moving and unmoving;
she is the support of all beings and the remover of the affliction of disease.
The powers of will, knowledge, and action are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others;
they exist in three ways as the very nature of power, effecting creation, maintenance, and destruction. In the form of Brahmā she creates, and in the form of Viṣṇu she protects.
In the form of Rudra, he shall withdraw this entire world of moving and non-moving beings.
In whose womb the entire universe revolves even today,
in whom it is dissolved at the end, and from whom it is born again;
having propitiated her, the three worlds attained the supreme state.
I shall tell you her thousand names; listen to them.
Oṃ. Of this mantra of the *Śrīmahātripurasundarīsahasranāmastotra*,
the venerable Lord Dakṣiṇāmūrti is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the Jagatī is the meter (*chanda*),
and its power is the inconceivable [splendor] of all that is manifest, secret, traditional, of the Kula, Kaula, Transcendent, Unveiled, Esoteric, and Ineffable.

The deity is Vāgīśvarī; *oṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*). Māyā-śakti is the *kīlaka* (stake) of the Kāmarāja-bīja. The individual soul (*jīva*) is the seed-syllable, Suṣumnā is the channel (*nāḍī*), and Sarasvatī is the power (*śakti*). This is the application (*viniyoga*) for the recitation (*japa*) for the sake of virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation.
[She resides] in the foundation (*ādhāra*), radiant as the orb of the rising sun.

O Śivā, those who meditate upon these three syllables of yours—the seed-syllable *Vāgbhava* (AIM), golden-hued; the *Manmatha* (KLĪM) syllable, resembling an indragopa insect; and the syllable established in the heart-lotus, joined with the Power (*Śakti*) residing in the positions of Viṣṇu and Brahmā, and radiant with the luster of the moon—they go to the state of supreme bliss.
The auspicious one, the lotus-born, the dark one, the formidable one, she who takes forms at will;
she who is named Kāmā, the giver of desires, the desirable one, desire itself, and she who moves according to her own will.
She is Kālarātri, Mahārātri, Kapālī, and Kālarūpiṇī;
she is Kaumārī, the liberation through compassion, and the destroyer of the impurities of the Kali age.
Kātyāyanī, the one whose hand is the support, the moonlight, the beloved of the lotus;
the giver of fame, the giver of intellect, wisdom, the knower of ethics, and the lover of ethics.
She is the consort of Maheśvara, the Great Illusion, possessed of great splendor;
she is the Sovereign Goddess, with a great tongue, most terrible, with great fangs and great arms.
She is the destroyer of the darkness of great delusion, the bestower of great liberation,
the annihilator of great poverty, and the crusher of great enemies.
She is Mahāmāyā, of great heroism, the destroyer of great sins;
she is the great sacrifice, composed of mantra, and dwells in the Maṇipūraka.
She is of the mind, the giver of honor, worthy of respect, the eye of the mind, and she who moves in battle;
she is the mother of the Gaṇas, the Gāyatrī, and she who is served by the Gaṇas and Gandharvas.
Girijā, Giriśā, Sādhvī, Giristhā, Girivallabhā;
Caṇḍeśvarī, Caṇḍarūpā, Pracaṇḍā, and Caṇḍamālinī.
Carvikā, who has the form of Carcikā; Caṇḍikā, who possesses a beautiful form;
the mistress of sacrifice, whose nature is sacrifice, and who is devoted to the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña).
She is the mother of sacrifice, the enjoyer of sacrifice, the mistress of sacrifice, and the source of sacrifice;
she is the perfection of the rites of successful sacrifice, the limb of sacrifice, and the protectress of sacrifice.
She is the performance of sacrifice, the form of sacrifice, the possessor of the limbs of sacrifice, and the protector of sacrifice;
she is the act of sacrifice, the sacrifice itself, and the abode of the ritual acts of sacrifice.
Jālandharī, the mother of the world, Jātavedā, the beloved of the universe;
she who has conquered her senses, who has conquered anger, the progenitor, and the giver of birth.
The Gaṅgā, the Godāvarī, the Gomatī, and the Śatadrū; the Ghargharā, the Vedagarbhā, the Recikā, and the Samavāsinī.
The Sindhu, Mandākinī, Kṣiprā, Yamunā, and Sarasvatī;
the Bhadrā, Rāgavipāśā, Gaṇḍakī, and Vindhyavāsinī.
The Narmadā, Sindhu, Kāverī, Vetravatī, and Sukauśikī;
the daughter of Mahendra (Goddess Śakrāṇī), as well as Ahalyā and Carmakāvatī.
Ayodhyā, Mathurā, Māyā, Kāśī, Kāñcī, Avantikā,
and the city of Dvārāvatī— these sacred sites (tīrthas) destroy even the greatest of sins.
She dwells in the midst of a lotus grove, residing within the filaments of the lotus;
she has a lotus-like face and eyes like those of the cakora bird; she stands upon a lotus and is born from the lotus.
She who utters the syllable *hrīṃ*, who wears the *kuṇḍala* earring, who dwells in the heart-lotus, and possesses beautiful eyes;
she who is adorned with the syllable *śrīṃ*, the goddess Lakṣmī, who utters the syllable *klīṃ* and destroys all afflictions.
Born from the mouth of Hari, peaceful, having made her abode in the mouth of Hari;
born from the mouth of Hari, peaceful, stationed upon the chest of Hari.
She is Vaiṣṇavī, she has the form of Viṣṇu, and her essential nature is that of the Mother of Viṣṇu;
she is the Māyā of Viṣṇu, the large-eyed one, radiant with expansive eyes.
She is the sovereign of the universe, the soul of the universe, the mistress of the universe, and she who possesses the form of the universe;
she is the sovereign of the universe, worshipped by Śiva, the mistress of Śiva, and the beloved of Śiva.
She is the mother of Śiva, known as Śivā, the giver of auspiciousness, and whose form is Śiva;
she is the sovereign of existence, worshipped by existence, the mistress of existence, and the leader of existence.
The mother of existence, accessible through existence, the destroyer of the thorns of existence;
beloved by existence, the bliss of existence, Bhavānī, the deluder of existence.
She is Gāyatrī and Sāvitrī, Brahmāṇī, whose form is Brahman;
she is Brahmeśī, the giver of Brahman, Brahman itself, Brahmāṇī, and the expounder of Brahman.
Durgā resides in the fortress, she is the form of the fortress, the difficult-to-attain one who destroys the suffering of those in distress;
she is easy to traverse yet difficult to reach, self-controlled, compassionate, the milch-cow of boons, and the remover of misfortune.
The destroyer of evil, difficult to perceive, hard to approach, and the annihilator of misdeeds;
five-faced, the fifth, full, and the dweller in the Pūrṇa-pīṭha.
Established in *sattva*, having the form of *sattva*, established in *sattva*, and originating from *sattva*;
established in *rajas*, having the form of *rajas*, and arising from the quality (*guṇa*) of *rajas*.
Abiding in darkness, having the form of darkness, she is of the nature of tamas and dear to those characterized by tamas;
born from the quality of tamas, she is also the sattvic and rājasic aspect.
She is the measure of time in the form of the kāṣṭhās, muhūrtas, nimiṣas, and thereafter the animeṣas;
she is the half-months and the months, and her very nature is the year.
Established in yoga, she is the embodiment of yoga; abiding in the kalpa, she is the very form of the kalpa;
her limbs are variegated with various jewels, and she is adorned with diverse ornaments.
She is the soul of the universe, the mother of the universe, the destroyer of all bonds;
she inspires confidence in all, she is the universe itself, and she is the contemplation of the power of the universe.
Resembling the flower of the barley plant and comparable to the flower of the pomegranate,
she has four limbs and four arms, and dwells in the conduct of the fourfold discipline.
She is the sovereign of all, she is everything at all times, she is the giver of everything at all times;
she is Māheśvarī, the primordial of all, Śarvāṇī, and the auspiciousness of all.
Nalinī, Nandinī, Nandā, Ānandā, Nandavardhinī;
she who pervades all beings and destroys the burden of corpses.
Richly adorned with all the ornaments of amorous grace, with noose and goad raised in her hands,
she possesses the splendor of thousands of millions of suns and a face resembling ten million moons.
She possesses the beauty of ten million Gaṇeśas, she is the destroyer of enemies like ten million Viṣṇus;
she is a lotus to the forest fire of ten million Dāvas, and she has a fierce form like ten million Rudras.
As deep as the limit of the ocean, possessing great strength like the limit of the wind,
as vast as the limit of space, she causes terror to the limit of Yama.
She is as high as ten million Mount Merus and bestows the prosperity of ten million hosts;
she is without a single coin, without support, devoid of qualities, and free from attributes.
Aśokā, free from sorrow and devoid of the threefold affliction;
Vasiṣṭhā, the mother of the universe, known as Viśvā, the nourisher of the universe; Citrā, whose limbs are wonderfully variegated, the source of all causes, the Sovereign of the Kula.
She of the pure smile is the power of will, the power of knowledge, and the power of action.
Pure, consisting of mindfulness, truthful, having the form of sacred revelation, and beloved of sacred revelation;
composed of great being, she is the essence of all beings, standing beyond the five elements.
Pārvatī, daughter of Himavat, she who stands on the further shore, whose form is the beyond;
Jayantī, Bhadrakālī, Ahalyā, the mistress of the lineage.
She is the sustainer of all beings, the mistress of beings, the abode of beings, and the creator of beings;
she is the power of the great Kuṇḍalinī, who increases great prosperity.
She has eyes like a swan, she is the form of a swan, she dwells upon a swan, and she possesses the form of a swan;
she resides in the center of the moon, sun, and fire, and she dwells within the circle of jewels.
She dwells upon a twelve-petaled lotus, resides within the solar disc,
is stainless, possesses the luster of the moon, and inhabits a sixteen-spoked [lotus].
Ḍākinī, Rākinī, Lākinī, Kākinī,
as well as Śākinī and Hākinī— these are the ones who dwell in the six cakras.
She who brings about creation, maintenance, and destruction; she who effects creation, preservation, and end;
she whose dear heart and throat belong to Śrīkaṇṭha; she known as Nandā; she who wears a garland of *bindus*.
The support of the sixty-four arts, resting upon the staff of the body,
she is Māyā, Kālī, Dhṛti, Medhā, Kṣudhā, Tuṣṭi, and Mahādyuti.
Hiṅgulā, Maṅgalā, Sītā, she who moves through the center of Suṣumṇā,
Paraghorā, Karālākṣī, Vijayā, and Jayadāyinī.
Dwelling in the lotus of the heart, she roars with terrifying and most formidable sounds;
born from the Liṅga of Space, she resides in the garden of the worlds.
She is both great and subtle, a skeleton-like form, terrible in appearance, and possessed of great strength;
born from the womb of Menakā, she resembles molten gold.
Abiding within, she is the seed-syllable of the peak, dwelling on the mountain of the three peaks;
she is called the phoneme, yet devoid of phonemes, and the divider of the fifty phonemes.
She is the Vidyādharī, the Sustainer of the World, the Apsaras, and the beloved of the Apsarases;
she is Initiation, the Daughter of Dakṣa, the Skillful One, and the Destroyer of Dakṣa’s Sacrifice.
Yaśasvinī and Yaśodā, born from the womb of Yaśodā;
Devakī, the mother of the gods; and Rādhikā, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa.
Arundhatī, Śacī, Indrāṇī, Gāndhārī, Gandhamālinī;
she who transcends meditation, she who is attainable through meditation, she who knows meditation, and she who upholds meditation.
Lambodarī, Lamboṣṭhī, Jāmbavantī,
Jalodarī, Mahodarī, Muktakeśī, and she who grants the attainment of liberation, desire, and wealth.
An ascetic devoted to austerity, possessing beautiful wings, dwelling in righteousness, bearing arrows and a bow, steadfast, a princess of Pañcāla, and fond of the fifth [note].
She whose limbs are secret, she who is most formidable, the essence of the secret, the stainless one;
bodiless yet residing within the body, she is the one who carries one across the ocean of saṃsāra.
Amṛtā, Niṣkalā, Bhadrā, Sakalā, Kṛṣṇapiṅgalā,
Cakrapriyā, Cakrāhvā, and Pañcacakrādidāriṇī.
Resembling a ruby and resembling the stainless sky,
she dwells below and has an upward form, residing within the upper lotus.
She is eternally established in the nature of cause and effect;
she is the knower of taste situated within the midst of tastes, abiding in fragrance and possessing the form of fragrance.
She is of the nature of the Supreme Brahman and dwells within the Supreme Brahman;
she is of the nature of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman), yet she resides in sound while being devoid of sound.

She is accomplishment, intellect, and supreme consciousness; she is the radiant one abiding in the center. She is the secret power of Śambhu, established in the principles (tattva) and having the nature of the principles.
She is the eternal Mother of Beings, beloved by the Lord of the Great Elements;
she is the pure preta, the accomplishment of Dharma, the increase of Dharma, and the unconquered one.
She who kindles desire, she who is ever fond of curiosity,
she who wears a mass of matted hair, she who is liberated, subtle, and adorned with the Śakti.
Clad in a leopard skin, wearing rags and bark garments,
she holds a trident and a *ḍamaru* drum, and is adorned with a garland of human heads.
She is of exceedingly fierce form and terrible, resembling the fire at the end of an aeon;
she is the accomplisher of the three worlds, the one to be attained, and she is affectionate toward those who seek spiritual perfection.
She consists of all knowledge, she is the essence, and she is the destroyer of the Asuras;
she is the subduer, the binder, the self-controlled, the compassionate, the milch-cow, and the one difficult to overcome.
Terrible like tongues of fire, with faces most horrific and even more horrific than the terrible,
she is Nārāyaṇī, she is Nārasiṃhī, and she dwells within the heart of Nṛsiṃha.
She is the Mistress of Yoga, the Embodiment of Yoga, the Mother of Yoga, and the Yoginī;
she is Khecarī, Khacarī, and Khelā, taking her refuge in the state of Nirvāṇa.
She is the female serpent, the daughter of the Nāgas, beautifully attired, and the leader of the Nāgas;
she blazes with the flames of poison and is adorned with a hundred artistic ornaments.
She has fierce faces and great faces, she who bears ten million serpent-hoods;
she is a being of great essence, a knower of the Dharma, and the bestower of supreme bliss through the Dharma.
She has a black head, a great head, and a terrible head; she possesses a beautiful face.
She is intoxicated by all the senses and the mind, and she consists of all the senses and the mind.
She bestows victory in all battles, she is intent upon every weapon,
she pacifies all afflictions, and she wards off all misfortunes.
Born from all sovereignty, the destroyer of all seizing spirits,
Mātaṅgī, the intoxicated Mātaṅgī, whose beloved maṇḍala is Mātaṅgī.
She dwells in the midst of the ocean of nectar, adorned with waist-bands;
she dwells in the midst of the ocean of nectar, wearing garments of coral and holding a lotus.
Seated in the center of a circle of jewels, her face slightly smiling,
she is Kumudā, Lalitā, Lolā, with eyes as red as lac.
Clad in the directions, she is the messenger of the gods and the supreme deity of the God of gods;
mounted upon a lion, she dwells on the Himalayan mountains.
Laughing with a loud, piercing laugh, she is formidable, the destroyer of the terrible Daityas;
she possesses the luster of extremely fierce red garments and is adorned with serpent-bracelets.
Adorned with strings of pearls, possessing lofty and full breasts,
having the form of red lotus petals, and with eyes rolling from intoxication.
She is the embodiment of all deities, the destroyer of the enemies of the gods;
she wields a sword, holds a trident in her hand, possesses a discus, and wears a garland of discs.
She holds a conch, a bow, an arrow, and a thunderbolt, and wields a vajra-staff;
she dwells in the midst of the ocean of bliss and is adorned with waist-bands.
Her limbs are radiant with various ornaments and adorned with diverse jewels;
she is the source of joy for the world and possesses the qualities of the wish-fulfilling gem.
The fourth state, who is bowed to by the three worlds, whose form consists of consciousness and bliss;
the goddess who gladdens the three worlds and destroys suffering and evil dreams.
It pacifies the burning of terrible fires, accomplishes kingdoms, deities, and wealth;
it destroys heaps of great offenses and removes the fear of great thieves.
Free from defects such as passion and the like, devoid of old age and death,
she dwells in the center of the lunar disc and is born from the ocean of nectar.
The Goddess is praised by all the gods and saluted by all the Siddhas;
she is the embodiment of inconceivable power, a great jewel, mantra, and medicinal herb.
There is a young girl composed of well-being, who dwells on the Malaya mountain;
she is the sustainer, the creator, and the destroyer, the knower of delight, and the bestower of delight.
She is Rudrāṇī, possessing the form of Rudra, the destroyer of the suffering caused by Rudra’s wrath;
she is all-knowing, knower of Dharma, knower of the essence of things, and compassionate toward the distressed.
Unstruck, three-eyed, free from burden, supreme bliss;
the supreme Ghorā, with fierce eyes, the wise one who bestows the highest excellence.
She is the letter of mantra, accessible through mantra, the garland of mantras, and the one possessing excellent mantras;
she is the bliss of faith, the greatly auspicious, free from duality, and whose nature is beyond the qualities (guṇas).
Dharaṇī, Dhāriṇī, Pṛthvī, Dharā, Dhātrī, Vasundharā—
she whose stability rests between Meru and Mandara, the beloved of Śaṅkara.

The illustrious one, the embodiment of glory, the most excellent, the bestower of fortune, the evoker of devotion; the giver of prosperity, the possessor of splendor, the abode of Śrī, the auspicious lady, and the refuge for those who possess prosperity.
Umā, Sāraṅgiṇī, Kṛṣṇā, Kuṭilā,
Kuṭilālakā, Trilocanā, Trilokātmā, Puṇyā, and Puṇyā are proclaimed as her names.
She is the nectar, whose resolve is truth; she is both real and unreal, the piercer of knots.
She is the Supreme Lord, the ultimate goal to be attained, the supreme knowledge, higher than the highest.
She of beautiful limbs, golden-hued, saluted by gods and asuras;
she is the mother of progeny, auspicious, and the bestower of abundance in wealth and grain.
Īśānī, Bhuvaneśānī, Bhavānī, Bhuvaneśvarī;
she who is honored by the infinite and the infinite, the essence of the world, and the source of the world’s existence.
Her nature is inconceivable, yet her power is conceivable; she possesses both a conceivable and inconceivable form.
She is accessible through knowledge, the embodiment of knowledge, the knower, and she abounds in wisdom.
She is black, of terrible form, a stream of nectar, the bearer of nectar;
she belongs to the sun, is radiant, the source of fear, and rests upon the sun’s eye.
Anasūyā, Kṣamā, Lajjā, Durlabhā, Bharanātmikā,
Viśvaghnī, Viśvavīrā, Viśvaghnī, and Viśvasaṃsthitā.
Established in morality, having the form of morality, moral, and bestowing morality;
she is the awakener, skilled in awakening, the restrainer, and likewise the bringer of enlightenment.
She is the illuminator of knowledge, whose nature is manifold, resembling a mass of lightning;
she is the source of the universe, the great source, the source of karma, and whose essence is love.
Rohiṇī is the pacifier of disease, the remover of great maladies and fevers;
she is the giver of essence and nourishment, the embodiment of nourishment, the bestower of honor, and beloved by humanity.
She who carries a dark body, she who is dark, she who is the sister of Kṛṣṇa;
she who belongs to Śambhu, she whose form is Śambhu, she who dwells in Śambhu, and she who originates from Śambhu.
Viśvodarī, Mother of Yoga, Yogamudrādhna-yoginī,
Vāgīśvarī, Yoganidrā, she who is served by millions of yoginīs.
The Kaulika, the slow maiden, she who dwells on the seat of erotic passion (śṛṅgārapīṭha),
the bringer of security, she who possesses all forms, the one of divine form, and the naked one.
Smoke-faced, smoke-eyed, and smoke-haired, she is ashy-grey;
she is Pinākī, Rudravetālī, and possesses the form of a great Vetāla.
Tapinī, Tāpinī, Dīkṣā, Viṣṇuvidyā, Ātmanāśrītā, Mantharā, Jaṭharā, Tīvrā, Agnijihvā, and Bhayāpahā.
She is the slayer of beasts, the one in the form of a beast, the killer of beasts, and the one who carries beasts;
she is the yellow one, the mother, the wise one, and the destroyer of the bonds of beasts.
She is the radiance of the moon, the crescent of the moon, adorned with the splendor of the moon;
her entire body is marked with saffron, and her eyes are heavy with nectar.
The goddess wears white garments and holds a lute and a book;
she is supported by the elephant Airāvata and a stream of lotuses, and is seated upon a white lotus throne.
The Goddess wears crimson garments, her eyes are like red lotuses; she is the insurmountable one, the savior, Tārā, the youthful, whose form is luminous.
She is the stream of nectar, the knower of Dharma, and the instructor of the Dharma;
she is the Mistress of Fortune, worshipped by the Fortunate, the Sister, and the Sovereign of Fortune.
She whose form is the *bhaga*, who is moistened by the *bhaga*, the womb of the *bhaga*, the bestower of the *bhaga*;
the Mistress of the *bhaga*, she who is to be worshipped through the *bhaga*, the sister, and the Leader of the *bhaga*.

The Mistress of the *bhaga*, whose form is the *bhaga*, whose secret is the *bhaga*, who brings forth the *bhaga*; she whose belly is the *bhaga*, who delights in the *bhaga*, who abides in the *bhaga*, and who is adorned with the *bhaga*.
She is the power that agitates all, as well as she who causes all to dissolve;
she is Mālinī, Mādhavī, Mādhvī, she whose form is honey, and she who is exceedingly fierce.
Bharuṇḍacandrikā, Jyotsnā, Viśvacakṣus,
Tamopahā, Suprasannā, Mahādūtī, Yamadūtī, and Bhayaṅkarī.
She is the intoxicating one, of great form, of divine form, worshipped by the gods;
she is the embodiment of consciousness, eternal, moist, and exalted by the intoxication of desire.
She who is the bliss of wine and absolute liberation, whose eyes are like wine, languid with intoxication;
the Sovereign of the Siddhas, the perfected lore, the primordial Siddha, and the source of all Siddhas.
She is the perfection of accomplishments, the mother of all that is accomplished, and the success that bestows the fulfillment of all aims;
she is composed of mind, transcends the qualities (guṇas), and has the nature of the supreme light.
She is the supreme lord, the supreme goal, the supreme shore, the supreme perfection, and the supreme destination;
she is stainless, the enchantress, the primordial one, and devoted to the drinking of honey.
She is the mother of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, proficient in all scriptures;
she is the knowledge that embodies all the gods and likewise embodies all the scriptures.
The Goddess consists of all knowledge; the Sovereign consists of all phenomena;
she is the sacrifice consisting of all sacrifices, and she holds authority over all mantras.
The Goddess who is the foundation of all prosperity, the supreme one who draws in all,
the agitator of all, and the bringer of all auspiciousness.
The goddess who attracts the three worlds, the goddess who causes all delight,
the goddess who utterly deludes all, and the goddess who causes all to be paralyzed.
The Goddess who causes the three worlds to yawn, likewise she who brings all under her control;
the Goddess who delights the three worlds, the bestower of all prosperity;
the Goddess who consists of all mantras, she who brings about the destruction of all dualities.
The Goddess who bestows all accomplishments, the Goddess who grants all prosperity,
the Goddess who makes everything dear, and the Goddess who brings about all auspiciousness.
The Goddess who bestows all desires, who liberates from all suffering,
who pacifies all death, and who destroys all obstacles.
The Mother is beautiful in all her limbs, the bestower of all good fortune,
omniscient, omnipotent, and the granter of the fruit of all sovereignty.
The Goddess consists of all-knowledge, she is the destroyer of all diseases,
her very nature is the support of all, and likewise she is the remover of all sins.
The Goddess consists of all bliss, she is the very embodiment of universal vision;
she is the Vidyā consisting of all Lakṣmī, the bestower of the fruits of all desires.
She who pacifies all calamities, bestows supreme bliss, resides in the triangle,
exists in three places, consists of three measures, and is established in a triple body.
She is the triple-confluence, the threefold path, the one abiding in the three, the triple-formed, and the sovereign of the three cities;
she is the mistress of the three luminaries, the presiding deity of the thirty [gods], and the dweller in the three cities who is threefold.
She is the knowledge of the three Vedas, the three-headed, the one belonging to the three worlds, and the one with three lotuses;
she resides within the three cavities, is threefold, is Tripura, and has the three cities as her essence.
Tripurāśrī, the mother of the three worlds, Tripurā, Tripurasundarī—
this is the thousand-name hymn (sahasranāma) of Tripurasundarī.
O son, this which is more secret than the secret has been proclaimed for your delight;
it must be guarded with effort and recited with diligence.
There is no merit greater than this; there is no austerity greater than this;
there is no hymn of praise greater than this; there is no goal higher than this.
This hymn called the *Sahasranāma*, which has issued from my mouth—
whosoever, being self-restrained and devoted, should recite it or listen to it with a concentrated mind.
One seeking liberation attains liberation; one seeking heaven shall reach heaven;
one desiring pleasures shall obtain pleasures; and one seeking wealth shall acquire wealth.
One who desires knowledge obtains knowledge; one who desires fame obtains fame;
one who desires a daughter obtains a daughter; and one who desires a son obtains a son.
A pregnant woman shall give birth to a son, and a maiden finds a virtuous husband;
even a fool obtains sacred learning, and even the lowly attains a higher state.
Especially on the day of the sun's transit,
on the new moon, the eighth day, the full moon, the fourteenth day, the ninth day, and on Tuesday.
Whether one recites it, causes it to be recited, or listens to it with a concentrated mind,
one is liberated from all sins and becomes equal to Kāmeśvara.
Possessing fortune and righteousness, he shall be beloved by all women;
the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile, will swiftly come under his control.
Just as the gods fled upon seeing Rudra, and the Dānavas upon seeing Viṣṇu;
just as serpents flee upon seeing Garuḍa, and elephants upon seeing a lion— so too do they flee like insects at the mere sight of his face.
For such a person, fear of fire or thieves shall never arise.
Various sins are pacified by that which is equal to Mount Meru;
therefore, one should listen to it, whereby obstacles are consumed like grass offered into a fire.
By reciting it even once, the destruction of all sins shall occur;
by reciting it ten times, perfection of speech is produced.
By reciting it even a hundred times, a man becomes a sky-walker (khecara);
he who recites it ten thousand times with a devoted mind [attains the same].
p. 190) O son, when a hundred thousand [recitations] are complete, the Mother, the nurse of the worlds, will certainly become manifest to the wise man who recites this king of hymns.
Freed from the bonds of worldly existence, he is equal to me; of this there is no doubt.
By reciting [this] even once, a person obtains the merit that is found in all sacred fords (tīrthas).
Whatever has been proclaimed in all the Vedas, that fruit is fully described:
having become powerful, O son, and possessed of wealth, one shall possess all prosperity.
At the end of the body, he will go to the supreme state, which is difficult even for the gods to attain;
there is no doubt that this occurs through the recitation of the King of Hymns.
Thus ends the Thousand-Name Hymn of Mahātripurasundarī, the Ṣoḍaśī, in the venerable Vāmakeśvaratantra, in the dialogue between Hara and Kumāra.
