having performed the morning duties and so forth, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with the mantra as follows:
Having drunk water with the three syllables—the seed-mantras of Lakṣmī, Māyā, and Kūrca—the practitioner [attains success].
Having wiped the lips with the Vāgbhava [syllable], one should wipe them twice with the two Māyā [syllables].
One should wash the hands with the *kūrca* and perform the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*) with these mantras.
With the syllables of Śrī Māyā, Kūrca, Vāk, Kāma, Tripuṭā, and Bhaga.
And with the *kāmakalā* and the *aṅkuśa*, [one should touch] the mouth, nose, eyes, and ears.
By touching the navel, heart, head, and shoulders, one becomes Śambhu in an instant.
Having sipped water (ācamana) in this manner, O Chinnamastā, one beholds her within a year;
thereafter, having performed the regulation of breath (prāṇāyāma), one should perform the sixfold ritual placement (ṣoḍhānyāsa).
At the end of the sixfold mantra, one should perform [the rite] that brings the three worlds under control.
Likewise, with the Śrī-bālā, Tripuṭā, Yoni, Prāsāda, and Praṇava [mantras].
[One should worship] with the Kālī-vadhū-aṅkuśa [mantras] and the Kāmakaḷā-kūrca-astro-mantras in due order.
The sixteenth [verse] consists of eighteen syllables, distinct from the syllables of the [preceding] mantra.
With these seed-syllables, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the letters of the alphabet upon their respective locations.
This is indeed proclaimed as the sixfold seed-syllable, which is of the nature of Brahman.
Indeed, by renouncing this, all indeed become vajra-bodies.
For they are endowed with all sovereignty and are liberated while living for ten years.
Then follows the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Ṛṣis and others.
For this mantra, Bhairava is the seer (ṛṣi), Samrāṭ is the meter (chandas), Chinnamastā is the deity (devatā),
the two *hūṃ* syllables are the seed-syllable (bīja), and *svāhā* is the power (śakti). Its application (viniyoga) is for the attainment of desired goals,
as follows:
Salutation to Bhairava the Ṛṣi on the head;
salutation to Samrāṭ the Chandas on the mouth;
salutation to the deity Chinnamastā on the heart; salutation to the seed-syllable Hūṃ Hūṃ on the private parts.
To the feet, Svāhā-Śakti, obeisance.
Then follow the ritual assignments (nyāsa) for the hands and limbs:
"Oṃ āṃ, svāhā to the sword-like limb, the heart," [is recited] over the two little fingers. "Oṃ īṃ, svāhā to the sword-like limb, the head," [is recited] over the two ring fingers.
*Oṃ ūṃ suvajrāya śikhāyai svāhā*—thus on the two middle fingers.
*Oṃ aiṃ pāśāya kavacāya svāhā*—thus on the two index fingers. *Oṃ auṃ aṅkuśāya netratrayāya svāhā*—thus on the two thumbs.
Oṃ āḥ surakṣa rakṣa asurakṣāya astrāya phaṭ—thus [one recites] over the palms and the backs of the hands;
likewise for the heart and other [limbs].
As it has been said in the Bhairavatantra:
First, one should utter the letter Ā, marked at its head with a bindu.
"To the sword, to the heart—svāhā! thus it is joined in the smaller [mantra].
And then, O Goddess, the syllable *īṃ*, possessing a radiance equal to ten million moons.
Then [the mantra] for the limbs of bliss should be recited, and immediately after that, for the head.
Then, joined with "svāhā," it should be recited while the fingers are held as a purifier (pavitra).
And then the syllable Oṃ should be uttered, its head marked with a bindu.
Then "Suvajrāya" should be recited, and immediately after that, "Śikhāyai."
Immediately after that, one should place "svāhā" at the end and in the middle.
Thereafter, one should also install the goddesses known as the twelve Mātṛkās.
Having uttered "pāśāya," one should then recite "kavacāya."
One should place the mantra ending in *svāhā* within the middle fingers immediately thereafter.
And then, O Goddess, the syllable Oṃ, and immediately after that, the goad.
Ending with "netratrayāya svāhā," [one should assign the mantras] to both hands at the thumbs.
The letter *a* ending in *visarga*, joined with *surakṣā-rakṣas-ayya*;
then the letter *aḥ* joined with *surakṣā-yas-ayya*, followed by the word *astrāya*.
One should place [the mantra] joined with the six syllables upon both hands.
In the heart, at the head, at the crest-lock, in the armor, and in the circle of the eyes.
This continues as far as the weapons in the four cardinal directions and the intermediate directions, respectively;
such is the statement of Bhairava in the Triśaktitantra.
One should first utter the Praṇava, followed by the letter Ā combined with the Bindu.
From such statements as these, the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the syllable *praṇava* upon the limbs of the hands is established.
Then, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) three times with the root mantra, from the head down to the feet, or from the feet up to the head.
Then, one should meditate on a meditation (dhyāna) within one's own navel: a white, half-open lotus;
and in the center of that lotus-bud is the mandala of the fiercely radiant one (the sun).
Resembling the hibiscus flower, it is like the red bandhūka.
It is adorned with lines of rajas, sattva, and tamas, and embellished by the circle of the womb.
In the center, however, is that great goddess, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns.
In her left hand, she holds her own severed head.
The goddess has her mouth wide open, repeatedly licking the tip of her tongue.
She was drinking streams of blood issuing from her own throat,
with her mass of hair disheveled and adorned with various flowers.
And in her right hand she holds a flaying knife, adorned with a garland of severed heads.
She is naked, extremely fierce, and stands in the pratyālīḍha posture.
The goddesses wore garlands of bones and had serpent-skins as their sacred threads.
And practitioners of mantra always meditate upon her who is above the desire for pleasure.
Always sixteen years of age, with full and elevated breasts.
When one is attached to perverse passion, one should meditate upon Rati and Manobhava.
Joined with Ḍākinī and Varṇinī through the union of the left and right [channels].
She is drinking the stream of blood gushing from the throat of the Goddess.
She was dark-complexioned, red-eyed, gentle, with loose hair and clad in the directions as her garment.
Holding a skull-cup and a chopper in her hands, through the union of the left and right [hands].
She was richly adorned with a serpent as a sacred thread, appearing as if composed of blazing radiance.
Standing in the pratyālīḍha posture, she is adorned with various ornaments and garments.
Always twelve years of age and adorned with a garland of bones.
On the left side, however, [he sees] the Ḍākinī, who resembles the fire of the Kalpa-ending sun.
She has matted locks of lightning, three eyes, and rows of teeth like a flight of cranes.
Her face was terrifying with bared fangs, and her breasts were full and elevated.
The Great Goddess, most terrible, with disheveled hair and naked.
She has a large tongue that lolls out and is adorned with a garland of severed heads.
Holding a skull-cup and a chopper in her hands through the union of the left and right [hands].
[He saw her] drinking the streams of blood spurting from the limbs of the goddess.
With a skull held in her hand, she was terrifying, yet more terrifying than the terrifying one.
While practicing these two, the wise one should meditate upon the Goddess.
The necessity of meditation is stated in the Tantra:
Whoever, having thus meditated upon Pracaṇḍacaṇḍikā, should worship her;
Immediately severing his head, the goddess drinks the blood.
"He drinks by means of that mouth"—this is the ellipsis. And thus:
"His own head, together with its skull, is filled with streams of blood."
Likewise, on the left arm, one should hold the extremely terrifying tongue that lolls out.
Thus it is stated in the Bhairavatantra; in that very same work:
"One should make the eastern petal white, and the southeastern one red in color."
The southern [direction] is black; thereafter, yellow, white, red, and white-and-black.
Then, one should make it yellow, situated in the middle of its pericarp.
In the middle of that, however, one should fashion the mandala of Caṇḍarocis.
The lines of rajas, sattva, and tamas are respectively red, white, and black.
Then, having placed the two Māyās together with the six-syllable mantra.
And one should surround the exterior of that wheel with a wall.
First red, then black, white, and yellow, in due order.
It was provided with four gates and presided over by guardians of the field.
This is its worship diagram (*pūjāyantra*). Or, for example:
First, one should arrange a triangle, and in its center, three mandalas.
In the center of that, one should place the yoni, provided with three gates.
Then, there is an external eight-petaled lotus and again three earth-mandalas.
One should write the *kūrcabīja* (the seed-syllable HŪM) in the center of the triangle, accompanied by the syllable PHAṬ.
Alternatively, this is the yantra described in that very meditation.
And so it is stated:
Furthermore, O Goddess, listen as I shall explain [it] to you in due order.
One should meditate on a lotus in one's own navel, resembling a circle of the sun.
It is joined with the wheel of the womb and is designated as the triad of qualities.
Therein, in the center, the ascetic should meditate upon the Great Goddess Chinnamastā.
Having the form of a lamp-flame, she abides as non-dual.
She is joined with the *yonimudrā*, and her eye is fixed upon her heart.
Listen now to this object of meditation for ascetics and householders alike:
within one's own body, situated at the lotus of the navel.
Untainted, devoid of qualities, subtle, and possessing a luster like the crescent moon of the new moon day.
But she who is accessible through meditative concentration alone, and is enveloped by the three qualities.
She who transcends time, transcends the qualities, and bestows nothing but liberation.
Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, one should perform the installation of the conch (śaṅkhasthāpana) as in the case of Tāriṇī.
Then follows the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā).
Salutation to the Support-Power (Ādhāra-śakti); salutation to Primordial Nature (Prakṛti); to Kūrma; to Ananta; to the Earth;

to the Ocean of Milk; to the Jewel Island (Ratnadvīpa); to the Wish-Fulfilling Tree (Kalpavṛkṣa). Below that, salutation to the Golden Lion Throne; to the Root of Bliss (Ānanda-kanda); to the Power of Will (Sambidvalā).

Salutation to the Lotus whose essence is all reality; to the *sattva* [quality]; to the *rajas* [quality]; to the *tamas* [quality]; to the *Ātman*; to the *Antarātman*; to the *Parātman*; salutation to the *Jñānātman*, *hrīṃ*.
In the center of the lotus is she who is afflicted by passion and desire. According to the Bhairava system, however, there is the *Ādhāraśakti* and the *Kūrma*.
After that, the knower of mantras should worship the Nāgarāja, as well as the lotus stalk and the lotus.
The mandala should be square, consisting of the qualities of rajas and sattva. Having fully worshipped Rati and Kāma, one should perform the worship of Śakti.

*Ratikāmopari vajravairocanīye dehi 2, ehi 2, gṛhṇa 2, mama siddhiṃ dehi 2, mama śatrūn māraya 2, karālike hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.* This is the *pīṭha-mantra*; one should worship everywhere with this mantra, preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*. Having meditated again, one should invoke [the deity].
O you who are described as the bestower of all accomplishments, O Ḍākinī of all accomplishments, O Vajravairocanī, bring [them] here, bring [them] here!
Having again uttered that mantra, having invoked [the deity] with the words "Stay here! Stay here! Be present here!

Be firmly established here!", and having performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breaths) with "Oṃ Ā Hrīṃ Kroṃ Haṃ Saḥ," one should perform the six-limbed (*ṣaḍaṅga*) ritual with "Oṃ Āṃ, svāhā to the heart, the possessor of the six limbs," and so forth.

Having performed the worship according to one's capacity and having made the offerings, one should present the *bali*. Thus: "O Vajravairocanī, give, give! Come, come! Seize, seize! Grant me success in the *bali*! Slay, slay my enemies! O Karālikā, hūṃ phaṭ svāhā! With this mantra, [one should offer] to the right of the Goddess.

Oṃ, salutation to Varṇinī on the left; Oṃ, salutation to Ḍākinī [on the right]. Then, having worshipped the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) upon the body of the Goddess, one should worship the Śaṅkhanidhi with "Oṃ, salutation to Śaṅkhanidhi" on the right, and the Padmanidhi with "Oṃ, salutation to Padmanidhi" on the left.
One should worship Lakṣmī, Lajjā, Māyā, and Vāṇī in the cardinal directions starting from the east. In the intermediate directions—

One should worship Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Īśvara, with Sadāśiva in the center, everywhere using the *praṇava* at the beginning and *namaḥ* at the end. Then, having offered five handfuls of flowers, one should worship the enclosures (*āvaraṇas*). [One should worship] in the southeast, northeast, southwest, northwest, in the center, and in the cardinal directions with "Oṃ."

Having worshipped the six limbs with "Ā Khaḍgāya hṛdayāya svāhā" and so forth, one should worship on the eight petals, starting from the east in order: *Oṃ hrīṃ Kālyai namaḥ*, likewise to Varṇinī, Ḍākinī, Bhairavī, Mahābhairavī, Indrākṣī, and Piṅgākṣī.
To Saṃhāriṇī [and so forth]. In all cases, one should worship with the *praṇava* (oṃ) at the beginning and *namaḥ* at the end. For example:
Ekānnāmā, Abhidhāṅkā, Kālī, Vvarṇinī, Ḍākinī, likewise Bhairavī preceded by "mahā" (Mahābhairavī), immediately after that Bhairavī, Indrākṣī, and then Sapiṅgākṣī.
She is the one who effects withdrawal. And the Śaktis are to be worshipped in order on the petals starting from the east.
Uttering the seed-syllable of modesty (*lajjābīja*) preceded by *praṇava* (*oṃ*) and ending with *namas*, [one should worship] in the center of the lotus:
*hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ namaḥ svāhā namaḥ*. To the right of the Goddess: *samrāṭchandase namaḥ*; to the left of the Goddess: *sarvavarṇebhyo namaḥ*; again to the right: *oṃ bījaśaktibhyāṃ namaḥ*.

On the tips of the lotuses, in the order starting from the east, one should worship Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Mahālakṣmī, everywhere using the *praṇava* at the beginning and *namaḥ* at the end. Then, in the four directions at the gates, [one worships] "Oṃ Karālāya namaḥ."
Salutation to Vikarāla; likewise, salutation to Atikarāla and Mahākarāla. As stated in the Bhairavīya:

"Karāla and Vikarāla are at the eastern gate; Atikarāla and Mahākarāla are in the west and north, respectively. Then, one should complete the ritual from the offering of incense (dhūpa) until the final dismissal (visarjana).

But in the rite of dismissal (visarjana), there is a distinction: having displayed the saṃhāra-mudrā and placed [the deity] within the añjali, [one exhales] through the left nostril, [visualizing the deity] mounted upon the yoni-mudrā and blazing like the flame of a lamp.
Like the moon in the dark fortnight, it gradually reaches a state of waning.

Having recited this mantra, one should cause Caṇḍaraśmi to enter [the disciple] with the words "On the northern peak," and so forth. Since this is a perfected *vidyā*, its preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) consists of one hundred thousand recitations. As for the offering of the sacrificial oblation (*bali*), however, it is according to the Bhairava tradition: the oblation should be offered at night with fish, meat, liquor, and the like. Or else—
With sweet offerings such as the drinking of honey and other displays of prosperity,
one should first utter the *praṇava* (Om), joined with the mantra that bestows all accomplishments.
Then the word *varṇinīye* should be uttered, followed by *sarvasiddhiprade*.
Then the name of the Ḍākinī should be recited, and after that, the name of the Goddess.
Then, immediately after this, one should say to this Bali: "Come, come!"
Then, having uttered "Seize! Seize!", immediately thereafter [attain] my accomplishment.
The illusion [mantra] "dehi dehi," followed by that [mantra] joined with "phaṭ svāhā."
Thus the bali-mantra has been fully explained; when this is worshipped, O Goddess of the Gods, it is honored. Thus ends the section on worship.
Then the Lord spoke this hymn:
"I praise the King of Hymns, the bestower of auspiciousness upon the daughter of Virocana."
At the navel is a white lotus, upon which shines the orb of the fierce-rayed sun;
therein, in its central third part, is the praised Chinnamastā, who bestows dharma, kāma, and artha, the sole essence of saṃsāra, and the mother of the three worlds, assuming a triple form.
I pay homage to Chinnamastā, the Yoginī who removes the fear of death, who is the mudrā of yoga. || 1 ||
Within that [lotus], there was not the great yoni-cakra, nor the radiant solar orb, red as a blossoming bandhūka flower, shining upon her face which is like a pure lotus.
In the midst of that,
I worship Him whose nature is like the splendor of ten million rising suns, seated upon the back of a beautiful woman who delights in the reverse act of sexual union with Pradyumna. || 2 ||

In her left hand she holds her own severed neck, and in her other hand a great sacrificial knife; she stands in the pratyālīḍha posture, clothed in the directions (naked), with her mass of hair disheveled,
drinking the streams of blood gushing from her own severed head— she who is supreme and equal to the rising sun.
She who shines with three eyes gleaming like the sky.
Except for her left [hand], she does not hold anything else;
she is of fierce form, loudly singing with streams of blood flowing from her deep throat, adorned with bones, and possessing a skull-topped lotus with a glittering knife.
Red in color, with hair slightly reddish, divested of garments,
possessing her own innate power (*ātmaśakti*), standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture with her thighs, her eyes bloodshot— the Yoginī, Yoganidrā. || 4 ||

Beholding her with garments as her directions, her hair disheveled, possessing a form as terrible as a mass of clouds at the end of an aeon, fierce, with formidable fangs, and with the brilliance of the tip of her flickering tongue darting from the cavity of her mouth;

With a pair of eyes flickering like lightning, possessing a terrifying form, and increasing [the power] of the Ḍākinī whose own throat has been instantly severed and whose blood flows from it—she who is like a serpent gliding upon the slope of the heart. || 5 ||

She whose lotus feet are placed upon the heads of Brahmā, Śiva, Viṣṇu, and others, and who is incessantly meditated upon at every step by the foremost of the lords of yogis and other perfected beings— she of inconceivable form.
In this cycle of existence,

I contemplate with my mind Chinnamastā— the essence of the world, the mother of the three realms, the most praiseworthy, the end of all that is desired, the bestower of what is sought, and the remover of the impurities of the Kali age.

I meditate with my mind upon that primordial Prakṛti for the complete accomplishment of all goals— she who, through her threefold nature, assumes the forms of Brahmā, Acyuta, and Śūlabhṛt (Śiva) as the transformations of the world consisting of the three guṇas, and who effects its creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
Men obtain gain at the pair of her smiling lotus feet. || 7 ||
I am devoted to the worship of union with the beloved woman of another; I am honored by the undertaking of the various dispositions of many people;
I am detached from the vulgar folk; I am established in Bhairavī; I am devoted to the feet of the Guru; I am Bhairava.
I am Śiva. || 8 ||
This hymn of great merit was spoken by Brahmā in ancient times;
it directly bestows all perfections and destroys even the greatest sins.
O Goddess, whether one recites this upon rising in the morning or even while in the presence of the Goddess, for such a person there shall be success that bestows all desired objects.
One will certainly obtain wealth, grain, sons, a wife, horses, elephants, the earth, great knowledge, and the eight supernatural powers (aṣṭasiddhi). // 11 //
In the forest of her own hips, adorned with a tiger skin; O you with protruding belly, who are short yet possess joints of indescribable beauty, and are graced by a garland of skulls;
O you who hold in your hand a scimitar as radiant as jasmine, bestowing knowledge upon wondrous women—at your feet [I bow].
O Mother, compassionate toward your devotees, O Mahāmāyā, let there be salutation unto you! || 12 ||
Thus ends the hymn to Chinnamastā.
Then the venerable Goddess spoke the armor-mantra (kavaca):
"Those various vidyās of Chinnamastā which have been told are well-guarded secrets."
O Lord of Life, with you as my protector, these have been heard and mastered by me. || 1 ||
Now I wish to hear the armor previously mentioned;
O Lord, let the armor named Trailokyavijaya be told.
Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, you who are saluted by all the gods; I shall proclaim the armor known as Trailokyavijaya, which deludes the entire universe. (3)
Consisting of all vidyās and directly bestowing victory over gods and asuras,
by its retention and recitation, the omnipresent Lord becomes a conqueror of the three worlds.
O Goddess of the Gods, because of its retention and recitation, Brahmā, Nārāyaṇa, and Rudra become the creator, the protector, and the destroyer of the worlds.
It should not be given to the disciples of others, especially to those who lack devotion;
it should be given to a devoted disciple who is dearer to one than even one's own life.
For the armor (kavaca) of the goddess Chinnamastā,
Bhairava is the seer (ṛṣi), Virāṭ is the meter (chandas), and the deity is Chinnamastakā.
The application for Trailokyavijayā and Muktā has been proclaimed.
May the syllable *oṃ hūṃ* protect my head, [and may] Chinnamastā, the bestower of strength, [protect me]. 8.
May the three-syllabled one, Hrīṃ Hrīṃ Aiṃ, protect the forehead and face;
may she, the naked one who bears a severed head and a sword, protect the eyes with Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Hūṃ Aiṃ.
May that Vidyā, beginning and ending with the Praṇava, protect the two ears forever:
*vajravairocanīye hūṃ phaṭ svāhā* for the eyebrows and so forth. (10)
May Chinnamastā, who bears a severed head and a chopper, protect my nose—O Vajravairocanīye, with the syllables of Śrī, Māyā, Kūrca, and Vāk, HŪṂ! 11.
"Hūṃ phaṭ svāhā" is the sixteen-syllable great vidyā, whose form is Brahman;
on her own side, she joyfully causes a young girl to drink a stream of blood.
May Chinnamastā, together with her own Śakti, protect the face at all times—she who holds a severed head and a sword, who is blood-red, and who grants the desires of the practitioner. (13)
May she, the fair-complexioned one, joined by the Ḍākinīs, protect me from all sides;
may Rāmā and the others protect my tongue, and may Lajjā and the others protect my throat. (14)

May the Vidyā beginning with *kūrcca* protect the heart; may the Vidyā beginning with *vāk* protect the pair of breasts; and may the Goddess of the Suras, the Vidyā encased by *ramā*, protect the two sides. (15)
May the Goddess Vidyā, naked and encased by Māyā, protect the region of the navel;
may the Goddess, encased by Kūrca, always protect the region of the back. (16)
May she who is encapsulated by the seed-syllable Vāk protect their midst, together with her Śakti;
[the mantra is]: *Īśvarī kūrca-vāgbīje vajra-vairocanīye hūṃ*. (17)
HŪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ! May the Great Vidyā Chinnamastā, whose radiance is equal to ten million suns and who is accompanied by her Śakti, always protect my two thighs. 18.
The syllable *hrīṃ hūṃ* is on the knees; *śrīṃ hraṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ* is the station of the *Ḍākinī*.
May she who abides in all vidyās and is eternal protect all my limbs forever. (19)
May the Yoginī Ekaliṅgā protect me from the eastern quarter;
may Ḍākinī and Śrī Mahābhairavī protect me in the south-east.
May Bhairavī protect [her] constantly in the southwest;
may Indrāṇī protect in the west; may Asitāṅgī protect in the northwest, and may she protect in the north.
May Saṃhāriṇī, together with her instrument, always protect [me] in the corner of Śiva;
thus may these eight powers, together with their instruments, protect [me] in the cardinal and intermediate directions. (22)
May *krīṃ krīṃ krīṃ* protect me in the east; may *hūṃ hūṃ* protect me in the southeast;
may *hrīṃ hrīṃ* protect me in the south; and may Kālikā protect me in the south.
May *krīṃ krīṃ krīṃ* protect in the southwest; may *hrīṃ hrīṃ* protect me in the west;
may *hrīṃ hrīṃ* protect in the northwest; and may *svāhā* always protect in the north. (24)
May Mahākālī, with sword in hand, always protect me in the northeast corner;
may Tārā, Māyā, Vadhū, Kūrca, and Phaṭkāra—the great mantra—protect me. (25)
May Tārā, bearing a sword and a knife, always protect me from the upper regions;
and may the virtuous Ekajaṭā, with the mantra *hrīṃ śrīṃ hūṃ phaṭ*, protect me in the netherworld.
May Tārā together with Mahānīla-Sarasvatī protect you in the sky.
Thus has been narrated to you the armor (kavaca) of the Goddess, which is the embodiment of mantras.
By holding and reciting this, the Lord Bhairava, known as Krodhabhairava, himself becomes the creator and destroyer of gods, demons, and the foremost of sages. (28)
By whose command the various Madhumatīs go to the abode of the practitioner, as do the Bhūtinīs and other Yoginīs, and the Yakṣiṇīs and other sky-farers (khecarīs). (29)
By the grace of that armor, they receive his command;
this very armor of the Supreme Brahman has been uttered from my own mouth. (30)

Having worshipped the Goddess with perfumes and other offerings, one should recite [the mantra] even once with the root-mantra; one shall thereby obtain the fruit of worship performed throughout an entire year. || 31 ||
One should wear it written on birch bark, or placed within a pill, or set in gold,
upon the right arm, or around the neck, or elsewhere.
Having become endowed with all sovereign powers, one shall bring the three worlds under one's control;
Lakṣmī shall dwell in one's home, and Vāṇī shall reside in the corner of one's mouth.
Weapons such as the Brahmāstra and others become harmless upon her body.
Whoever worships Chinnamastā without knowing this armor will quickly meet death by the stroke of a weapon. (34)
Thus ends the *Chinnamastā-kavaca*, named *Trailokyavijaya*, from the *Śrī-bhairava-tantra*, in the dialogue between Bhairavī and Bhairava. (p. 232)
Then Śrī Pārvatī, with a heart full of devotion, spoke: "I have properly heard from the lotus of your mouth the instructions regarding worship and other rites."
I now wish to hear about the heart of Chinnamastā.
Śrī Mahādeva said:
O beloved, dear as my own life, until this day I have not spoken of this to anyone;
yet, because you have asked, I shall tell it to you out of affection for you, my dear.

Om. Of this *Śrīcchinnamastā-hṛdaya-stotra-mantra*, Bhairava is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Samrāṭ is the meter (*chanda*), Chinnamastā is the deity (*devatā*), Hūṃ is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), Oṃ is the power (*śakti*), and Hrīṃ is the pin (*kīlaka*). Its application (*viniyoga*) is for recitation with the purpose of destroying enemies.
Oṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ; Oṃ hūṃ śirase svāhā; Oṃ hrīṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ; Oṃ klīṃ netratrayāya vauṣaṭ; Oṃ aiṃ kavacāya huṃ; Oṃ hūṃ astrāya phaṭ.
Thus is the ritual placement of the hands (*karanyāsa*). Now, the meditation (*dhyāna*): She has a reddish luster and red hair;
she holds a blood-stained flaying-knife upon her lotus-hand; she possesses the splendor of the dark night;
and she drinks from the thick, crimson stream of blood flowing from the severed head of her own body, from its sharp edge.

I meditate upon Chinnamastā, who resembles a fierce wind that scatters the mass of clouds of obstacles, who is served by hosts of Siddhas, whose eyes are like lotuses, and who destroys the demons with her deceptive sword. || 1 ||
I bow to the supreme goddess Chinnamastā, who holds a severed head, whose neck is covered by a mass of severed heads, and who is clothed in garments of fine linen. || 1 ||
For the sake of all prosperity, I worship Chinnamastā, the bestower of auspiciousness, whose lotus-feet are always served by the hosts of gods.
I bow to that Goddess Chinnamastā, who is born in every age for the sake of the yoga-sacrifice among sacrifices, and who is the destroyer of the Dānavas. 3.
I pay homage to Vairocanī, the one of excellent hips, who was magnified by Vāmadeva; she possesses the radiance of ten million suns and is adorned with eyes the color of lightning. 4.
I take refuge in the feet of that fierce Yoginī who repeatedly satiates the other Yoginīs with streams of blood gushing from her own throat.
I worship him, by whose single-syllable mantra *hūṃ* one who recites it with a concentrated mind causes his enemy to be reduced to ashes.
I bow to that Chinnamastā who, when a man afflicted by suffering correctly remembers the mantra *hūṃ svāhā*, cuts away his distress as if it were severed. 7.
I worship that Chinnamastā, by whose mere sidelong glance cruel spirits and other malevolent beings flee far away in an instant. (8)

May she who protects the surface of the earth, who possesses patience and freedom from anger, who is highly skilled, whose side is cleared of deceitful rogues, who is characterized by forbearance in cutting away [evil],
who has the gods as her excellent wings, who provides inexhaustible instruction for the subjects of the earth, and who is free from the senses— may she be victorious, may she be victorious!
Chinnamastā is the devourer of her enemies. || 9 ||

May Chinnamastā Karālī, the dark-hued Kali who cuts away the fragments of the impurities of the Kali age like the hand of a wielder, who illuminates the blue water-lilies of the gods with her light, and who strikes terror into the ranks of the demon hosts— triumph, triumph!
May the Goddess of Speech be auspicious— she whose majesty shines intensely as she sustains the world, whose splendor is manifested by supporting the powers of worldly existence and liberation,
and who illuminates the lotuses of the twice-born like the form of the sun.
Chinnamastā is Bhavānī. || 11 ||
O Mother, quickly take up this fierce and sharp sword to instantly sever my host of enemies; let it be so. Sever the heads of my wicked foes, and grant me my desired glory.
O Chinnamastā, forgive me. || 12 ||

She whose neck is severed, whose head is severed, who holds a severed skull and remains uninjured; she who brings about the welfare of the crushed, who is beautiful-eyed, and who is capable of covering the lords of the earth.
Vairocanī, of excellent gait, delighted by the offering of oblations;
she whose lotus-feet are worshipped with offerings, and who is fully honored by Vāsudeva. || 14 ||
Whoever, having risen at dawn, remembers these twelve names dear to Chinnamastā, their enemies shall perish. (15)
Remembering whom, all the hosts of gods immediately become ever enriched with prosperity;
having struck down the multitudes of their enemies, they take refuge with brightened faces and tranquil minds.
May that praiseworthy Chinnamastā—who is constantly resorted to by him who possesses such resolve, and who is herself served by Śrī, Īśa, and others—bear fruit most abundantly for you today. 16.
O Pārvatī, how can the enemy of one who desires to slay his foe without knowing this heart come to destruction before long? (17)
If a person desires the swift destruction of an enemy, they should recite this;
Chinnamastā, being well-pleased, bestows the desired fruit. (18)
It pacifies enemies, is meritorious, bestows desired fruits, grants long life and health, and is a means of merit for those who recite it. (19)
Thus ends the Śrī Chinnamastā-hṛdaya-stotra, from the Śrī Nandyāvarta, in the dialogue between Mahādeva and Pārvatī.
(p. 234) Then, Śrī Pārvatī spoke the one hundred and eight names,
the supreme, auspicious thousand names dear to Chinnamastā.
O Śambhu, you have described the Sadyojāta [mantra], which instantly cuts down one's enemies. || 1 ||
Again I ask, O Lord, have mercy upon me:
what should a man do who is unable to recite the Thousand Names? (2)
"What does he recite, O Lord? Tell me that, O Compassionate One.
Śrī Sadāśiva said:
"He always recites the one hundred and eight names."

One certainly attains the fruit of reciting the Thousand Names. Om. Of this hymn of the one hundred and eight names of Śrī Chinnamastā, Sadāśiva is the seer (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandas), and Śrī Chinnamastā is the deity (devatā) for me.
The application is for the purpose of attaining all perfections during the recitation.
Oṃ! Chinnamastā, the Great Vidyā, the Most Terrifying, the Large-Bellied One;
Caṇḍeśvarī, the Mother of Caṇḍa, the Destroyer of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa. || 4 ||
She is Mahācaṇḍā, Caṇḍarūpā, Caṇḍikā, and Caṇḍakhaṇḍinī;
she is Krodhinī, Krodhajanani, Krodharūpā, Kuhū, and Kalā. || 5 ||
She who is afflicted by anger, possessed of anger, and the one who brings about the destruction of anger;
she is Vajravairocanī, Vajrā, Vajrakalpā, and Ḍākinī. || 6 ||
Delighting in the activities of the ḍākinīs, she is honored by the activities of the ḍākinīs;
she delights in the company of the ḍākinīs and is filled with love for the ḍākinīs. || 7 ||
She carries a skull-topped staff, she is short of stature, and she holds a sword and a skull-bowl;
she feeds on corpses, is accompanied by spirits, and dwells in the company of the deceased.
She carries severed heads, she who has cut through fierce spells, and she who is variegated;
she is of terrible form, of terrible gaze, of terrible roar, and thick-bellied.
The Yoginī is devoted to yoga and intent upon the sacrifice of recitation;
she consists of the circle of the womb, she is the womb, and she is the one who sets the circle of the womb in motion. || 10 ||
She is Yonimudrā, she who is to be approached through the yoni, and she who dwells within the mechanism of the yoni;
she is the form of the yantra, composed of the yantra, the mistress of the yantra, and worshipped by means of the yantra. || 11 ||
Kīrti, Kapardinī, Kālī, Kaṅkālī, Kalavikāriṇī, Āraktā, Raktanayanā, and she who is devoted to drinking blood. || 12 ||
Bhavānī, the bestower of prosperity, prosperity itself, the giver of prosperity, and Bhairavī;
she who is devoted to the conduct of Bhairava and is served by the Bhairavas and spirits. || 13 ||
The goddess Bhīmeśvarī is formidable, devoted to a terrible roar;
she is to be propitiated by Śiva, praised by Śiva, and the one who carries one across the ocean of worldly existence.
Bhadrakālī, she of auspicious body, of auspicious form, and the auspicious one;
she of auspicious form, Mahābhadra, Subhadrā, and Bhadrapālinī. (15)
She is of auspicious nature, with a beautiful countenance and a lovely face;
she is served by the Siddhas, the bestower of success, the source of all accomplishments, herself perfected, and attended by those who have attained perfection.
Bestower of auspiciousness, auspicious, pure, [yet] containing impure beings, bringing about the auspicious;
the supreme goddess consisting of vision, she is the one who effects the withdrawal of [false] views. || 17 ||
Śarvāṇī, she who goes everywhere, she who is everything, the performer of all auspiciousness;
Śivā, the peaceful one, whose form is peace, Mṛḍānī, who is afflicted by love. || 18 ||
Thus, O Goddess, this hymn most difficult to obtain has been told to you;
it is more secret than the secret, and must be concealed with great effort.
What is the use of speaking much more in your presence, O beloved of my life? O Goddess, [I have described] killing, enchanting, and thereafter, eradication.
Rites such as immobilization (stambhana), as well as supernatural powers and accomplishments, all are achieved without doubt by reciting this at the three times of day. || 21 ||

O fair-faced one, those best of men who, with undistracted minds and endowed with devotion, recite this most excellent hymn constantly as uttered by me, shall suffer no defeat at the hands of their enemies. (22)
Thus ends the hymn of one hundred and eight names of the illustrious Chinnamastā.
Then the Goddess spoke the Thousand Names:
"Speak, O God, Great God, you who are the best among those who know all the scriptures."
Have mercy, O Lord of the World; speak to me, O Master.
The goddess Pracaṇḍacaṇḍikā desires the welfare of all the worlds;
and everything concerning her—her hymn of praise, armor, and so forth—has been told.
O Lord of Gods, you who are affectionate toward your devotees, please graciously reveal to me now the auspicious thousand names of Chinnamastā.
Śiva said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the most enchanting [account] of Chinnā;
it must be guarded with great effort if one desires one's own welfare.
And this must not be spoken of anywhere, even when one's life-breaths have reached the throat;
listen to that, O Great Goddess, for I shall tell it all to you.
It is accomplished without worship, without meditation, and without recitation;
likewise, O Goddess, it is accomplished without meditation and without the purification of the elements and so forth.
Success shall come from mere recitation; this is the truth, the absolute truth, O fair-faced one!
Formerly, on the peak of Kailāsa, in the assembly hall of all the gods, [it was proclaimed].
(236) He asked: Listen, O fair-faced one, how it was told.

Of this *Śrīpracaṇḍacaṇḍikāsahasranāmastotra*, Bhairava is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Sammṛāj is the meter (*chandas*), Pracaṇḍacaṇḍikā is the deity (*devatā*), and its purpose is for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
This is the application for the recitation.
Pracaṇḍacaṇḍikā, Caṇḍā, Caṇḍadevī,
Avināśinī, Cāmuṇḍā, Sucaṇḍā, Capalā, and Cārudehinī.
With a lolling tongue, moving red, and a face resembling a beautiful moon;
with eyes like those of a cakora bird, she is fierce in her cries, restless, and intoxicating to the mind.
She is volition, the abode of consciousness, whose form consists of the knowledge of the digits of consciousness;
she is the goddess who causes great terror, yet she bestows boons and grants fearlessness.
She who is rich in compassion, whose very form is fearlessness, and who liberates one from the bonds of existence;
she is Bhavānī, the Sovereign of the World, and the one who carries one across the ocean of worldly rebirth.
She is the ocean of existence and the liberation from existence; she is the destroyer of the bonds of worldly life.
She is the Bhāgīrathī, she resides in the divine fortune, and she bestows the enjoyments of good fortune.
Kamalā, the bestower of desires, Durgā, who liberates from the bonds of difficulty;
she who is difficult to behold, who possesses an inaccessible form, who is hard to comprehend, and the destroyer of misfortune.
The Goddess is the eternal remover of the suffering of the wretched, the perpetual dispeller of grief,
eternally composed of bliss, and the constant bestower of auspiciousness.
She is the accomplisher of all aims, the very embodiment of all supernatural powers (siddhis),
the power that agitates all, and the supreme one who causes all to be enchanted.
She possesses the power to enchant all, her very nature is universal intoxication;
she is all-knowing, the bestower of accomplishments, and the embodiment of the knowledge of success.
She is both with parts and without parts, perfected, beyond parts yet consisting of parts;
she knows the Kula, possesses the form of the Kula, and bestows the bliss of vision.
She is of noble birth, capable of assuming any form at will, and enchanting;
she dwells within the lotus, has a face like a lotus, and possesses the gait of a lordly elephant.
Kularūpā, Koṭarākṣī, the bestower of the sovereignty of Kamala;
Kuntī, Kakudminī, Kullā, Kurukullā, and Karālikā.
She is the Mistress of Desire, the Mother of Desire, the liberator from the torment of desire;
she is the embodiment of desire, the essence of desire, and the creator of the wonder of desire.
She whose heart is compassion, whose form is the mantra *krīṃ krīṃ*, the hollow one, the mace-bearer,
the night-lotus, she who is absolute liberation, and she who dwells in the lineage.
She who possesses beautiful hair, she who is worshipped by Keśava, she who is the destroyer of the Daitya Keśin;
she who removes affliction, she who is free from affliction, and she who annihilates the multitude of afflictions.
Karālī has a terrifying mouth; she is the destroyer of the Karāla asuras;
she bears a sword of formidable hide; she is the annihilator of the Karāla clan.
Wearing anklets and devoted to bracelets, she carries an excellent skull-cup;
with a sword in hand and three eyes, she holds a severed head and a blade.

She who destroys the wicked, the slayer of the wicked, she who flows, she who moves through the sky, she who is eternal, the Gaṅgā, she who is worshipped by Gautama, Gaurī, and she who dwells among the Gandharvas.
The goddess is worshipped by the Gandharvas in the sky, served by hosts of Gandharvas, the source of the sound of the Gaṇas, devoid of qualities yet the essence of all qualities.
She is the embodiment of virtue, the bestower of virtues, and the one who instills reverence for excellence;
she is the mother of Gaṇeśa, the profound, and the illuminator of the light of the sky.
She is fair-limbed, accessible at Gayā, and dwells in the abode of Gautama;
she is to be known as the beloved of Gadādhara, attainable through knowledge, and the sovereign lady of Guha.
She is Gāyatrī, possessed of qualities, beyond qualities, and the sovereign of qualities;
she is the goddess who is the mother of Gaṇeśa and the bestower of boons upon Gaṇeśa.
The eternal goddess is praised by the leader of the Gaṇas, worshipped by the leader of the Gaṇas;
she is the beloved of Girīśa, the goddess adored by Girīśa.
She is the giver of destinies, the destroyer of destinies, she who is sung of, she who was served by the Teacher Gautama,
she who is worthy of worship by the Guru, she who is united with the Guru, and she who is intent upon the service of the Guru.
She whose gateway is fragrance, who is rich in fragrance, whose essence is fragrance, and who creates fragrance;
she who is worshipped by the Lord of the Gods (Indra), and who bestows satisfaction upon the Lord of the Gods.
The beloved of the Lord of the Gods, she who is worshipped by the Lord of the Gods,
she who is to be served by the Lord of the Gods, and she who bestows joy upon the Lord of the Gods.
She is the power of song, accessible through song, and the bestower of the power of song;
she is the science of song, perfected in song, and her mind is delighted by song.
She who transcends song, who is sung in song, who is filled with the joy of song,
who is delighted by the lord of the Gandharvas, and who is adorned with the qualities of the Gandharvas.
She is served by the hosts of Gandharvas, she dwells in the midst of the hosts of Gandharvas;
she is skilled among the hosts of Gandharvas and is worshipped by the hosts of Gandharvas.
She delights in the hosts of Gandharvas and is adorned by the hosts of Gandharvas;
she has a gurgling voice, a terrible form, and makes a fierce *ghurghura* sound.
Born from drops of perspiration, having the nature of drops of perspiration;
sounding like a bell, possessing a deep resonance, having the form of a cloud, and having a belly like a cloud.
She is of terrible nature, the giver of dense [blessings], delighting in the sound of bells;
she is the fierce Caṇḍālinī, the formidable one, the destroyer of the most terrible and violent forces.
She is the subduer of terrible dānavas, the destroyer of terrible dānavas;
she is free from terrible deeds and the like, yet she is devoted to terrible deeds.
The Goddess consists of the terrible principle (ghoratattva), she is the liberator from the terrible principle;
she is devoid of terrible actions and the like, yet she is filled with terrible actions and the like.
She is devoted to terrible deeds and the like, she is the one who increases terrible karma;
she is the subduer of terrible spirits and the destroyer of terrible vetālas.
She is the subduer of terrible forest fires, the destroyer of formidable enemies,
endowed with fierce mantras, and worshipped with fierce mantras.
She whose mind is the formidable mantra, who bestows the fruit of the formidable mantra,
who is the treasury of the formidable mantra, and who has made her abode in the formidable mantra.
The Goddess Ghoramantreśvarī has her mind fixed on the meaning of the terrible mantra;
she knows the reality of the meaning of the terrible mantra and has reached the further shore of the meaning of the terrible mantra.
She is the manifestation of the meaning of the terrible mantras, the awakener of the meaning of the terrible mantras;
she is the collection of the meanings of the terrible mantras, the birthplace of the meaning of the terrible mantras.
Devoted to the recitation of the terrible mantra, intent upon the recitation of the terrible mantra;
she whose abode is the letter *ṅa*, adorned with the syllable *ṅa*.
She whose form is beyond the letter Ṅa, who embodies the syllable Ṅa;
she of variegated form, the multicolored channel, with beautiful hair and a radiant luster.
She is the restless one, appearing restless, beautiful in form, and fierce;
she consists of the four Vedas, she is the impetuous one, and she is adorned by hosts of Cāṇḍālas.
She who cuts down the outcastes, who eradicates fierce heat,
who possesses four arms, who has a fierce form, and who destroys Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa.
Candrikā, Candrakīrti, and likewise Candrakānti;
Candrāsyā, Candrarūpā, and she whose nature is like the moon-crested Lord.
She is the beloved of the moon-crested Lord, her mind is ever-satisfied by the moon-crested Lord;
she is the charming consort of the cakora bird’s kinsman, and she is worshipped by the kinsman of the cakora bird.
She whose form is the discus, who consists of the discus, whose very nature is the shape of the discus;
she who is beloved by the Discus-handed One (Viṣṇu), and who bestows affection upon the Discus-handed One.
She who possesses the supernormal knowledge of Cakrapāṇi, she who bestows boons upon Cakrapāṇi,
she who is intoxicated by the boon of Cakrapāṇi, and she whose very form is Cakrapāṇi.
Cakrapāṇīśvarī is eternally saluted by Cakrapāṇi;
she has arisen from Cakrapāṇi and is the locus of Cakrapāṇi’s virtues.
Candrāvalī, Candravatī, possessing a splendor equal to ten million moons,
her lotus-feet anointed with sandalwood paste, and her head adorned with sandalwood.
She of beautiful renown, of beautiful eyes, adorned with the beautiful moon;
she of beautiful ornaments, of beautiful attire, and the bestower of beautiful garments.
Her limbs are adorned with beautiful ornaments; she is the bestower of boons upon the four-faced one;
she is worshipped by the four-faced one; and she is the refuge of the four-faced one.
Caturvaktrā, Caturbāhā, Caturthī, Caturdaśī, Citrā, Carmaṇvatī, Caitrī, Candrabhāgā, and Campakā.
She has fourteen forms, she follows the fourteen Yamas,
she delights in the fourteen Yamas, and she is dear to the fourteen Yamas.
She who abides in deception, whose form is that of a flaw, the giver of illusion, the one with illusory streaks;
likewise Chinnamastā, the severed one, who bears a severed head.
She who bestows victory, whose form is victory, the victorious one, the deluder of victory;
she who is Jaya, who abides in life, and who dwells in Jālandhara.
Jvālāmukhī, the bestower of flames, resembling a fiercely blazing fire;
she who is venerated by the world, worshipped by the world, and devoted to the protection of the world.
The earth is the support of the world, the remover of birth, death, and old age;
she is the mother, the birthplace, the giver of birth, and the one who is ever-victorious.
She is the flame that removes the disease of fever, filled with garlands of flames;
she is the sovereign of the enemy of Jambha, who brings about the majesty of the enemy of Jambha.
She who is praised by the enemy of Jambha, she who destroys the enemies of the enemy of Jambha;
Jayadurgā, she who is to be propitiated for victory, Jayakālī, and Jayeśvarī.
Victory to Tārā! Victory to the Transcendent One! Victory to the beloved of Śaṅkara!
You are the giver of water, the daughter of Jahnu, and the one who causes terror to the ocean.
She who subdues the ocean of diseases, she who destroys the fever of the ocean;
the Mistress of the moving world, the remover of dullness, and the dispeller of the mass of stupor.
She transcends those seized by dullness, she is the dispeller of the disease of ignorance,
the giver of birth and the destroyer of birth, and she is accompanied by the sound of victory.
She who is united with the yoga of recitation, she who delights in the yoga of recitation;
she who is fond of the yoga of recitation, she who is to be recited, she who transcends recitation, and she whose sound is victory.
The wife abiding in the state of being a wife, she who fulfills the state of being a wife;
resembling the hibiscus flower, she who is worshipped with hibiscus flowers.
Delighted by the hibiscus flower, adorned with the hibiscus flower,
possessing a radiance like the hibiscus flower, and having the form of the hibiscus flower.
Jānakī, the daughter of Janaka, is the very embodiment of Jamadagni;
her limbs are released by the gale-force wind, and she dwells amidst the whistling of the storm.
She who utters the sound "jhaṅ," she who is like a violent storm, and Jhaṅkarī;
she whose essential nature is the anusvāra of the letter ña, and she who resounds with the "ṭavaṭṭ" sound.

She who utters the sound "ṭaṅkāri," she who speaks with the sound "ṭaku," she whose form is the syllable "ṭha," as well as Ḍiṇḍimā, Ḍimbhā, and she who resounds with the drum-like sound of "ḍiṇḍu-ḍiṇḍima."
She is composed of the ḍhakkā drum and consists of the sound of the ḍhila; she delights in the sounds of dance.
She is the ḍhakkā, the Mistress of the ḍhakkā, and likewise her form is the very sound of the ḍhakkā.
She who delights in the sound of the ḍhakkā drum, whose mind is satisfied by the sound of the ḍhakkā;
she who begins with the letter ṇa, who consists of the syllable ṇa, and whose essential nature is the primordial syllable ṇa.
Tripurā is composed of the three cities, possesses the three powers, and consists of the three qualities;
she is the dark one (Tāmasī), the sovereign of the three worlds, Tripurā, and the mistress of the triple Veda.
She who possesses the three knowledges, the three forms, the three eyes, and the three bodies;
she who delivers, she who is tremulous, she who is Tārā, and she who is worshipped by the enemies of the stars (the Asuras).
She is worshipped by the enemy of Tāraka, the bestower of boons upon the enemy of Tāraka;
she is the mother of the enemy of Tāraka, slender, youthful, and possessed of a tremulous luster.
She possesses the three forms, resides in the triple city, and holds the excellent trident;
she is the wielder of the trident, composed of the Tantra, and expert in the Tantric scriptures.
Her form is that of Tantra, her embodiment is austerity; she is the very nature of Tantra and Mantra, appearing like streaks of lightning, and bestowing the knowledge of reality.
The Goddess is the sovereign of the knowledge of reality, who rejoices in the knowledge of reality;
she consists of the triple Veda, is served by the triple Veda, possesses three syllables, and is the sovereign of the three syllables.
She is the destroyer of suffering, the one who uproots the multitude of afflictions;
she is the creator of fear, the remover of fear, the giver of protection, and the subduer of terror.
She is the mistress of lunar days, the embodiment of the lunar day, residing in the lunar day, and worshipped by the lunar day;
she is Tilottamā, the giver of sesame seeds, delighted by sesame seeds, and the sovereign of sesame seeds.
She consists of the three qualities, has the form of the three qualities, is the triple city, and has the triple city as her essence;
she is the triple peak, has the form of the triple peak, and dwells in the midst of the triple-peaked mountain.
She is Trijaṭā and Trinetrā, most beautiful with three eyes;
she is the third, three years of age, threefold, and the sovereign of the three measures.
She who dwells in the triangle, the mistress of the triangle, situated in the center of the triangular yantra;
she who is the three junctions (trisandhyā), worshipped at the three junctions, the three-footed one, and the foundation of the three-footed.
She who abides in her place, she who stands upon dry land, and she who dwells in the blessed region;
she whose form is the letter *tha*, and likewise she whose form is gross.
She has thick hands and is likewise stout; she reveals the form of steadfastness.
She is Durgā, the destroyer of the suffering of distress, and the liberator from the bonds of difficulty.
The Goddess is the destroyer of the Dānavas, the slayer of the lords of the Danujas;
she is the eternal bestower of wives and offspring, who bears half of Śaṅkara’s body.
She possesses divine limbs, she is the mother of the gods, and she is the destroyer of those who harm the gods;
she removes the suffering of the wretched and eradicates the affliction of the distressed.
The mother of the distressed, served by the distressed, the destroyer of the pride of the wretched;
the goddess who slays the Danujas, Devakī, beloved of the gods.
She who is fond of the water of the Danavas, she who is long, she who is worshipped by the water of the Danavas;
she who has a long voice, a long body, and who destroys long-lasting miserable rebirths.
Long-eyed, long-sighted, with long hair, she is naked;
she is dear to the sky-clad ones, self-controlled, and her very nature is that of the sky-clad ones.
She who is free from suffering, the remover of suffering, the one who carries one across the ocean of suffering;
she who pacifies the poverty of suffering, yet brings about the poverty of suffering.
She who bestows suffering, who is difficult to endure, whose sole nature is the refutation of the wicked;
she who is the left-hand path of the gods, who is served by the gods, and who bestows divine power.
Dāminī, beloved of Dāminī, more beautiful than a hundred Dāminīs,
served by hundreds of Dāminīs, adorned with garlands of lightning.
Content with the state of divinity, she stands in the midst of a hundred deities;
moist with compassion, she is the very form of compassion, and is wholly devoted to the giving of mercy.
The Goddess is compassionate by nature, whose essence is compassion, and who is established in an ocean of compassion;
she is the soul of the ten sciences and the very embodiment of the ten sciences.
She is the earth, the giver of wealth, the sustainer, the blessed one, intent on grain, the auspicious one;
she is the embodiment of Dharma, the most excellent, that which is to be attained, and the sphere of the wise.
She is the sovereign queen of the Lord of Dharma, whose form is the activity of Dharma;
she is the mistress of wealth, the science of archery, attainable through the bow, and the bestower of boons upon the wielders of the bow.
Virtuous in nature, sporting in the Dharma, and free from worldly religious duties;
a bestower of Dharma, devoted to the Dharma, and the destroyer of those who pervert the Dharma.
She is the mistress of Dharma, the embodiment of Dharma, and the bestower of boons upon the King of Dharma;
she abides in the house of Dharma, possesses the nature of Dharma, and is the very essence of both righteousness and unrighteousness.
Bestower of wealth, beloved of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera), bestower of abundance in riches and grain;
abiding place of abundance in riches and grain, and destroyer of [excessive] riches and grain.
Established in the Dharma, steadfast in the Dharma, always delighting in the path of the Dharma;
having made her abode in the seed of the Dharma, she is the excellent guardian of the seed of the Dharma.
She is the sovereign of the seeds of Dharma, the form of the seeds of Dharma, and she who moves within the Dharma;
she is born from the seeds of Dharma and rests upon the seeds of Dharma.
Praised by the lords of mountains at every breath,
she is the daughter of the lord of the great mountains and is herself worshipped by the lords of the earth.
Dwelling in the home of the lord of mountains, she is the protectress of the lord of mountains;
she is the destroyer of all the afflictions of the lord of mountains and the protector of Dharma.
She is ever-new, stainless, eternal, and worshipped by the king of mountains;
she is the Mistress of the Nāgas, the Mother of the Nāgas, the Daughter of the Nāgas, and the Naked One.
She is unstained, free from conceptual construction, hairless, and free from affliction;
she is without food, formless, and has the nature of the stainless.
She is the Nāginī, possessing the splendor of the nāgas, praised by the nāga kings;
she knows the qualities of the nāga kings and bestows happiness upon the nāga kings.
She who constantly goes to the world of the nāgas, who dwells in the world of the nāgas,
the sovereign of the nāga-world, the sister of the nāgas, and she who is worshipped by the nāgas.
Seated in the midst of nāgas, she causes agitation through the delusion of the nāgas;
she is fond of dance, possesses dancing, and is devoted to dance and song.
The Mistress of Dance, the Dancer, whose form is dance, she who is without support;
the Consort of Nārāyaṇa, dwelling among kings, wearing a garland of human skulls and bones.
She who always delights in human flesh, she who eternally delights in human blood;
the sovereign queen of men, she who possesses the form of a woman and whose very nature is that of a woman.
Worshipped by throngs of women, standing in the midst of women, clad in fresh garments,
she is Narmadā in the form of a river, situated at the confluence of rivers.
She who is well-pleased by Narmadeśvara, she whose form is Narmadeśvara;
Padmāvatī, lotus-faced, dwelling within the filaments of the lotus.
Dependent upon fine silken garments, adorned with rubies,
she is eternally bestowing supreme joy and dwells upon the seat of the hungry ghosts.
Intoxicated by the fullness of rasa, her beloved is overwhelmed with love;
she is purified by the wind from the sacred corpse, the supreme mistress who is one's own very self.
She is eternally devoted to her beloved vows, the bestower of supreme love;
she is fond of flowers, possesses the heart of a lotus, and dwells within the nature of the lotus.
She is the embodiment of the *Phetkāriṇī Tantra*, the one who roars like a jackal and a jackal-dog;
she is the flute-player, the one in the form of a courtesan, and Bagalā who possesses a form at will.
She is the earth consisting of speech, she who is to be approached with confidence, the excellent woman known as Vāgbhavā;
she is the giver of intellect, the embodiment of intellect, knowledge, and the very nature of debate.
She is the youthful one whose form consists of the aged; she is speech residing within words;
she is Varuṇā, the possessor of eloquence; she is the Heroine adorned with the ornaments of heroes.
Her feet are worshipped by Vīrabhadra, and she is the mother of Vīrabhadra;
she delights in the path of the Vedas, her form is the Vedic mantras, and she is fond of the syllable *vaṣaṭ*.
Vaishnavi is indeed associated with the playing of the lute, devoted to the playing of the lute,
possessing the resonance of the lute, and having the very form of the sound of the lute.
Devoted to the conduct of Vaiṣṇavas, intent upon the conduct of Vaiṣṇavas,
she is served by Viṣṇu, the wife of Viṣṇu, possessing the form of Viṣṇu, and having a beautiful countenance.
The sovereign of the universe, the mother of the universe, the creator of the universe;
she who is the form of the universe, the mistress of the universe, and the destroyer of the universe.
Bhairavī, worshipped by Bhairava, served by the Bhūtas and Bhairavas,
the mistress of Bhairava, likewise Bhīmā, she who grants satisfaction to the Lord Bhairava.
She is the beloved of Bhairavādhīśa, the protectress of Bhairavādhīśa;
she is Bhīmeśvarī, the mother of Bhīma, and she is devoted to the word "Bhīma."
She is of terrifying form, the mistress of the terrible, the formidable one who bestows the boon of fearlessness;
her lotus feet are worshipped by Bhīma, and she is the protector of Bhīma and Bhairava.
She is the destroyer of the demon Bhīma, the annihilator of terrible wickedness;
she is the one who exists in all worlds, the one worshipped by the universe, the source of existence, and the eternal bestower of prosperity.
She who bestows fearlessness and destroys fear, she whose form is fearlessness itself;
she who is unshakable amidst terrifying sounds, and the destroyer of fear and dread.
She is measured and yet appears intoxicated, possessing a nature like one frenzied with wine;
she is venerable, charming, and full of pride, auspicious and captivating to the mind.
She is to be honored, most worshipful, the crusher of wicked buffalo-demons,
the slayer of the demon Mahiṣāsura, Mātaṅgī, who dwells within illusion.
The Mādhvī is the seal consisting of honey, whose form is the mantra of Mudrikā;
she is the messenger of Mahāviśveśvarī, illuminating with the light of the moon upon her crest.
The Goddess whose very nature is glory, who bestows the path of yoga,
the Yoginī who is attainable through yoga, the Mistress of the South, and she whose form is yoga.
She is the limb of sacrifice, composed of yoga, consisting of recitation, and having recitation as her essence;
she is known as the Age (Yuga), she is the end of the Age, and she dwells within the circle of the womb.
She is not born from a womb; she is the yogic sleep that bestows the bliss of yoga.
She is Ramā, the beloved of Rati, eternal, and the one who increases passion and delight.
Ramaṇī, born of the Rāsa, the delightful one, fond of the Rāsa, the essence;
she who yearns for battle, who stands in the fray, and the bestower of the excellent stage.
Revatī, Raṇajaitrī, Rasodbhūtā, Raṇotsavā, Latā,
Lāvaṇyarūpā, and Lavaṇābdhisvarūpiṇī.
She is worshipped with cloves and flowers, she has a flickering tongue, and she is a licker;
she is the mistress, she dwells in the forest, she loves forest flowers, and she is the most excellent.
The mistress of life, whose form is intellect, the bestower of wisdom, and whose essence is the enlightened;
she is the pacifier, white in color, the consort of Śaṅkara, and the speaker of auspiciousness.
She is of the nature of peace, of the nature of power, and dwells within the power-bindu;
she is the sovereign of all, the giver of all, the mother of all, and the night.
Śāmbhavī is the bestower of perfection, the perfected one, shining with the resonance of the Suṣumnā;
she resides in the midst of the thousand petals and dwells within the thousand-petaled lotus.
She who is beloved by Hara, who is meditated upon by Hara, whose form is the seed-syllable *hūṃ*,
the sovereign of Laṅkā, the tremulous one, and she who is worshipped with hair and flesh.
She is the secure one, the bestower of security, the emaciated, and whose nature is like a drop of milk;
she eternally grants a distracted mind and delights in silken garments;
she is the severed, she is of severed form, hunger itself, and her form is the sound of sneezing.
The Goddess, who consists of all castes, is the bestower of all prosperity.
She is the bestower of all prosperity, adorned with both fortune and adversity;
she is the embodiment of living beings, the fulfiller of all aims, and worshipped by all the gods.
She is the sovereign of all, the mother of all, the omniscient one, whose essence is nectar;
she is the ocean, the Mandākinī, the Gaṅgā, and the personification of rivers and the sea.
She who has beautiful hair and loose hair, the Ḍākinī of excellent complexion;
the giver of knowledge, the sky of knowledge, she who dwells within the lunar mandala.
Residing in space, eternal, having the form of the supreme ether,
she is Annapūrṇā, the Great Eternal One, born from the essence of Mahādeva.
Maṅgalā, Kālikā, Caṇḍā, the exceedingly terrifying Caṇḍanādā, the destroyer of the Asura Caṇḍa, Cāmuṇḍā, and Capalātmikā.
Fierce, with hair like yak-tail whisks, wearing swinging earrings,
she is eternally adorned with a garland of severed heads and delights in the severed and the whole head.
She holds a sword in her hand, she holds a shaven head in her hand, she has excellent hands, and she is the bestower of boons;
she eternally bears a sword and shield, and she is the supreme goddess who holds a noose and a goad.
She holds a trident in her hand, she has the hand of Śiva, she delights in the resonance of the bell;
she is the Sun who bears the bow and arrow, she has a serpent in her hand, and she is the daughter of the Mountain.
She is the slayer of the demon Mahiṣāsura and the destroyer of Raktabīja;
she is red in form, with red limbs and red hands, bestowing fear.
She is dark-hued, the upholder of the Dharma, another who holds a noose and a goad;
she eternally bears a bow and arrows, and is the destroyer of Dhūmralocana.
The supreme form of the deity residing beyond is Śarvāṇī, the transcendent Śāradā;
her limbs are adorned with various colors, and she is the fulfiller of manifold desires.
Clad in animal skins and garments, she is the supreme wielder of the flower-weapon;
she is enriched with garlands dyed with saffron and graced by necklaces of pearls.
Adorned with golden earrings, seated upon a golden throne,
with beautiful limbs and a golden luster, she is Śāmbhavī in the form of the cart.

She is the vidyā of all the lords of the world, the one who causes delusion and utter confusion; she is the most auspicious, whose form is creation, and who is the guile that severs the veil of illusion.
She who bears the severed head is eternal, bestowing eternal bliss;
she is Nandā, Pūrṇā, and Riktā—the lunar days that constitute the full sixteenfold cycle.
Kuhū is the form of the Saṃkrānti, sporting at the five lunar nodes;
she eternally wields the five arrows, bestows the joy of the fifth state, and is the supreme goddess.
She who desires the five petals, she who sports with the five nectars,
the Pāñcālī goddess, the fifth, she who spreads forth the five red [essences].
She who bears five arrows, the eternal, the constant giver, devoted to compassion;
she who eternally delights in flesh and the like, accessible to the sacrificial animal, and ruled by the Supreme Lord.
She is the supreme secret, overwhelmed with supreme love;
she is of noble birth, established on the path of Keśinī, and the illuminator of the path of the Kula.
She is the essential nature of both Kula and Akula, consisting of the ocean of Kula, and is Kula itself.
She is Rukmā, Kālarūpā, and the one who causes the trembling of Time.
She is the embodiment of grace, auspicious, and saluted by both the Kula and Akula traditions;
she is the bestower of Kubera’s wealth and the supreme mother of Kumāra.
She who abides in the form of a maiden, the Mother worshipped by maidens;
the goddess with the eyes of a deer, whose face is like the sun, the unconquered Aparājitā.
Kuṇḍalī is the excellent army of plantains, free from evil paths;
she is of infinite form, dwelling in the infinite, and residing in the ocean of bliss.
The Goddess whose nature is *īlā* causes fear through the distinction between *i* and *ī*;
she is the channel *iṅgalā* and *piṅgalā*, whose form is the syllable *ikāra*.
Umā is the form of origination and the destroyer of high states;
she is to be propitiated by the Ṛgveda and worshipped by the Yajurveda.
Chanted by the Sāmaveda, she speaks through the Atharvaveda;
she is the form of the syllable *Ṛk*, yet she is the Ṛkṣā whose true nature is beyond syllables.
Her conduct is like that of a serpent-guarded fortress; she is the embodiment of the syllable *ikāra*;
she is *Oṃkāra*, abiding in the *praṇava*, and her essential nature is the form of *Oṃkāra* and the rest.
Abiding in both direct and reverse order, she arises from the letter *tha*;
enriched with the seed-syllables of the fifty letters, she is the garland of fifty severed heads.
The number eleven and the sixteenth [deity] Chinnamastaka are to be worshipped as the young maidens of the six limbs, yet they are devoid of the form of the six limbs themselves.
She who eternally resides in the six-faced one, the Sovereign of the Universe, whose abode is the six maces;
she who consists of the garland-mantra, the Mother of mantra-recitation, and who is languid with passion.
The power that is the sovereign of the entire universe, the bestower of all bliss—
thus ends the excellent thousand names of the illustrious Chinnamastā.
This has been taught according to the sequence of worship, bringing happiness to practitioners;
it must be kept secret, kept secret, kept secret—of this there is no doubt.
At midnight, a man with his hair loosened, filled with devotion,
should recite the Thousand Names after having performed the ritual chanting and worship.
The accomplishment of knowledge shall come to him through the practice of six months;
by whatever means possible, he should remain devoted to the Goddess.
One may paralyze all the worlds, delude even a king,
attract the power of the gods, and slay the enemy of the gods.
O beloved, by reciting and speaking [this], enemies become servants, evils go to destruction, and even death goes to its end.
By the grace of Praśastā, what on this earth cannot be accomplished?
This is the supreme secret, the great means for securing well-being.
By holding [this] on one's arm, great accomplishment is attained; there is no doubt in this matter.
There exists no knowledge equal to this, O Maheśvarī;
he who studies it even once becomes a master of all accomplishments.
On a Friday, on the eighth lunar day of the dark fortnight, on the new moon, on a solar transit, and on the full moon;
Listen to the full fruit for him who recites this knowledge:
having chanted it one hundred and eight times, he should then recite the *Nāmasahasra*.
By praising the Great Goddess with devotion, one is liberated from all sins;
being completely freed from all sins, one becomes a lord of all supernatural powers (*siddhi*).
On the eighth lunar day, or at midnight, a man who has gone to a crossroads should offer an oblation of black-gram and rice and recite the Thousand Names.
Within the altar of Sudarśa, according to the ritual procedure for three months,
Durjaya was born, who could assume any form at will and possessed great strength and prowess.
A person should recite even just the mantra known as Kumārīpūjana;
by the recitation of this mantra, one shall become a master of all supernatural powers (siddhis).
Thus has been told to you, O Goddess, the supreme means for all accomplishments;
by reciting and praising the Great Goddess, one is liberated from all sins.
O Goddess, this which is honored by all the gods must not be disclosed;
it is the supreme secret and must be guarded against the presence of the uninitiated.
Thus, that mortal who here recites this praise of Chinnamastā— which is the cause of all prosperity and is most auspicious—
becomes as wealthy as the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) and is held in honor by kings.
The refuge of people, the knower of spiritual accomplishments.
Thus ends the *Śrīcchinnamastāsahasranāmastotra*, spoken in the dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī within the *Śrīviśvasāratantra*.
Thus ends the Chinnamastā Tantra within the Śāktapramoda.
Composed and compiled by the sovereign King Śrī Siṃha Bahādura, the son of the illustrious Rājādeva and lord of the capital of Śrī Śivahara.
The Sixth Tantra, the Tripurabhairavī-tantra, contained within the Śāktapramoda.
This has been edited by the learned Śrī Raghurāja Dubejī, a descendant of the aforementioned royal preceptor.
Printed and published by Śrī Kṛṣṇadāsātmaja Khemarāja at his own ‘Śrī Veṅkaṭeśvara’ Press.
Om, salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. Now begins the Śāktapramoda.
Now, the Tripurabhairavī Tantra.
Now, the meditation on Bhairavī:
[She who possesses] the luster of a thousand rising suns, wearing a saffron silken garment and a garland upon her head.

I bow to the Goddess who wears a gentle smile, whose breasts are smeared with red sandalwood paste, who holds a rosary, a book, the Vidyā, and the gestures of fearlessness and boon in her lotus-like hands; she possesses the splendor of a three-eyed, radiant lotus-face and wears a crown of jewels and the cool-rayed moon.

(p. 250) Now, the extraction of the yantra: one should then draw a lotus provided with eight petals, its pericarp enriched with nine triangles, and joined with four gates, together with the enclosure of the earth (bhūgṛha).
Now, the extraction of the mantra:
One should join the letter 'A' with Īśāna (the letter 'H'), and thereafter join it with 'Saiṃ'.
Then one should utter 'Hasakarī', and after that, one should recite 'Hasaiṃ'.
This eight-syllable mantra of Bhairavī has been proclaimed;
it bestows all prosperity upon one who recites it or even through its mere retention.
Now the mantra: *hasaiṃ hasakarīṃ hasaiṃ*.
Now, regarding the procedure for worship:
having performed the rites beginning with the morning duties and ending with the breath-control (prāṇāyāma), one should perform the ritual placement on the seat (pīṭhanyāsa).

Having performed the placement [of mantras] according to the previously stated sequence, beginning with *ādhāraśakti* and ending with *hrīṃ jñānātmane namaḥ*, one should place [the following] on the filaments of the heart-lotus starting from the east: *oṃ icchāyai namaḥ*, likewise *jñānāyai namaḥ*,
*kriyāyai*, *kāmadāyinyai*, *ratyai*, *ratipriyāyai*, *nandāyai*, and in the center.

Having performed the placement [of mantras] ending with "aiṃ parāyai namaḥ, aparāyai namaḥ, hasauṃ sadāśiva-mahāpreta-padmāsanāya namaḥ," one should perform the placement of the seer (ṛṣi) and the others.
p. 251) For example: "Salutation to Dakṣiṇāmūrti on the head;
salutation to the Paṅkti metre on the face; salutation to the deity Tripurabhairavī on the heart;
salutation to the Bāgbhava seed-syllable on the secret place; salutation to Śaktikāśakti on the feet."
"Salutation to Kāmarājāya-kīlaka, who is in all limbs. And likewise, in the Dakṣiṇāmūrti-saṃhitā: "One should place the sage Dakṣiṇāmūrti on the head in due order;
one should know the metre to be Paṅkti and place it on the face; [then] the deity."
In my heart is Tripureśānī; she is said to be the seed-syllable Vāgbhava.
The seed-syllable of Śakti is Śakti herself, and Kāmarāja is the Kīlaka;
thereafter, from the navel down to the feet, is the mantra "Haṃsa-re-namaḥ."
One should place the seed-syllable of desire (*kāma-bīja*) from the heart down to the navel.

[The mantra] *sakalaḥ riṃ namaḥ* is for the head, ending at the heart; *haṃsareṇa namaḥ* is likewise. Thus, the first seed-syllable is on the right hand, the second on the left hand, and the third on both hands.
Just as [one places them] at the crown, the root-support, and the heart, one should likewise place the three seed-syllables with the conch-shell gesture.
As it is stated in the Nibandha:
Likewise, the knower of the Vāgbhava mantra, [visualizing] from the navel down to the feet.
One should place the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja) from the heart down to the navel.
Then, one should place those three [syllables] from the head down to the region of the heart.
Then one should place [the syllables] once on the first hand, twice on the second hand, and three times on both.
And one should again place the three seed-syllables in sequence at the crown, the base, and the heart.
Then follows the arrangement consisting of the nine wombs.

The first seed-syllable is on the right ear, the second seed-syllable on the left ear, and the third seed-syllable on the chin. In this manner, [the remaining syllables are placed] on the two temples, the face, the eyes, the nose, the shoulders, the belly, the two elbows, the flanks, the knees, the penis, the feet, the private parts, the sides, the heart, the breasts, and the throat.
As it is stated in the Nibandha:
One should perform the nyāsa consisting of the nine yonis with the three seed-syllables in sequence.
Again on the ears, the chin, the temples, and once more on the face.
One should also place [the seed-syllables] upon the two eyes, the two shoulders, and again upon the abdomen.
Then, [one should place them] on the two elbows, the two sides of the abdomen, the two knees, the head, the crown of the head, the two feet, the private region,
the two flanks, and the lotus of the heart.
Then one should place Rati and the others upon the two breasts and at the region of the throat.
Now follows the ritual placement (nyāsa) of Rati and the others.
At the *mūlādhāra*: *aiṃ ratyai namaḥ*; in the heart: *klīṃ prītyai namaḥ*; between the eyebrows:
*manobhavāyai namaḥ*; again, between the eyebrows: *sauḥ amṛteśyai namaḥ*; in the heart: *klīṃ yogeśyai namaḥ*; at the *mūlādhāra*: *aiṃ viśvayonyai namaḥ*.
As it says in the Nibandha:
"She places delight in his mouth, affection in his heart, and the god of love between his eyebrows."
Having performed the placement (nyāsa) with the three seed-syllables of Bālā in these locations in reverse order.
And these [goddesses], Amṛteśī, Yogeśī, and Viśvayoni, [are worshipped] in this sequence.
Having performed the placement of the seed-syllables in reverse order, one should carry out the placement of the forms (mūrttinyāsa).
Now follows the ritual placement of the forms (mūrttinyāsa).
On the head: *hasaroṃ*, obeisance to Īśāna, the mind-born one (*manobhava*).
In the mouth: *hasareṃ*, obeisance to Tatpuruṣa, the god of love (*makaradhvaja*).
In the heart: *hasarūṃ*, obeisance to Aghora, the youthful god of love (*kandarpakumāra*).
At the secret place: *hasarīṃ vāmadevamanmathāya namaḥ*.
At the two feet: *hasarāṃ sadyojātakāmadevāya namaḥ*.

In this manner, one should install the five forms, beginning with Īśāna and Manobhava, in the upward, eastern, southern, northern, and western faces, preceded by their respective seed-syllables and so forth.
As it is stated in the Nibandha:
All their respective offerings and so forth [should be made] to Īśāna, the mind-born one, upon the crown of the head.
One should assign Tatpuruṣa and Makaradhvaja to the mouth.
Then follow Hṛdya, Aghora, Kumāra, and so forth, ending with Kandarpa.
Having placed the Manmatha-mantras, beginning with Vāmadeva, in the secret region.
Then, one should place Sadyojāta and Kāmadeva at the two feet.
In the upward, eastern, southern, northern, and western faces, those [offerings].
One should arrange them as before; Bhṛgu is situated in the fire of the sky.
The seed-syllables for these are conceived as the five short vowels beginning with *a*, which are known as the Truths (*satya*).
Then, one should place the five arrows and the five objects of desire upon the fingers of both hands.
*Yathā-drāṃ draviṇeśyai namaḥ* on the two thumbs; *drīṃ śobhinyai namaḥ* on the two index fingers; *klīṃ vaśīkariṇyai namaḥ* on the two middle fingers;
*pluṃ ākarṣiṇyai namaḥ* on the two ring fingers; *strīṃ unmādinyai namaḥ* [on the two little fingers].
On the two little fingers: likewise, *hrīṃ* to Kāma, *klīṃ* to Manmatha, *aiṃ* to Kandarpa, *pluṃ* to Makaradhvaja, *strīṃ* to Mīnaketana. As it is stated in the Jñānārṇava:
One should place the five arrows, in their proper sequence, upon the fingers of the hand.
The application of the ritual placement (nyāsa), however, is here performed using feminine gender endings, because it is seen as such in the Tantra.
