One should [worship] the Supreme Goddess in sequence, beginning with the thumb and ending with the little finger.
Having written the two final letters of the [vowel] series, one should then place the letter *ta* situated in fire (*ra*) in sequence.
Adorned with a face and an eye on the left side.
It is said that there are two arrows, located on the ground of Mādana.
O fair-faced one, the fourth [form] is the form of sound (nāda), enriched with the science of vowels.
Joined with the face of his beloved and adorned by her left ear.
O Dear One, the Moon, together with its limbs, is conjoined with the *bindu* and the *nāda*.
O Pārvatī, O Great Goddess, hear the names of the five arrows.
Agitation, liquefaction, subjugation, and likewise that known as attraction.
And Unmāda, O Supreme Goddess—these are the names in their proper sequence.
Desire is to be understood as residing in that very place; now listen as I describe their seeds.
O Supreme Goddess, the Vāgbhava [syllable] consists of the seed-syllable of Parā in the middle of the arrows.
Then, O Dear One, the seed-syllable of the woman follows in sequence, preceded by the fourth and the five arrows.
In the Tripurāsāra:
The fifth [syllable] is joined with the end of the pure eye (ī) and possesses the qualities of the leftward-moving wind (ya);
the sun (ra) moves with the horse of Hari (e), ending with the dot of space (m); and Bhṛgu (sa) is joined with the supreme (ha) situated at the end of the earth (la).
O Goddess, O beloved, listen to these names of the five objects of desire.
They are known by the names Kāma, Manmatha, Kandarpa, and Makaradhvaja.
O Maheśānī, the fifth is proclaimed as Mīnaketu.
O Goddess, O beloved, hear now the names of the five ends of desire.
One should place [the syllables] in the locations of Kāma, Manmatha, and Kandarpa’s arrows.
One should place these [syllables] upon the body; after that, the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa) follows.
Then follow the ritual assignments (nyāsa) of the hands and the limbs.
Hasaraṃ to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*.
Svāhā hasarīṃ to the two index fingers, *namaḥ*. Hasarūṃ to the two middle fingers, *vaṣaṭ*.
HŪM, [I offer] the sacrificial cakes with the two ring fingers.
I laugh with the two little fingers; vauṣaṭ!
Hrasaḥ, with both palms and backs of the hands, phaṭ!
The same applies to the heart and other [limbs], as stated in the Nibandha.
The ritual application of the limbs (aṅgakriyā) is considered to be performed with the first seed-syllable joined with the six long vowels;
thereafter follows the placement of the arrows (bāṇanyāsa).
On the head: *drāṃ* to Drāviṇī, *namaḥ*; in the secret place: *klīṃ* to Ākarṣiṇī, *namaḥ*; in the heart: to Sammohinī, *namaḥ*.
As stated in the Nibandha:
"One should place Drāviṇī, beginning with *drāṃ*, upon the head, and Kṣobhiṇī, beginning with *drīṃ*."
One should place *klīṃ vaśīkaraṇīṃ* in the mouth and *klīṃ* preceded by the seed-syllable in the secret place.
Again, the *ākarṣiṇī* [mantra] is in the heart, joined with *sa*, *rgā*, *laḥ*, *bhṛgu*, and *sai*.
Thus, in this manner, the placement of the arrows (vāṇanyāsa) has been described as that which causes delusion.
By this [it is shown that] madness (*unmāda*) and delusion (*sammohana*) are synonyms; having placed the *kāmas* in these locations, as in the *Śrīkrama*:
"O Goddess, on the forehead, in the mouth, in the heart, at the navel, and in the secret place."
Having assigned the Kāmas and the [seed-syllables] beginning with Tārā and Subhagā to these [locations].
The word "one should perform the placement" (*nyaset*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. Following that is the placement of Subhagā and the others:
*aiṃ klīṃ lūṃ strīṃ subhagāyai namaḥ* on the forehead; *auṃ klīṃ brūṃ strīṃ bhagāyai namaḥ* between the eyebrows; *bhagasarpiṇyai namaḥ* on the face.
p. 254) On the necklace: *namaḥ* to Bhagamālinī; on the throat: *namaḥ* to Anaṅgā; in the heart:
*namaḥ* to Anaṅgakusumā; at the navel: *namaḥ* to Anaṅgamekhalā; at the base of the penis: *namaḥ* to Anaṅgamadanā; in the heart: [five times]. As in the Nibandha: on the forehead.
In the space between the eyebrows, on the face, and upon the necklace, throat, and heart.
In the navel and the seat [of the heart] are the five stars and so forth, beginning with Subhagā.
O Goddess, the auspicious *bhaga* should be deposited by the practitioner according to the prescribed rite.
Then Bhagasarpiṇī, and immediately after her, Bhagamālinī.
She was Anaṅgānaṅgakusumā, and furthermore, Anaṅgamekhalā.
The serpent of the passion of the bodiless god [Kāma] was slow with gentle, languid glances.
Vāk, Kāma, Bīja, Klūṃ, Trīṃ, and Sa—these are the five Tārās as they have been proclaimed.

Now, the placement of ornaments (bhūṣaṇanyāsa): *aṃ namaḥ* on the head; *āṃ namaḥ* on the forehead; *iṃ īṃ* on the eyebrows; likewise on the ears; *uṃ ūṃ* on the eyes; *ṛṃ ṝṃ* on the nose; *ḷṃ ḹṃ* on the cheeks; *eṃ* on the upper lip; *aiṃ* on the lower lip; *oṃ* on the row of teeth; *auṃ* on the mouth; *aṃ* on the chin; *aḥ* on the chin.

Kaṃ on the back; khaṃ and ṅaṃ on the two sides of the neck; ghaṃ and ṅaṃ on the two breasts; caṃ and chaṃ at the roots of the two arms; jaṃ and jhaṃ on the two elbows; jaṃ and jhaṃ on the two feet; ñaṃ on the two big toes; ñaṃ and ṭaṃ on the two feet; ṭhaṃ and ḍaṃ on the backs of the two hands.
Ḍhaṃ at the navel, taṃ in the secret place, thaṃ on the thighs, daṃ dhaṃ on the knees, naṃ paṃ on the shanks, phaṃ baṃ at the joints,
bhaṃ maṃ on the feet, yaṃ on the big toes, raṃ on the hips, laṃ on the throat, and vaṃ on the neck.

One should place *laṃ* in the heart, *śaṃ* in the secret place, *kṣaṃ* in the two ears, *ṣaṃ* in the two cheeks, and *saṃ* on the crown of the head. One should place [the syllables] upon the horse-stand (*hayasthā*) at the binding. One should install the Lords (*īśvarān*) upon the head, the forehead, the pair of eyebrows, ears, and eyes, the chest and cheeks, the thighs and back, the row of teeth, the mouth, the chin, and the throat.

With a concentrated mind, one should place the letters from *ka* to *va* in these locations: on the two sides, on the pair of breasts, at the two armpits, on the two elbows, then on the region of the back,
then on the navel, again on the secret organ, then on the two thighs, the two knees, the two calves,
then on the two buttocks, and finally on the two toes of the feet.

The most excellent of preceptors, having firmly established the powerful [deities] who are invincible to Rākṣasas upon the hips, the neck-ornament, the back, the belly, the heart, the private parts, the ears, the cheeks, and the head, should then assign the gods to their respective chariots.
Then, having formed the three-part mudrā, one should meditate.

She possesses the splendor of a thousand rising suns, wears a crest-garland of crimson silk, has breasts smeared with red pigment, and holds a rosary, the gesture of fearlessness, and the boon-granting mudrā; she is the Vidyā.

I bow to the Goddess, who possesses the splendor of a three-eyed, radiant lotus-face, who holds [it] with her lotus-hands, who wears a crown of cool-rayed moons, and who smiles gently. Having meditated thus and worshipped her mentally, one should perform the ritual installation of the conch (*śaṅkhasthāpana*).
Having thus worshipped with "Obeisance to Ādhāraśakti and the others, whose nature is *hrīṃ* and knowledge," [one worships] on the filaments in the east and so forth, and in the center: Icchā, Jñānā,
Kriyā, then Kāminī, Kāmahāvinī, Ratī, Ratipriyā, Nandā, and the ninth, Manonmanī— these [are the goddesses].

One should worship [the deities] with [mantras] beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*. Thus: *parāyai namaḥ*, *aparāyai namaḥ*, *parāyai namaḥ*, *parāvatyai namaḥ*, and "Salutation to the Great Corpse-Lotus-Throne of Sadāśiva.
Having thus worshipped, one should worship the lineage of gurus mentioned in the Śrīvidyā [tradition] in the space between the east and the north, as stated in the Nibandha:
Vāgbhava, Rohita, Śrīkaṇṭha, Lohita, and Nala.
To Dīrghavāṇī, Parā, and again to Aparā behind her— [I offer] Sadāśiva, the great preta,
ending in the feminine suffix -ī (ṅe), seated upon a lotus throne before me.
With this mantra, one should offer a seat to the most excellent and venerable Guru.
One should worship and then perform the ritual preparation in the space between the east and the center.
Having first invoked the deity into that [liṅga] with five *praṇavas*,...
Tāra, Vāk, Śakti, Kamalā, and Hasakhapla-yaśas are thus remembered.
If one is unable to do that, [one should recite]: *oṃ gurubhyo namaḥ*, *oṃ gurupādukābhyāṃ namaḥ*;
likewise, *paramagurubhyo namaḥ*, *paramagurupādukābhyāṃ namaḥ*;
*oṃ parameṣṭhigurubhyo namaḥ*, *parameṣṭhigurupādukābhyāṃ namaḥ*.
To the teachers, to the sandals of the teachers... [in this composition on the yantra for worship].
A lotus provided with eight petals, enriched with a central pericarp containing nine yonis.

Then, one should draw an underground chamber (bhūgṛha) provided with four doors. With the mantra "Aiṃ Hrīṃ Saḥ Ha Saḥ Krehyaiṃ," one should perform the visualization of the form within the Bindu-cakra using the Tri-khaṇḍa mudrā, meditate upon the Goddess, and invoke her:
"Oṃ, O Queen of Gods, who are easily accessible and auspicious, accompanied by Your retinue!"
"Remain steadfast as long as I worship you. Having thus invoked [the deity], one should say with affection:

"Oṃ namo ugrakoṇe manobhavāya namaḥ" (Salutation to Manobhava in the northeast corner). Then, one should begin the worship in the filaments at the corners starting from the southeast, in the center, and in the cardinal directions, using the previously mentioned limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*). Now, in the *Jñānārṇava*:
One should worship the directional binding (digbandha) in the center between Agni, Īśa, Asura, and Vāyu. Then, in the north:
"Drāṃ, obeisance to Drāviṇī; Drīṃ, obeisance to Kṣobhiṇī. In the south:
"Klīṃ, obeisance to Vaśīkariṇī; [Klūṃ], obeisance to Ākarṣiṇī."
In the southeast: *sammohinyai namaḥ*. Likewise, in the north: *hrīṃ kāmāya namaḥ*, *klīṃ manmathāya namaḥ*. In the south:
*aiṃ kandarpāya namaḥ*, *pluṃ makaradhvajāya namaḥ*. In the southeast: *strīṃ mīnaketanāya namaḥ*. As [prescribed].

In the *Jñānārṇava*: "In the two directions of the north and [the northeast], and in the southeast, one should worship the five arrows in sequence. One should likewise worship the five arrows as one would the divine arrows."
Like the arrow [mantra]. Then, in the eight wombs starting from the east: *aiṃ klīṃ strīṃ saḥ namaḥ to Subhagā*.
Thus: Aiṃ 4 Bhagāyai namaḥ; Aiṃ Bhagasarpiṇyai namaḥ; Aiṃ Bhagamālinyai namaḥ; Aiṃ 4 Anaṅgāyai namaḥ; likewise, Aiṃ 4 Anaṅgakusumāyai namaḥ; Aiṃ 4 Anaṅgamekhalāyai namaḥ; Aiṃ 4.
Salutation to Anaṅgamadanā. Then, on the eight petals starting from the east: Oṃ, salutation to Asitāṅga and Brāhmī; Oṃ, salutation to Umā and Maheśvara;
Oṃ, salutation to Caṇḍa and Kaumārī; Oṃ, salutation to Krodha and Vaiṣṇavī; Oṃ—
Salutation to Uttaravārāhī and [her consort], Oṃ; salutation to Kāpālīndrāṇī and [her consort], Oṃ;
salutation to Bhīṣaṇacāmuṇḍā and [her consort], Oṃ; salutation to Saṃhāramahālakṣmī and [her consort], Oṃ.

As stated in the *Nibandha*: "In the eighth [wheel] and in the sixth power (*śakti*), one should worship Subhagā and the others, as well as the Mothers beginning with Bhairavī, who are overwhelmed by the intoxication of passion. Having worshipped them duly upon the eight petals up to the offering of flowers, one should then worship Indra and the other [directional deities] outside of that, from the incense offering until the final dismissal."
One should conclude the ritual action (*karma*). However, after the food offering (*naivedya*), the fourfold *bali* offering mentioned in the *Śrīvidyā* [tradition] should be given.

The preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for this consists of ten hundred-thousand recitations (*japa*), and the fire oblation (*homa*) is twelve thousand. As stated in the *Nibandha*: "Having received initiation, one who has conquered the senses should recite the mantra one hundred-thousand times according to the principles (*tattva*)."
One should offer oblations of flowers produced from the *akṣa* tree equal in number to thousands of suns. Thus ends the worship.
Then, in this hymn, Śrī Bhairava said:
"Even Brahmā and the other gods do not know [the Lord] in His subtle form, even with hundreds of praises."

We praise her who is the primordial form of the world yet without beginning, who possesses the luster of fresh saffron from her slightly contracted [limbs], and who is the mother of all speech. || 1 ||
She possesses the splendor of a thousand suns suddenly risen;
her hands bear the marks of the knowledge-gesture, the rosary, the boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness;
her lotus-face is adorned with three blue-lotus eyes.
O Lord of Tripura, we worship you, who are resplendent with the weight of your pearl necklaces. || 2 ||

O Goddess, those of dull intellect do not recognize you— who are beautiful with the flow of vermilion, bowed by the weight of your breasts, and attainable only as the fruit of merit accumulated in previous lives— because they are distracted by mutual strife and the divisions of pride.
O Mother, form! || 3 ||
The sages declare you to be gross, while the Vedas praise you as subtle; others call you the abode of all speech,
O Bhavānī, and still others say you are the root of the worlds.
We consider him to be an ocean of boundless compassion. || 4 ||
They meditate upon you in their hearts as one adorned with a crescent moon, white as the autumnal moon, consisting of fifty syllables,
holding a book, a rosary, and a jar of nectar.
And she holds the gesture of exposition with her lotus-like hands and possesses three eyes. || 5 ||
You are Śambhu, whose half-body is embraced by the Daughter of the Mountain;
you are Viṣṇu, O Mother, whose body is entwined by Kamalā; you are Padmodbhava, the abode of Speech—those for whom you are the source of all actions in this world, O Tripurā.
You alone. || 6 ||
I bow to you, the Supreme Goddess, who, having resorted to the four states beginning with the "Supreme" (para) arising from the Vāgbhava syllable, utter them as they are prescribed by the words,
and who [manifests] through the instruments such as Time (kāla).
I never forget that [form] made of wine within my heart. || 7 ||

Having restrained the breath and conquered the six internal enemies, they gaze with an unwavering mind at the tip of their own noses and meditate upon Him who bears the crescent moon as His crest-ornament, situated at the crown of the head.
O Mother, Your form is like the rising sun to those who are accomplished.
"O Daughter of the Mountain, O Sole Mother of the World, it is the declaration of the Vedas that having obtained half the body of the Enemy of Manmatha, you bring about the creation of the worlds;
this is the truth, for were it not so, there would be no stability for the entire universe. (9)
O Mother, having performed worship with flowers of the celestial trees upon your throne in the caves of the Golden Mountain,
the wives of the Siddhas, their lotus-eyes reddened by tasting the essence of nectar, sing together with the Kinnarīs.
One should worship the Goddess, whose body is the play of lightning and who brings forth splendor;
she departs from her own abode for the royal capital of Śiva,
causing the lotuses of the Suṣumnā path to blossom.
Her limbs are sprinkled with the supreme nectar. || 11 ||
O Mother, I take refuge in you, the source of bliss, the abode of the Vedas, whose body is pure consciousness,
and whose lotus feet are worshipped by Brahmā, Śiva, and Viṣṇu.
In Tripura, which is the birthplace and abode of good fortune, [he dwells] exactly as it is.
She who, in the form of the Moon, creates the world that brings about all purposes;
she who, in the form of the Sun, sustains it by her own power;
and she who, as the essence of Brahmā, withdraws that entire universe at the end of the age.
I never forget that autumnal [scene] in my mind. || 13 ||
She is Nārāyaṇī, the one who carries across the ocean of hell;
she is Gaurī, the pacifier of weariness;
she is Sarasvatī, the bestower of knowledge, adorned with three eyes.
O daughter of the king of mountains, the wise call you by these names. || 14 ||
O Mother of the World, those who praise you in succession with these twelve verses shall attain perfection of speech after reaching you, and they shall obtain supreme glory.
Thus, O Goddess, I have told you this five-limbed [teaching] consisting of Bhairavī;
it is secret, most to be concealed, and must be guarded like one's own womb.
Thus ends the Śrī Bhairavī Stotra, within the description of the Five-Limbed Section (Pañcāṅgakhanda) in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara from the venerable Rudrayāmala.
Then Śrī Pārvatī spoke the armor-mantra (kavaca):
"O God of gods, O Mahādeva, you who are learned in all the scriptures!"
Have mercy, O Lord of the World; you are a knower of Dharma, O Great-minded One. || 1 ||
Tell me truly the divine armor (kavaca) of that Bhairavī who was previously described as the Vidyā beginning with Tripura.
Having heard her words, the Lord of the World spoke to the goddess Bhairavī, who possessed a divine form and wonderful speech.
Īśvara said:
I shall proclaim the armor of the Great Vidyā, which is difficult for all to obtain.
Listen to it according to the prescribed rite; having heard it, you must keep it secret even unto death.
By whose grace I sustain all the three worlds;
from whom everything has arisen, and in whom it still abides even today. (5)
The mother and father are blessed by the world, for they are the very embodiment of the Brahman of the universe;
they are the bestowers of perfection (siddhi) and are themselves perfected, yet they remain unperfected among wicked beings.
May the Goddess Kakārī—benefactor of all beings, whose very nature is all beings, the beloved woman who grants all desires—protect me. (7)
May the Goddess Ekārī, whose nature is the Mūlādhāra, protect me;
may the Goddess Ikārī, who bestows abundant all-encompassing happiness, protect me. (8)
May the goddess Lakārī, the beloved of Indra, protect me;
may the goddess Hrīṃkārī, the beautiful consort of Śambhu, protect me at all times. (9)
May Mahāmāyā Śambhavī protect [me] with these syllables on the head;
may the goddess Mā, Śarvāṇī, the consort of Hara, protect me at the syllable *ka*.
May the Goddess who destroys all sins protect me in the syllable *ma*;
may the Goddess who always assumes any form at will protect me in the syllable *ka*. (11)
May the Goddess, the beloved of the enemy of Śambara, always protect me at the syllable *ka*; may the Goddess, who assumes the form of the earth-supporting mountain, protect me at the syllable *pa*.
May the Goddess Hrīṃkārī protect me, she whose body consists of half the letter Ā;
may Mahāmāyā, the beloved of Kāma and Rāhu, protect [me] with these syllables.
May the Goddess Sāvitrī, the bestower of all things, protect me with the letter *ma*;
may she whose nature is the sky of the digit (*kalā*) protect me everywhere with the letter *ka*.
May the goddess Lakṣmī, who possesses all auspicious marks, protect me with the syllable *la*;
may the goddess Tribhuvaneśvarī protect me everywhere with *hrīṃ*. (15)
May Mahāmāyā, whose nature is Śakti, protect [me] with these syllables;
may she who is Vāgbhava protect my head, and may Kāmarājikā protect my face.
May she whose nature is Śakti protect the heart; may Sundarī, who bestows the perfection of the yantra, protect [me] forever; Sundarī provides complete protection. 17.
May the beautiful one, red in color, who grants all things, protect me always;
may the beautiful one, adorned with various ornaments, protect me at all times. 18.
May she who is beautiful in all her limbs, who bestows auspiciousness everywhere, who generates delight for the world, and whose form is Śambhu, protect me always. 19.
May she who consists of all mantras protect us;
may she who bestows all prosperity, the goddess who embodies all Lakṣmī, grant supreme bliss. || 20 ||
May the auspicious Goddess, who possesses various treasures such as conch-shells, protect me at all times;
may the Goddess Padmanidhi, the bestower of auspiciousness, protect me always.
May Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the sage, protect me everywhere on my head;
may the Sureśvarī, whose nature is the Paṅkti meter, protect my mouth.
May Śaṅkarī, who consists of the eight perfumes, always protect my heart;
may Sarvasammohinī protect me, and may Saṅkṣobhiṇī always protect me.
May she who bestows all accomplishments protect [me]; may she who effects all attractions protect [me];
may she who agitates always protect; may she who holds power protect at all times. (24)
May Ākarṣiṇī always protect; may Sammohinī always guard;
may the goddess Rati always protect; may Bhagāṅgā protect at all times. (25)
May Maheśvarī always protect me; may Kaumārī protect me at all times; may she who causes universal delight protect me; may she who brings all under her control protect me. (26)
May Kṣemaṅkarī always protect me, as well as Sarvāṅgasundarī,
Sarvāṅgayuvati, and she who bestows all good fortune upon everything.
May Vāgdevī protect [me] always; may Vāṇinī protect [me] always;
may Vaśinī protect [me] always; may she who bestows the great siddhis protect [me] forever. (28)
May Sarvavidrāviṇī protect me; may Gaṇanātha always protect me;
may Goddess Durgā always protect me; may Baṭuka protect me at all times. (29)
May Kṣetrapāla always protect, and may Āvariśāntikā protect;
may Ananta protect at all times, and may Varāha protect at all times.
May the Earth protect me always, as well as the golden lion-throne;
and may the red nectar protect me perpetually at all times. (31)
May the ocean of wine protect me always; may the wish-fulfilling tree protect me always.
May the white umbrella protect me always; may the red lamp protect me always. (32)
May the Nandana garden protect me constantly for the attainment of all perfections; likewise, may the guardians of the directions and all the multitudes of dualities protect me at all times. (33)
May the mounts always protect; may the missiles protect at all times;
may the weapons always protect; may the Yoginīs protect at all times. (34)
May the Siddhas protect [me] always; may the Goddess, the bestower of all accomplishments, grant success.
May the Goddess, beautiful in every limb, likewise protect me at all times. (35)
May the Goddess, whose form is bliss, whose nature is consciousness, and whose essence is consciousness—the eternally beautiful Sundarī, the beauty of existence—protect [us] forever. (36)
May Sundarī always protect me in a terrifying temple, in a narrow pass, on an inaccessible mountain, or even in a forest or a wilderness. (37)
O Pārvatī, this has been declared as the Kavaca, along with the extraction of its mantras;
he who, having become restrained, pure, and self-controlled, recites it at the three junctions of the day, [attains success].
Whatever is in one's mind shall have all its purposes accomplished for him, using either gorocanā, saffron, or red sandalwood. (39)
With white *svayambhū* flowers, when Mars, Saturn,
or Jupiter are [in the ascendant], one should perform it in a cremation ground, a wilderness, an empty house, or a temple of Śiva.
Having worshipped the yantra according to one's own capacity, and having likewise worshipped the mantra of Kumārī as well as the lineage of gurus (gurupaṅkti), [one should proceed]. || 41 ||
Then, having offered an oblation to the Goddess with men, cats, pigs, mongooses, buffaloes, and rams, and having worshipped her according to the prescribed rite, || 42 ||
Having held it upon his neck or on his right arm with gold placed in the middle,
on an auspicious lunar day, under a favorable asterism, and likewise at the rising of the sun.
And having worn this armor, a person shall obtain all accomplishments;
for even in hundreds of years, one cannot fully describe the majesty of this armor.
But I am able, O Great Goddess, to describe its fruit:
there is neither the result of famine nor likewise any affliction there. (45)
It pacifies all obstacles and destroys all diseases. || 46 ||
It bestows protection upon all living beings and grants the fruits of the four aims of life;
it must never be spoken of or given to anyone whatsoever.
Having obtained the mantra according to the prescribed rite, the wise one should worship it constantly;
even among those, I consider the armor (kavaca) in its divine form to be most difficult to attain.
Having obtained the grace of the Guru and acquired the well-guarded lore, one also obtains therein the divine armor, which is difficult to find in the three worlds. (49)
Whoever, being restrained and pure, should recite even a single verse or a single hymn, for him there shall be the accomplishment of all goals; so it was proclaimed by Śaṅkara. (50)
The Guru is the god Hara himself, and Pārvatī is his wife;
for him who worships them as non-different, success is not far off. (51)
Thus ends the Śrī Bhairavī Kavaca from the Śrī Rudrayāmala, in the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī.
Then, on Mount Meru, the sovereign of mountains, Pārvatī, intent upon meditating on Śiva, questioned his heart with a desire for supreme grace.
Śrī Pārvatī said:
O Blessed One, many dharmas have been heard from the lotus of your mouth;
yet I desire to hear once more the supreme Bhairavī-stotra.
The illustrious Śaṅkara said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the hymn called Bhairavīhṛdaya,
which is supremely meritorious and the cause of all auspiciousness.
By the mere hearing of which auspiciousness certainly arises, and even without meditation and the like, Bhairavī becomes thoroughly pleased. (4)

Om. Of this Śrī Bhairavī-hṛdaya mantra, Dakṣiṇāmūrti is the seer (ṛṣi), Paṅkti is the meter (chandas), Bhayavidhvaṃsinī Bhairavī is the deity (devatā), the syllable Ha is the seed-syllable (bīja), Rīṃ is the power (śakti), and Raiḥ is the pin (kīlaka). Its application (viniyoga) is for recitation with the purpose of destroying all fears.
Now, the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*):
*oṃ hrīṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *oṃ śrīṃ śirase svāhā*, *oṃ aiṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, *oṃ hrīṃ kavacāya huṃ*, *oṃ śrīṃ netratrayāya vauṣaṭ*, *oṃ aiṃ astrāya phaṭ*.
Thus is the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa). Now, the meditation (dhyāna):
I bow to Ambikā, who is meditated upon by the gods, the three-eyed one, whose form is like a forest fire for the destruction of the dense host of asuras;
she is fierce, adorned with red garments, possessing a formidable appearance with a pair of breasts joined in the intensity of passion,
and whose forehead-mark shines with the crescent moon as her beautiful ornament.
I meditate upon Bhairavī, the mother of the three worlds, whose limbs are filled with vermilion. || 1 ||
To her who bestows the path of the Vedas upon all beings wandering in cyclic existence, who dispels the terrible suffering [of saṃsāra], who rends asunder the enemies of the gods,
who grants liberation from worldly existence, who is a sun whose light shatters the darkness of rebirth, and who cuts through the cycle of becoming— [I bow].
I always worship Bhairavī. || 1 ||

I always worship Bhairavī, who possesses the splendor of a fresh rain-cloud, whose chest is adorned with a long-hanging serpent-garland and the crescent moon, who has three beautiful lotus-eyes, who is praised by hosts of gods, who brings about the destruction of the cities of the gods, and who manifests through the power of Śiva.
To her who alone bears the burden of the entire unbroken circle of the earth, whose self is cultivated by sublime devotion,
who bestows both prosperity and future well-being,
and who moves within the ocean of worldly existence while bringing about the expansion of that very world— [to her I bow].
I always worship Bhairavī, who dwells within the heart. || 3 ||
[This is] the sweet, melodious speech of her whose lotus-face possesses a luster that rivals the moonlight of the autumn moon, which is itself worthy of being worshipped for its wondrous beauty.
I always worship Bhairavī, who is adorned with a garland of serpents and a garland of human heads, and who bestows devotion, liberation, and prosperity.
Worship her who possesses a face endowed with three eyes—the moon, the sun, and fire; she who bestows sacrificial fees upon the lords beginning with Narāntaka and Antaka;
she whose fierce Candrahāsī sword is formidable in severing off heads; and she who illuminates the intellect of Tamasā.
[He worships] Mi-bhairavī always. || 5 ||
I worship her who bears the trident,
the triple mark, the triple-sectioned rosary, and the triple staff; who is intensely impassioned by the three qualities (guṇas), whose nature is the inconceivable consciousness,
who shatters the lineage of the hosts of enemies of Indra and the gods, and who manifests through the power of worldly existence.
[He should worship] Bhairavī always. || 6 ||
I worship her whose body possesses the radiance of a solar orb with its brilliantly blazing rays, who has shattered the vast masses of darkness in every direction,
whose mind is fixed on the increase of the eternal dharma and conduct of the twice-born, and whose lotus-face has the splendor of a blooming water-lily.
[He worships] Bhairavī always. || 7 ||

I gaze upon the lotus-face of Bhairava, who possesses a moon-like forehead and a nose graced by a white parrot resting upon it— a face whose cheeks are radiant with the luster of swinging golden earrings, and which resembles a blue lotus longed for by cakora birds.
[He should worship] Bhairavī always. || 8 ||
Those who recite this hymn known as the *Hṛdaya-saṅgata* incessantly never fall into the blind well that is saṃsāra;
rather, they become radiant, possessing abundant devotion and liberation, and consequently, [the Lord] becomes gracious toward them.
And Bhairavī is one whose mind is filled with joy. || 9 ||
The fame of one who is ever resplendent triumphs throughout the world; for him, there is no defeat whatsoever in the three worlds.
For one who always recites this auspicious praise with undistracted mind, even his riches shall increase.
They bestow constant happiness. || 10 ||
All rites such as recitation and worship, as well as those consisting of the chanting of hymns and the like,
do not equal even a sixteenth part of this Heart of Bhairavī.
What is the use of speaking much more on this matter? Listen, O Goddess Maheśvarī;
there is no merit greater than this in the three worlds.
Thus ends the "Hymn to the Heart of Bhairavī" from the *Śrī-bhairavī-kula-sarvasva*.
Then the Goddess Śatānāmā said:
"O Blessed One, dweller of Kailāsa, Lord of Prāṇa, ocean of mercy!"
O you who are affectionate toward your devotees, [herein lies] the one hundred and eight names of Bhairavī. || 1 ||
"I have not heard it, O Lord of the gods; speak it, O you who are compassionate toward the distressed.
Śrī Śiva said:
"Listen, O beloved, to the one hundred and eight names of the Great Gopī."
This [practice] of Bhairavī bestows auspiciousness, is worthy of service, and grants all prosperity;
by its mere performance, what on this earth is not accomplished? (3)
Oṃ! Bhairavī, worshipped by Bhairava, bestower of prosperity, creator of beings, noble Brāhmī, the wish-fulfilling cow, the giver of all success. || 4 ||
The Goddess, adored by the three worlds, the crusher of the demon Mahiṣāsura;
she who destroys delusion, whose garland is of jasmine flowers, and who annihilates great sins. || 5 ||
The wrathful one, the abode of anger, with eyes red with rage, the new moon;
she who is Tripurā, the support of the three cities, the three-eyed, the formidable Bhairavī.
Devakī, the mother of the gods, the destroyer of those wicked toward the gods;
the beloved of Dāmodara, the long one, Durgā, the destroyer of misfortune. || 7 ||
She has a protruding belly, long ears, and pendulous breasts;
she is Praty-aṅgirā, who is present at every step and destroys the suffering of those who bow before her. || 8 ||
Prabhāvatī, Guṇavatī, Gaṇamātā, Guheśvarī, daughter of the Ocean of Milk, Kṣemyā, and the one who ordains the protection of the world. || 9 ||
She is the great pestilence, the great delusion, the great wrath, and the great river;
she is the destroyer of great sins and the bestower of great delusion. || 10 ||
Vikarālā, Mahākālā, Kālarūpā, and Kalāvatī; she who bears a skull and a khaṭvāṅga staff, and who carries a sword and a skull-bowl. || 11 ||

She is the maiden (Kumārī), who delights in saffron (Kuṅkumaprītā), and is colored rosy-red with saffron (Kuṅkumāruṇarañjitā); she is the mace Kaumodakī, the night-lily (Kumudinī), and the bestower of fame through her renown (Kīrttyā Kīrttipradāyinī). || 12 ||
She is ever-new, eternal, and the protectress of Nandikeśvara;
she is Ghargharā, whose roar is like the sound of a water-pot, formidable, and of a terrible form.
She is the destroyer of the Kali age, the destroyer of the dharma of the Kali age, and the destroyer of the curiosity of the Kali age;
she is the youthful maiden, beloved by Keśava, and the warder-off of the multitude of afflictions.
She is the greatly intoxicated, the greatly exhilarated, the great knowledge, and that which consists of the earth;
she is the great sacrifice, the great speech, and the upholder of Mount Mandara. || 15 ||
She bestows liberation and bestows delusion; she is the delusion that grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
She is intent upon loud, boisterous laughter and wears tinkling anklets.
She with long fangs, long face, and long nose, the one who dwells in the long [lake];
she is the destroyer of the sons of Danu, the wicked one, and the shatterer of suffering and poverty. || 17 ||
She is of difficult conduct yet the destroyer of faults, the wife of Dama, and devoted to compassion;
she is born of the mind, composed of Manu, and the increaser of Manu’s lineage.
Śyāmā, Śyāmatanu, Śobhā, Saumyā, and Śambhuvilāsinī—thus have these one hundred and eight divine names been recounted to you. (19)
O Goddess of the gods, O Sovereign of the Suras, for your pleasure, this which is not to be revealed and must be kept secret should be recited with great effort. 20.
O Dear One, having meditated upon the Goddess and drunk the divine liquor with the five "M"s,
one should constantly worship with devotion and recite this auspicious hymn.
Within six months, even he shall become equal to Gaṇanātha;
what is the use of much speaking here before you, O beloved of my life?
O Omniscient One, you know all things, yet you ask me again;
[this teaching] should not be given to the disciples of others, and especially not to those who revile it. (23)
Thus ends the hymn of one hundred and eight names of the illustrious Bhairavī.
Then Mahākālabhairava spoke the Thousand Names:
"Now, O Maheśānī, I shall declare the thousand names of the Goddess."
O Great Goddess, by whose grace one may obtain the fruits of the four aims of human life. || 1 ||
This hymn, which pacifies all diseases, destroys all death, and brings about all accomplishments—there is no praise superior to this. (2)
There is no knowledge higher than this, and no sacred ford (tīrtha) is remembered as superior to this;
from it all has arisen, and in it all still abides even today.
O Maheśvarī, all that shall go to dissolution at the time of the cosmic dissolution;
I bow to the goddess Tripurā, who is Bhairavī and the liberator from fear. || 4 ||
The venerable Lord is the seer (*ṛṣi*) of this *Śrītripurabhairavīsahasranāmastotra*, which directly bestows all accomplishments and destroys great sins;
the *paṅkti* is the meter (*chanda*), the Primordial Power (*Ādyā Śakti*) is the meter, and the goddess Tripurabhairavī is the deity (*devatā*).
The application is for the purpose of accomplishing all desired aims during the recitation.
Tripurā, the supreme sovereign goddess, who dwells in the perfection of yoga;
she is the goddess consisting of all mantras and the promoter of all accomplishments.
The auspicious Goddess, whose nature is the support of all, bestows all prosperity;
she is the Yoginī, the Mother of Yoga, and the promoter of yogic accomplishments.
She is the object of meditation for yogis, composed of yoga, and she dwells within the yoga of yoga;
she is sport, play, and pastime, and she sets in motion the form of time.
Kālamātā, Kālarātri, Kālī, Kāmalavāsinī,
Kamalā, Kāntirūpā, Kāmarājeśvarī, and Kriyā.
Kaṭu, Kapaṭakeśā, Kapaṭā, she who has the form of an unchaste woman (Kulaṭākṛti), Kumudā, Carccikā, Kānti, and she who is always beloved by Kālarātri.
Her intellect bestows both dharma and adharma; she is of terrible form and most formidable.
She is the bell that rings with a deep *gharghara* sound, and she is forever fond of the resonance of the bell.
The intellect is always subtle, subtler, gross, and exceedingly gross;
it is the ultimate truth, possessed of truth, and dwells within the convention of truth.
She is forgiveness, she is formidable, and likewise she is the one who utters a terrifying roar;
she is of the form of a whirlwind, the remover of fear, the giver of fear, and the destroyer of fear.
The Goddess who dwells in the cremation ground, who resides in the abode of the cremation ground;
she whose seat is a corpse, whose food is a corpse, whose body is a corpse—she is both Śivā and Aśivā.
Feeding on corpses from the region of the throat, wearing ornaments of corpses,
she is the bumpy one with beautiful teeth, the truthful one who dwells at the place of the true appointment.
She whose body is truth, whose food is truth, who dwells in those who speak the truth;
she whose abode is truth, who is attached to truth, and who fulfills her vows of truth.
She is unattached and free from attachment, yet well-attached and the deluder of attachments;
she is the illusory intellect, the Great Illusion, and she who delights in the great sacrifice.
She who dwells in the two mouths from which streams of flowing blood issue;
she who is the essence of truth, whose contact is truth, and who brings about union with truth.
Unattached yet delighting in attachment, she is the perfect attachment dwelling within attachment;
eternally true and the great truth, she is the noose of flesh and the excellent flesh.
Eaters of flesh, bearers of flesh, consumers of flesh, devourers of flesh;
drinkers of blood, lovers of blood, red-hued, and fond of blood.
She whose food is blood, who is fond of blood, who destroys those who revile blood;
she who delights in drinking blood, the youthful maiden, whose realm is red, the intensely radiant one.
She who dwells in the Svayambhū flower, she who is eager for the Svayambhū flower,
she whose food is the Svayambhū flower, and she whose seat is the one who censures the Svayambhū.
She who delights in the Svayambhū flower, she who originates from the Svayambhū flower,
she who is enriched by garlands of Svayambhū flowers, and she who is the destroyer of those who revile the Svayambhū.
She who sports with the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*, she whose intellect is ever fixed on the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*,
she who acts for the pleasure of the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*, and she who originates from the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*.
She whose essence is semen, who produces semen, who is exceedingly pure semen, and who is the excellent pearl;
she who is worshipped by those who worship semen, and who reviles those who revile semen.
She who wears red garlands, she who possesses red flowers, she whose blossoms are like red flowers;
her limbs are anointed with red sandalwood, yet she scorns red sandalwood.
Matsyā, Matsyapriyā, Mānyā, Matsyabhakṣā, Mahodayā;
Matsyāhārā, Matsyakāmā, and Matsyanindakanāśinī.
She who has squinting eyes, likewise the cruel one, the destroyer of cruel armies;
she whose limbs are cruel, she whose limbs are like thunderbolts, she whose limbs are marked by wheels, and she who is born from the wheel.
She whose body is a wheel, who wears a garland of wheels, who dwells within a skeleton of wheels;
she whose navel is deep, who removes fear, who bestows fear, and who takes away fear.
She who bestows fear, she who is terrified by fear, she who is fearless, she who roars terribly;
she who is beautiful, she who is auspicious, she who is truth, she who is secure, and likewise she who brings security.
Adorned with vermilion, she whose form resembles vermilion,
whose nose is reddened with dye, who possesses a beautiful nose, and whose nostrils are well-sunken.
She is short, pot-bellied, tall, long-nosed, and large-breasted;
she is crooked, fickle, fierce, and the most formidable goddess with a fierce roar.
Aticaṇḍā, Mahācaṇḍā, Śrīcaṇḍā, Caṇḍaveginī,
Cāṇḍālī, Caṇḍikā, Caṇḍaśabdarūpā, and Cañcalā.
Campā, Campāvatī, Costā, Tīkṣṇā, Tīkṣṇapriyā,
Kṣati, Jaladā, Jayadā, Yogā, and Jagadānandakāriṇī.
She is the one worshipped by the world, the Mother of the world, the earth, and the patient endurer of the world;
she is the one to be born, the mother of victory, the victorious one, and likewise the giver of victory.
She is the Mother, the Sustainer of the World, known as Jayā, whose very form is victory;
she is the Mother of the Universe, honored by the world, the Glory of Victory, and the Bringer of Triumph.
Jayinī, Jayamātā, Jayā, and likewise Vijayā;
Khaḍginī, Khaḍgarūpā, Sukhaḍgā, and Khaḍgadhāriṇī.
She who has the form of a sword, who holds a sword in her hand, who possesses a sword, who is beloved by the sword;
she who gives swords, whose nature is the sword, and who is born from the body of the sword.
Khaḍgā, Khaḍgadharā, Khelā, Khaḍginī, Khaḍgamaṇḍinī;
Śaṅkhinī, Cāpinī, Devī, Vajriṇī, Śulinī, and Mati.
Vālinī, Bhindipālī, Pāśī, Aṅkuśī,
Śarī, Dhanuṣī, Caṭakī, Carmā, Dantī, and Karṇanālikī.
Musalī, she who takes the form of a plowshare, she who dwells in the multitude of quivers;
she whose abode is the quiver, the remover of the quiver, and she whose form arises from the quiver.
She who possesses quivers, who is free from the fatigue of the quiver, whose limbs are like quivers, who is fond of quivers;
the Goddess who wields various missiles and originates from various weapons.
Lakṣā, Lakṣaharā, Lābhā, Sulābhā,
Lābhanāśinī, Lābhahārā, Lābhakarā, Lābhinī, and Lābharūpiṇī.
Dharitrī, Dhanadā, Dhānyā, Dhanyarūpā, Dharā, Dhanuḥ,
Dhuraśabdā, Dhurāmānyā, Dharāṅgī, and Dhananāśinī.
The destroyer of wealth, the gain of wealth, she who is obtainable through wealth, the great bow;
the unpeaceful, the form of peace, and the dweller in the path of the breath.
She is served by the hosts of the sky and the stars; she is the beloved of speech, which is the limb of the Gaṇas;
she is the bestower of the Gaṇas and the destroyer of the Gaṇas; she is to be attained, and she is beautiful in her coming and going.
She who moves when one is to go, she who destroys the calculation, she who removes disease, she who increases disease;
she who is stability, she who destroys stability, and she who brings an end to stability, she who belongs to the lineage.
She is the giver, the doer, the beloved, love itself, the bestower of what is dear, the increaser of what is dear,
the destroyer of what is dear, the auspiciousness of what is dear, and she whose body is the root of the tree of love for the beloved.
She who is beloved by her husband, who is destined for love, who dwells in what is dear, and who abides in the home;
she who is well-established, whose form is stable, who bestows stability, and who is adorned with the peacock of steadfastness.
Cañcalā, Capalā, Colā, Capalāṅganivāsinī,
Gaurī, Kālī, as well as Chinnā, Māyā, Mānyā, and Harapriyā.
Sundarī, Tripurā, Bhavyā, the dweller in Tripureśvara;
the Goddess who destroys Tripura and who takes away the life-breath of Tripura.
Bhairavī resides in Bhairava; she is the beloved body of Bhairava.
She is the limb of Bhava, has the form of Bhairava, and is the most cherished consort of Bhairava.
Kāladā, Kālarātri, Kāmā, Kātyāyanī,
Kriyā, Kriyadā, Kriyahā, Klaibyā, and likewise Priyaprāṇakriyā.
He is Krīṅkārī, Kamalā, Lakṣmī, Śakti, Svāhā, the Pervasive One (Vibhu),
the Lord (Prabhu), Nature (Prakṛti), and the Spirit (Puruṣa), possessing both the form of the Puruṣa and the non-Puruṣa.
The Supreme Person himself, and Māyā Nārāyaṇī, the Intellect;
likewise Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and Vaiṣṇavī.
Vārāhī, Cāmuṇḍā, Indrāṇī, Haravallabhā,
Bharggī, Māheśvarī, Kṛṣṇā, Kātyāyanī, and Pūtanā as well.
The Rākṣasī, the Ḍākinī, Citrā, Vicitrā, and likewise Vibhramā;
Hākinī, Rākinī, Bhītā, Gandharvā, and Gandhavāhinī.
Kekarī, Koṭarākṣī, Nirmāṃsā, Alūkamāṃsikā,
Lalajjihvā, Sujihvā, Bāladā, and Bāladāyinī.
Candrā, Candraprabhā, Cāndrī, and she who is intent upon the splendor of the moon; Amṛtā, Mānadā, Pūṣā, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭī, Rati, and Dhṛti.
Śaśinī, Candrikā, Kānti, Jyotsnā, Śrī, Prīti, Aṅgadā, Pūrṇā,
Pūrṇāmṛtā, Kalpalatikā, and Kalpadānadā.
She is of noble resolve, with hands capable of creative action, and the creator of the wish-fulfilling tree;
she is known as Kalpā, she is worthy of the Kalpa, and she is praised by those who find bliss in the Kalpa.
Sūcīmukhī, Pretamukhī, Ulkāmukhī, Mahāsukhī,
Ugramukhī, Sumukhī, Kākāsyā, and Vikaṭānanā.
Kṛkalāsyā, Sandhyāsyā, Mukulīśā, and Ramākṛti; Nānāmukhī, Nānāsyā, and she who assumes various forms.
She is worshipped by all, the mother of all, named by all, and the source of all beings;
she is the Sun, possessing solar radiance, the very splendor, abiding within the solar orb.
Sūryakānti, Sūryakarā, Sūryākhyā, Sūryabhāvanā, Tapinī, Tāpinī, Dhūmrā, Marīci, Jvālinī, and Ruci.
She is the giver of heaven, the giver of enjoyments, the all-encompassing, the awakener, the sustainer, and the patient one;
she is the giver of the ages, the destroyer of yoga, the worthy one, the destroyer of the unworthy, and the increaser of yoga.
She is established within the fire-maṇḍala, she dwells in the center of the fire-maṇḍala,
she has the form of the fire-maṇḍala, and she is designated as the fire-maṇḍala.
She whose splendor is fire, whose passion is fire, who bestows fire, who destroys fire,
who is the activity of fire, and who is the consumer of fire— this digit (kalā) is ever established in fire.
Dhūmrārciṣā, Ujjvalinī, as well as Visphuliṅginī,
Śūlinī, Surūpā, Kapilā, and Havyavāhinī.
The various radiant goddesses are the consorts of the Supreme Brahman;
the goddess consists of the light of Brahman and has the nature of the Great Brahman.
The Supreme Self, supreme, meritorious, the giver of merit, the increaser of merit,
the bestower of merit, she whose name is merit, who possesses the fragrance of merit, and whose body is beloved.
She whose body is merit, who performs meritorious deeds, who censures the censurers of merit;
she who brings about the time of merit, who is merit itself, who is supremely meritorious, and who is a garland of merit.
In ancient times, she was Puṇyakhelā, Puṇyakelī, and equal in name to Puṇyā;
she is to be served by merit, sported with by merit, and is the beloved of ancient merit.
She is the life-force of the Puruṣa, her essential nature is the self of the Puruṣa;
she possesses the limbs of the Puruṣa, she is the female counterpart of the Puruṣa, and she is eternally a portion of the Puruṣa.
She who possesses beautiful flowers, whose life-breath is flowers, who takes away flowers,
who is dear to flowers, who loves flowers, who wears garlands of flowers, and who is worshipped by those who worship flowers.
Puṣpahā, Puṣpamālā, and Puṣpanindakanāśinī;
Nakṣatraprāṇahantrī and Nakṣatrālakṣavandakā.
She who possesses a garland of a hundred thousand, she who wears a necklace of a hundred thousand, she who is a hundred thousandfold, she whose very nature is a hundred thousand;
she who is the stars, she who is the auspicious constellation, she who devours the stars, and she of great exaltation.
She who wears great garlands, she who is highly honored, the Great One worshipped by the Mothers;
she who is the youngest of the Great-Great Ones, the Great Mahākāleśvarī.
Mahāsyā, Vandanīyā, Mahāśabdanivāsinī,
Mahāśaṅkheśvarī, Mīnā, Matsyagandhā, and Mahodarī.
Lambodarī, Lamboṣṭhī, Lambanimnatanūdarī,
Lamboṣṭhī, Lambanāsā, Lambaghoṇā, and Lalatsukā.
Atilambā, Mahālambā, Sulambā, Lambavāhinī,
Lambārhā, Lambaśakti, Lambasthā, and Lambapūrvikā.
She possesses four bells, she is the great bell, and she always delights in the sound of bells;
she loves musical instruments, is devoted to music, is the beautiful music itself, and is the destroyer of [worldly] music.
Ramā, Rāmā, Subālā, and she whose nature is delightful; she who is most beautiful, the giver of delight, Rambhā, she with thighs like plantain stalks, and the beloved of Rāma.
She who loves desire, who creates desire, whose limbs are desire, the delightful one, Rati;
she who is dear to Rati, Rati herself, the beloved of Rati, and she who is served by Rati.
Surabhi, Surabhī, Śobhā, Dikśobhā, Śubhanāśinī,
Suśobhā, Mahāśobhā, Atiśobhā, and Pretatāpinī.
She who is greedy, greatly greedy, very greedy, and the increaser of greed;
she whose limbs are greed, who is to be honored by greed, the serpent of greed, and the illuminator of greed.
She who delights in greed, who possesses great greed, who reviles and censures greed;
(p. 270) she who dwells in the limbs of greed, who is both fragrance and foul odor, and who destroys all odors.
Gandhāṅgī, Gandhapuṣṭā, Sugandhā,
Premagandhikā, Durgandhā, Pūtigandhā, Vigandhā, and Atigandhikā.
Padmāntikā, Padmavahā, Padmapriyapriyaṅkarī,
Padmanindakanindā, and Padmasantoṣavāhanā.
The goddess is the supreme red lotus, always fond of the red lotus;
she possesses the fragrance of the red lotus and dwells within the red lotus.
She wears a garland of red lotuses, she is enchanting with her red lotuses;
she has beautiful eyes like red lotuses and assumes the very form of the red lotus.
She is Vaiṣṇavī, worthy of worship by Viṣṇu, and she dwells within the bodies of Vaiṣṇavas; she is worshipped by those who adore Viṣṇu, and her form is established within the Vaiṣṇava.
Residing within the body of Nārāyaṇa, she is captivating to Nārāyaṇa;
she is of the very nature of Nārāyaṇa and abides in the mind of Nārāyaṇa.
Born from the body of Nārāyaṇa, she is the beloved form of Nārāyaṇa;
she is the woman (Nārī) who is beyond counting among the consorts of Nārāyaṇa, and she is dear to the abode of Nārāyaṇa.
Worshipful to Hara, supreme to Hara, the beloved of Hara, the patient one;
the destroyer, residing within the body of Hara, and ever intent on the worship of Hara.
Born from the body of Hara, dwelling upon the limbs of Hara, she is the new moon;
she is the one to be worshipped by the worshippers of Hara, and is ever intent on saluting Hara.
Born from the body of Hara, she is the constant resort for Hara’s sport;
she is free from association with the Suganas, unattached, and the destroyer of attachment.
She is solitary, devoid of people, and difficult to access; she wards off the afflictions of distress.
She brings an end to the body of distress, possesses a form that is difficult to attain, and dwells within those who are destitute.
She is the maker of the deceased, beloved of the deceased, and born from the bodies of the deceased;
she dwells within the limbs of the deceased, is the deceased herself, and the crusher of the bodies of the deceased.
She is the Ḍākinī, the Yoginī, Kālarātri, and the one ever dear to Time;
she is the destroyer of Kālarātri, the Black One, whose body is dark and whose form is vast.
She has a dark body and a curved form; she possesses a vajra-body and assumes the nature of a vajra.
Bearing various bodies, she is the blessed one who dwells within the sequence of the six cakras.
She dwells in the *mūlādhāra* and is ever situated in the *mūlādhāra*;
she is the form of wind, of great form, and resides on the path of the wind.
The Goddess, joined with the wind, the maker of the wind, who fills the filler of the wind,
assumes the form of the wind and moves along the path of the Suṣumṇā.
Abiding in the body, having the form of the body, and being meditated upon within the body, she is the auspicious Dehikā;
she is in the form of the channels, in the form of the earth, and dwells in the locations of the channels.
Iṅgalā and Piṅgalā, as well as Suṣumnā who dwells in the center,
perform what is dear to Sadāśiva and assume the form of Mūlaprakṛti.
Amṛteśī is the great Śālī, dwelling in the limbs of erotic sentiment;
she is the one who brings about arising, maintenance, and destruction, and she resides in the state of dissolution.
She is associated with the great dissolution, the performer of creation and withdrawal;
she is Svadhā, Svāhā, the bearer of oblations, the oblation itself, and always fond of oblations.
She is the abode of the oblation, the consumer of the oblation, and she who has arisen from the body of the oblation;
she is the play of the oblation, whose nature is that of the wish-fulfilling cow, and who is born of beauty.
Surabhī, Nandanī, Puṇyā, Yajñāṅgī, Yajñasambhavā,
Yajñasthā, Yajñadehā, Yonijā, and Yonivāsinī.
Born not from a womb, she is both real and unreal, possessing a crooked body;
she is Ahalyā, the wife of Gautama, accessible to him, yet born of Videha and the destroyer of the body.
Gāndhārī, Draupadī, Dūtī, Śivapriyā, Trayodaśī,
Pañcadaśī, Paurṇamāsī, Caturdaśī, and Pañcamī.
The sixth, the ninth, the eighth, the tenth,
as well as the eleventh and the twelfth— these, in the form of doorways, bestow fear.
Through the transition [of the breath], she is of the nature of the *sāman*, noble-born yet the destroyer of the lineage;
she is the beloved of the lineage, emaciated, the water-jar, and the one who increases the body of the jar.

She is the disciplined one, of noble lineage, the seeker, the inner witness, the follower, and the dawn; she is the giver of rivers and oceans, peace itself, the embodiment of tranquility, and the bringer of perfect peace.
She is hope, thirst, hunger, and agitation; she dwells in the form of perturbation;
she flows to the ocean like the Gaṅgā; she is beauty, sacred revelation, tradition, fortitude, and the earth.
She is day and night, the body composed of the five elements, and the one with a beautiful form;
she is rice-grain, Chinnamastā, and she who wears a serpent as a sacred thread.
Varṇinī, Ḍākinī, Śakti, Kurukullā, Sukullakā, Pratyaṅgirā, the other goddess Aparā, Ajitā, and Jayadāyinī.
She who is Jaya and Vijaya, the slayer of Mahiṣāsura,
the destroyer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, and the annihilator of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa.
She is the slayer of Niśumbha and Śumbha, the destroyer of Raktabīja;
she is Kāśī, the resident of Kāśī, Madhurā, Pārvatī, and the Supreme.
Aparṇā, the goddess Caṇḍikā, Mṛḍānī, Ambikā, and Kalā;
she is white, black, and of every color, with a form like a digit of the autumn moon.
Rukmiṇī and Rādhikā are indeed proclaimed as [forms] of Bhairavī;
by chanting the names of the Goddess, one attains [the merit of] more than eight thousand [recitations].
Even one joined with a great sin (mahāpātaka) is liberated; there is no doubt in this matter.
[These sins are: the killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, theft, and violating the teacher’s wife.
Even ten million great sins (mahāpātaka) as well as minor sins (upapātaka) are all destroyed in that very instant by this hymn spoken by Bhairava.
By reciting or even remembering the entire [text], or even a single verse,
or by reading it oneself or causing others to read it, one shall be immediately released from bondage.
O Maheśvarī, [this applies] at the king’s gate, in battle, in a fortress, in a narrow pass, on an inaccessible mountain, in a wilderness, on a mountain, or even on a boat.
When the danger of fire or a difficult pass has arisen, or when one is beset by lions and tigers,
a mortal is liberated from every peril through recitation and remembrance [of this].
A sonless man obtains a son, and a poor man becomes wealthy;
a brahmin devoted to all the scriptures shall obtain the fruits of all sacrifices.
O Maheśvarī, [it grants] the stambhana of fire, wind, and water, as well as the stambhana of movement; likewise, it is used for killing, inciting hatred, and expulsion.
With undistracted mind, one should write the hymn using yellow orpiment and saffron;
through this, whether performed by a preceptor or by Vaiṣṇavas, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices.
Subjugation [of others] occurs right here, and all accomplishments (siddhis) arise;
having become pure at dawn, at midday, and at the onset of night.
Whether one recites it oneself or causes others to recite it, one shall obtain the fruit of all sacrifices;
even a wicked king, like a servant, shall become mute before a debater.
O Maheśvarī, on a Sunday, Tuesday, or Thursday,
one with undistracted mind should write out this hymn using *gorocanā* and saffron.
By wearing [this] placed within gold, one obtains the fruits of all sacrifices from the Guru or from Vaiṣṇavas, and shall attain all desires.
O Maheśvarī, it should be worn by women on the left hand and likewise by men on the right hand, on Sundays, Tuesdays, or Saturdays.
Or if one writes it during the time of Saturn, one will certainly obtain all accomplishments;
whether in a wilderness or in a cremation ground, at night during the hour of midnight.
And in an empty house, O Goddess of gods,
the practitioner should diligently draw [the mandala] when Jupiter has entered the sign of Leo and the sun is situated in Cancer.
When Jupiter has entered the sign of Pisces, the practitioner should write with diligence;
having seen a woman in her menses, he should always write while remaining in that state.
One should carefully draw [the deity] using fragrant white flowers and fragrant sandalwood paste mixed with musk and deer-essence.
Having written it down, recited it, and also retained it with undistracted mind,
one should worship a young maiden and likewise worship women.
Having worshipped with flowers, perfumes, sandalwood, and garments,
one should worship with vermilion and red flowers through the yoga of devotion.
Alternatively, O Goddess, one should worship virgins up to ten years of age;
there, one obtains all desired fruits even at that very moment.
In this, there is no dependence on perfected beings (*siddhas*) and the like, nor is there any concern regarding friends, enemies, or defects;
O Mistress of the Gods, it bestows perfection through mere recitation (*japa*), without the need for deliberation.
At all times and in all undertakings, having offered a bali-oblation according to the prescribed rite, one should worship Śivā every day with six thousand [recitations].
One should worship the goddess Pārvatī— who is Bhairavī and the essence of Tripura— with Svayambhū flowers and offerings day and night.
One should feed ten or twelve Brahmins daily;
O Goddess, by this rite one should constantly worship Bālā.
Whoever recites this for one month at the three junctions of the day according to this rite shall obtain a son if childless, and if destitute, shall become wealthy.
O Goddess, by this method, after three months or likewise after four months, one’s purpose will be accomplished.
One shall be liberated from long-term illness; in the fifth month, one becomes a preeminent poet;
and likewise, O Goddess, in the sixth month, one attains all sovereign powers.
In the seventh [birth], one attains the power of moving through the sky; in the eighth, great splendor;
in the ninth, all supernatural accomplishments (siddhis); and in the tenth, one is honored by the world.
On the eleventh day one becomes subject to kings, but on the twelfth, one becomes Indra;
he who recites it even once obtains the fruit of worship.
Whoever, being restrained and pure, recites even a single complete verse,
obtains the fruit of worship as declared by Bhairava.
In the conjunction with the long-lived Prīti, especially during the Brāhma and Aindra yogas,
as well as on the fifth and sixth lunar days, it remains effective wherever one may be situated.
No fear exists there, nor any defect such as illusion;
by reciting this even once, a mortal is liberated from all distress.
O Goddess, what more need be said? One shall obtain all desired fruits.
Thus ends the *Śrītripurabhairavīsahasranāmastotra*, composed by Mahābhairava in the *Śrīviśvasāra*.
Thus ends the Tripurabhairavī Tantra within the Śāktapramoda.
Composed and compiled by His Majesty King Śrī Rājā Deva Nandana Siṃha Bahādura, the Lord of the capital of Śiva-Hara and possessor of the Goddess of Fortune.
The seventh Tantra within the Śāktapramoda, the Dhūmāvatītantra.
This has been edited by Paṇḍita Śrī Raghurāja Dubejī, a descendant of the aforementioned royal preceptor.
Printed and published by Śrī Kṛṣṇadāsātmaja Khemarāja at his own Śrī Veṅkaṭeśvara Press.
Bombei.
Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. Now begins the Śāktapramoda.
The Dhūmāvatī Tantra:
Now, the meditation on Dhūmāvatī—
she is discolored, flickering, wicked, tall, and clad in soiled garments.
With disheveled hair, harsh, a widow, and with sparse teeth.
Mounted upon a chariot with a crow as its banner, with pendulous breasts,
holding a winnowing basket in her hand, with extremely harsh eyes, shaking her hands, she was endowed with excellent qualities.
But she who has a prominent nose, is exceedingly crooked, and has squinting eyes,
is constantly afflicted by hunger and thirst, brings fear, and is a source of quarrels.
(p. 278) Now, the extraction of the diagram (*yantra*): In a ritual procedure (*kalpa*) not previously mentioned, one should draw a lotus diagram with eight petals;
therein, it should have a six-cornered pericarp and be adorned with four gates.
Now, the extraction of the mantra:
the two letters *da* and *ta*, followed by the seed-syllable ending with *sarvīśa* (the letter *i*) and a bindu (*m*), and then *dhūmāvatī* (the letter *u*) and *dviṭha* (the letter *la*).
This is declared to be the mantra of Dhūmāvatī, which effects the subjugation of enemies.
Now the mantra:
*dhū* *dhū* *dhūmāvatī* *ṭhaḥ* *ṭhaḥ*.
Now the ritual procedure for worship (*pūjāvidhi*).
Therein, one should first perform the Nyāsa of the Ṛṣi and so forth: "Obeisance to the sage Pippalāda on the head;
obeisance to the Nicṛt metre on the mouth; obeisance to Dhūmāvatī on the heart."
Now, the ritual placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa):
Oṃ dhāḥ, salutation to the heart; Oṃ dhīṃ, svāhā to the head; Oṃ dhūḥ, vaṣaṭ to the tuft of hair;
Oṃ dhaiṃ, hūṃ to the armor; Oṃ dhauṃ, vauṣaṭ to the three eyes; Oṃ dhaḥ, phaṭ to the weapon.
Then, the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*):
*oṃ dhāḥ* to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*; *oṃ dhīṃ* to the two index fingers, *svāhā*;
*oṃ dhūṃ* to the two middle fingers, *vaṣaṭ*; *oṃ dhaiṃ* to the two ring fingers, *hūṃ*.
Oṃ dhauṃ, to the two little fingers, vauṣaṭ. Oṃ dhaḥ, to the palms and backs of the hands, phaṭ.
Then there appeared a widow, pale, restless, black, tall, and clad in soiled garments; her hair was disheveled, her skin was rough, and her teeth were sparse. || 1 ||

Mounted upon a chariot with a crow as its banner, with pendulous breasts, holding a winnowing basket in her hand, with extremely harsh eyes, shaking her hand, she is endowed with excellent qualities. (2)
With a greatly protruding nose, exceedingly crooked, and squinting eyes, she is constantly afflicted by hunger and thirst, a source of fear, and a locus of quarrels. (3)
Having meditated thus, one should establish the vital breaths and so forth. It is as follows:
Ā Hrīḥ Kroṃ Ya Ra La Va Śa Ṣa Sa Hoṃ Oṃ Kṣa Sa Ha Saḥ Hrīḥ Oṃ Ha Saḥ.
Here are the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) of the illustrious Dhūmāvatī; here are her vital breaths.
Ā HĪ KROṂ YA RA LA VA ŚA ṢA SA HOṂ OṂ KṢA SA HA SAḤ HRĪṂ OṂ HA/SAḤ | The life-force (jīva) of the illustrious Dhūmāvatī is stationed here.
OṂ HRĪṂ KROṂ YA RA LA VA ŚA ṢA SA HOṂ OṂ KṢA SA HA/SAḤ HRĪṂ OṂ HA/SAḤ.
All the sense organs of the illustrious Dhūmāvatī are present here.
Ā Hrīṃ Kroṃ Ya Ra La Va Śa Ṣa Sa Hoṃ Oṃ Kṣa Sa Ha Saḥ!
O illustrious Dhūmāvatī, [your] speech, mind, eyes, ears, nose, and vital breaths, having come here—
May they remain happily for a long time, svāhā!
Then, having meditated upon oneself as having the form of the deity.

Having performed the breath control (prāṇāyāma), the placement of the Ṛṣis and others (ṛṣyādinyāsa), the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa), and the hand placement (karanyāsa), one should perform the placement of the Mātṛkā (mātṛkānyāsa). In that regard: "Om, of this Mātṛkā-mantra, Brahmā is the Seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is the meter (chandaḥ), Mātṛkā-Sarasvatī is the deity (devatā), and the consonants are the seed-syllables (bīja)."
The vowels are the *śaktis*, both [vowels and consonants] together are the *kīlaka*, and the application (*viniyoga*) is for the sake of attaining one's desired goal.
On the head: salutation to Brahmā, the seer (*ṛṣi*). In the mouth: salutation to Gāyatrī, the meter (*chandas*).
In the heart: salutation to Mātṛkā-Sarasvatī, the deity (*devatā*). At the *liṅga*: salutation to the consonants, the seeds (*bījas*).
Salutation to the Śaktis, the vowels, at the two feet; salutation to the Kīlaka consisting of both [the consonants and vowels] at all limbs.
Now, the six-limbed assignment (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa):
a, ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa, ā—salutation to the heart.
i ca cha ja jha ña ī—svāhā to the head;
u ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa ū—vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock;
e ta tha da dha na aiṃ—hūṃ to the armor.
Oṃ pa pha ba bha ma auṃ netratrayāya vauṣaṭ; a ya ra la va śa ṣa ha kṣa aḥ astrāya phaṭ.
The placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*) is as follows: *a ka kha ga gha ṅa ā* to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*;
*i ca cha ja jha ña ī* to the two index fingers, *svāhā*.
u ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa ū—*vaṣaṭ* with the two middle fingers;
e ta tha da dha na aiṃ—*hūṃ* with the two ring fingers;
oṃ pa pha ba bha ma auṃ—*vauṣaṭ* with the two little fingers.
A Ya Ra La Va Śa Ṣa Sa Ha Kṣa Aḥ, phaṭ with both palms and backs of the hands.
Now, the placement of the Mātṛkās (mātṛkānyāsa):

on the forehead, *a* namaḥ; on the perimeter of the mouth, *ā* namaḥ; on the right eye, *iṃ* namaḥ; on the left eye, *īṃ* namaḥ; on the right ear, *u* namaḥ; on the left ear, *ū* namaḥ; on the right nostril...
*Ṛ* namaḥ on the left nostril; *Ṝ* namaḥ on the right cheek; *Ḷ* namaḥ on the left cheek;
*Ḹ* namaḥ on the upper lip; *E* namaḥ on the lower lip; *AI* namaḥ on the upper row of teeth.
Oṃ namaḥ; on the row of lower teeth, auṃ namaḥ; on the head, aṃ namaḥ; on the mouth, aḥ namaḥ;
at the base of the right arm, ka namaḥ; at the elbow, kha namaḥ; at the wrist, ga namaḥ;
at the base of the fingers, gha namaḥ; at the tips of the fingers, ṅa namaḥ; at the base of the left arm...
Ca, salutation; at the elbow, Cha, salutation; at the wrist, Ja, salutation; at the base of the fingers, Jha, salutation;

at the tips of the fingers, Ña, salutation; at the base of the right thigh, Ṭa, salutation; at the knee, Ṭha, salutation; at the ankle, Ḍa, salutation; at the base of the toes, Ḍha, salutation; at the tips of the toes...

Ṇa/Namaḥ at the root of the left thigh; Ta/Namaḥ at the knee; Tha/Namaḥ at the ankle; Da/Namaḥ at the base of the toes; Dha/Namaḥ at the tips of the toes; Na/Namaḥ on the right side; Pa/Namaḥ on the left side; Ba/Namaḥ on the back; Bha/Namaḥ at the navel; [Ma/Namaḥ] at the abdomen.

*Maṃ*, salutation to the self of the skin in the heart; *yaṃ*, salutation to the self of blood in the right shoulder; *raṃ*, salutation to the self of flesh in the crown of the head; *laṃ*, salutation to the self of fat in the left shoulder;
*vaṃ*, salutation to the self of bone from the heart to the tip of the right arm; *śaṃ*, salutation to the self of marrow.
From the heart to the tip of the left arm: *ṣaṃ* to the *majjātman*, *namaḥ*; from the heart to the tip of the right foot: *saṃ* to the *śukrātman*, *namaḥ*;
from the heart to the tip of the left foot: *haṃ* to the *ātman*, *namaḥ*.
From the heart to the crown of the head: *kṣaṃ paramātmane namaḥ*.

Thus ends the external placement of the Mātṛkās (bahir-mātṛkā-nyāsa). Thereafter, one should worship the Goddess with mental offerings. In that regard, one should pray with this mantra: "O Dhūmāvatī, welcome to you; be present here now. Accept this mental worship, which has been contemplated according to its true purpose."
Then, one should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times using a rosary made of [the appropriate] beads. Thus concludes the procedure for mental worship.
Now follows the external worship.
Therein, having performed the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) and other rites,

one should first perform the three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) known as inhalation (*pūraka*), retention (*kumbhaka*), and exhalation (*recaka*) by reciting the root mantra four, sixteen, and eight times respectively; thereafter—
One should perform the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) and so forth, as follows:

*dhāṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*; *dhīṃ* to the head, *svāhā*; *dhūṃ* to the tuft of hair (*śikhā*), *vaṣaṭ*; *dhaiṃ* to the armor (*kavaca*), *hūm*; *dhauṃ* to the three eyes, *vauṣaṭ*; *dhaḥ* to the weapon (*astra*), *phaṭ*. Thus.
One should perform the binding of the directions with a snap of the fingers.
Thus is the ritual placement of the hands (karanyāsa).
Dhāṃ to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*; dhīṃ to the two index fingers, *svāhā*; dhūṃ to the two middle fingers, *vaṣaṭ*;
dhaiṃ to the two ring fingers, *hūm*; dhauṃ to the two little fingers, *vauṣaṭ*.
PHAṬ with both the palms and the backs of the hands joined together.
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and so forth in this manner, one should perform the setting out of the *arghya* offering. It is as follows:

Having fashioned a mandala consisting of a triangle, a circle, a hexagon, and a square, and having written "im" [within it], one should worship the triangle with the root mantra (mūlamantra). Then, having worshipped the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) upon the six parts [of the body], one should worship the four corners of the square as follows:
"Obeisance to Pūrṇagiri-pīṭha" in the east; "Obeisance to Uḍḍīyāna-pīṭha" in the south;

"Oṃ, obeisance to the seat of Kāmarūpa," thus in the west; "Oṃ, obeisance to the seat of Jālandhara," thus in the north. Having worshipped [them] in this manner, one should worship in the center with: "Oṃ, obeisance to Ādhāraśakti."

Having established the Yantrikā, which is adorned with a triangle within a hexagon, with the root mantra and the word *namaḥ*, one should sprinkle it with water from the general *arghya* vessel, reciting: "O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Sarasvatī, Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī! Be present in this water!"
Oṃ! O Sun, the sacred fords within the belly of the universe have been touched by your rays; by that truth, O God, O Maker of Day, grant me a sacred ford.
Having invoked the sacred sites with these and other [mantras], one should offer a flower with the *vauṣaṭ* mantra while employing the *aṅkuśa-mudrā*.

Having displayed the *gālinī-mudrā* with the syllable *vaṣaṭ*, having rendered [the offering] nectar-like by means of the *dhenu-mudrā* with the syllable *vam*, having meditated upon the chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), having worshipped and performed the ritual of integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*), having displayed the *śaṅkha-mudrā*, and having worshipped the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) within the hexagon, one should meditate upon the goddess Dhūmāvatī as before.

One should perform the invocation (*āvāhana*). It is as follows: reciting the root mantra, one should say, "Oṃ, O Blessed One Dhūmāvatī, come here! and, having pressed the two thumbs against the root joints of the extended and joined fingers, one should invoke her while reciting the root mantra: "O Goddess Dhūmāvatī, stay here! [This is done] with the hands facing downward.

One should establish [the deity] with the mudrā while reciting the root mantra. With the lotus-mudrā (padmamudrā), one should offer a seat of flowers and other offerings. Then: "O Goddess, you whose nature is imperishable, seated comfortably upon this excellent seat, may you be firmly established here; be gracious, O Supreme Sovereign."

Reciting the root mantra, one should consecrate [the image] with the previously mentioned mudrā, saying, "Be established here. Having established the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) according to the previously mentioned procedure for the installation of the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*), one should then perform a threefold sprinkling with the water of the *arghya* offering while reciting the root mantra. Then follows the water for washing the feet (*pādya*).

Reciting the root mantra: "I offer this *arghya* to Śrī Dhūmāvatī; *namaḥ*," one should place it at her feet. Then, reciting the root mantra: "I offer this *ācamanīya* to Śrī Dhūmāvatī; *namaḥ*," one should place it in her mouth.

Having recited the root mantra, [one should say]: "To the venerable Dhūmāvatī— along with her limbs (sāṅgāyai), along with her weapons (sāyudhāyai), along with her vehicle (savāhanāyai), and along with her retinue (saparivārāyai)—
I offer this madhuparka consisting of honey, ghee, sugar, curd, and milk."
One should place the word "mi nāma" in the mouth.

Reciting the root mantra again, one should offer the water for sipping (ācamanīya) by saying, "I present this to Śrī Dhūmāvatī, together with her limbs," and so forth, ending with "namaḥ," and place it in her mouth.

Reciting the root mantra, one should offer this *arghya* with the words "I offer this to Śrī Dhūmāvatī together with her limbs (*sāṅgāyai*)," and so forth, ending with "namaḥ," and place it upon the head.
Having recited this root-mantra, [one says] "I offer this turmeric-based unguent, along with its ancillaries, to the venerable Dhūmāvatī; obeisance."
Oṃ! O Sovereign Goddess, whose own form is immersed in the ocean of the awakening of supreme bliss, I offer this bath, complete with its primary and secondary limbs.
Reciting the root mantra and saying, "I offer this bathing substance to Śrī Dhūmāvatī together with her limbs," and so forth,
one should bathe [the deity] a hundred times, a thousand times, or as many times as one is able, ending with "I offer salutation."
Reciting the root mantra, "I offer this garment to Śrī Dhūmāvatī, svāhā," and so forth, ending with "namaḥ," one should present the garment.
Reciting the root mantra, "I offer this upper garment to Sāṅgā," and so forth, one should present the upper garment with the words, "I offer this to Śrī Dhūmāvatī; obeisance."
Reciting the root mantra, "I offer this sandalwood paste, along with its ancillaries, to Śrī Dhūmāvatī; obeisance."
Having recited the root mantra over these unbroken grains, [saying] "To Śrī Dhūmāvatī, together with her limbs," and so forth, I offer them; obeisance!
Reciting the root mantra while offering these flowers with the words "to Śrī Dhūmāvatī, together with her limbs, etc., vauṣaṭ," [one should perform the offering].
Having worshipped the bell with the sounds of "Victory! (jayadhvani), "O Mother! (mātaḥ), and "Svāhā!", while reciting the root mantra:
"Oṃ, endowed with the essence of the forest-king, rich in fragrance, and most enchanting..."

"May this incense, to be smelled by all the gods, be accepted. Reciting "This incense [is offered] to Sāṅgā," and so forth, saying "I offer this to Śrī Dhūmāvatī, obeisance," one should ring the bell with the left hand while joining the right thumb and index finger.

Displaying the incense mudrā and proclaiming the qualities of the deity, one should fumigate [the deity] from the region of the navel while reciting the root mantra. Reciting "This handful of flowers is offered to [the deity] with her limbs," and so forth,
ending with "I offer this to Śrī Dhūmāvatī, namaḥ," one should present three handfuls of flowers.
Oṃ! This great lamp, brilliantly radiant, which dispels all darkness, the light that shines both within and without—may this lamp be accepted.
While reciting the root mantra, forming the lamp-mudrā by joining the middle finger and the thumb, one should display the lamp toward the region of the eyes.
A ghee lamp is on the right, and an oil lamp is on the left.
Oṃ! I offer this accomplishment of the worthy vessel, consisting of various kinds of meat and many sorts of food;
O Goddess of Gods, please accept it out of compassion.
Reciting the root mantra and displaying the *grāsamudrā*, one should offer [the food] with water from a conch shell.
Oṃ, O Goddess of the lords of gods, you who are the supreme cause of attaining everything.
In this [vessel] filled with unbroken bliss, accept this excellent water.
Thus, having offered water, one should duly offer a handful of water according to the ritual.
Oṃ, [this is] endowed with cardamom, cloves, camphor, and betel leaf.
O Goddess, please accept this betel leaf offered with its share of areca nut.

Reciting the root mantra and saying, "I offer this betel leaf (tāmbūla) along with its ancillaries to Śrī Dhūmāvatī, [Oṃ] Namaḥ," one should place it in the region of the mouth using the *tattvamudrā*. Then, one should offer three handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*). Furthermore, one should offer a sacrificial oblation (*bali*) according to one's capacity, following the procedure for offering a *bali*.
Thus ends the venerable ritual procedure for the worship of Dhūmāvatī.
Now, the hymn of praise:
at dawn she is a maiden holding a flower bud while chanting her rosary;
at midday she is of mature form with a blossoming face and beautiful eyes; and at night—

May that Goddess Kālikā, the Mother of the three worlds, protect you—she who at twilight appears in the form of an old woman, with her pair of breasts dissolved away, wearing a garland of skulls, she who is the Goddess of gods. || 1 ||
Having tied the mass of matted hair of the lotus-born Brahmā to the tip of his skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga),
having made a garland for his chest from the heads of the foremost Daityas and a crest-ornament for his head from the feathers of Garuḍa,
and having taken in his hand the great horn of Yama’s buffalo filled with the blood of the gods;
May Bhairava protect you, who, at the time of the dissolution of the world, rejoices while being praised by Kālarātri.

Constantly devouring fragments of bone amidst a multitude of manifest *kaṭakaṭa* sounds, emitting fierce laughter— *kahakaha-haha-hāsa*— among the *pretas*, she of the emaciated limbs perpetually intent upon spreading the *ḍamaru* sound from her lotus-face.
May this Caṇḍikā protect us, wandering about and uttering the sounds "jhajha-majha-majha. || 3 ||

A mass of bells producing the sounds *ṭaṇ-ṭaṇ-ṭaṇ-ṭaṇ-ṭa-ṭaṇ-ṭā-prakara-ṭama-ṭa-mānā-ṭa-ghaṇṭā*, carrying forth the sounds *sphem-sphem-sphem* and the harsh laughter of jackals, terrifying with the clashing of its roar; wearing a garland of dangling severed heads, uttering the sounds *lala-hala-hala-hā*, and devouring raw flesh with its ever-moving jaws.
May she who devours Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, having repeatedly crushed them with "maṭa maṭa maṭa," purify [us]. || 4 ||

In his left ear is the moon surrounded by the dissolution [of time], and in his right the orb of the sun; around his neck is a necklace of constellations; upon his excellent and formidable mass of matted hair is a garland of severed heads;
and resting on his shoulder is the burden of Brahmā’s skull, together with a hand holding the banner of the lord of serpents.
May Bhadrakālī, who sustains all during the dissolution and bestows auspiciousness, take away my fear. || 5 ||
With her hair in a single braid smeared with oil, her ears adorned with shining earrings made of tin,
and having fashioned the beauty of her lotus-feet with a single iron anklet,
she who is naked and wears barley as ear-ornaments devours this world while riding a donkey.
O Goddess, you alone are she who rains down [blessings], whose arms are outstretched like banners, and who holds a sword.
