O Lord served by the sages, we here take refuge in your lotus feet— which are soft yet provide shelter and bestow bliss,
and which are the refuge sought by hosts of gods such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva—
and we serve them forever.
O Mother, this must be done. || 19 ||
Whoever, endowed with devotion, recites this hymn to the heart of Bagalā, Bagalā shall become pleased with him by virtue of that recitation. (20)
The devotee who, intent on the yellow meditation, listens without conceptualization,
shall become stainless while alive and, upon death, attain liberation.
He who recites this with devotion day and night on the Mahāṣṭamī of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina attains the favor of Bagalā.
The mortal who, clothed in yellow garments, recites this in the temple of the Goddess while meditating upon the Sovereign Bagalā, his enemies shall perish. (23)
He who is always devoted to yellow conduct, adorned with yellow ornaments, and constantly meditating upon Bagalā, shall daily recite this supreme Heart-Stotra. 24.
Nothing whatsoever is seen to be difficult to obtain for him upon the surface of the earth;
his enemies fall into exhaustion merely by the sight of him. (25)
Thus ends the Śrī-Bagalāhṛdayastotra in the Bagalā-paṭala of the Uttarakhanda of the Siddheśvara-tantra.
Then Nārada, uttering a hundred names, said: "O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, whose nature consists of creation, preservation, and dissolution!"
Now, recite the one hundred and eight names of Ambāgalā.
The Blessed Lord said: Listen, my child, I shall proclaim the one hundred and eight names of the Great Goddess Pītāmbarī, a hymn that destroys all sins.
By the mere recitation of which a debater instantly becomes mute in an instant, and the paralyzing of enemies occurs—this I speak as the truth, the absolute truth. (3)

Oṃ. Of this hymn of one hundred and eight names of the illustrious Pītāmbarī, Sadāśiva is the seer (ṛṣi), the Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandas), the illustrious Pītāmbarī is the deity (devatā), and it is employed for recitation (japa) for the sake of pleasing the illustrious Pītāmbarī.
Oṃ! Bagalā is the consort of Viṣṇu, the beloved of both Viṣṇu and Śaṅkara;
she is Bahulā, the mother of the Vedas, and also the progenitress of Mahāviṣṇu. || 1 ||
She who takes the form of the great fish, the great tortoise, and the great boar;
she who is dear to Narasimha, the delightful one, and she who appears as the dwarf and the young brahmin student. || 2 ||
She is the very embodiment of the son of Jamadagni, the beautiful Rāmā who is worshipped by Rāma;
she is Kṛṣṇā, Kapardinī, Kṛtyā, Kalahā, and Kalavikāriṇī. || 3 ||
She is the embodiment of intellect, the consort of the Buddha, and the shatterer of Buddhist heretics;
she is the form of Kalki, the remover of strife, and the destroyer of the misfortunes of the Kali age.
Resembling ten million suns, enchanting ten million gods of love,
she is the solitary, firm Kālī, the digit who bestows absolute liberation.
She belongs to Keśava, she is worshipped by Keśava, she is a young maiden, and she is praised by Keśava;
she has the form of Rudra, she is the embodiment of Rudra, she is Rudrāṇī, and she has Rudra as her deity.
She is the form of the constellations, she is the constellations herself, and she is worshipped by the Lord of the Constellations;
she is eternally beloved by the Lord of the Constellations and saluted by the Sovereign of the Constellations. || 7 ||
She is the female serpent (nāginī), the mother of serpents (nāgajananī), she who is praised by the serpent kings (nāgarājapravanditā);
she is the sovereign of serpents (nāgeśvarī), the daughter of serpents (nāgakanyā), the lady of serpents (nāgarī), and the daughter of the mountain (nagātmajā).
The daughter of the king of mountains, worshipped by the king of mountains,
she is like a fresh rain-cloud, yellowish-dark, and the creator of beauty.
Red, blue, dense, white, and brilliant white—she bestows good fortune;
she is beautiful, auspicious, gentle, golden-hued, and the giver of the heavenly state.
She causes fear to enemies, brings about the destruction of foes, and is likewise the passionate woman, illusion, the paralyzer, the deluder, and the auspicious one. (11)
She who causes the destruction of passion and hatred at night, the destroyer of the Raurava hell;
she is the Yakṣiṇī, the assembly of the Siddhas, the Mistress of the Siddhas, and the embodiment of spiritual perfection.
She who brings about the destruction of the Lord of Laṅkā, she who is worshipped by the enemy of the Lord of Laṅkā;
she who is the river of the lineage of the Lord of Laṅkā, she who took away the great Rāvaṇa. || 13 ||
The Supreme Goddess is worshipped by the multitudes of gods, dānavas, and siddhas;
she is the supreme atom-form, the ultimate, and the destroyer of the dependent.
The bestower of boons, she who is to be propitiated by those seeking boons, she who is solely devoted to the granting of boons;
she who loves the land of Varada, the heroic one adorned with the ornaments of heroes. || 15 ||
The goddess Vāṇī bestows wealth and bestows much; she is the embodiment of Brahman and possesses a beautiful countenance.
She bestows strength, wears yellow garments, and is adorned with golden ornaments.
"Beloved of yellow flowers, wearing a yellow necklace, having a yellow form"—thus, O Brahmin, the one hundred and eight names have been told to you. (17)
Whoever recites it, causes it to be recited, or listens to it with a concentrated mind—his enemy shall go to destruction immediately; there is no doubt in this matter. || 18 ||

If a person, purified and full of devotion, recites this while meditating upon Pītāmbarā at the time of dawn, all his prosperity shall quickly come to pass and his enemy shall meet with destruction. (19)
Thus ends the hymn of the one hundred and eight names of Śrī Bagalā, from the dialogue between Nārada and Viṣṇu in the Viṣṇuyāmala.
Then, at the preeminent abode of the gods, the daughter of the King of Mountains addressed Maheśvara, the God of Gods, who was being praised with the collection of his thousand names.
The Goddess said:
O Supreme Creator, O Supreme Abode, O Primal One, O Supreme Lord!
O Beloved, please recite the thousand names beginning with Bagalāmukhī.
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the thousand names of the supreme Brahmāstra-vidyā, which bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life.
O Goddess, more secret than the secret, it is worshipped by all the Siddhas; this most highly guarded Vidyā is concealed within all the Tantras.
Especially in the Kali age, she bestows a flood of great siddhis;
it must be guarded, guarded, and guarded with great effort.
O lady of virtuous vows, this truth is not to be disclosed, like one's own private parts;
it obstructs the hosts of obstacles and deludes those who belong to others.
She is the paralyzer of the king's armies and the confounder of opposing disputants. And in the past, during the terrible time of the single ocean, [there was] the Supreme Bhairava. (7)
Accompanied by Sundarī, the divine Keśava, the destroyer of afflictions,
sat upon the serpent-throne and entered into yogic sleep.
And at the time of sleep, O Goddess, that eternal hymn consisting of a hundred names, which causes the great pillar [of stability], was proclaimed by me. 9.
"Recite the supreme thousand names of some god.
The Blessed Lord said: "Listen, O Śaṅkara, Lord of Gods, to this supreme and most secret [teaching]."
I have told this by whose grace Viṣṇu is the Lord of all lords;
it must be guarded with effort, for its disclosure causes the loss of spiritual success.

Om. Of this mantra of the Thousand Names of Śrī Pītāmbarī, the Seer (ṛṣi) is the Blessed Lord Sadāśiva, the Metre (chandas) is Anuṣṭubh, the Deity (devatā) is the auspicious Pītāmbarī who brings the world under control, and the Application (viniyoga) is for the purpose of attaining all desired accomplishments through recitation.
Now, as for meditation:
[one should visualize her] clothed in yellow garments, with full and elevated breasts, enriched by the splendor of a crown of matted locks, and seated comfortably upon a yellow ground. || 12 ||
She bears the tongue and the mallet of the enemy, possessing supreme beauty;
she is renowned throughout the three worlds in all the Āgamas and Purāṇas.
Listen, I shall tell you of that Great Goddess, the primordial source of creation, preservation, and destruction, who must be guarded with every effort.
I bow to that Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), the Goddess who destroys the world, who brings about freedom from old age and death, and who bestows great sovereignty. 15.
Having first extracted the Praṇava (Om), one should then utter "Sthiramāyā," followed by "Bagalāmukhī" and "sarve" for the speech of all the wicked. 16.
"Paralyze the mouth and feet," "Nail down the tongue, O wise one," and "Destroy"— one should then utter these along with the *tāra* (Oṃ) and the stable *māyā* (Hrīṃ).
The mantra ending with *vahnipriyā* bestows the fruits of the four aims of life;
it is the Brahmāstra, the Brahma-vidyā, and the eternal Mother of Brahmā. (18)
Brahmeśī, Brahmakaivalya, Bagalā, and Brahmacāriṇī;
she is eternal bliss, eternally perfected, eternal in form, and free from all ailment. || 19 ||
Mahāmāyā is the sustainer, she who brings security through her side-long glances;
she is Kamalā, Vimalā, and Nīlā, resting upon the qualities of the luster of jewels.
She who loves desire, who delights in desire, whose very nature is the desire for desires;
she is Maṅgalā, Vijayā, Jāyā, and the bringer of all auspiciousness. || 21 ||
She is the beloved woman, desired by lovers, the passionate one, and she who moves according to her will;
she is dear to desire, delighting in desire, and whose nature transcends both desire and its absence. || 22 ||
Kāmākhyā, who dwells within the seed-syllable of desire (kāma-bīja), residing in the sacred seat of desire (kāma-pīṭha);
she is the bestower of desires, the destroyer of desires, Kālī, Kapālī, and Karālikā. || 23 ||
The enemy of Kaṃsa, the lotus-born, the fulfiller of desires, the beloved of the Lord of Kailāsa,
Kātyāyanī, the one with beautiful hair, compassion itself, and the enjoyer of amorous play.
Kriyākīrti, Kṛttikā, Kāśikā, Mathurā, Śivā, Kālākṣī, Kālikā, Kālī, and Dhavalānanasundarī. (25)
She is Khecarī and Khamūrti, the small one (Kṣudrā), the destroyer of petty hunger;
she holds a sword in her hand, is devoted to the sword, possesses a sword, and is fond of a skull-bowl.
Gangā, Gaurī, Gāminī, Gītā, Gotravivardhinī, Godharā, Gokarā, Godhā, and Gandharvapuravāsinī. || 27 ||
Gandharvā, Gandharvakalā, Gopanī, Garuḍāsanā, Govindabhāvā, Govindā, Gāndhārī, and Gandhamādinī. || 28 ||

The fair-limbed one, the embodiment of the cowherd maiden, the dweller in the assembly of cowherd women, the fragrant one, she who moves with the gait of a lordly elephant, the peerless one, the beloved of the wielder of the mace, and the one who transcends the planets. 29.
Terrible, most terrible, and of terrible form, she has thick hips and dense radiance;
she is powerful as the lord of the Daityas, a striker of bells, and possesses a dreadful resonance.
Ḍākinī, Umā, Upendrā, Urvaśī, and she whose seat is a serpent;
she who is supreme, exalted, and noble, dwelling in the highest station. || 31 ||
Cāmuṇḍā, Muṇḍitā, Caṇḍī, and she who removes fierce pride;
Ugracaṇḍā, Caṇḍacaṇḍā, and the destroyer of the fierce Daityas. || 32 ||
Caṇḍarūpā, Pracaṇḍā, and Caṇḍācaṇḍaśarīriṇī;
the four-armed Pracaṇḍā, who dwells within all that is moving and unmoving. || 33 ||
She consists mostly of Kṣatriyas, she carries their heads, she is deceptive, more deceptive, and full of guile;
she has the form of a Kṣatriya, she assumes the state of a Kṣatriya, and she is the destroyer of the Kṣatriyas. || 34 ||
Jayā, Jayadurgā, Jayantī, the supreme Jayadā, Jāyinī, Jayinī, Jyotsnā, the beloved of Jaṭādhara, and Jitā. (35)
She who has conquered her senses, conquered her anger, who is ever victorious,
the sovereign of people, who has conquered death, who is beyond old age— the daughter of Jahnu, the daughter of Janaka.
Jhaṅkāra, Jhañjharī, Jhaṇṭā, Jhaṅkārī, Jhakaśobhinī, Jhakhā, Jhameśā, Jhaṅkārī, the one who bestows the auspiciousness of the womb. || 37 ||
Jhañjharā, Jhamurī, Jhārā, Jharājharatarā, Parā, Jhañjhā, Jhametā, Jhaṅkārī, and Jhaṇākalyāṇadāyinī. (38)
Īmanā, Mānasī, Cintyā, Īmunā, Śaṅkarapriyā, Ṭaṅkārī, Ṭiṭikā, Ṭīkā, Ṭaṅkinī—these belong to the Ṭa-group (Ṭavargagā). 39.
She who is the *ṭāp* and the *ṭopā*, whose mind is established in the *ṭaṭa*, and who is dear to *ṭama*;
she who bears the syllable *ṭha*, the *ṭhīkā*, the *ṭhaṅkarī*, and who is dear to *ṭhikara*. || 40 ||
She who dwells in the ṭha-syllable, she who bestows security, the sovereign mistress, she whose delight is in stilling;
she who laughs with the ḍa-sound, the ḍākinī, the devourer, the terrifier, and she whose delight is in the ḍamaru drum. || 41 ||
She who possesses the sound of the *ḍakhiṇī* and the *ḍaḍa*, whose beloved is the sound of the *ḍamaru*;
she who is the *ḍhakkā*, the *ḍhakkī*, and the resonance of the *ḍhakkana*, awakened by the sound of the *ḍhola*.
Ḍhāminī, delighted by the abode, illuminator of the Ḍhaka-tantra, the Mother who possesses manifold forms, the bestower of the siddhi of aṇimā. || 43 ||
The silent one, the imitator, abiding within the subtle sun;
Tārā, the possessor of tantras, whose form is the essence of tantra, the ascetic woman.

She who possesses waves, who is devoted to the ultimate reality, who is the embodiment of the Tantras, whose form is the Tantra, who is the very nature of austerity, who bestows the ultimate reality, and who surpasses all through her love for austerity. || 45 ||
Devoted to the worship of the tantras and yantras, she dwells in the Talātala realm;
she is the giver of the throne, the giver of little, the one desired, the steadfast, and the most stable state. || 46 ||
She is beloved by the Lord of the Stump (Śiva), intent on stability, ever-abiding, and the bestower of stations;
she is sky-clad, the embodiment of compassion, and the tamer of the forest fire through her self-control.
Durgā is the supreme goddess beyond all difficulties, the destroyer of wicked Daityas;
she is the joy of self-restraint and is devoted to bestowing compassion upon the Daityas.
She is the destroyer of the suffering of those in distress, the self-controlled, the humble, and yet devoid of hypocrisy;
she is dear to the sky-clad ascetics, the embodiment of humility, and the shatterer of the pride of the Daityas. || 49 ||
She who subdues, whose teeth are beautiful, the destroyer of the lord of the Dānavas;
she who is compassion, the earth, the subduer, and who sports upon blades of Darbha grass.
She is Dhariṇī, Dhāriṇī, and Dhātrī; the beloved of the supporter of the earth;
the daughter of the mountain-king; the goddess Sudharmā, who practices righteousness. || 51 ||
She is the knower of Dharma, pure, stainless, the giver of wealth, and the increaser of riches;
she is steadfast, wise, most wise, and the bestower of the accomplishments of the steadfast.
She who is Dhanvantari, the steadfast one upon the earth, whose nature is meditation, she who is to be meditated upon;
she who is Nārāyaṇī, Nārasiṃhī, and the supreme man of eternal bliss.
Naktā, Naktāvatī, Nityā, resembling a dark blue cloud, blue-limbed, clad in blue garments, and dwelling on the Blue Mountain. (54)
Inlaid with deep blue flowers, possessing a luster like that of the blue jambū fruit, she is the sixteenth Vidyā known as Nityā; she is eternal and brings forth perpetual bliss. (55)
Narmadā, Nandanā, Ānandā, the increaser of the joy of those who rejoice; Yaśodā, the daughter of Ānanda, she who dwells in the Nandana grove. || 56 ||
O destroyer of serpents, O elder of serpents, O serpent-wife, O female serpent;
you by whom all people are bowed down, you who possess salutation—homage to you! (57)
Pārvatī was clad in yellow garments, adorned with yellow ornaments,
wearing yellow silk raiment, possessing a yellow luster, and having tawny hair.
She is devoted to worship with yellow flowers and is herself worshipped with yellow flowers;
she possesses supreme splendor, is the mistress of the ancestors, and is the destroyer of enemy armies. || 59 ||
She is the supreme, the dependent, the supreme mantra, higher than the highest; she is supreme knowledge, supreme accomplishment, and the bestower of the supreme abode. || 60 ||
She is the flower, the one possessed of flowers, the eternal, adorned with garlands of flowers;
she is the ancient one, prior to all else, and the bestower of supreme accomplishment.
She is yellow, possessing beautiful hips, yellow-hued, with full and elevated breasts;
she is the middle of all love and joy, and she is as graceful as a lotus petal.
Padmāvatī, lotus-eyed, Padmā, lotus-faced, supreme;
seated upon a lotus, fond of the lotus, whose nature is like a ruby. || 63 ||
She is the purifier, the drinking vessel, the bowl, the supreme gift, the giver of boons, and the auspicious one;
she is established among the spirits, the supreme bliss, and whose nature is the Supreme Brahman.
The Goddess is the beloved of the Lord of Jinas; she is fond of the blood and flesh of sacrificial victims (paśus);
she delights in the flesh of animals; she is Parṇā; and she is devoted to the supreme nectar (amṛta). || 65 ||
She who holds the noose, she who is the noose itself, she who slays the bound, she who speaks for the bound;
her face is like a full-blown lotus, and her body is like a full-blown blue water-lily.
She bestows supreme bliss, she destroys the bonds of the individual soul with her lute,
she is the sound of "phūt," she is the supreme "phut," she is the frothy one, and her eyes are like full-blown blue lotuses.
Phaṭmantrā, Sphaṭikā, Svāhā, Sphoṭā, and she whose nature is Phaṭ; Sphāṭikā, Ghuṭikā, Ghorā, and she whose form is the crystal mountain. || 68 ||
The excellent woman, the bearer of boons, Vārāhī, the most excellent Vāsukī;
she who dwells in the bindu, the mistress of the bindu, the Goddess of Speech, residing in the wheel of the bindu. || 69 ||
She is the Vidyādharī with wide eyes, beloved by the inhabitants of Kāśī;
she is the knowledge of the Vedas, the three-eyed goddess, and she who assumes many forms throughout the ages of the universe.
The power of Brahmā, the power of Viṣṇu, five-faced, beloved of Śiva;
the Goddess who dwells in Vaikuṇṭha and bestows the station of Vaikuṇṭha. (71)
She is the form of Brahmā, the form of Viṣṇu, and the Great Goddess of the Supreme Brahman;
she is beloved by Bhava, born from Bhava, the form of Bhava, and the most excellent of Bhava.
She who has reached the further shore of existence, the sustainer of worldly life, the one who fulfills the desires of the fortunate;
she who is auspicious, most auspicious, the bestower of prosperity, and the destroyer of the demon Śumbha.
Bhavānī, Bhairavī, Bhīmā, Bhadrakālī, Subhadrikā, Bhaginī, she whose form is the bhaga, Bhagamānā, and Bhagottamā. || 74 ||

She who is dear to Bhaga, the Sovereign Goddess, she who possesses fortune, she who creates fortune; she who is created by Bhaga, she who is endowed with good fortune, she whose form is fortune, and she who consumes fortune. || 75 ||
The Goddess is fond of the bhaga and liṅga, devoted to the bhaga and liṅga, her very nature is the bhaga and liṅga, and she finds delight in the bhaga and liṅga. || 76 ||
The Goddess is delighted by the bhaga and liṅga; she dwells within the bhaga and liṅga.
She is garlanded with bhagas, possesses the power of the bhaga, is the support of the bhaga, and has the bhaga as her garment.
She whose speed is fortune, whose ornament is fortune, the sovereign of fortune, whose form is auspiciousness;
she who enjoys the union of the *bhaga* and the *liṅga*, and who brings forth the nectar of the *bhaga* and the *liṅga*.
Delightful through the union of the bhaga and liṅga, established in the placement of the bhaga and liṅga, the excellent worship of the bhaga and liṅga, and endowed with the bhaga and liṅga. || 79 ||
She is detached from the vulva and the phallus, yet she is encompassed by the vulva and the phallus;
she is Mādhavī, honored by Mādhava, sweet, and proud of her sweetness.
She is the gentle smile, the great illusion, the enchantress, the most excellent greatness;
she is the great delusion, the great knowledge, the most terrible, and the great memory. || 81 ||
She is high-minded, proud, joyful, and sweet-faced;
she is Menikā, the venerable one, full of self-respect, and adorned with jewels and gems. || 82 ||
Mallikā, Maulikā, Mālā, the most excellent among those who wear garlands (Mālādharamadottamā), Madanāsundarī, Medhā, Madhumattā, and Madhupriyā. || 83 ||

She has a gait like that of an intoxicated swan, possesses a great roar like that of an intoxicated lion, is beloved by Mahendra, is formidable, and wears a crest-jewel; she is the daughter of the twin-born [Agni]. 84.
Mahākālī, Mahākālī, Mahābuddhi, Mahotkaṭā, Māheśvarī, Mahāmāyā, and the slayer of the demon Mahiṣāsura. || 85 ||
She possesses sweet fame, she walks with the gait of an elephant in rut, she is fond of intoxication, she delights in meat, and she brings about the desires of those who are intoxicated. || 86 ||
The Goddess is beloved of sexual union, she is great bliss, the great festival;
she is the radiance, the essence of passion, illusion, and the bestower of mind and intellect. || 87 ||
She is Mohā and Mokṣā, Mahālakṣmī who bestows the supreme state;
she is Yamunā in the form of Yama, and Jayantī who grants victory. (88)
She who belongs to Yama, who possesses the power of Yama, who is victorious in battle, the increaser of Yadu’s lineage;
she is Ramā, the beautiful woman, the wife of Rāma, the one adorned with a garland of jewels, and she whose beloved is Rati. || 89 ||
Seated upon a jeweled lion-throne and adorned with precious ornaments,
she was a delightful woman, charming and devoted to the essence of passion.
She is the bliss of delight, she who possesses delight, the one who increases the lineage of the Radhus,
she who shines through her lover, and she who is born from the jewel exceeding the stream of nectar.
She is the river whose nature is the aesthetic flavor (rasa), and she brings happiness to the king of night;
she is born of the seasons, the giver of the seasons, prosperous, the form of the seasons, and beloved by the seasons. || 92 ||
She who loves red, she who possesses redness, she who is colored, she whose teeth are red;
she is Lakṣmī, Modesty, the Creeper, and she whose eyes are fixed upon her playful gestures.
She is Līlā, the playful one; she is Līlāvatī, the strip of cloth that delights through the bristling of her hair;
she abides in Brahman, has the form of Brahman, and is praised by Brahman as the Veda.
Born from Brahmā, a portion of Brahmā, the consort of Brahmā, the awakener of Brahmā;
she is the wife of the Vedas, the form of the Vedas, the woman, the humble one, and the dweller. 95.
She is the child, the young woman, and the aged; she is devoted to the practice of Brahman;
she dwells in the Vindhya mountains and resides in the Vindhya; she is adorned with the pair of dots and the single dot.
She is possessed of knowledge, the upholder of the Vedas, the all-pervading one, the digit of the peacock, fond of the left-hand path (vāmācāra), the fire, and devoted to the left-hand path. || 97 ||
The Goddess delights in the left-hand path (vāmācāra), she is the most beloved of Vāmadeva;
she is the awakened faculty of intellect, the fully enlightened one, and she is garlanded with the conduct of the Buddhas. || 98 ||
She is the liberator from bondage, belonging to Varuṇa, and having her abode in the waters;
she is auspicious, beloved of Śiva, pure, possessing pure limbs, and white in color. || 99 ||
She who loves white flowers, she who is white, she who is devoted to the auspicious dharma;
she who dwells in the white, she who is pure, she whose form is white, and she who loves white sacrificial animals. || 100 ||
She who abides in semen, she who possesses semen, she who is semen, she whose form is semen, and she who is the essence of semen;
she who has six faces, she who has six limbs, and she who dwells in the six cakras. || 101 ||
She is endowed with the six knots, sixfold, the mother of the six, and consisting of the six;
she is the goddess who is the youth of the six limbs, the self-controlled one whose nature is the six limbs. 102.
She who has six faces, she who possesses the six flavors, she who is the sixth, she who is beloved by the Lord of the Sixth;
she who proclaims the six cows, she who is the sixteenfold one, and she whose nature is the sixteen-fold ritual placement (ṣoḍhā-nyāsa). || 103 ||
She is the piercer of the six chakras, whose essential nature resides within the six chakras;
she is the form of the sixteen vowels, six-faced, and endowed with six arms. (104)
She is the very nature of Sanaka and the others, the supreme refuge of the Śiva-dharma;
she is the perfected Seven-Syllabled One, pure, the mother of the gods, and the most excellent of vowels. (105)
She is the perfected lore, the mother of perfection, the perfected one, whose nature is perfection;
she is the destroyer, the beloved of Hari, the necklace, the deer-like one, and likewise she is endowed with a necklace.
She is the form of Hari, the stream of Hari, the fawn-eyed one, and the beloved of Hari;
she is fond of causes, devoted to causes, and the embodiment of both the beneficial and the harmful.
She is forbearance, the one possessed of forbearance, the patient one, adorned with tiny bells;
she is the destroyer of decay, the sovereign of the earth, and she who is most beautiful with a slender waist. || 108 ||
She is unknowable and leafless, she who reclines upon the remnants of Ahalyā;
she is contained within herself and exists within the virtuous as one whose form is infinite.
Formless, stainless, and half-formed, she is endowed with infinite virtues;
she is one's own wisdom, the knower of knowledge, ignorance, and knowledge itself—the lotus-eyed goddess.
Aparājitā, Jātavedā, Ajapā, Amarāvatī, Alpā, Svalpā, Analpā, and others, she who bestows the siddhi of aṇimā. || 111 ||
The Goddess, endowed with the perfection of form and characteristics, bestows the eight siddhis;
the lotus-faced Goddess grants the happiness of worldly enjoyments. 112.
The primordial knowledge, the first of all things, bestowing the first accomplishment;
the Goddess whose form is the sound *sīt*, adorned with every seat. 113.
She is beloved by Indra, Indrāṇī, the dweller in Indraprastha;
she is Indrākṣī, Indravajrā, and likewise Indramadyokṣaṇī. || 114 ||
Īlā, Kāmanivāsā, Īśvarī, the beloved of the Lord, Jananī, Īśvarī, Dīnā, and Bhedā, who performs the deeds of the Lord. (115)
Umā, Kātyāyanī, Ūrdhvā, Mīnā, and Uttaravāsinī;
the goddess Umāpati-priyā, Śivā, and she whose form is the syllable Oṃ. (116)
She is the crest-jewel upon the head of the lord of serpents, the beloved of the serpents and the serpent-like ones;
she dwells in the garden, is a garland, and is adorned with excellent jewels.
She whose teeth and head are turned upward, who is supreme, and whose hair stands erect; she who bestows the perfection of Umā and is seated upon a serpent-throne. || 118 ||
The daughter of the sages, whose meter is the sages, she who bestows supernatural power and perfection;
she whose parting of the hair is a festival of festivals, she who fulfills desires, and she who is endowed with all virtues. || 119 ||
Elā, Ekāravidyā, and likewise Eṇīvidyādharā;
she is endowed with the circle of the syllable Oṃ, the supreme digit of the syllable Oṃ.
Oṃ, you who speak, O Speech adorned with the syllable Oṃ;
you are Aindrī, holding a thunderbolt in hand, Oṃ, you who dwell beyond the worlds. || 121 ||
She whose seed-syllable is in the center of the syllable Oṃ, who bears the form of "Oṃ Namaḥ," whose nature is that of the Supreme Brahman, and who is the beloved of the finest silken garments. 122.
Adorned with the syllables of the *akṣa* beads, she consists of the mantras *oṃ*, *aḥ*, and *phaṭ*;
though without mantra, she is the very form of mantra, endowed with the splendor of her words.
She is the form of the syllable Om (praṇava) and again she partakes in the utterance of Om;
she is the form of the syllable Hrīṃ, the possessor of the syllable Hrīṃ, and adorned with the seed-syllables of speech.
Hṛllekhā, Siddhiyogā, and Hṛtpadmāsanasthitā; Bījākhyā, Netrahṛdayā, Hrīṃbījā, and Bhuvaneśvarī. (125)
The syllable *klīm* is Kāmarāja, and Klinnā bestows the fruits of the four aims of life;
the Goddess is Klīṃ-Klīṃ-Klīṃ-Rūpikā, bearing the name Krīṃ-Krīṃ-Krīṃ. (126)
She whose seed-syllable is the power of Kamalā, adorned with the noose and the goad, the Great Vidyā consisting of the syllables Śrīṃ Śrīṃ, is likewise Śraddhā and Śraddhāvatī. (127)
Oṃ aiṃ klīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ! Parā and Klīṅkārī are the supreme digit (kalā), whose essential nature is the syllables Hrīṃ, Klīṃ, and Śrīṃ, and who bestows the fruits of all actions. || 128 ||
She is the most wealthy of all, the goddess of all, and likewise the bestower of all accomplishments;
she is omniscient, possesses all powers, and is the giver of the splendor of speech.
The Goddess who bestows all liberation, who grants all enjoyments, who is beloved by the Lord of Qualities (Śiva), who is the auspicious Left-hand path, and who bestows all powers. || 130 ||
She is composed of all bliss, the bestower of all accomplishments, the Goddess who is the sovereign of all cakras, and likewise the sovereign of all siddhis. || 131 ||
She who makes everyone dear, she who bestows all happiness, the Goddess who grants all bliss, and she who bestows the bliss of Brahman. || 132 ||
She is the bestower of what is desired by the mind, endowed with the increase of the mind;
she begins with the letter 'A' and ends with the letter 'Kṣa'; she is Durgā, the destroyer of the suffering of distress.
Padmanetrā, Sunetrā, Svadhākārī, Svāhākārī, Vaṣaṭkarī, Svavargā, Devavargā, and Tavargā are likewise endowed [with these qualities]. || 134 ||
Antassthā, Veśmarūpā, Navadurgā, Narottamā, Tattvasiddhipradā, Nīlā, and likewise Nīlapatākinī—[these are the goddesses]. (135)
Nityarūpā, Niśākārī, Stambhinī, Mohinī, Vaśaṅkarī, Uccāṭī, Unmādī, and Karṣiṇī. || 136 ||
Mātaṅgī, Madhumattā, Aṇimā, and Laghimā—these are the eternal Siddhas who bestow liberation and grant eternal bliss. (137)
She has red limbs and red eyes, is adorned with red sandalwood paste,
possesses slight accomplishment and is well-disposed, and her luster is like that of a divine Cāraṇa or a parrot.
Transmigration, all-encompassing knowledge, and the day adorned by grain;
these are the first, the second, the third, and the fourth. (139)
The fifth and the sixth are pure, and likewise the seventh;
as are the eighth, the ninth, the tenth, and the eleventh. || 140 ||
The twelfth, the thirteenth, the fourteenth, and the full moon;
likewise the new moon, the prior full moon, and the subsequent full moon. (141)
She is armed with a sword, a discus, a mace, and likewise a trident;
she holds a *bhuśuṇḍī* weapon, a bow, and arrows, adorned with all manner of weapons.
She is the Mistress of the Kula, possessed of the Kula, devoted to the Kula-conduct, deeply enamored with the rites of the Kula, and the promoter of the Kula-conduct. || 143 ||
Salutations ever to Kīrti, Śrī, Ramā, Rāmā, and Dharmā;
to Kṣamā, Dhṛti, Smṛti, Medhā, and she who dwells in the Kalpa-tree.
Ugrā, Ugraprabhā, Gaurī, Vedavidyāvibodhinī, Sādhyā, Siddhā, Susiddhā, and likewise Viprarūpā. (145)
Kālī, Karālī, Kālyā, Kalā, the destroyer of the Daityas, Kaulinī, and Kālikā—she whose syllables are the letters Ka, Ca, Ṭa, Ta, and Pa. || 146 ||
Jayinī, Jayayuktā, Jayadā, and likewise Jṛmbhinī;
Srāviṇī, Drāviṇī, the goddess Bharuṇḍā, and Vindhyavāsinī. || 147 ||
She has become light, she is the giver of victory, and she is filled with garlands of flames;
she is divided, she is manifold radiance, she is differentiated, and she possesses diverse forms.
Aśvinī and Bharaṇī are the winds born from the stars;
Vinatā is known as the daughter of Kaśyapa, as is Diti, the daughter of Diti. (149)
Kīrti is the goddess beloved by Kāma; she increases fame through fame.
She is smeared with fresh flesh and brandishes a freshly whetted sword.
The southern, northern, eastern, and western directions are likewise remembered, as well as the southeastern, southwestern, northwestern, and northeastern directions. || 151 ||
Extending from the upper part of the body downwards, she is white, black, red, and yellow;
she consists of the four aims of life, the four castes, and is composed of syllables with four morae.
She who has four faces, who is the four Vedas, who is the four branches of knowledge, and who has four mouths;
she who consists of the four groups, who is the mother of the four, and who bestows the fruits of the four aims of life. (153)
She is the sustainer and the ordainer, the female companion dwelling with her lord;
she rejoices in wine and joy, she is the delighter, and the daughter of Menakā. || 154 ||
Ūrddhakālī, Siddhikālī, Dakṣiṇākālikā, Śivā, Nīlī, Sarasvatī, Sāttvambagalā, and Chinnamastakā. (155)
The sovereign of all, the perfected lore, the supreme goddess;
she who is vermilion-red, whose limbs are vermilion-red, and who dwells upon a vermilion-red lower lip.
She possesses the color of the finest vermilion and is adorned with vermilion ornaments;
she is the ever-awake Mother of the World and the beloved of the Lord of the Universe.
The goddess beloved by Janārdana, endowed with victory and bestowing victory;
she who brings joy to the world and causes delight to the world. 158.
She is the bestower of the gift of knowledge, the sacrifice, Jānakī, the beloved of Janaka;
she is Jayantī, the giver of victory, eternal, and possesses a splendor equal to a blazing fire. || 159 ||
Vidyādharā, Bimboṣṭhī, the dweller on Mount Kailāsa, Vibhavā, Vaḍavāgni, and Agnihotraphalapradā; || 160 ||
The supreme goddess is the very form of mantra, and likewise she is the form of the Guru;
she is Gayā, Gaṅgā, Gomatī, Prabhāsā, and Puṣkara as well. (161)
The Goddess who delights in the Vindhya mountains, who dwells upon the Vindhya range, who is exceedingly beautiful, and who is the destroyer of the demon Kaṃsa. || 162 ||
She who holds the trident, she who has the trident in her hand, she who is the thunderbolt, and she who wields the thunderbolt;
Durgā, Śivā, the bestower of peace, Brahmāṇī, and she who is dear to the Brāhmaṇas. || 163 ||
She is the leader of all worlds and the remover of all diseases;
she is auspicious, beautiful, pure, partless, and the supreme digit.
She is the Sovereign of All, the Mother of the Universe, the Graceful One with a beautiful countenance;
she is Sadāśivā, Umā, Kṣemā, Caṇḍikā, and she of fierce valor.
The Goddess consists of all the gods; she removes the fear of all the scriptures;
she is saluted by Brahmā, Śiva, and Viṣṇu; and she is the bringer of all auspiciousness. (166)
She is the Yoginī, the Mother of Yoga, residing in the heart of the Lord of Yogins;
she is the Consort of the Yogins, possessed of yoga, the Yoginī who is the bliss of the Lord of Yogins. 167.
The Goddess who is bowed to by Indra and the other gods, the Sovereign beloved of Īśvara;
she bestows purity, removes fear, and strikes terror into those who hate her devotees. (168)
She is the dress of worldly existence, the passionate woman, the Bharuṇḍā who causes fear; she has the form beloved by Balabhadra and is the one who carries one across the ocean of saṃsāra. || 169 ||

She consists of the five elements, she is all beings, the manifestation, and the upholder of manifestation; she is borne by a lion, the great delusion, and the destroyer of the noose of delusion. (170)
She is the stable, the intoxicating wine, the seal, and the bearer of the seal and mallet;
she is Sāvitrī, the Great Goddess, and the leader of those dear to others. 171.
Yamadūtī, Piṅgākṣī, Vaiṣṇavī, and likewise Śaṅkarī;
Candrapriyā, Candraratā, and Candanāraṇyavāsinī. (172)
She who is joined with Candanendra, the destroyer of the fierce Daityas, the sovereign of all, the Yakṣiṇī, as well as Kirātī and Rākṣasī. || 173 ||
The goddess Mahābhogavatī is the bestower of great liberation;
she is the destroyer of the universe, the one whose form is the universe, and the agent of the universal dissolution. || 174 ||
The goddess Dhātrī desires to bring about the welfare of all worlds;
she is Kamalā, the bestower of subtle [grace], and the destroyer of Hara. || 175 ||
Worshipped by the Lord of the Gods, she is the perfected one (Siddhā) and possesses great splendor;
the Goddess, possessing supreme form, is the attractor of the three worlds. (176)
Thus, O Goddess, the thousand names beginning with "Pīta" have been told to you;
whether one recites them or causes others to recite them, O Beloved, all perfections shall be attained. 177.
Thus was this supreme method for causing great paralysis proclaimed to me by Viṣṇu, O Pārvatī, to be practiced at dawn, at midday, and at the time of twilight. (178)
One who recites this with a single-minded focus will attain all accomplishments;
whoever recites it even once, the destruction of all sins shall occur. (179)
Whoever recites it twice shall become equal to Vighneśvara;
by reciting it three times, O Goddess, everything is accomplished in every way.
By the power of this hymn, O lady of excellent vows, one becomes manifest;
he who seeks liberation attains liberation, and he who seeks wealth attains wealth. (181)
One seeking knowledge obtains knowledge endowed with logic and grammar;
after one year, greatness is attained and the destruction of enemies occurs. || 182 ||
The lord of the earth, Vaśa, would be equal to him in his remembrance;
O beloved, for whoever should always recite this with devotion, prosperity shall surely come to pass.
The excellent representative of the leader of the assembly, who is devoted to poetry and the poet, must always be guarded with great effort, like the lover of one's own mother. 184.
One should always be endowed with reason and always be endowed with power;
he who recites this constantly shall become equal to Śiva. (185)
While living, one shall enjoy the fruits of dharma and wealth; when dead, one shall become a lord of liberation.
This is true, truly so, O Great Goddess; it is true, truly so, there is no doubt. (186)
By the power of this hymn, one rejoices together with the God;
and all the gods of pure mind rejoice through the recitation of this king of hymns. 187.
Clad in yellow garments and anointed with yellow perfumes, she shall possess supreme fame arising from the highest joy, O beautiful goddess. (188)
Thus ends the hymn of the thousand names of Pītāmbarī, in the dialogue between Viṣṇu and Śaṅkara within the *Utkataśambara-nāgendraprayāṇatantra* in sixteen thousand verses.
Thus ends the Bagalāmukhī Tantra in the Śāktapramoda. Śrī! [Composed by] Siṃha, the son of the illustrious Rājādeva, the lord of the capital city of Śivahara.
The Ninth [Chapter] from within the Śāktapramoda, composed and compiled by the noble lord Bahādur.
The Mātaṅgītantra,
edited by Paṇḍita Śrī Raghurāja Dube Jī, a descendant of the aforementioned royal preceptors.
This has been published by Śrī Kṛṣṇadāsātmaja Khemarāja at his own Śrī Veṅkaṭeśvara Press.
Having been printed and published at Bombay;
salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
Śāktapramoda; then the Mātaṅgītantra;
then the meditation on Mātaṅgī.

She has a dark-complexioned body, wears the moon upon her crest, and possesses three eyes; she is seated upon a jeweled lion-throne and holds in her staff-like arms the Vedas, a sword, a shield, a noose, and a goad.
(p. 332) Now follows the construction of the yantra: one should draw a beautiful yantra consisting of a hexagon and an eight-petaled lotus.
Therein, the knower of mantras should perform worship with hibiscus flowers (javā).
Now follows the extraction of the mantra:
first the Praṇava (Om), then Māyā (Hrīṃ), the Aṅkāmabīja (Klīṃ), and Kūrcaka (Hūṃ).
The mantra consists of *mātaṅgī*, followed by *ṅe* and *yuta*, then the weapon (*astra*), ending with the wife of fire (*vahnijāyā*).
Now the mantra: Oṃ hrīṃ klīṃ hūṃ mātaṅgyai phaṭ svāhā.
Now follows the procedure for worship:
I shall now describe the Great Goddess Mātaṅgī, the bestower of all spiritual accomplishments.
By the mere worship of her, one certainly attains the perfection of speech.
Then, the mantra consists of the Praṇava, Māyā, the Kāmabīja, and the Kūrcaka; followed by Mātaṅgī joined with the syllable *ṅe*, the Astra-mantra, and ending with the Vahnijāyā (Svāhā).
The sage of this [mantra] is Dakṣiṇāmūrti; Virāṭ is proclaimed as the meter;
the goddess Mātaṅgī is the deity, the bestower of all accomplishments.
The practitioner, composed in mind, should perform the placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) and the placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*);
he should effect this with the seed-syllable (*bīja*) preceded by the *praṇava*, conjoined with the six long vowels.
One should draw a beautiful yantra consisting of a hexagon and an eight-petaled lotus;
there, the knower of mantras should perform worship with hibiscus flowers.
With a well-concentrated mind, one should worship the eight powers upon the eight petals;
the powers are Rati, Prīti, Manobhavā, Kriyā, and Śuddhā.
Having worshipped these eight Śaktis— Anaṅgakusumā, Anaṅgamadanā, and Madanālasā— along with the offering of oblations, [one should proceed].
Then the practitioner, with a steady mind, should meditate upon the supreme Goddess—
dark-limbed, crowned with the moon, three-eyed, and seated upon a jeweled lion-throne.

Having thus meditated upon the Great Goddess, who holds in her staff-like arms the Vedas, a sword, a shield, a noose, a goad, and the boon-granting gesture, [one should worship her] with delightful perfumes and flowers.
As for the food offering to Mahādevī, it should be milk-rice mixed with sugar;
during the time of the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa), one should recite the mantra six thousand times.
The practitioner, together with the Śaktis, should offer oblations ten times that amount using clarified butter along with sugar and honey,
and with fuel-sticks made from the wood of the Brahma-tree.
Having thus performed the preliminary honors,
the practitioner of mantras should carry out the ritual procedure at a crossroads, in a cremation ground, or in the midst of a sacred field (kalā).
One should offer fish, meat, milk-rice, and guggulu incense;
this should always be performed at night by the practitioner who is ever-perfect.
By this mere application, poetic composition is certainly produced;
one will certainly effect the immobilization of fire, the immobilization of water, and the immobilization of speech.
The minister conquers his enemies just as Tārkṣya [conquers] the race of serpents;
in scripture, debate, and poetry, he is like another Bṛhaspati.
By this very procedure, Mātaṅgī bestows success;
indeed, having come to that house, Kubera grants wealth.
One should not worship the Supreme Deity without fish and without meat.
Thus ends the *Tantrasāra*.
Now, regarding this hymn to Mātaṅgī, Īśvara said:
"O Mother, by worshipping the lotus-feet of yours, Brahmā and the other gods attained widespread fame."
Some lords of sages attained liberation, while others attained supreme glory through devotion.
I bow to the Goddess Mātaṅginī, who wears the crescent moon as her crest-jewel,
she who respectfully awakens her beloved to the meaning established by the attainment of the sacred tradition.
Your lotus-feet, which are radiant with anklets that have learned the rhythmic steps of unartificial speech, shine at their edges with the steady crowns of bowing gods.

I meditate upon that Mātaṅginī, whose heart is auspicious, who makes her path meaningful with her two feet as she strikes her sweet-toned lute, who wears playful garments, and whose hips are like pure, radiant orbs.
I bow to the consort of Śambhu, who has placed ear-ornaments of palm leaves, whose lotus-like eyes roll from the intoxication of honey-wine, who possesses full breasts,
whose splendor is like a flash of lightning, and who is adorned with priceless jewels. (5)

O Mother, Sovereign of the worlds, I remember with devotion your waist, enriched by the three folds of skin and marked by a line of fine hair that is difficult to perceive; it bears the splendor of the luster of a blue lotus.

With her beauty and side-glances, she who adorns her mass of hair with a garland of kadamba flowers like a mine of lotuses—I meditate upon that daughter of the forest-dweller in my heart; may I contemplate her with cheeks as rosy as bimba fruits. (7)

O Great Goddess, O Consort of Śaṅkara, may your face—with its playful locks of hair swaying, its long eyes, and the mark of vermilion placed upon your bimba-red lips—be graced by this hymn of praise. 8.
Those humans who, endowed with devotion, praise Mātaṅginī, the goddess presiding over speech,
constantly attain supreme prosperity and dwell upon the slopes of Kailāsa in the hereafter.
Thus ends the Mātaṅgī-stotra from the Rudrayāmala.
Then the Goddess spoke the Mātaṅgī-kavaca:
"Excellent, excellent, O Mahādeva! O Lord of the Gods, please speak."
The divine armor of Mātaṅgī, which bestows all perfections upon men. || 1 ||
The illustrious Lord said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the auspicious armor (kavaca) of Mātaṅgī;
it must be kept secret, O Great Goddess, and one should perform the recitation while observing silence.

Of this Śrīmātaṅgī-kavaca, Dakṣiṇāmūrti is the seer (ṛṣi), Virāṭ is the meter (chandaḥ), Mātaṅgī is the deity (devatā), and the application (viniyoga) is for the attainment of the four aims of human life.
Oṃ! May Mātaṅginī protect my head, Bhuvaneśī my eyes, Toḍalā the pair of my ears, and Tripurā my face. (3)
May Mahāmāyā protect my throat, and likewise Māheśvarī my heart;
may Tripuṣpā protect both my sides, and Kāmeśvarī my anus.
Likewise, Caṇḍī is on the two thighs, Harapriyā on the two shanks,
Mahāmāyā on the pair of feet, and Kuleśvarī on all the limbs.
May Vaiṣṇavī always protect the limbs and the minor members;
may she who is established as Mātaṅgī always protect the aperture of Brahmā (the crown of the head).
May Mahāpiśācinī protect [him] constantly on the forehead;
may Sumukhī protect the two eyes, and may the Goddess protect the nose. (7)
May Mahāpiśācinī protect [me] at the beginning; may she always guard my mouth.
May Lajjā protect my mind at the end, and Sammārjanīkarī my lips. (8)
May the Great Goddess, who is the three letter 'ca's along with the visarga at the region of the chin and throat, protect my heart forever. 9.
May the restless [Gaurī] protect the navel; may Kālikā protect the eyes;
may Cāmuṇḍā protect the belly, and likewise may Kātyāyanī protect the generative organ.
May Ugratārā protect the anus; may Ambikā protect the feet;
may Śarvāṇī protect the arms; and may Caṇḍabhūṣaṇā protect the heart.
May Mātṛkā protect [the tongue] on the tongue; may Puṣṭikā protect it in the east;
may Vijayā guard it in the south; and may Medhā protect it in the west.
May Sudayā protect in the southwest; may Lakṣmaṇā protect in the northwest;
and may the goddess Mātaṅgī, the bringer of auspiciousness, protect in the northeast.
May the Queen of the Gods protect in the southeast, and may Bagalā protect in the north;
may the Great Goddess, who acts for the welfare of the gods, protect from above.
May Vashini, who possesses all forms, protect me eternally in the netherworld (pātāla).
[The mantra consists of] the Praṇava, then Māyā, the seed-syllable of Kāma, and the Kūrca syllable. || 15 ||
The mantra of Mātaṅginī, ending with the weapon-syllable (phaṭ) and the consort of fire (svāhā), consists of eleven and a half syllables; may she protect me always everywhere. 16.
Thus, O Goddess, I have told you this supreme armor named Trailokyamaṅgala, which is more secret than the secret and difficult even for the gods to obtain. (17)
Whoever recites this constantly becomes an abode of prosperity;
he shall attain supreme and incomparable sovereignty—of this there is no doubt. (18)
If one worships the Guru according to the prescribed rites and recites this armor-mantra (kavaca),
one will certainly attain sovereignty, the state of being a great poet, and perfection of speech.
But for him who is constant, Mātaṅgī shall perform auspiciousness;
so too shall Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and those gods who are the best of the Suras. (20)
O Goddess, upon seeing that practitioner, the Brahma-rākṣasas, Vetālas, Grahas, and other classes of spirits become filled with shame. || 21 ||
Whoever wears this armor will certainly obtain all accomplishments (siddhis);
even kings shall become his servants, and he shall accomplish the six rites.
One becomes successful everywhere; what is the use of further words?
If a man should worship Mātaṅgī without knowing this armor (kavaca), [he gains nothing]. 23.

One will certainly become short-lived, destitute, and foolish; of this there is no doubt. Therefore, one should always maintain devotion toward the Guru and firm resolve regarding the armor-mantra (kavaca). || 24 ||
To him, the goddess Mātaṅginī bestows all supernatural attainments (siddhi). || 25 ||
Thus ends the armor (kavaca) of Mātaṅginī, which bestows swift results, within the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the Nandyāvarta.
Then once, filled with curiosity, Bhairavī— who delights in the welfare of all beings— questioned Bhairava, who is served by spirits, regarding the Heart-mantra. || 1 ||
The illustrious Bhairavī said:
"O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, you who cherish all living beings!
I desire to know that which is beneficial to all creatures."
By the recitation of which mantra and by the chanting of which hymn shall there be, in every way, the attainment of the highest welfare for all beings who desire prosperity? (3)
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, out of affection for you; O beloved, though it is generally to be kept secret, I shall tell you all of that which brings about auspiciousness, happiness, and prosperity.
It bestows all prosperity upon those who constantly read and hear it; it is the supreme granter of auspiciousness, bringing about the attainment of knowledge, sovereignty, and happiness. (5)
This *Hṛdayastotra* of Mātaṅgī shatters suffering and poverty;
it is the most auspicious of all auspicious things and bestows every happiness. (6)

Oṃ. Of this mantra of the Śrīmātaṅgī-hṛdaya-stotra, Dakṣiṇāmūrti is the seer (ṛṣi), Virāṭ is the meter (chandas), Mātaṅgī is the deity (devatā), Hrīṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja), Hūṃ is the power (śakti), and Klīṃ is the pin (kīlaka). Its application (viniyoga) is in recitation for the sake of attaining all desired objects.
Now, the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*):
*oṃ hrīṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *oṃ klīṃ śirase svāhā*, *oṃ hūṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, *oṃ hrīṃ netratrayāya vauṣaṭ*, *oṃ klīṃ kavacāya hūṃ*, *oṃ hūṃ astrāya phaṭ*.
Thus is the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa);
now follows the meditation:
[one should visualize her] as dark-complexioned, with a forehead marked by a digit of the moon, and possessing three lotus-eyes.
Seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, bestowing the desires of her devotees,
with a pair of lotus-feet served by the hands of hosts of gods,
possessing the luster of blue lotuses and fine silken garments, she is like a forest fire to the thicket of night-stalking demons— [the Goddess] holding a noose and a conch.
And he is joyful, holding in his four excellent lotus-like hands a shield and a goad.
I meditate upon Mātaṅgī, who brings [all things], who bestows desired fruits, and who is full of joy. || 7 ||
Salutations to Mātaṅgī, whose body is soft and joyful, who bestows the supreme welfare upon those embodied beings whose minds are absorbed in meditation on her lotus feet.
Salutations to the Goddess, who is to be constantly served in the assembly by the wise with divine intellects, whose heart is moist with compassion,
and whose mind is fierce in its destruction of evil.
O Supreme One, he who, with the heart of a seeker, recites this mantra becomes a poet and, being well-disciplined, masters the ritual manuals at every step.
Furthermore, his speech dances gracefully, as if it were the charming dance of the Goddess herself, composed of immortal nectar.
And Palitā is on the rasanā. || 9 ||
O Mother, those who meditate upon Your form and constantly mutter the revolving mantra shall never suffer defeat;
indeed, they mostly become those who adorn their heads with garlands of kadamba flowers.
They were under the sway of the throngs of young women. || 10 ||
Those who, having uttered a thousand names, worship even Your pair of lotus-feet with a thousand lotuses— yet, inferring that those feet also possess the dative case-ending *te*,
they always worship them separately with each name, thus performing the rite with ten thousand names.
The pair of whose lotus feet are bowed to by Devavrata.

O Mother, those who are most meritorious and whose inner hearts find singular delight in love for your feet offer you an oblation— placing fish, meat, or even a beautifully shining dark fruit, as is pleasing to the King— for your pleasure.
Oh, how great is their fortune, for the entire impurity of the three worlds has been brought under their control! 12.

O Mother, those who meditate upon your lotus-face— its smile revealing its inner radiance, adorned by the shimmering rays of earrings that do not sway, and its eyebrows acting as hovering bees— are never again struck by the agitation of worldly existence. They are the ones whom Lakṣmī attends.
He does not abandon their excellent abode. || 13 ||
This most excellent hymn known as the *Hṛdaya*, composed of flowers from the minds of the wise, is to be served; it grants desired fruits immediately and is exceedingly charming.
For those men who constantly hear or recite this praise, nothing in this world is difficult to attain.
That which is unattainable even for the gods.
By the recitation of this hymn, one who desires wealth obtains wealth; one who desires a wife obtains a beautiful and beloved spouse; and one who desires a son obtains a son. (15)
One seeking knowledge obtains various forms of knowledge that bestow prosperity;
one seeking victory certainly attains victory by reciting this. || 16 ||
One whose kingdom has been lost shall regain a kingdom endowed with all prosperity;
by reciting this in his heart, he shall possess wealth equal to that of Kubera.
What is the use of saying more in this regard? Whatever a person desires, they shall obtain all of it by reciting the *Hṛdayastotra* of Mātaṅgī. (18)
Thus ends the Śrīmātangīhṛdayastotra in the venerable Śrīdakṣiṇāmūrttisaṃhitā.
(p. 338) Now, the hymn of one hundred names.
Śrī Bhairavī said: "O Blessed One, I wish to hear the hundred names of Mātaṅgī."
That which is secret in all tantras and has not been revealed by anyone.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim that which is the most secret of secrets;
it must not be told anywhere, but is to be read as the supreme beyond the supreme.
O Goddess, by reciting it even once, all obstacles and calamities perish instantly, like a heap of cotton in a fire.
By reciting this, the goddess Mātaṅgī becomes pleased with him.
The fruit that is proclaimed for the recitation of the *Sahasranāma* (Thousand Names),
that same auspicious fruit of the *Nāmāṣṭaśataka* (Eight Hundred Names) is multiplied ten million times.

For this *Śrīmātangī-śatanāma*, the venerable Mataṅga is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the Anuṣṭubh is the meter (*chanda*), Mātangī is the deity (*devatā*), and the application (*viniyoga*) is for the sake of pleasing Mātangī during recitation.
Mahāmattamātaṅginī is the embodiment of accomplishment, as are the Yoginī, Bhadrakālī, and Ramā;
Bhavānī bestows both fear and joy, is endowed with prosperity, is worshipped by the world, and brings about the attainment of wealth and power.
The mother of the lord of people, whose gaze is like a dense cloud, worshipped by the Lord of Wealth, the courageous pond, the one of excellent limbs;

the most excellent one, whose form is light, who can take any form at will, the joyful one, the bestower of great fame; the tube-like ear, the dark one (Kālī), whose form is as formidable as the female organ (bhaga), whose body is the bhaga, who is called bhaga, the giver of delight to the bhaga, and the one of terrifying form.
Bhavānī is the great Kauśikī, full of treasure, a young maiden, who delights in the joy of youth.
She is the Great Cause, the Cause, whose nature is action; she is the bearer of the skull, renowned as Mahāsiddhakhaṇḍā;
she is fond of the syllable *ma*, whose form is pride, the Great Mistress, intensely radiant, her body the abode of the play of dance.
Forgiving, of peaceful nature, the maker of night, bestower of imperishable joy,

endowed with prosperity, Bhavānī; worshipped by Bhava, whose essence is prosperity and truth, illuminated by her own splendor, possessing rays as radiant as the sun, mother of the lord of the earth, whose gaze is upon the abode of wealth, honored by the Lord of Wealth, and the most wise.

She whose limbs are like those of a fisherwoman; she who is preeminent, whose form is radiance, whose nature is the vital breath, who possesses a supreme essential nature, and who is fond of her own true form;
she who wears swaying earrings, who is full of desire, who is joined with her beloved, who dwells on the mountain of skulls, and who is the remover of the god of death.
She who is fond of the Kadamba tree, the hollow-dweller, whose body is the peak, the one who follows the sequence, the bestower of fame, whose form is the ear, and the auspicious one.
She whose limbs are forgiveness, whose nature is the waning of passion, the night, she who is the end of decay, she who is called destruction, she who dwells within the realm of dissolution;
she who is like a sneeze, the passionate woman, the corrosive one, the nourisher of milk, she whose body is auspiciousness, and Śākambharī.
Śākadehā.
Mahāśākayajñā, Phalaprāśakā, Śakāhvā, Śakāhvāśakā, and Śakā; Śakākṣāntaroṣā, Suroṣā, Surekhā, and Mahāśeṣayajñopavītapriyā.

She is Jayantī, Jayā, Jāgratī, and Yogyarūpā; she whose name is satisfied by the practice of *japa* and meditation, who is the very form of victorious life-force, whose body is golden with victory, who is the blazing Jayajvālinī, the Night, and she who possesses the form of Yama.
She is the form of the Mother of the World and the protector of the world; she is Svadhā, ending with Vauṣaṭ, both slow and swift.
She possesses six limbs, has the form of a great *alambara*, holds a lion in her hand, and is the captivator, the captivator, and the captivator.

She is the Great Auspiciousness (*Mahāmaṅgalā*), the auspiciousness of love and fame; she is the destroyer of Niśumbha and the remover of Śumbha’s pride. She is the seed of bliss (*Nandabījā*) and the essential nature of liberation; likewise, she is the foremost fierce one (*Caṇḍā*) who delivers from the calamities of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa.

She is the intensely fierce (*Pracaṇḍā*), the most fierce (*Apracaṇḍā*), and possesses the great fierce velocity (*Mahācaṇḍavegā*). She is the one with waving chowries (*Calaccāmarā*), the chowrie itself (*Cāmarā*), and the moon-like fame (*Candrakīrti*).
May she, whose body is radiant with variegated ornaments and pure gold, and who is accompanied by the singing of beautiful songs, protect us from misfortune.
Thus, O Goddess, I have told you the one hundred and eight names;
they are to be kept secret in all tantras and must always be concealed.
Through the constant practice of these, Maheśvara, the Great Lord himself, becomes manifest.
And it should be recited with great devotion at the three junctions of the day for the arising of happiness.
Nothing whatsoever becomes difficult for him in an instant through contact;
whatever has been done by oneself is what is obtained, therefore one should always turn back from it.
The Goddess always dwells in his presence with great respect;
indeed, those things which are obstacles for you become excellent opportunities in his presence.
Through his grace, they indeed become friends;
poisons do not approach them, nor do diseases touch them.
All spider-bites and eruptions are pacified at that very moment;
the man shall be freed from old age and grey hair and live for an eon.
Moreover, what need is there for much speaking? One shall obtain the fruit of his presence, as great as the fruit of the Thousand Names previously proclaimed by me.
A mortal obtains all that through the grace of Mahāmāyā.
Thus ends the Śrī Rudrayāmala, the hymn of one hundred names of Mātaṅgī.
Then the Lord of a Thousand Names said:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall now declare the supreme reality according to its true nature."
This supreme thousand names of Sumukhī is beneficial for the attainment of success.
He who recites the Thousand Names shall be victorious everywhere;
for him there is no defeat, whether in an assembly or in a great battle.
O Goddess of the gods, just as the Goddess becomes pleased and well-disposed toward him through his recitation,
so does the practitioner become Śiva himself.
The merit of thousands of horse-sacrifices and tens of millions of Vājapeya sacrifices is produced by reciting this even once; she becomes gracious and her countenance turns favorable.
Mataṅga is its seer (ṛṣi), the Anuṣṭubh meter is proclaimed as its goddess,
and Sumukhī is the application (viniyoga) for the sake of attaining all prosperity.
Having meditated thus, one who desires his own spiritual accomplishment should recite this:

"The Goddess, sixteen years of age, seated upon a corpse, reeling with the intoxication of honey-wine, dark-limbed, clad in crimson garments, possessed of full breasts, and adorned with a garland of *guñjā* berries."
One should meditate upon the Blessed Lady Ucchiṣṭacāṇḍālī in the lotus of the mind, holding in her two hands a stainless skull-cup and a sharp knife.

Oṃ! She who has a beautiful countenance, she who is served by wisdom, she who is full of nectar, she who bears the moon upon her crest; she whose face is equanimous, she who is the means of accomplishment, and she who faces all the virtuous gods.
She who generates all prosperity, she who flows with joy, she who dwells by the ocean;
she who is the consort of Śambhu, she who is gentle, she who is to be propitiated, and she whose essence is nectar.
She is the deer-marked one, the shore, the garland of the forest of beauty,
the lotus-eyed one, the forest-dweller, the forest itself, and she who delights in the forest.
She is the swift one, the bestower of speed, the impetuous, residing in the throat, possessed of great strength;
she is Kālī, beloved of Time, playful, Kamalā, and the mistress of Time.
Kamalā, Kamalasthā, Kamalasthākalāvatī,
Kulīnā, Kuṭilā, Kāntā, Kokilā, and Kalabhāṣiṇī.
Kīrākelikarā, Kālī, Kapālinī, Kālikā, Keśinī, Kuśāvartā, Kauśāmbhī, and Keśavapriyā.
Kālī, Kāśī, resembling Mahākāla, the bestower of hair;
she who possesses earrings, who abides in the lineage, and who is adorned with earrings and armlets.
She is the lotus-pool, the night-lily, the increaser of joy for the white water-lily;
she is fond of sacrificial pits, radiant with sacrificial pits, deer-eyed, and noble.
Her waist is like a mirror-dish, resonant with sound; it is a source of saffron flowers, rich with the splendor of gold, and its hips are adorned with tinkling bells.
She is the one of harsh senses, the ultimate limit, the moonlight, and she who possesses itching;
she is the wearer of matted hair, the deceitful one, the chalk-pen, and the one with a sweet voice.
Kīrahastā, Kumārī, Kurūḍhakusumapriyā,
Kuñjarasthā, Kujaratā, Kumbhī, Kumbhastanī, and Kalā.
Kumbhīkāṅgā, Karabhorū, Kadalī, Kuśaśāyinī, Kupitā,
Koṭarasthā, Kaṅkālī, and Kandalālayā.
Dwelling in a skull, possessing hair, with trembling locks,
clad in a garment of *kadamba* flowers, standing upon a *kadamba* tree, she who bears the affection of saffron.
Kuṭumbinī, Kṛpāyuktā, Kratu,
Kratukarapriyā, Kātyāyanī, Kṛttikā, Kārttikī, and Kuśavartinī.
She is the consort of Kāma, the bestower of desires, the mistress of desire, and she who is saluted by Kāma;
she whose form is desire, whose delight is desire, she who is named Kāmā, and the deluder of knowledge.
She who holds a sword, she who moves through the sky, she who is limping, she whose eyes are like those of a wagtail, she who is a bird;
she who moves with difficulty, she whose roar is harsh, she who dwells on the desert, and she who is fond of play.
She who possesses the rays of the sun, she who is playful, she who holds a skull-topped staff and a skull-bowl, she who is fierce and the destroyer of the wicked;
she who is renowned, she who is free from fragmentation, and she who delights in the destruction of obstacles.
Khaṇḍapriyā, Khaṇḍakhādyā, Khaṇḍhasindhu, and Khaṇḍinī; Gaṅgā, Godāvarī, Gaurī, Gotamī, and also Gautamī.
Gangā, Gayā, Gaganagā, Gāruḍī, Garuḍadhvajā;
Gītā, Gītapriyā, Geyā, Guṇaprīti, Guru, Giri;
Gauḥ, Gaurī, Gaṇḍasadanā, Gokulā, Goḥpratāriṇī.
The protector, the one who possesses cows, the hidden one, and she whose humming is concealed and absorbed.
She who moves like an elephant, the cowherd woman, the cowherd girl, she who is fond of the victory of the cow-pen,
the host, the daughter of the mountain-king, the leader of cows, and the dweller in Gokula.
She has firm breasts, a firm luster, and firm thighs;
she possesses a deep resonance, utters the sound "ghuṃ," causes the "ghukṣa" sound, and is surrounded by owls.
She who is fond of the sound of the bell, the bell itself, the mare, and she who is borne by mares;
she of terrible form and the Terrible One, she who delights in clarified butter and whose collyrium is clarified butter.
Ghṛtācī, Ghṛtavṛṣṭi, Ghaṇṭā, she who is surrounded by jars and bells;
she who dwells in the jar, she who is the act of joining, she who destroys, and she who wards off destruction.
Cañcarīkī, Cakorī, Ca, Cāmuṇḍā,
Cīradhāriṇī, Cāturī, Capalā, Cañcu, Citā, and Cintāmaṇisthitā.
Her beak consists of the four castes; she is a marvelous teacher of thieves;
she is the wonderful consort of the universal monarch; she is marked with wheels and delights in the wheel.
She is the movement of the mind, the activity of consciousness, volition, and the beloved of volition;
she is the wielder of the bow, the delight in the *campaka* flower, the fierce one, and the dweller among the *caṇḍālas*.
Long-lived, she dwells at the root of the tamarind tree;
she resides within the umbrella, she is the cutter, the one who causes cutting, and the severer.
Chucchundarī, she whose affection is deceptive, whose sound resembles that of a muskrat;
Chalinī, the giver of the parasol, the severed one, the cutter of the *chiṇṭi*-plant, and the radiant splendor.
Chadminī, chāndasī, chāyā, charū, and also chandākarī;
jayadā, jayadā, jātī, jāyinī, jāmalā, and jatuḥ.
She who is fond of the Jambu tree, who abides in life, who is mobile, who is dear to all that moves,
who loves the Java flower, who is to be meditated upon, who is the life of the world, and the source of the world.
She is the foremost among the beings of the world, intent on conquering the life-force of the world;
she is fond of her lineage, established in living, and possesses a luster like that of a rain cloud.

She is the one to be born, the benefactor of people, the wife, the birthplace, the devourer of the demon Jambha, and the destroyer of Jambhu; she is the giver of victory, the abode of the world, the victorious one, and the conqueror of the distress of fever.
She is Japā, Japatī, Japyā, Japāhā, Jāyinī, and Janā;
she whose knees are made of Jālandhara, who dwells in the net of light (Jālaukā), and whose ornaments are the objects of recitation (Jāpya).
She consists of the life-force of the world, she is the living soul, she is Jaratkāru, and she is beloved by the people;
she is the earth devoted to procreation, and she is the swift one who brings splendor to the universe.
She who protects the world with her legs, she who delights in nutmeg,
she who loves jasmine flowers, she who is a flame, she who destroys birth, and she who possesses the form of the *jāti* flower.
Jīmūtavāhanaruci, Jīmūtā,
she who is made of worn-out rags, the wearer of tattered garments, the aged one, the blazing one, and the destroyer of the net.
She is the caste that causes the agitation of the world, yet she is the destroyer of that worldly agitation;
she is the slander of people, yet she is the living mother dwelling in the home.
She who is beloved by the people, who dwells upon the knees [of the world], who resides in the water, who relieves the distress of those in water,
who is born from the water, who is the shore of the ocean, and who dwells within the circle of the waters.
Jalamuktā, Jalārohā, Jalajā, Jalajekṣaṇā,
Jalapriyā, Jalaukā, and likewise Jalāṃśobhavatī.
Victory to Jayā, whose body flashes like water, who shines with blazing fire,
who consists of the sound *jhiñjhā*, who is full of the *jhillā* bird, and who produces the clanging sound *jhiñjhājhaṇat*.
She who is the tempest, the one who causes leaping, the leap itself, and the remover of fear from those who leap;
she who abides in the sound *ṭaṅkāra*, the maker of the *ṭaṅka* sound, and the one who effects the *ṭaṅkāra* through her own sins.
Making the sounds *ṭaṅkāra* and *uṭṭaka*, spitting, clothed in froth,
the Ḍākinī and the Ḍāmirī, resounding with the noise of the ḍiṇḍima drum.
She who shines with the radiance of the sound "ḍa," she who is scorching, likewise Tāpinī,
Taruṇī, Tundilā, Tundā, Tāmasī, and she who is dear to Tamas.
Tāmrā, Tāmravatī, Tantus, Tuṇḍilā, Tulasambhavā,
Tulākoṭisuvegā, Tulyakāmā, and Tulāśrayā.
Tudinī, tuninī, tumbā, tulyakālā, and tulāśrayā; tumulā, tulajā, tulyā, and likewise tulādānakarī.
Equal in speed and equal in course, it resounds with the clanging of its scales;
it has copper-colored lips, copper-colored leaves, and causes the agitation of darkness.
Tvaritā, Jvarahā, Tīrā, Tārakeśī, Tamālinī, Tamodānavatī, Tāmatālasthānavatī,
Tamī, Tāmasī, Tamisrā, Tīvrā, and Tīvraparākramā.
Standing on the bank, anointed with sesame oil, the young woman possesses the brilliance of the sun.
Tilottamā, whose crest-jewel is the lord of the stars (the moon) marked with sesame seeds,
who loves sesame flowers, Tārā, the mistress of the stars, the housewife.
She is the consort of Sthāṇu, the maker of stability, the increaser of abundant prosperity;
she is the cosmic abiding, the essence of steadfastness, the most massive, the architect of the universe, and she whose form is vast.
She who possesses vast regions, she who is the vessel, she who increases through contact with the dry land;
she who holds the staff, she who possesses elephants, she who is the bond, she who is destitute, and she who is compassionate toward the wretched.
She is the goddess, the consort of the gods, Diti, the lightning, and the ornament of the deities;
she is compassion, the possessor of self-restraint, affectionate toward the distressed, and has breasts like pomegranates.
She who fashions the forms of the gods, who destroys the wealth of the Daityas, who is bowed to by the deities,
who delights in swinging on a swing, who is compassionate, and who consists of the essence of the divine couple.
Established in the ten lamps, she is the destroyer of defects, yet the creator of defects;
she is Durgā, the pacifier of the suffering of distress, difficult to approach, and dwelling in the inaccessible;
she is the destroyer of foul odors, situated in the difficult, and the bringer of the cessation of suffering.
She is foul-smelling, sounding like a drum, dwelling in darkness, situated afar, and residing at a distance.
She is the giver of gifts, the destroyer of evil diseases,
the subduer, the bearer of the burden, the foremost, the leader, and the bestower of wealth.
She whose roar is wisdom, the supporter of the earth, the giver of Dharma, whose mind is steadfast;
she who wields the bow, the vital channel, and whose form is the rogue of the channels.
She is smoke-colored, a drinker of smoke, smoky, and delighting in smoke;
she is Nandinī, the joy of Nandinī, and the girl who brings joy to Nandinī.
The Narmadā is ever-new, the rim of sport, free from the sound of restraint,
stainless, the support of the Vedas, a flowing river, and the beloved of the naked.
Blue, devoid of jewels, extinguished, free from greed, devoid of qualities, bowed down;
blue-necked, effortless, and born of the stainless one.
Nirguṇḍikā, nirguṇḍā, nirnnāsā, and nāsikābhidhā;
patākinī, patākā, patraprītiḥ, and payasvinī.
The plump wife with full breasts, subsisting on air, composed of the night;
she is Parāparaparākālī, whose beloved is he who enjoys the fulfillment of all tasks.
She who abides in the wind, who is the wind, who increases the joy of the wind;
she who causes the increase of cattle, who is the flowering one, the nourisher, and the increaser of nourishment.
She who possesses flowers, who holds a book in her hand, who dwells upon the surface of the full moon;
she is the fleshy mass, the wielder of the noose, the noose itself, the destroyer of dust, the dusty one, and the sacrificial animal.
She is the clever one, the one who holds an axe as her supreme hope,
the noose-holder, the destroyer of sin, the wife of the Lord, the fallen, and the one whose husband has fallen.
She is the Piśācī, the slayer of Piśācas, and the one who delights in the flesh-eaters;
she is the giver of drink, the bearer of the drinking vessel, and she is intent on the act of giving drink.
Peyāprasiddhā, Pīyūṣā, Pūrṇā, Pūrṇamanorathā,
Pataṅgābhā, Pataṅgā, and Paunaḥpunyapibāparā.
Muddy and submerged in mud, a drink and situated in a cage;
the fifth [syllable] and the five sacrifices, death and the fifth unpleasant thing.
Picumandā, Puṇḍarīkā, Pikī, Piṅgalalocanā,
Priyaṅgumañjarī, Piṇḍī, Paṇḍitā, and Pāṇḍuraprabhā.
She whose seat is the *preta*, who dwells in the *priyāla* tree, who is pale-white, and who removes catarrh;
she who possesses fruit, who bestows fruit, who is the glory of fruit, and whose ornament is fruit.
Phūtkārakāriṇī, Raphārī, Phullā, and she whose face is like a full-blown lotus (Phullāmbujānanā); Sphuliṅgahā, Sphītamati, and likewise Sphītakīrttikarī.
She is the illusion of the child, the enemy of Bala, the powerful one who increases strength;
she is the player of the flute, the forest-dweller, and even the mother of Brahmā.
The bestower of knowledge, the Great Knowledge, the awakener, the giver of awakening, the mother of the Buddhas, the Buddha herself, Vanamālāvatī, the most excellent.
The bestower of boons, the daughter of Varuṇa, the lute, intent upon playing the lute;
she who delights, the abode of delight, the consort of Viṣṇu, the beloved of Viṣṇu.
She is the physician and the medical treatment, helpless yet renowned throughout the universe;
she is overwhelmed by the flood of knowledge, the shore that bestows wealth, and free from all feverish affliction.

She is the one who utters cries, she who makes things distinct, she whose lips are like the *bimba* fruit, she who is fond of the *bimba*, she who dwells in the Vindhya mountains, she who is worthy of worship by others, she who stands in the station of heroes, and she who is the supreme *vit*.
She is to be known through the Vedanta, she is Vijaya, the bestower of victory and triumph;
she is free from conflict, the eulogist, the barren one, and the remover of the bondage of those worthy of worship.
She is Bhaginī, Bhagamālā, Bhavānī, and the destroyer of worldly existence;
she is Bhīmā, Bhīmānanā, Bhīmābhaṅgurā, and Bhīmadarśanā.
She is the Bhilla woman, the land of the Bhillas, the timid one, the Bharuṇḍa bird, the terrifying,
the one who moves through the vulva, the vulva itself, the form of the vulva, and the abode of the vulva.
Seated upon the vulva-throne, possessing the fullness of existence, delighted by the resonance of the kettledrum;
terrifying, with a terrifying roar, she moves about, adorned with serpents.
She is the descendant of Bharadvāja, the bestower of enjoyments, the destroyer of worldly existence, adorned with prosperity;
she is the giver of land, the grantor of earth, the sovereign of the world, and the one who bestows nourishment.
She is the female bee, the producer of honey, the forehead-mark, and she who resides within the lineage of kings;
she is the Mother, the captivating one, the illusory power, the proud one, the enchantress, and the earth.
Mahālakṣmī, intoxicated with passion, Madirā, whose abode is wine,
exalted by intoxication, seated upon an elephant, Mādhavī, the crusher of the spring season.
Modā is the maker of joy; Medhā resides in the center of the pure;
Madyapā is established in the craving for flesh; Modinī is intent upon sexual union.
Mūrdhāvatī, Mahāmāyā, Māyā, the abode of majesty,
Mahāmālā, Mahāvidyā, Mahāmārī, and Maheśvarī.
Honored as the consort of Mahādeva, Mathurā is adorned by Mount Meru;
she is Medasvinī, Milindākṣī, and the crusher of the demon Mahiṣāsura.
She resides in the mandala and dwells in the vulva; she is proud with the passion of wine.
She is the giver of liberation, the garland of severed heads, the garland itself, and she who sports with the garland.
Mātaṅginī, Mātaṅgī, and also Mātaṅgatanayā;
Madhusravā, Madhurasā, and Bandhūkakusumapriyā.
She is the night, adorned by the lord of the night (the moon),
colored with red lac, fond of barley sprouts, the watch of the night, the Yavana woman, and the destroyer of the Yavanas.
She who destroys Yama, she who is like Yama, she whose form is that of the sacrificer;
she who is the sacrifice, she who performs the sacrifice, she who knows the sacrificial formulas, she who is the source of glory, and she who causes the trembling of the wicked.
She is the Yakṣiṇī, the mother of the Yakṣas, the bearer of Yaśodā’s burden;
she is the one who bestowed the thread of glory, the Yāmā, and also the performer of sacrificial rites.
Yaśasvinī resides in the letter Ya; she dwells further in Stambha;
she is Rañjitā, the wife of a king, Ramā, Rekhā, Ravī, and Raṇā.
She who possesses dust, she who is variegated by dust, she who is the delighter, she who is the night,
she who is the lord of the night, she who is afflicted by disease, she who is the night, she who is the queen, she who bestows sovereignty, and she who increases the kingdom.
She is possessed of kings, she is royal policy, and likewise she dwells in silver;
she is delightful to lovers, she is the beautiful woman, she is the delight of Rāma, and she is Rati;
she is semen, she is pleasure, she is the enthusiasm for passion, she is the destroyer of disease, and she is the cause of disease.
She is the theater, she who possesses the theater; she is passion, she who is passion, she who knows passion, and she who creates passion through compassion.
Rāmikā, Rajakī, Revā, Rajanī, Raṅgalocanā;
she who wears red skins, the dyer, she who dwells in color, and she who carries color.
Ramā, who delights in the fruit of the plantain tree; Rambhorū, the beloved of Rāghava;
Raṅgā, sweet as the limbs of the stage; and Rodasī, whose roar is great.
She who causes obstruction and destroys disease, who bears beautiful form and flows with the removal of illness;
she is the singer, praised by bards, the kinswoman, and she whose lips are like the *bandhūka* flower.
She is the one who is worshipped and she who is being worshipped; she is the one who causes flight and she who is the knower of the Vedas;
she is free from agitation and free from skulls; she dwells in the *viṅka* and is affectionate toward the *viṅka*.
