others, such as Brahmā and Īśāna, possess only a portion of his power, just as [the sparks from] a fire. || 165 ||
In the same way, his other power is Śrī, who is the locus of compassion;
she consists of the sixfold attributes such as knowledge and is declared to be the supreme Prakṛti.

Having meditated thus, having offered a flower upon one's own head, and having worshipped with mental offerings (*mānasopacāra*), one should meditate again, place [the flower] on the body of the maiden, and say: "This is the seat; *aiṃ hrīṃ hūṃ hsauḥ*, obeisance to Sandhyā-Kumārī."

p. 394) Having thus uttered the preceding seed-syllables, one should worship [the goddesses] with the sixteen services beginning with the seat, using their names in the dative case in the order of the years, such as "Salutation to Sarasvatī Kumārī" and so forth.

This water: *aiṃ* salutation to Sandhyā; this foot-water: *hrīṃ* salutation to Sandhyā; this ornament: *śrīṃ* to Sarasvatī; this perfume: *hūṃ* salutation to Sandhyā; these flowers: *hsauḥ* salutation to Sandhyā; this incense: *aiṃ* salutation to Sandhyā; this...

*Dīpaḥ* (the lamp): *hrīṃ* to Sandhyā. This is the *naivedya* (food offering): *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hūṃ hsauḥ*, I offer this to Sandhyā. The sword, garlands, collyrium, saffron, and so forth should be offered with this mantra ending in *namaḥ*.
In all cases, the specific qualification "to Kumārī" (kumāryai), ending in the dative case, must be supplied.
Then follows the six-limbed worship (ṣaḍaṅgapūjā).

In that regard, the sequence for the maiden is as follows: holding her heart with the right hand, one should visualize it as consisting of great splendor and white in color; then, having visualized the head as white in color and composed of all things, one recites: *aiṃ hrīṃ hūṃ hsauḥ, to the heart of the Kula-maiden, *namaḥ*.
Then, having visualized the head as white in color and composed of all things...
Having meditated on the crest (*śikhā*) with *haiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ aiṃ śirase svāhā* as having the luster of blue collyrium (*nīlāñjana*),

one should then meditate on the armor (*kavaca*) with *oṃ śrīṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ* as having the first dawn-like appearance and great splendor. Then, with *aiṃ kulavāgīśvari kavacāya hūṃ*, one [meditates on] the three eyes.
Having visualized [the hand] as containing all seeds, possessing great luster, red in color, and blazing like ten million hibiscus flowers,
one should offer two *tāla* slaps with the index and middle fingers upon the palm of the left hand, reciting: *aiṃ kuleśvarī netrābhyāṃ vauṣaṭ* and *hrīṃ astrāya phaṭ*.

Then, having meditated upon Bālabhairava together with his retinue within her sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍabila*), one should worship him with: "These perfumes and flowers, salutation to Bālabhairava together with his retinue. Likewise: "These perfumes and flowers, *aiṃ*, salutation to Siddhajā, the eastern face; likewise to Jayā, the northern face."

Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Kubjikā, to the western face; Aiṃ Kālikā, to the southern face; Oṃ Bhāskara, to each of the guardians of the directions (dikpālas); to Vīrabhadrā, to Mahākanyā, to Kaulinī, to Kulagāminī, to Aṣṭādaśabhujā, to Kālī, and to Caṇḍadurgā.
One should worship with [mantras] beginning with Oṃ and ending with Namaḥ.
Then, having recited the root mantra of the Kumārī or one's own mantra as many times as possible,
having performed *prāṇāyāma*, having offered the recitation (*japa*), and having recited the hymn (*stava*), the armor (*kavaca*), and so forth,
one should prostrate with either eight or five limbs and give the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the worship of the maiden (kumārīpūjā).
Now, O Lord, listen as I shall explain the propitiation of the Kumārīs;
by the mere act of propitiating them, the accomplishment of the Kula is certain. (1)
O beloved, I satisfy with a hundredfold repetition of the root mantra you who sport in the lap of the primordial lotus situated within the family of the young.
I satisfy Śrī Sarasvatī, who possesses the limbs of yoga with the primordial lotus, the maiden, by means of the substances of my lineage for the sake of your satisfaction. (3)
I propitiate her who shines within the six petals of the beautiful root-support lotus with the Śrī-bīja, solely for the sake of enjoyment and liberation. (4)
I satisfy Kālikā with the nectar of the Kula, using her own seed-syllable, she who moves toward the secret sign of Viṣṇu through the unfolding of the waves of self-consecration (svādhiṣṭhāna).
Now I satisfy Kuleśvarī, the auspicious one consisting of great splendor, who resides upon the lotus called Svādhiṣṭhāna and is the head of the suns. 6.
In the centers of the lotuses at the Maṇipūra, I satiate the goddess Umā, Pārvatī, whose body is enchanting, with the seed-syllable Māyā (Hrīṃ).
In the center of the lotus of the Maṇipūra, I satisfy Māninī, who is worshipped as supreme in the three worlds, for the sake of the pure-minded one’s true awakening. (8)
I satisfy Kubjikā, the goddess who dwells in Maṇipūra, who is Raudrī, who increases supreme bliss, and who moves through the sky. 9.
I satisfy the Great Goddess, who is intent upon the practice of mantra; I satisfy the Yoginī Kālasaṃdarbhā, whose face belongs to the Kula.
I propitiate the Great Goddess Aparājitā, the Mistress of the Kula, who bestows power and mantras, who is fierce, and who is filled with a flickering tongue. 11.
I satisfy Rudrāṇī, who is beloved by the great Kaulas, who is perfected, who bestows the happiness of the world of Rudra,
who possesses rays like those of Rudra, and who is fond of honey.
I satisfy Bhairavī, who is perfected by the sixteen vowels, who destroys the Mahāraurava hell, and whose mind is intoxicated by the great wine. 13.
O Mother, I gratify Mahālakṣmī, the Goddess who bestows boons upon the three worlds, who is surrounded by the garland of Śrī-bījas, and who is the source of worldly sovereignty. 14.
I propitiate the benefactress of the worlds, who is beloved by people for her capacity to bring about welfare and misfortune,
the mistress of the sacred seats beginning with the seat of the seed-syllable *Ramā*.
I satiate with nectars Jayantī, the mother of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, the mother of the Sun, and the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) veiled by Māyā. (16)
I offer libations to the supreme-faced one, the joy of the lineage who has reached the further shore;
I offer libations to the goddess Ambikā, Māyā-Lakṣmī, who dwells within the heart.

And for the sake of the happiness of all those possessing the knowledge of consciousness, [I worship] the auspicious Śrīṣoḍaśī, who is joined with the sixteen auspicious Smaras, at the soles of the two lotus-feet.
I perpetually satisfy you, who are seated upon a beautiful throne inlaid with rubies from the ocean of bliss, resting in the center of a white lotus.

Those who always remain well-established in the complete satisfaction of the limbs of praise, who possess the supreme liberation through the cause of the gift of knowledge, and who are free from the nature of illusion—they go [to that state]. There are no hosts of enemies on the circles of the earth, nor any kings who cause misfortune; they all bring [all others] under their control.
They become eternally possessed of the fullness of yoga in an instant. || 19 ||
If a human being recites this [text] known as liberation, which consists of satiation,
he shall become endowed with the eight sovereign powers and behold me within a year.
O Lord, O Master, by practicing for one month, one becomes a great yogi;
he shall swiftly agitate the three worlds and obtain the fruit of his desires. || 21 ||
He who recites this with single-minded devotion shall obtain the fruit of libations;
through the recitation of this hymn to Kumārī, he attains the fruit of worship.
He who does not perform the worship of Kumārī and the daily auspicious hymn will become like a corpse; death shall await him at every step.

Thus ends the hymn consisting of the libation to the Kumārī, within the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī concerning the determination of the divine state, in the section on perfected mantras, in the arrangement of the service to the Kumārī, in the Mahātantroddīpaṇa of the Rudrayāmala, Uttarakhanda.
Now, regarding the *Kumāristotra*,
Bhairava said:
"The Vidyā residing in Vārāṇasī, possessing rays like ten million moons rising over the lord of gods."

They worship for the sake of prosperity Kumārī— the daughter of the Mountain— who is born of Speech (Vāgbhava), who is the beloved of the Three-eyed Lord (Śiva), who moves with subtle actions, who cuts through fierce agitation, who is the nurse of the three worlds, who dwells in the lotus at the root of the excellent tree, and whose face is like the moon. || 1 ||

One should meditate upon the auspicious Bālikā, who is worshipped by hosts of gods such as Śiva and Indra, by ascetics seeking liberation, and by those desiring excellence; she who possesses the constant arising of virtues, who brings about the rise of the best of the twice-born, who shines with white luster, who is the Supreme Goddess, and the doer of good.
I worship Viśālā, Ananā, Aṅgāyatrī, Gaṇamātā, Indrapatnī, Kṛṣṇā, and Vṛddhā. || 2 ||
I bow to the Mother who is worshipped by children and women, who is endowed with excellent qualities,
who bestows liberation upon the learned, who is the nourisher (Dhātrī), the ever-new Śukla-Sarasvatī,
Vāgvādinī, and Caṇḍikā.
I worship her who is the beloved of Hara in the Svādhiṣṭhāna [cakra], who grants what is dear,
who bestows the knowledge of Vedānta, who is eternally intent on the welfare of liberation, and whose form is consciousness, appearing in the body of Yoga. 3.
I bow to the maiden worshipped by the gods in a palace fashioned from a multitude of various jewels,
whose face is the sole seed of the Siddhānta in the mind, dwelling in the Nandana grove;
O Goddess, having abandoned the digit of maidenhood, grant wealth to this body which is otherwise devoid of purpose.
She is Mahyamātṛkumārikā, and she consists of radiant energy through her threefold form.

Having abandoned all else, I always take refuge in the lotus feet of the youthful Lord Baṭuka; I worship her who, with the playful grace of her path crowded with Hālāhala-Karālikās, brings forth the fragrance of the nectar from the lotuses of her hands, and bestows boons exceeding even those of the god of love.
I worship the young maiden upon a white lotus on her head. || 5 ||

I ever worship in the heart-lotus, upon its solar petals, the virtuous Kālikā, who is composed of light, who removes the fear of the sun, who dwells in the waters of splendor that destroy the heat of the great sins of strife caused by the power of the sun’s radiance, and who is the wisdom of the crescent moon.
O Kumārī, you who bring about direct accomplishment, O Immaculate One, I bow to you, the primordial Sovereign Goddess.
I bow to the eternal Śrīkulakāminī, the virtuous Kaulavatī, the Kaulā, Ambikā, Nānāyogavilāsinī,
the divine maiden, and she who is endowed with constant austerity.
I bow to you, O beloved of Śiva, who are adorned with the daughter of the king of mountains, and who abide in a particular dialect that dwells upon the specific meaning of the Vedānta.

I bow to Kaumārī, who wears a garland of skulls, who instills the fire of agitation in the hosts of enemies, whose auspicious eyes possess a red luster, who is the supreme path that bestows the realization of liberation;
she who is the consort of Bhogavatī, whose husband is the lion of fragrance throughout the three worlds, and who is beloved by the five-faced one.
I worship her who removes fear from women and who wards off snakes and other dangers.

Those who constantly worship the beautiful Śrī Kubjikā— the moon-faced one, who delights in the great splendor of her two feet and arms, who causes the destruction of delusion and other afflictions, and who bestows excellent fortune— will suddenly become the crest-jewel of the lords of kings.
They declared that his lordship pervades the three worlds, whose life-span has the attainment of prosperity as its fuel.
[He who is] the Lord of the World of the Yogīs, the beloved, accompanied by the Śrī-Kālasaṃdarbha,
proceeding toward the ocean of splendor, the illuminator of the fruits of desire like a celestial tree—
for the destruction of the sins of the worlds, [he is joined] with Śivā, the Vidyā known as Śrī.
I meditate upon the wish-fulfilling tree, whose very life-breath is the Dharma and who is the eternal deity, as I prostrate myself. 10.

Those of meritorious intellect who joyfully worship Bhairavī— the one whose knowledge is unsurpassed, who is unconquered, who dwells in the heart of Madana, whose face is intoxicated with fragrance, whose sandals reside within the lotus of the heart, who is adorned with the marks of the lineage, and who is the daughter of Atri— [they dwell] amidst the ocean of supreme bliss.
[She who] bestows fearlessness with her all-enveloping splendor, [is worshipped] for the sake of liberation and true renown. || 11 ||
I bow to Rudrāṇī,
whose face possesses the splendor of ten million suns, whose limbs are adorned with various ornaments, whose arms are marked by the signs of her noble lineage, and who bestows supreme bliss.

I bow to the noble lady of the Kula, who is endowed with the glorious Māyā and Kamalā, who resides in the heart, whose function is the seed of the lineage, who takes the form of Vāgbhava, and who arises from the seed-syllable HŪM. || 12 ||
I bow to Varabhairavī, whose face is as black as the Destroyer (Kāla) upon the surface of the earth, who is as red as a lotus stalk or a flower, and who purifies the defects of the world.
I bow to her who removes the fear of the world, who is the supreme one, who delights in yoga, who is the mistress of yogis, and who bestows all enjoyments upon me even amidst a thousand calamities.
I bow to that Goddess Mahālakṣmī, the sovereign knowledge who bestows empire, who directly grants the eightfold prosperity on earth, who destroys the agitation of the lineage,
and who resides within the beautiful lotus of the Svādhiṣṭhāna for the sake of Viṣṇu’s infinite glory.
She who bestows the status of royalty, the auspicious one, the Mistress of the Kilaka, [is worshipped] at all times.

I praise Vāruṇī, the sovereign of the seats (*pīṭha*), the destroyer of the Asuras, the auspicious leader of the Vidyās, adorned with all ornaments, who removes the agitation of the three worlds; she who is the mistress of the *pīṭha*-dwellers and who covers all things with her shadow over the three realms.
She who acts for the welfare of the victorious ones, the Sovereign whose very form is bliss.

Śākinī, who is the field-knower (kṣetrajñā), whose limbs are agitated by intoxication, the beloved consort of Śambhu, the Lord of the Auspicious Baṭuka; she who moves within the great bliss of the wise,
and who directly removes the agitation of one's own mind through the emergence of both self and other.
I bow to Mahābhairavī, who reveals the meaning of the Vākya and whose nature is silver. 16.
I bow to her whose face is like a perfectly full moon, who is conceived within the lotus of the heart, who bears upon her head a hundred petals like a cloud from the great ocean of nectar,
who bestows the fruit of salutation, and who possesses the power to bring all kingdoms under control.
The Supreme Mother, who destroys the fetters of the sense-objects. || 17 ||

I worship you, O excellent Kālikā, who directly burns the three worlds, whose body is filled with nectar, who is the goddess of the junctions (sandhyā) and others, and who is the essence of the Kalās and the supreme master of the Kula; O best of deities, I bow to you daily in the fire of the Siddhas.
Through devotion. || 18 ||
O you whose feet are the fire that consumes the fuel of devotion, if you grant me [this], then I shall give my wife, who is like a great vessel of honey, as a slave in this place. (19)
By the grace of this hymn, one shall become a lord of poetry and speech;
divine, a master of the great siddhis, and devoted to the state of a hero. || 20 ||
He indeed attains victory everywhere and becomes beloved of Hara;
he quickly becomes a master of speech and a man capable of assuming any form at will.
The Mahāvīra certainly becomes a divine animal;
gradually he shall attain the eight siddhis and will certainly become eloquent. (22)
All sciences become propitious, and all the lords of the directions are satisfied;
fire attains coolness, and one may effect the solidification of water. (23)
In this world, that man shall become wealthy, possessed of sons, and a king;
in the next world, he shall dwell in Vaikuṇṭha and in the presence of Śiva on Kailāsa.
O Mahādeva, he who recites this constantly from the very beginning is indeed liberated;
for he certainly beholds the lotus-feet of the Great Vidyā.
Thus ends the Kumārīstotra.
Now, the Kumārī-kavaca:
Hereafter I shall fully proclaim the auspicious Kumārī-kavaca, known as the "Auspiciousness of the Three Worlds," which destroys even the greatest of sins. (1)
Through recitation and retention, people become great perfected ones and illuminators;
[so too did] Śakra, the glorious lord of the gods, and Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods. (2)
The King of Dharma is a formidable fire composed of perfect splendor;
and Varuṇa himself is indeed the worshipful god and the sovereign lord of the waters. || 3 ||
The great wind, the all-destroyer; Kumāra, the lord of elephants;
the lord of wealth, the beloved of Śambhu; and all the gods who are the lords of the directions. || 4 ||
You alone are the Lord, the singular Self, the Master of all, whose arising is stainless;
by the recitation of this armor, all kings shall become lords of wealth.
May the Praṇava, who is the true nature of the twilight (sandhyā) and possesses the power of illusion (māyā), protect my head;
may Mahāmāyā and Śrīsarasvatī protect the upper part of my forehead.
Kāmākhyā is Baṭukeśānī, while Trimūrti is indeed my forehead; Cāmuṇḍā is the form of the seed-syllable, and Kālikā is my mouth.
May she who dwells in the sun protect me eternally, as well as my two eyes;
may the ascetic Umā, whose nature is the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma), protect the pair of my ears.
May Vāgdevī Mālinī protect the tip of my tongue;
may Kuṃbhikā, who takes any form at will, protect the tips of my teeth. (9)
May that Goddess, whose form is the Praṇava, eternally protect my head;
may she, whose essence is the Śakti-bīja and whose nature is Svāhā, protect my upper and lower lips.
May Aparājitā, the most fierce, protect my throat;
may Rudrāṇī, joined with Svāhā, always protect my neck with the seed-syllable *kṣauṃ*.
May the sixteen-syllable Vidyā, possessing sixteen beautiful tones, protect the heart;
may Mahālakṣmī, the foremost goddess, protect both arms everywhere.

May she whose nature is all mantras protect my belly, as the mistress of the sacred seat (pīṭha); likewise, may the goddess of the heart, whose essence is the Vāgbhava mantra, protect the pair of my sides.
The youthful goddess, whose nature is the seed-syllable of Māyā, dwells in my waist;
the Yoginī Kullukā, surrounded by her retinue, dwells in my pair of shanks.
May the goddess Ambikā, who penetrates the meaning of the mantra, protect all my limbs;
may the stainless goddess protect the tips of my hair, and the one who fascinates men protect the tip of my nose.
May the goddess Caṇḍikā protect my chin, and may Kumārī always protect [me];
may the goddess Lalitā protect my heart, and Parvatavāsinī my back. (16)
May the goddess Triśakti, the Ṣoḍaśī, always protect the secret liṅga;
may Ambikā protect it in the cremation ground, and Bhairavī within the womb of the Gaṅgā. 17.
May Vajradhāriṇī, who reveals the mantras and yantras of the five mudrās in empty dwellings, always protect me at the crossroads. (18)
Seated upon a corpse-seat, fierce, and adorned with a garland of severed heads, may the Sovereign Lady, who is the very form of Śakti, protect me in the Liṅga. (19)
May Mahābalā protect [me] in the forest; may Raṇapriyā protect me in the great wilderness;
and may Sarasvatī protect me in the great waters, in the pond, and in the midst of enemies.
May the Earth protect me always on the great path of the sky;
may Rājalakṣmī, the maiden beloved of her family, protect me in the midst of battle. (21)
May Ardhanārīśvarī protect my soles;
may Mahī, who assumes the form of a young maiden, protect me as the Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā) of nine hundred thousand verses.
Resembling ten million suns and as cool as ten million moons, may Vāṇī—the bestower of boons and the beloved of Baṭukeśvara—protect me. 23.

Thus, O Lord, I have related to you this most wonderful armor (kavaca), which bestows a noble lineage upon a maiden and leads one to the further shore of the meaning of the five principles (pañcatattva). 24.
Whoever should recite [this] with the fivefold reality (pañcatattva), along with the hymn and the armor (kavaca), shall attain the siddhi of traveling through the sky; of this there is no doubt. (25)
By the grace of this armor-mantra, one shall quickly become possessed of a vajra-body;
the yogi who recites it becomes a master of all siddhis and a possessor of gnosis.
In disputes, in legal proceedings, in battle, in an assembly of noble families,
on the great road, in a cremation ground, and through the arising of the perfection of yoga— 27.
Having recited it, one obtains the fruit; this is the truth, the truth, O Kuleśvara!
This auspicious armor of subjugation grants victory everywhere.
One who observes meritorious vows and recites this daily shall certainly become a glorious ascetic;
and the maiden Siddhavidyā bestows the highest perfection.
Whoever recites or even hears this shall become a wish-fulfilling tree,
bestowing enjoyment, liberation, contentment, nourishment, royal fortune, and abundant prosperity.
Having worn it, the best of practitioners becomes victorious;
by reciting this auspicious armor, the wise man accomplishes even that which is impossible to achieve.
For those of noble lineage, there is great happiness; it bestows dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
On the day [of the lunar month], one should always worship a young girl at night.
By means of a specific ritual application, one may bring the three worlds under control,
even by means of meat as food, or with fish, together with the mudrā.
The practitioner [should worship] with various kinds of food and edibles, with fragrant substances,
with garlands, with ornaments of gold and silver, and with fine garments.
O Maheśvara, having worshipped, recited mantras, and offered libations to the fair-faced goddess through sacrifices, gifts, austerities, and ritual practice, [one attains success].
Whoever, having offered praise, recites the Kumārī-kavaca with single-minded devotion,
shall quickly attain perfection and become a sovereign lord of kings.
If one writes this armor-mantra on birch bark and wears it, he obtains the fruit of his desire, whatever dwells within his mind. (37)
On Saturdays and Tuesdays, on the ninth, the eighth, and the fourteenth day, and especially on the full moon day during the dark fortnight. || 38 ||
Having written it down, the wise person should preserve it while facing north;
even if burdened with great sins, he shall be liberated from all transgressions. (39)
Holding a woman by her left arm, one should touch all auspicious objects;
she shall be beloved, possessed of many sons, and endowed with every prosperity. || 40 ||
Likewise, one should wear the illustrious Puruṣottama on the right arm;
in this world, he shall possess a divine body and a splendor equal to that of a lion. (41)
Possessing the speed of the wind and free from disease, he goes to the supreme world of Śiva;
having pierced through the solar orb, he attains the highest liberation.

This auspicious armor, which bestows supreme happiness upon the worlds, removes pride and deceit, grants devotion at the feet of the Blessed One, and arises from the ocean of bliss for those who recite it for the sake of liberation.
And those people who study this incomparable Dharma, which is the sole cause for destroying the terrible impurities of the Kali age, attain liberation in an instant. || 43 ||

Thus ends the Kumārī-kavaca, the determination of the [nine] Bhās, within the Siddhamantra-prakaraṇa, in the Kumārī-kavacollāsa, in the arrangement of the service to the Virgin (Kumāry-upacaryā-vinyāsa), in the Mahātantroddīpana of the Uttaratantra of the Rudrayāmala.
Now, another hymn:
O Kaumārī, who art worshipful by the world, who art venerable by the world, whose very nature is all-pervading power; accept this worship, O Mother of the World! Salutations be unto you! (1)
I worship Tripurā, the support of the three cities, she who is three years old and whose form is knowledge—the Goddess who is the triple embodiment and is adored by the three worlds. || 2 ||
I worship the auspicious Goddess Kalyāṇī, the mother of all well-being, whose heart is compassion, who transcends the divisions of time, and who is the very essence of Time.
I worship Lakṣmī and Rohiṇī, who are the substratum of qualities such as atomization (aṇimā), whose essence consists of the letters beginning with 'A', and who possess infinite powers.
I worship Kālikā, who acts according to her will, whose limbs are beautiful, who has the nature of the Wheel of Time (Kālacakra), who grants desires, and whose form is noble with compassion. || 5 ||
I always worship the goddess Caṇḍikā, who possesses fierce valor, and who shatters Caṇḍavīra, Caṇḍamāya, and Caṇḍamuṇḍa.
I worship Lakṣmī, the consort of Śambhu, who bestows eternal bliss, who is peaceful, who is saluted by all the gods, and who is the self of all beings. 7.
I always worship with devotion Durgā, the destroyer of the suffering of distress, who dwells within the miseries of worldly existence during difficult and insurmountable tasks.
I worship the goddess Subhadrā, who is beautiful, radiant with all colors, the bestower of happiness and good fortune, and the mother of Subhadrā.
Thus ends the Kumārīstotra; thus concludes the Kumārītantra within the Śaktapramoda. Śrī.
Contained within the *Śāktapramoda*, compiled by King Siṃha Bahadur, the son of the illustrious Rājā Deva and sovereign of the capital of Śivahara.
The twelfth tantra: the procedure for the offering of bali,
composed by the scholar Śrī Raghurāja Dubejī of the lineage of the aforementioned royal preceptor.
This has been thoroughly revised by Khemarāja, son of Śrī Kṛṣṇadāsa.

Mumbai.
Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. Now begins the *Śāktapramoda*.
Herein follows the procedure for the offering of the sacrificial oblation (*balidāna*).

Facing north himself, he should bring forward a beautiful, well-nourished, and joyful person with unimpaired limbs who has bathed and wears a garland around his neck; facing east, he should recite the following with palms joined in reverence.
Oṃ! Vārāhī, Yamunā, Gaṅgā, Karatoyā, Sarasvatī, Kāverī, Candrabhāgā, Sindhu, Bhairava, and the oceans.
"Be present here for the purpose of performing the ritual bath for the sacrificial animal. Thus, having invoked the sacred bathing places (tīrthas).
Oṃ! Agni was the sacrificial animal; with him they sacrificed. He won this world in which Agni dwells; that shall be your world, and you shall conquer it. Drink these waters.
Oṃ! Vāyu was the sacrificial animal; with him they sacrificed. He conquered this world in which Vāyu dwells. That shall be your world;
you shall conquer it. Drink these waters. Oṃ! Sūrya was the sacrificial animal; with him they sacrificed. He conquered this world in which Sūrya dwells. That shall be your world...
That will come to pass; you shall conquer it; drink these waters.
Oṃ, I purify your speech; I purify your breath;
I purify your eye; I purify your ear; I purify your penis; I purify your anus.
I purify your conduct;
may your mind swell with strength; may your speech swell with strength.
May your vital breath swell.
May your eye be nourished.
May the end of the ear swell;
may that which is harsh in you, whatever it may be, swell for you;

Having bathed [the deity] with the mantras: "Obeisance to you through that purity; Svāhā to the auspicious days," [one recites]: "Oṃ, bind, bind the sacrificial animal with its horns and other limbs for the sake of the animal-sacrifice in the center of the pillar that produces wisdom."
"O pillar in the form of a fragment of the cosmic egg, bind the animal, bind it!
HVAḤ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ! OṂ HRĀḤ HRĪḤ HRŪḤ CĀḤ! To Caṇḍikā, I sprinkle this animal—SVĀHĀ!
Thus is the sprinkling.

Then, having performed the ritual release with "tatassaśṛṅgādyavayavampaśumokṣaṃ kuru kuru svāhā," and saying "forgive me" (*kṣamasva*) while applying vermilion (*sindūra*) to the forehead, one should offer the water for the feet (*pādya*) and other honors with "oṃ chāgapaśave namaḥ."

Having offered flowers with the mantra "Oṃ, obeisance to Agni, the presiding deity; Hrīṃ, obeisance to such-and-such deity, the recipient," one should worship the deities of the limbs of the sacrificial animal.
As follows: on the head, *oṃ rudhiravadanāyai namaḥ*; on the forehead, *oṃ śārṅgiṇyai namaḥ*;
between the eyebrows, *oṃ bhaṅgāyai namaḥ*; on the eyes, *oṃ trinetrāyai namaḥ*;
on the ears, *oṃ pārvatyai namaḥ*; on the nose, *oṃ gaurīyai namaḥ*; on the chin, *oṃ*...
Salutation to Caṇḍikā; on the row of teeth: *oṃ ugracaṇḍikāyai namaḥ*; on the tongue:

Vaiṣṇavyai namaḥ; on the four feet, oṃ Caṇḍapriyāyai namaḥ; on the two sides, oṃ Sarvaiśvaryai namaḥ; at the region of the hips, oṃ Virūpākṣāyai namaḥ; on the tips of the hooves, oṃ Kauśikyai namaḥ; on the tail, oṃ Prahārṣiṇyai namaḥ; on all the limbs, oṃ.
Having worshipped with "Obeisance to the presiding deities of the animals," one should release them.
Oṃ Tat Sat. Today, in the month of Āśvina, in the bright fortnight,

on the [specified] lunar day, during the great festival of the deity [Name] in the autumn season marking one year [since the passing], for the sake of pleasing the deity [Name], this animal is offered to the goddess [Name] by [Name] of the [Name] gotra.
Having uttered, "I shall cause [this person] to be killed by the fire-god and his attendants," one should recite this while standing with palms joined in reverence.
Oṃ! Goat, you have appeared through my good fortune in the form of an offering.
Then I bow down to him who possesses all forms and who possesses the form of Bali.
Animals were created by Svayambhū himself for the sake of sacrifice.
Therefore, I shall kill you; thus, killing in a sacrifice is not killing.
"You are born from an animal womb for the sake of rituals such as worship and fire-offerings."
May that goddess be satisfied with those blood and flesh of yours.

Then:
We know Him as the Lord of Creatures and their bonds; we meditate upon Him who severs the head [of Māyā].
May that animal impel us forward.
Thus one should whisper into the ear.
Then, having brought forth a sword and written the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*, one should meditate upon it.
[He saw] Kṛṣṇa with the Pināka bow in hand, and [the goddess] who has the form of Kālarātri.
With fierce red faces and eyes, adorned with red garlands and unguents.

And drinking blood, he was devouring a mass of raw flesh.
Having thus meditated on the sword and grasped it.
Oṃ! And you, Rasanā, are the embellisher of the world of the gods for Caṇḍikā.
Having thus consecrated with the mantra.
Having worshipped with water for the feet and other offerings, saying "Aiṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to the Sword," one should again worship:
"Oṃ, salutation to Mahādeva" at the hilt; "Oṃ, salutation to Yama" at the edge; and "Oṃ, salutation to Brahmā" at the tip.
Oṃ! You are the sword, the destroyer of the wicked, the blade with a sharp edge, difficult to approach.
Śrīgarbha, Vijaya, and Dharmapāla—homage be to you!
Thus, these eight names of yours were spoken by the Creator himself.
Your birth star is Kṛttikā, and your presiding deity is the Lord Maheśvara.
And the god Dhātṛ, Janārdana, shall provide you with a golden body.
O Father, O Grandfather, O God, protect me always.
Resembling a dark blue cloud, with sharp fangs and a lean belly.
Bhāvaśuddha, Amarṣaṇa, and likewise Atitejas.
Having offered a flower with the mantra "Oṃ, homage to the one with sharp fangs."
Having taken up a sword with "Oṃ hrīṃ phaṭ," and having recited "Oṃ kāli kāli Vajreśvarī, homage to Lohadaṇḍā," [one should strike] at the neck of the goat.
"O Sword, cut, cut quickly! Phaṭ phaṭ! Svāhā!"—facing east, one should oneself face north and offer the bali, or facing north, one should oneself face east; with a single stroke, one should cut it.

Then, having taken blood in a vessel made of clay or similar material and divided it into four parts: in the northeast, *oṃ vidārikāyai namaḥ*; in the southeast, *oṃ pūtanāyai namaḥ*; in the southwest, *oṃ pāparākṣasyai namaḥ*; in the northwest, *oṃ kauśikyai namaḥ*. *Oṃ tatsad adya amuke...*
On the [specific] lunar day of the bright fortnight of the month of [month], during the great festival of the deity [name] in the autumn season marking the anniversary,
for the sake of pleasing the deity [name] for ten years on behalf of [name] of the [gotra] lineage, to the goddess [name].

Having made the formal resolve (saṅkalpa), "I shall offer the blood of a goat," [one recites]: Oṃ Kāli Kāli Mahākālike, O destroyer of sins! Accept this blood and this sacrificial offering (bali), O granter of boons, O you with beautiful eyes!
This is the blood offering.
One should give [the offering] with the mantra "Oṃ dakṣayajña."
Then one should say: "Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Kauśiki, may you be nourished with blood."
Then, having placed flaming lamp-wicks upon their heads: *Oṃ tatsat*.

Today, in the month of [name], in the fortnight of [name], on the lunar day of [name], during the great festival of [name] occurring in the autumn season of the year, for [name] of the [name] lineage...

Having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*): "Desiring to obtain merit that is progressively greater than before, born from seeing, saluting, touching, worshipping, bathing, and satiating the illustrious goddess [Name],

consume the bali offering; salutations be to you. Then, taking the blood of a rhinoceros: Oṃ, whoever I touch with my foot, and whoever I behold with my eye—may each and every one come under my control.

"If he were equal to Śakra," thus one should apply the *tilaka* on the forehead. In the case of a ram-sacrifice (*meṣāghāta*), the word "ram" (*meṣa*) should be substituted accordingly. Having formed the resolve, "I shall give," one should give each [offering] individually. The gift of the head (*śīrṣadāna*) is likewise. Then, having recited the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) according to one's capacity and having offered it, one should prostrate;
this is the procedure taught in the Nandikeśvara Purāṇa.
Now follows the ritual procedure for the offering of the tantric *bali*.

Having stationed an animal endowed with auspicious marks before the Goddess, one should release it according to the procedure to be described. As it is stated in the *Yāmala*: "Having stationed before the Goddess an animal possessed of the proper characteristics..."

Then, one should drive away the malevolent spirits by scattering white mustard seeds; having sprinkled [the area] with arghya water, protected it with the Astra-mantra, veiled it with the Kavaca-mantra, rendered it nectar-like with the Dhenu-mudrā,
and worshipped the sacrificial animal (paśu) with scents, flowers, and unbroken rice grains while reciting the root mantra seven times with the Tattva-mudrā.

we meditate upon Viśvakarman; may that Jīva inspire us. Then, with the mantra "Hrīṃ Kāli Kāli Vajreśvari, obeisance to Lohadaṇḍā," one should worship the sword (khaḍga). Then...

Then, having worshipped everywhere with the mantra "Salutation to the sword endowed with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Śakti," one should prostrate.
One who is intent on the purpose of the spear should [use] a sword that is like a whetstone for donkeys.
O Lord of the Sword, you who swiftly sever the sacrificial animal—homage be to you!
Then, with the great formula: "Desiring to please such-and-such a deity, I offer this animal to such-and-such a goddess; I give it unto you. Then he should present it.
According to the prescribed rite, let this be offered unto you.
Then one should cut off the sacrificial portion.
Then one should offer blood mixed with meat to the Goddess.
Then one should offer the *bali* to the remaining *baṭukas* and others, as follows:

Having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings while reciting "HŪṂ YĀ BAṬUKĀYA NAMAḤ," one should offer the bali-oblation in the northwest (vāyavya) with the mantra as before. Having worshipped while reciting "HŪṂ YĀ YOGINĪBHYO NAMAḤ," one should offer the bali-oblation in the northeast (īśāna) with the mantra as before.
Having worshipped with "Hūḥ Kṣāḥ! Salutation to the Guardian of the Field," one should offer a bali-oblation in the southwest with the mantra as before.
Having worshipped with "Hūṃ Gā Gaṇapataye Namaḥ," one should offer an oblation (bali) to Aṅgaṇeśa in the southeast corner with the mantra as before. Thus ends the *Tantrasāra*.
Now follows the procedure for the fire-oblation (homapaddhati).
Regarding that, first is the method for the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), the altar (sthaṇḍila), and so forth, as stated in the Matsya Purāṇa:
A person should diligently have the ground made to slope toward the northeast.
It should slope toward the northeast, being low in the east or low in the north; this is stated in the Vasiṣṭha-pañcarātra and in the Vijñāna-lalitā.
The square pit (kuṇḍa) is suitable for all [rites] and bestows everything.
Caturasram means four-cornered.
In the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa: "When one thousand [oblations] are to be offered, one should construct a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit."
That [fire-pit] should be two cubits for ten thousand oblations, and four cubits for a hundred thousand oblations.
In [a mandala] measuring two cubits and so forth, it is joined with its consort (yāmala).
It is constructed by means of the diagonal line of each preceding pit.
The measure of each successive sacrificial pit is proclaimed to be infinite.

The measurement of each subsequent *kuṇḍa* is determined by the diagonal cord (*koṇasūtra*) of the preceding *kuṇḍa*, which is measured from the northeast corner (*īśāna*) to the cord placed at the southwest corner (*nirṛti*).
That very measurement is the conventional measure of two cubits (*dvihasta*) and so forth for the successive *kuṇḍas*.
But it is measured by the doubling of the standard hand-span and so forth.
If that were the case, then that which is measured as two cubits and so forth would result in having the dimension of four cubits.
Like the measurement of a farmer’s land; [as stated] in the Vasiṣṭha-pañcarātra.
The depth of the excavation shall be equal to the width of the pit.
In one hand, there are three girdles, measuring three, four, and three finger-breadths respectively.
In a two-cubit square pit, those [lines] should be known as six, four, and three finger-breadths [in width].
In a pit measuring four cubits, those [lines] should be eight, six, four, and two finger-breadths [in width].
Like a celibate student wearing a girdle.
Encircled by a rim and fashioned from clay.
And those [walls], leaving aside a neck (kaṇṭha) of one finger-breadth outside the excavated area, measure four fingers and so forth in height and breadth, respectively.
Those contrary to this, as stated in other tantras, are inconsistent with worldly convention.
In the Piṅgalāmata, there are four Vedas, three fires, two eyes, six tastes, three qualities, and eight, six, and four [units] for the Vasus and the pairs of Tarks;
this is the rule for the girdles of a single pit, after leaving one finger-breadth from the edge. Regarding a single pit:
The duties pertaining to the western direction are stated in the *Vasiṣṭha-pañcarātra* within the section on the determination of great gifts (*mahādāna-nirṇaya*).

In eating, in liberation, likewise in nourishment, and similarly in the restoration of the worn-out; always in the *homa*, always in pacification—[the fire] is situated in the western direction (*vāruṇī-dik*). The yoni of the fire-pits (kuṇḍas) measuring one muṣṭi, one aratni, and one hasta has been declared.
It is distinguished by a length, width, and height of six, four, and two finger-breadths respectively.
One should make the tip of the vulva one finger-breadth deep and slightly downward-facing.
In other sacrificial pits, one should increase the size of the vulva by one finger-breadth at each stage.
One should likewise increase even the tip of the vulva by means of this very sequence of duality.
Starting from the base, the stalk should extend to the middle of the yoni, being perforated with a hole.

By the phrase "like the leaf of the *aśvattha* tree," these girdles have a base four finger-breadths wide, with their width gradually decreasing according to the stated sequence until it reaches one finger-breadth at the end.

In the Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā: "Therefore, having examined [the site] thoroughly, an auspicious altar (vedikā) should be prepared in this manner, or a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) measuring one cubit, in the case of a concise fire-rite (homakarma).
This is also stated in the Kriyāsāra.
