the foremost among the wise, the most excellent, the highest of all the supreme deities.
The bestower of the knowledge of Śiva, the illustrious one, the crested one, the beloved of Śrīparvata;
he who holds a thunderbolt in his hand, the possessor of the sword of the perfected ones, the slayer of Narasiṃha. || 94 ||
He is the celibate student, the wanderer of the world, the practitioner of Dharma, and the lord of wealth;
he is Nandi, the Lord of Joy, Joy itself, the one who maintains the conduct of the auspicious moment, and the pure one. || 95 ||
The overseer of signs, the overseer of gods, the overseer of yoga, the bringer of the age;
he whose splendor is heaven, who has gone to heaven, the master, the celestial sound, the one possessing the most excellent voice, and the one whose voice is like that of the celestial realm.
The supervisor of awakening, the creator of the seed, the performer of dharma, the source of dharma;
he is indeed Śambhu—deceit and greed—and the Great Lord of all beings. (97)
Dwelling in the cremation ground, three-eyed, he is a bridge of incomparable form;
transcendent of the world, possessed of clear vision, the three-eyed one adorned with serpents. (98)
The enemy of Andhaka, the hater of Maya, whose essence rests upon the shoulder of Viṣṇu;
the bestower of welfare, possessing the quality of destruction, the enemy of Dakṣa, and the breaker of Pūṣan’s teeth. 99.
Pūrvajanī, Khaṇḍaparaśu, Sakala, Niṣkala, Muni, Akāla, Sakalādhāra, Pāṇḍuroga, Mṛga, and Naga. || 100 ||

The full one, the fulfiller, the meritorious, the delicate, the one with beautiful eyes; he who possesses all limbs, the protector of cattle, the one dear to Akrūra, the one of holy fame, the one free from ailment. || 101 ||

He who is as swift as thought, the founder of a religious order, the one with matted hair, the lord of life, the bringer of the end of life, the eternal, he whose seed is wealth, and the bestower of wealth. || 102 ||
Sujāti, Satkṛti, Siddhi, Sajāti, Kālakaṇṭaka, Kalādhara, Mahākālabhūta, and Satyaparāyaṇa. || 103 ||
He is the creator of worldly beauty, the abode of supramundane bliss,
composed of splendor, possessing radiance, the foremost among those honored by the world, and the subtle atom.
He of the pure smile, serene in soul, invincible, and difficult to transcend;
composed of light, with limbs free from disease, the beloved of Gaṅgā, and the Lord of Waters.
He who holds the lute made of a gourd, the one of great body, the sorrowless, the destroyer of grief;
the protector of the three worlds, the lord of the three worlds, the purity of all, the one who is beyond the senses. || 106 ||
The Lord whose characteristic is unmanifest is both manifest and unmanifest, the protector of the people; he is the Supreme, Śiva, Vasu, Nāsā, Sāra, Māna, Nandana, and Amaya.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Prajāpāla, Haṃsa, Haṃsagati, Vaya, Vedhā, Vidhātṛ, Sraṣṭṛ, Saṃhartṛ, and Caturmukha. || 108 ||
He who dwells on the peak of Kailāsa, the inhabitant of all, the ever-moving one, Hiraṇyagarbha, Druhiṇa, the Lord of Beings, and the Sovereign of the Earth. || 109 ||
The true yogin, the knower of yoga, the bestower of boons, the beloved of the Brahmins;
the beloved of the gods, the lord of the gods, the source of the gods, and the contemplator of the gods. || 110 ||
The one with uneven eyes, the one with deformed eyes, the bull, the enhancer of the bull;
free from possessiveness, free from egoism, free from delusion, and free from affliction.
The destroyer of pride, exalted by his own majesty, the transformer of all things; the conqueror of thousands, possessing a thousand rays, he is affectionate by nature and upright. || 112 ||
The lord of the past, the future, and the present; the source of prosperity and the destroyer of misfortune;
the goal and the non-goal; the great treasury; and the one who is solely expert in the affairs of others. (113)
Free from thorns, a source of joy, guileless, and a crusher of deceit; full of courage, truthful, devoted to fame, and one who has fulfilled his obligations—such is Sātyaki.
Unshaken, perceiving virtues, not of a single nature, and not performing a single action;
well-pleased, gracious-faced, subtle, easy to deal with—such is the southern wind.
The bearer of the mass of joy, the leader, the increaser of manifest love, unconquered by all beings, Govinda, the vehicle of living beings. || 116 ||
Unsupported, self-supported, perfected, pure in form, whose wealth is glory;
the bearer of the boar’s tusk, the hero, the powerful one, the sole lord. 117.

He is the illuminator of the Vedas, the sole kinsman of the Vedas, the author of many works, the one who cherishes the Śrīvatsa mark, the source of auspiciousness, the most peaceful and noble, and one whose fame is equal [to all]. 118.

He is the further ornament, prosperity, the creator of beings, and the source of well-being; he is immovable, yet his body is devotion; he is the destroyer of time and the Lord of the partless. || 119 ||
He is devoted to truth, a great renouncer, eternally peaceful, and the supreme refuge;
his conduct is for the sake of others, he is the granter of boons, desirous of entering [the world], and profoundly wise.
Bestower of auspiciousness, creator of auspiciousness, possessing an auspicious name, auspiciousness itself;
one who accepts virtues even when unasked, a non-doer, with the luster of gold. || 121 ||
He is naturally auspicious, impartial, the slayer of enemies, and the destroyer of obstacles;
he bears a crest-lock, wears armor, carries a trident, has matted hair, a shaven head, and wears earrings.
Deathless, the all-seeing lion, a mass of splendor, a great jewel;
incalculable, the immeasurable self, heroic, and skilled in valor.
Vaidya, Viyogin, Saptavīra, Munīśvara, Anukrama, Durādharṣa, Madhura, and Priyadarśana. || 124 ||
The Lord of the gods, the Savior, the All-Sound, the one whose movement scorches [the world],
the Destroyer of Time, the Maker of Time, the Doer of Good, and the one who has made Vāsuki his garment.
The great archer, the lord of the earth, the stainless one, the unrestrained;
the sun among luminaries, the one who crosses over, the fortunate one, the bestower of perfection, and the means for attaining perfection.
He who is both manifest and unmanifest, the one worthy of praise, broad-chested, and long-armed;
the source of all, free from fear, and beloved by Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
Untainted, whose nature is free from attachment, without blemish, the destroyer of blemishes;
he who is to be praised, who loves praise, the praiser himself, whose form is all-pervading, and who is undisturbed. (128)
He is the means to the faultless state, the honored mass of knowledge,
possessed of tranquil intellect, unimpaired, ever-joyful, and eternally beautiful.
The destroyer of evil, the lord of those who uphold the Dharma, endowed with resolve, the lord of the night;
he whose vision is the teacher of the supreme goal, and who is affectionate toward those who take refuge in him by the gods.
Soma, the knower of tastes, the giver of tastes, who takes all sentient beings as his object of support,
praised the bull-bannered god with these thousand names.
Śambhu indeed made his request and worshipped Śaṅkara;
for the sake of testing Hari, the Lord Maheśvara [placed] lotuses [before him]. || 132 ||
The Lord of the World concealed that single lotus;
he reflected upon it in his heart, wondering, "Where indeed has the lotus gone? (133)
Let it go, let it go; my eye is not indeed like a lotus.
Having made that very [eye] into a lotus, I worship the Moon-crested Lord. 134.
Having thus understood the heart of Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor, the Teacher of the World appeared while he was still uttering the words, "Not so! Not so! (mā mā).
And at the very spot where worship was performed by Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul,
he quickly descended from that royal mandala.
Having prostrated before Śambhu, who possesses the form described above and has arisen from a mass of splendor, and having stood before him, he offered a special hymn of praise. || 137 ||
Having become serene of countenance, he stood facing Śambhu;
seeing him thus, Hari shone like ten million suns. (138)
Janārdana prostrated before the Lord Śambhu, the God of gods;
then Mahādeva Śaṅkara, as if smiling,
spoke to him as he stood with his palms joined in reverence while gazing at the universe.
Śaṅkara said: "O Janārdana, I have understood all this purpose of the gods;
I give to you this beautiful discus named Sudarśana."
O you of noble vows, contemplate that form which was seen by you, which brings happiness to all the world, and which was created for the benefit of all the lords of the gods.
Even on the field of battle, by recollecting this desired discus, this form, and this thousand names, which destroy the suffering of the gods, [one attains victory]. || 142 ||
"Those who always listen with devotion shall attain unfailing success.
Having spoken thus, he gave him a discus possessing a radiance equal to ten thousand suns. (145)
Viṣṇu also, having bathed there, then took [the water] while facing north;
having paid homage to the God, he then spoke these words again: (144)
"Listen, O Lord; tell me, O Creator of the World, what should be meditated upon and what should be recited by me for the sake of destroying the suffering of the worlds. (145)
Thus questioned by him at that time, Śiva, being well-pleased, spoke: "My form, which indeed destroys all calamities, is to be meditated upon. (146)
For the sake of destroying manifold sufferings, one should recite my thousand names; today, this discus should always be worn by me for the pacification of all calamities.
And others who shall constantly recite it or cause it to be recited—for them, suffering does not arise even in a dream; of this there is no doubt. (148)
If one recites it a hundred times when kings are in distress—complete with its ancillaries and performed according to the prescribed rules—that person obtains auspiciousness. (149)
This is the supreme leader of vidyās, which brings about the destruction of diseases;
those men who shall recite it here with a specific aim will obtain the most excellent fruit.
They obtain the unsurpassed, true fruit; of this there is no doubt—provided they rise early in the morning and perform my worship. (151)
Whoever recites this constantly in my presence, for such a person success is not far off;
having attained success in this world, they shall attain that which arises in the next world. 152.
O Lord of the Gods, by my grace, the reciter shall always attain [this];
he attains liberation through union (sāyujya-mukti), of this there is no doubt. 153.
Having spoken thus to Viṣṇu, Śaṅkara, with a delighted mind, touched him with both hands and spoke again. 154.
"I am the bestower of boons, O best of gods; choose whatever boons you desire.
I have indeed been forever won over by your devotion and by this hymn of yours. (155)
Having been addressed thus by the God of gods, he bowed down to that God of gods and said: "O Lord, if grace is now to be bestowed upon me beyond this. (156)
O Lord, you must especially show compassion toward me because of your merciful nature;
O Mahādeva, be gracious to me, for my devotion is fixed upon you—grant me this supreme boon.
"I desire nothing else, O Lord, than that my devotees should never suffer distress.
Having heard those words of his, Bhava became exceedingly compassionate.
Then the Great God, whose mark is the cool-rayed moon, touched him with faith and spoke to that Acyuta, who is supreme bliss: 159.
Devotion to me is [the cause of my being] venerable and worthy of worship even by the gods; indeed, your name, O Viśvambhara, is the supreme destroyer of sins. (160)
"It shall come to pass, O best of gods, through my grace; of this there is no doubt.
Having spoken thus, the Lord Rudra, who is blue-and-red (Nīlalohita), vanished.
The Blessed Lord Janārdana, having received the auspicious discus at the word of Śaṅkara, performed this hymn of praise continuously with meditative concentration.
He recited it and taught it, provided with offerings by his devotees;
may others who shall read it likewise obtain that same fruit. (163)
Thus has been told that which removes the sins of those who hear it as it was requested;
O noble ones, what further words shall I speak next?
Thus ends the hymn of the thousand names of Śiva.
Thus ends the Śivatantra within the Śāktapramoda.
Composed and compiled by the sovereign King Śrī Rājā Deva Nandana Siṃha Bāhādura, the lord of the capital city of Śiva-hara and the possessor of royal fortune.
The Gaṇeśatantra, the fifteenth [treatise] within the Śāktapramoda.
This has been edited by the learned Śrī Raghurāja Dubejī, a descendant of the aforementioned royal preceptors.
Printed and published by Śrī Kṛṣṇadāsātmaja Khemarāja at his own Śrī Veṅkaṭeśvara Press.
Mumbai. Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. Now begins the Śāktapramoda.
Now begins the Gaṇeśatantra;
now the meditation on Gaṇeśa:
One should meditate upon an island made of the nine gems in the ocean of sugarcane juice.
Its shores were washed by those waves, and it was fanned by gentle breezes. || 1 ||
It was crowded with celestial trees and creepers such as the mandāra and pārijāta,
and its ground was reddened by the radiance of emerging jewels.
In its center, one should visualize a Pārijāta tree made of nine jewels, illuminating the quarters of the sky with the rising sun and moon.
It is constantly attended by the six seasons that increase delight;
beneath it, upon a great pedestal fashioned as a lotus of the Mātṛkās, [he sits].
One should meditate upon Mahāgaṇapati, who is endowed with a triangle within a hexagon.
[I worship] Him whose face is like that of the lordly elephant, who has the moon as His crest-jewel, whose three eyes have the luster of the rising sun,
and who is eternally embraced by His beloved, who rests upon His own lap with her lotus-hand;
[I worship Him] who holds the citron, the mace, the bow, the trident, the discus, the lotus, the noose, and the blue lotus.
I worship Him who carries in His hands two jeweled jars, white as lotuses, along with His own tusks.
He repeatedly warded off with his two ear-flaps the bees whose minds were longing for the flood of ichor flowing from the hollows of his temples.
He was gladdening the practitioner, who was overwhelmed by his own spiritual power, with showers of jewels streaming forth from the mouths of ruby jars held at the tips of his hands.
Adorned with a crown of rubies and decorated with jewel ornaments.
(p. 504) Now, the extraction of the yantra: there is a hexagon and a triangle, and outside of that, everything else is like the *mātṛkā*-yantra.
Now follows the extraction of the mantra: One should first utter the seed-syllables of Śrī, Śakti, Smara, Bhū, and Vighna;
then [one should say] "Ṅe" (ṅenta), followed by Gaṇapati, and finally "Varada" at the end of "Vara."
Having uttered [the mantra] "bring all people under control" (*vaśamānaya*), followed by two *ṭha* syllables;
this is declared to be the twenty-eight-syllable mantra beginning with Tārā.
Now the mantra:
Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ Gaṇapataye, O bestower of excellent boons, bring all people under my control!
Ṭhaḥ Ṭhaḥ.
Now, the procedure for worship:
having performed the rites beginning with the morning duties up to the placement on the seat (pīṭhanyāsa), and having placed the previously mentioned powers of the seat (pīṭhaśaktis).
Namely: in the filaments and in the center [of the lotus]: to Tīvrā, to Jvālinī, to Nandā, to Bhogadā, to Kāmarūpiṇī, to Ugrā, to Tejovatī, to Satyā, to Vighnanāśinī.
Above that, in the center: *namaḥ* to the one seated upon the lotus of all powers (*sarvaśakti-kamalāsana*). In all cases, [the names] begin with the *praṇava* (Oṃ) and end with *namaḥ*.

One should perform worship. Then, one should carry out the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and so forth: "Oṃ, salutation to Gaṇaka, the seer, on the head; salutation to Nicṛt-Gāyatrī, the meter, on the mouth; salutation to Gaṇapati, the deity, on the heart. Then follow the ritual placements of the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*): Oṃ Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ Glauṃ Gaṃ Gāṃ...

To the two thumbs, *namaḥ*. *Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ gīṃ*, to the two index fingers, *svāhā*. 6. Likewise, *gūṃ* to the two middle fingers, *vaṣaṭ*. 6. *gaiṃ* to the two ring fingers, *hūm*. *gauṃ* to the two little fingers, *vaṣaṭ*. 6. *gaḥ*.

*Phaṭ* with both the palms and the backs of the hands. In this manner, [the placement] is performed on the heart and other limbs. However, some maintain that one should perform it with one's own seed-syllable located within the six seed-syllables of the *tattvas*, using the long vowels, as in: *Oṃ gāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *Śrīṃ gīṃ śirase svāhā*. This is because of the specific injunction: "Because of the mention of the qualified [seed-syllables] alone."
Now follows the ritual procedure for worship according to the sequence of the sixteen offerings; now follows the meditation.

One should meditate upon the god who has a single tusk, ears like winnowing baskets, and the face of an elephant; who possesses four arms and holds a noose and a goad, while bearing sweetmeats in his hands.
He wears a garland made of red flowers around his neck and holds a supreme, auspicious [lotus] in his hand;
he is the granter of boons to his devotees and is eternally served by Siddhi and Buddhi.
Bestowing success and intelligence upon men, granting virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation, it is praised by Brahmā, Rudra, Hari, Indra, and other supreme ṛṣis. Thus is the meditation.
p. 506) Now, the invocation: "Come, O Support of the World, worshipped by the best of gods and asuras;
O Lord of the helpless, Omniscient One, honored by the immortals. Thus ends the invocation.
"Then, O Lord, a divine golden lion-throne, endowed with various jewels, was offered by me; please sit upon it there. Thus [ends] the seat.
Now, the water for the feet:

"O Lord of the gods of gods, O Lord of all, O Gaṇapati, accept this water for the feet brought from all sacred bathing places, accompanied by fragrance, flowers, and unbroken grains. Thus is the water for the feet.

Now, O you of unfailing power, please make fruitful this *arghya* offered by me, consisting of coral, pearls, betel nuts, gems, betel leaves, gold, the eight fragrances, flowers, and unbroken rice grains.
Thus is the *arghya*.

Now, for the water for sipping: "O Lord, please accept this excellent water for sipping, which has been requested from all the sacred bathing places such as the Gaṅgā, and which is scented with camphor, cardamom, cloves, and other fragrances. Thus ends the water for sipping.
"Let the beautiful oil, perfumed with *campaka*, *aśoka*, *bakula*, *mālatī*, *mallikā*, and other flowers, and which is the cause of smoothness, be accepted. Thus ends the section on oil.
Now follows the milk-bath:
"This milk, produced from the wish-fulfilling cow, the supreme sustenance for all beings, purifying and intended for sacrifice, is offered for the purpose of bathing. Thus ends the milk-bath.
Now, the curd-bath:
"This excellent curd, produced from the milk of a cow, pure, all-pervading, and pleasing, has been brought by me for the purpose of bathing; please accept it. Thus ends the curd-bath.
Now, the ghee-bath:
"The ghee produced from fresh butter, the cause of all satisfaction, the food of the deities according to their respective limbs, is offered for the bath. Thus ends the ghee-bath.
Now, the honey-bath:
"O God, this honey produced from red bees, which increases all splendor and brings about all nourishment, is offered for the purpose of the honey-bath. Thus ends the honey-bath.
Now, the sugar bath:
"O you who desire to bathe, accept this most beautiful sugar, produced from the essence of sugarcane, which removes impurities, offered by me. Thus ends the sugar bath.
Now, the molasses bath (*guḍasnāna*):

"Molasses, produced from the essence of sugarcane, which is the cause of all sweetness, delicious, and dear to all, and which bestows nourishment, has been brought for the bath. Thus ends the molasses bath.
Now, the *madhuparka*: (p.

507) "This *madhuparka*, filled with curd, honey, and clarified butter, contained in a bronze vessel and covered with another bronze vessel, has been brought by me for the sake of worship; please accept it. Thus ends the *madhuparka*.
Now follows the bath with pure water:
"O Lord, O Ruler of the Gods, please accept this well-scented water brought from all sacred fords by me through prayer, so that you may bathe properly. Thus ends the bath with pure water.
"Alternatively, take this pair of red garments offered by me— priceless, exceedingly fine, and a shield against the shame of the world of the gods. Thus [is the offering of] the garment.
"O Supreme Lord, please accept with devotion this sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) made of silver and this golden *brahmasūtra* adorned with red silk. Thus ends the section on the sacred thread.
Then, by your command, I shall apply many ornaments made of gold, set with numerous gems, upon each of your limbs. Thus ends the section on ornaments.
Now, O Lord, I anoint you with sandalwood endowed with the eight fragrances, the most excellent red sandalwood;
upon these twelve limbs, have mercy. Thus, [the offering of] sandalwood.
Now, for the sake of beauty, I shall offer unbroken grains (akṣatāḥ) mixed with red sandalwood and rice upon the tilaka; accept them, O Supreme Lord. Thus, the unbroken grains.
Now, for the flowers:
"Take the *pāṭala*, the *karṇikāra*, the *bandhūka*, the red lotus, the *mogra*, and the jasmine flower—these most enchanting blossoms. Thus, the flowers.
Now for incense:
"O ten-ingredient guggulu incense, which produces all fragrances and causes the destruction of all sins, please accept this which has been offered by me. Thus ends the incense.
Now, for the lamp:
"O Omniscient One, Lord of all worlds, supreme destroyer of darkness! Accept this auspicious lamp; O God of gods, salutations be unto you. Thus ends the lamp offering.
Then, as for the food offerings:
milk-rice mixed with sugar, accompanied by various kinds of cooked foods,
enriched with the beauty of diverse side dishes, and unsurpassed boiled rice of the *śāli* variety.
Combined with curd, milk, and ghee, and endowed with cloves and cardamom;
accompanied by powdered black pepper and filled with *kvathikā* dumplings.
A paste made from *methī* seeds mixed with mustard seeds and grains,
along with buttermilk, asafoetida, cumin, pumpkin, black pepper, and powdered *māṣa* beans.
It was provided with well-prepared, well-cooked, and fried *vaṭakas*,
along with *modakas*, *apūpas*, *laḍḍukas*, *śaṣkulis*, *maṇḍakas*, and other such delicacies.
The food offering (naivedya) should also be prepared with *parpaṭa* cakes mixed with *amṛtā*;
likewise, there should be excellent soup accompanied by turmeric, vermilion, and salt.
"Take this food along with the ocean-vessel and partake of it with reverence. Thus ends the offerings of food (naivedya).
Now, one may drink at will this fragrant water for sipping, which brings complete satisfaction;
for when you, the Great Self who are eternally satisfied, are satisfied, the entire world is satisfied.

"I give you this well-scented water for the purpose of the *uttarāpośana* (the final sipping after a meal); I give you this water again for the purpose of purifying your mouth and hands. Thus [is the offering of] *ācamanīya*.
Now, as for fruits:
pomegranate, sweet citron, rose-apple, mango, jackfruit, and so forth;
grapes, plantain, ripe mango, jujube, and the fruit of the date palm.
"O Lord of Gods, please accept these fruits: the coconut, the orange, the citron, and likewise the cucumber. Thus ends the section on fruits.
Then he performed the sipping of water (ācamana), the rubbing with unguents (udvarttana), and so forth.
I give you water again for the sake of purifying your face and hands;
accept this beautiful sandalwood paste, auspicious for anointing the hands and limbs.
"Please accept this excellent powder, made from various fragrant substances, known as Sugandhi;
it is meritorious, aromatic, and beautiful. Thus ends the hand-massage.
Now, may this vermilion—
produced from beautiful *śālūra* [lotus roots], originating from the essence of bamboo, a powder for adorning the parting of the hair, and dyed with lac— be yours. Thus ends the section on vermilion.
Then, the betel:

betel-leaf enriched with camphor and areca nut powder, combined with the juice of khadira and other ingredients, mixed with cardamom and cloves, and provided with saffron filaments. Thus ends the description of the betel.

"Now, O Lord, for the sake of attaining the complete fruit of worship that may have been deficient or excessive in its materials, I place this golden coin as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) before You. Thus ends the dakṣiṇā.
Then [the mantra for] the garland:
"O Supreme Lord, please accept this beautiful garland strung with auspicious white, yellow, and red lotus flowers. Thus ends the garland.
Now, the *dūrvā* grasses— either green or white in color, each consisting of five or three leaflets—
I have offered twenty-one sprouts of *dūrvā*. Thus ends the *dūrvā* offering.
Then, O Lord, I shall perform twenty-one circumambulations;
O Lord of Gods, may my sins perish at every step. Thus ends the circumambulation.
Now,
accept these lamps, which bestow sight, prepared in vessels made of udumbara wood, silver, bronze, or gold.
O Supreme Lord, accept this beautiful lamp, which resembles the moon, which wards off the waves [of affliction], and which is illuminated by five lamps within a five-spoked vessel.
Just as this ash is seen, so too destroy all evil. Thus [ends] the ārārttika.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for worship. Now follows the King of Hymns to Gaṇeśa:
Oṃ, we know that Supreme Person; we meditate upon the one with the curved trunk.
May that Dantī inspire us.

I worship the elephant-faced god, whose feet are bowed to by hosts of deities, who is adorned with the crescent moon as a crest-ornament, and whom the virtuous proclaim as the primordial syllable *Oṃ* and whom the Vedas themselves extol.

I bow to that Lord of Obstacles (Vighneśvara), who resembles a rain-cloud and is capable of extinguishing the forest fire of saṃsāra for those intent on worshipping his lotus feet, by means of the continuous streams of ichor flowing from him.

Who could forget the son of the enemy of Ananga (Kārttikeya), who, with the rhythmic flapping of his own ears, warded off the swarm of intoxicated bees clinging to the mud of fresh saffron used as body-unguent; he who,
having brought the water of the Gaṅgā residing in the matted locks of Śambhu with his lotus-like hand—
Devoted with faith, they worship the elephant-faced one who worships Śiva from afar through his divine sports;

I, however, out of simplicity, worship that elephant-headed one as he washes the breasts of the Mountain King’s daughter with the spray of his trunk for his own sake during his enjoyment of her youth.
The sprays released from the tip of the elephant's trunk by her as it was raised up, and discharged through the opening of its ear-fan,
wander across the courtyard of the sky like stars, possessing a luster equal to pearls, appearing as if they were the very essence of Time.
While the Lord of Kailāsa was sporting in the ocean mounted upon his elephant, as the flood of water overstepped its shores, the gods, fearing the end of the kalpa, praised him with Vedic hymns.
O Goddess with the face of a Naga, clad in an upper garment made of naga-skins, while you were sporting with hosts of celestial youths,
those two— the ball and the moon— attained you, having abandoned the passage of time for a moment.

I take refuge in Heramba, who is as tawny as the sun, the sole friend of the gods, the sages, and his devoted followers, who incessantly teaches the meaning of all the scriptures with his five faces that are ever-beaming with joy.

My heart does not abandon that elephant-faced one (Ganeśa), whose lotus-feet are exceedingly small yet who, out of compassion, fulfilled the purpose of the Earth; he who, though causeless himself, became the cause [of her success] according to the words of the Seers.

I worship that son of the moon-crested Lord, who is a mass of bliss, whom Satyavati’s son formerly drew as a portrait with the tip of his tusk and offered to him, and who is propitiated by the austerities of his own son.
Worship the primordial Vighnarāja, who is the abode of the Vedas, the abode of hymns of praise, the playful incarnation of the Supreme Self’s form,
and who is non-different from the serpent-natured or the Puruṣa-natured [Lord].

I worship Him who holds a noose and a goad, with His trunk raised in the gesture of granting boons, and who sprinkles the bodies of Śiva and Śivā with thick streams of spray resembling pearls that stream forth from the hollow of His trunk.

I constantly worship that son of Śambhu whom the knowers of the Vedas call Brahman— the manifold yet singular, born from a limb, possessing a single tusk, whose nature is consciousness, and who is the primordial seed of the universe.

I worship Him who deludes the entire universe, whose eyes are restless with gazing at the lotus-face of His beloved resting on His own lap, and whose smiling lotus-face is restrained by the power of intoxication.
For those who, having previously propitiated you, O Elephant-faced One, study all the scriptures, there is nothing further to be learned from them;
if there were, then everything [else] would be as if unreal.
I take refuge in that golden-hued Lord of the Universe, the ancient Ka, who dwells within the solar orb; the virtuous enter Him through the yoga of the time of dissolution, O Gajānana.
I worship that Puruṣa, the Vedānta-sung, the Self residing in the heart, a mass of bliss;
O Gajānana, by the splendor of whose majesty the darkness of obstacles of people goes to its dissolution.
May he who, out of childish innocence, desiring to pull at the crescent moon from Śambhu’s mass of matted hair with his trunk— only to find its teeth broken off— bestow prosperity upon us.

I always worship that Lord, whose face is like a rutting elephant, who extends his trunk for the sake of warding off obstacles, removing bolts, and preventing misfortune, using coconuts, plantains, and other fruits— He who is my constant desired goal.

Those who duly praise with this hymn the primordial one, whose face is like that of the king of elephants, and who is to be propitiated by numerous sacrifices and manifold austerities, become the abode of all prosperity.
Thus ends the Gaṇeśastavarāja.
Then the Lord spoke the armor-mantra: "Listen, O beloved, I shall declare the armor-mantra which grants all accomplishments."
Having recited it and having caused others to recite it, one is liberated from all distress.
O Goddess, if one recites the mantra of Gaṇeśa without knowing his armor (kavaca),
success will not arise for him even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Oṃ! May Āmoda protect the head; may Pramoda protect above the eyebrows;
may Sammoda protect the pair of eyebrows; and may Gaṇādhipa protect the space between the eyebrows.
May Gaṇakrīḍa, whose eyes are joined with his nose and who is the leader of the hosts,
protect my face for the sake of all accomplishments— he who is adorned by the play of the Gaṇas.
May Sumukha protect my tongue; may Durmukha always protect my neck.
May Vighneśa protect my heart, and may Vighnanāśa protect my chest.
May Gaṇānāṃ Nāyaka always protect the pair of my arms.
The creator of obstacles resides in the belly, and the remover of obstacles resides in the linga.
May Gajavaktra protect my waist, Ekadanta my hips, Lambodara always protect my private parts, and Aruṇa my secret region.
May he who has a serpent for his sacred thread protect me always at the pair of my feet;
may the reciter (Jāpaka) protect me always, and may the Lord of the Gaṇas protect my knees and shanks.
May the yellow-hued Gaṇanāyaka protect [me] always on every limb;
O Maheśvarī, whoever should recite this daily concerning Gaṇeśa.
This armor, known as Sarvasiddha, destroys all obstacles;
it directly bestows all accomplishments and liberates one from all sins.
It directly bestows all prosperity and causes the destruction of all enemies;
[it wards off] the afflictions of the planets, fevers, diseases, and others such as the Guhyakas.
O Goddess, through mere recitation and retention, this armor, worshipped by the gods, brings about destruction [of obstacles] at that very moment; it bestows wealth and grain.
O Maheśānī, there is nothing equal to this *kavaca* in the three worlds; O Maheśānī, on this earth, there is nothing equal to this *kavaca* of the turmeric [deity].
"What is the use of other worthless talk, wherein one's life would only be spent?
Thus ends the Gaṇeśa-kavaca in the Viśvasāra-tantra.
Now the Upaniṣad: Oṃ laṃ svāhā! May He protect us both; svāhā! May He nourish us both; svāhā! May we acquire vigor together.
May our study be luminous; may we never harbor hatred toward one another.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace!
Oṃ Laṃ! Salutations to Gaṇapati; you alone are the manifest reality.
You alone are the sole creator; you alone are the sole sustainer.
You alone are the sole destroyer;
you alone are indeed all this, for you are Brahman;
you are eternally the manifest Self.
I speak the *ṛta*; I speak the truth. Protect me; protect the speaker; protect the listener.
Protect the giver; protect the establisher; protect the one who has studied the Vedas and the student; protect from behind.
[He recites] "ava purastāt" [at the front].
Protect from above; protect from below; protect from the zenith; protect from the nadir.
Protect me from all sides; protect me everywhere! You are composed of speech; you are composed of consciousness.
You are composed of bliss; you are composed of Brahman; you are the non-dual existence-consciousness-bliss.
You are Brahman manifest before the eyes; you consist of knowledge and consist of realized wisdom.

This entire world is born from you; this entire world abides in you; this entire world shall go to dissolution in you. You are earth, water, fire, air, and space. You are the four steps of speech. You are beyond the three qualities (guṇas).
You transcend the three bodies; you transcend the three times. You abide eternally in the *mūlādhāra*;
you consist of the three powers (*śaktitraya*). Yogis meditate upon you eternally. You are Brahmā, you are Viṣṇu, you are Rudra, you are Indra, you are Agni, you are Vāyu, you are Sūrya.
You are the Moon, O Brahman; bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ om!
Having first uttered the *gaṇas* and so forth, one should thereafter utter the *varṇas* and so forth.
The anusvāra is further beyond; it is obstructed by the syllable *tāra*, which is white like a crescent moon.
This is your human form; the letter *ga* is its prior form.
The letter *a* is the middle form; the *anusvāra* is the final form.
The Bindu is the form of the subsequent [vowel]; the Nāda is the conjunction; the Saṃhitā is the euphonic combination.
This is that very Vidyā of Gaṇeśa; Gaṇa is the seer, and Nicṛt Gāyatrī is the meter.
The deity is Gaṇapati. Oṃ gaṃ, salutation to Gaṇapati.
We know the One-Tusked One; we meditate upon the Crooked-Trunked One. May that Elephant-nosed One inspire us.
Having one tusk and four hands, he holds a noose and a goad.
Holding a rosary and a boon-granting gesture in his hands, he has a mouse as his emblem.
With a red protruding belly, ears like winnowing baskets, and clad in red garments.
To the God whose limbs are anointed with red sandalwood paste, who is well-worshipped with red flowers,
who is compassionate toward his devotees, the cause of the universe, and the infallible one.
He who constantly meditates thus upon that which was manifested at the beginning of creation— arising from Prakṛti and beyond Puruṣa— is the best of yogis among yogis.
Oṃ, salutations to the Lord of the Hosts; salutations to the Lord of the Gaṇas; salutations to the Lord of the First;
let there be salutation to you, the pot-bellied one, the single-tusked one, the destroyer of obstacles, the son of Śiva, whose form bestows boons. Salutations!
Whoever studies this Atharvaśīrṣa becomes fit for union with Brahman; he is not afflicted by any obstacles; he prospers in happiness in every respect; he is liberated from the five great sins.

Studying in the evening, one destroys the evil committed during the day; studying in the morning, one destroys the evil committed during the night; by practicing both morning and evening, one becomes free from sin.

One who studies this everywhere remains free from obstacles; one attains dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. This Atharvaśīrṣa must not be given to one who is not a disciple. If anyone should give it out of delusion, he becomes a sinner. By reciting it a thousand times, whatever desire one studies [to fulfill], that is attained through this.
One should accomplish [the rite]. By this, one consecrates Gaṇapati; he becomes eloquent.
"On the fourth [day], he mutters while fasting; he becomes possessed of knowledge"—this is a statement from the Atharvaveda.
One should know that the practice beginning with Brahmā ensures that one never fears; this applies to one who worships with blades of dūrvā grass.

He who sacrifices with parched grains (lāja) becomes like Vaiśravaṇa. He who sacrifices with a thousand sweetmeats (modaka) becomes possessed of fame and becomes wise. He who sacrifices with fuel-sticks (samidh) soaked in clarified butter (ājya) obtains everything; he obtains everything. Eight.

Having correctly instructed the Brahmins, one becomes as radiant as the sun. By reciting [the mantra] during a solar eclipse at a great river or in the presence of an image, one becomes perfected in the mantra.
One is liberated from great obstacles; one is liberated from great faults.

One is liberated from great transgression. He becomes all-knowing; he becomes all-knowing—he who knows thus. This is the Upanishad. May He protect us both; may He nourish us both; may we work together with vigor; may our study be brilliant; may we not hate each other. Om. Peace! Peace! Peace!
Peace! Thus ends the Gaṇapatyopaniṣad.
Now, the hundred names: Oṃ, Gaṇeśvara, Gaṇakrīḍa, and likewise Mahāgaṇapati.
The creator of the universe, whose face is the universe, the invincible, the conqueror of Dhūrjati, the Victorious One. || 1 ||
He is beautiful of form, the abode of all eyes, and takes recourse in the heroic posture (vīrāsana).
He is the sovereign of yoga, situated upon the stars, the Primordial Person (puruṣa), whose ears are like those of an elephant. || 2 ||

He has variegated marks, dark teeth, and a crescent moon upon his forehead; he is four-armed, possesses the splendor of Śambhu, has the sacrifice as his body, is the soul of all, and is strengthened by the Sāman chants.
He has the mountain ranges for his shoulders, the sky for his navel, and the groves of Kalpa trees for his abode;
he has a deep navel, a broad belly, a full chest, and mighty arms.
He had broad shoulders, a neck like a conch shell, full lips, and a prominent nose;
he was complete in all his limbs and endowed with all the auspicious marks.
Bearing a sugarcane bow and a trident, his abode blossomed with splendor;
holding a rosary and possessing the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā), he brings about victory.
Desiring the beloved woman, he is fondly caressed by the play of Mālinī;
he is Amoghasiddhi, the support, yet devoid of both support and the supported.
Dark as the petal of a blue lotus, pure as the orb of the moon;
witness of karma, performer of karma, and bestower of the fruits of both karma and non-karma. || 8 ||
Holding a water-pot, disciplined, with matted hair and wearing a waist-thread,
he is the embodiment of compassion, tawny-hued, and described as one who moves through secret ways.
He who dwells in the cave, who resides in the ocean of the cave; he who is the jar and the pot, the interior of the jar;
he who is full bliss, supreme bliss; the giver of wealth, the upholder of the earth. || 10 ||

The greatest of the great, the foremost of the Brahmas, the friend of those devoted to Brahman, the knower of Brahman, beloved by the knowers of Brahman; the auspicious one, the abode of all beings, the bestower of enjoyments, and the high-minded one.
The most excellent one, Vāmadeva, the venerable one, the warder-off of the thunderbolt;
the creator of the universe, the eye of the universe, the invocation, and the consumer of the *havya* and *kavya* offerings. (12)
He is independent, one whose resolve is true, and likewise an increaser of good fortune;
he is the bestower of fame, the remover of grief, and the giver of the fruits of the three aims of life. || 13 ||
He has four arms and four tusks, born on the fourth lunar day;
he is the Puruṣa with a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet.

He who can assume any form at will, whose movement is at his pleasure, the elephant, the protector of the continents, the lord of the sacred field, the sustainer of the earth, who abides in dissolution, and who is fond of sweetmeats. || 15 ||

He who paralyzes the mouths of opponents, who purifies the minds of the wicked, the Blessed One who is easily attained through devotion, the performer of sacrifices, and the beloved of those who offer oblations. 16.
Thus, these one hundred and eight names of the wise Gaṇarāja, the god of gods, have been proclaimed as the very essence.
Having extracted the thousand names, I have proclaimed this captivating [work];
having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and remembered the Lord Gaṇeśvara.
If one recites this hymn with devotion, Gaṇarāja becomes pleased. || 18 ||
Thus ends the hymn of one hundred and eight names of the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
Then Vyāsa said: "How did Gaṇeśa teach the thousand names?"
Tell me that for the sake of Śiva, O you who are intent upon the grace of the world.
Brahmā said:
O God of gods, O Foe of Tripura, it is said that during your endeavor to conquer the three cities,
you became indeed overwhelmed by obstacles due to the failure to worship Gaṇeśa.
Having mentally determined that cause of the obstacle,
he then worshipped Mahāgaṇapati with devotion according to the prescribed rite.
The Great Gaṇapati himself, being personally gratified by the worship of Śambhu, was asked by Aparājita for the means to pacify obstacles. || 4 ||
It is the sole remover of all obstacles and the bestower of the fruits of all desires;
then he spoke this thousand names of his own to him.

Of this mantra, the *Śrī Mahāgaṇapati Sahasranāmamālā*, Gaṇeśa is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Mahāgaṇapati is the deity (*devatā*), the various meters (*chandas*) are the meters, "Gaṃ" is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), "Tuṇḍa" is the power (*śakti*), and "Svāhā" is the pin (*kīlaka*). [This is recited] for the purpose of pleasing Mahāgaṇapati by means of the destruction of all obstacles.
This is the application for the recitation (japa).
Mahāgaṇapati said: Oṃ! Lord of the Gaṇas, who sports with the Gaṇas, Master of the Gaṇas, Sovereign of the Gaṇas;
he with the single tusk, the curved trunk, the elephant face, and the great belly. (6)
Lambodara, Dhūmravarṇa, Vikaṭa, Vighnanāyaka, Sumukha, Durmukha, Buddha, Vighnarāja, and Gajānana. || 7 ||
Bhīma, Pramoda, Āmoda, Surānanda, Madotkaṭa, Heramba, Śambara, Śambhu, Lambakarṇa, and Mahābala. || 8 ||
Nandana, Lampaṭa, Bhīru, Meghanāda, Gaṇañjaya, Vināyaka, Virūpākṣa, Dhīra, Śūra, and Varaprada. || 9 ||
Mahāgaṇapati, beloved of wisdom, the one who quickly bestows grace;
the favorite of Rudra, the presiding lord of the Gaṇas, the son of Umā, and the destroyer of sin. || 10 ||
The teacher of the Kumāras, the son of Īśāna, whose vehicle is a mouse;
he who is fond of success, the lord of success, the perfected one, and the Vināyaka of success. || 11 ||
Avighna, Tumbaru, Siṃhavāhana, Mohinīpriya, Kaṭaṅkaṭa, Rājaputra, Śālaka, Sammita, and Amita. (12)
He is the source of the Kūṣmāṇḍa Sāman, the invincible, the conqueror of Dhūrjaya, the victorious;
he is the lord of the earth, the lord of the world, the imperishable lord of all beings.
The creator of the universe, whose face is the universe, whose form is the universe, the treasure-house, the radiant one;
the seer among seers, the bull among sages, the friend of Brahman, the Lord of Brahman. || 14 ||
The eldest king, the lord of treasures, beloved by the lord of treasures,
he dwells within the golden city and resides in the center of the solar disc.

He who destroyed the waters of the ocean with the blow of his hand, who shattered the teeth of Pūṣan, who takes delight in the playful sport on Umā’s lap, who bestows liberation, and who protects the lineage. 16.
Wearing a crown, earrings, and necklaces, adorned with a forest garland, he is composed of mind;
having destroyed the fortune of the Daityas through his aversion, he has conquered the earth by treading upon it with his feet.

Sadyojāta, who wears a girdle of gold and muñja grass; the remover of ill omens, the remover of bad dreams, the victorious, the possessor of qualities, and the one established in the sound of the *nāda*. || 18 ||
He is beautiful, the abode of all eyes, and takes recourse in the heroic posture (vīrāsana).
He wears yellow garments, has broken teeth, and has made the crescent moon his crest-ornament.
Citrāṅka, Śyāmadaśana, Bālacandra, Caturbhuja, Yogādhipa, Tārakastha, Puruṣa, and Gajakarṇaka. || 20 ||
The lord of the Gaṇas, victory, the steadfast one, the lord of elephants, the bearer of the banner; the god of gods, the life-breath of Smara, the lamp, and the pillar of wind. || 21 ||
The wise one, the bestower of boons, the resonance, he whose clouds are pierced by resonance;
he whose tusks are like those of a boar, the conqueror of death, whose garment is a tiger skin. || 22 ||
He who holds the power of will, the protector of the gods, the crusher of the Daityas;
he who was born from the mouth of Śambhu, the remover of Śambhu’s anger, and the source of Śambhu’s laughter. (23)

He whose splendor is Śambhu, who removes the sorrow of Śivā, who brings happiness to Gaurī, who is born from the body of Umā, who is the source of Gaurī’s luster, and who is born from the celestial river. || 24 ||
He whose body is the sacrifice, who possesses a great roar, whose stature is like a mountain, and whose face is auspicious;
he who is the self of all, the self of all the gods, whose head is Brahman, and whose hearing is the quarters of space.
The jar of the universe is His forehead, the sky of consciousness is His brow, and truth is the hair upon His head;
He is the one whose opening and closing of His eyes causes the birth and dissolution of the world, and whose eyes are the sun and the moon.

Dharma, the most virtuous, has the lord of mountains as his single tusk, is strengthened by the Sāman chants, has the planets and constellations for his teeth, speech for his tongue, and Vāsava for his nose. || 27 ||

With his hand placed between his eyebrows, intoxicated with the pride of the knowledge of Brahman, he has the principal mountain ranges for shoulders, the moon and sun for bells, and Rudra for a neck. (28)
He has the rivers and streams for his arms, the serpents for his fingers, and the stars for his nails;
he has the sky for his navel, Śrī for his heart, Mount Meru for his back, and the oceans for his belly. (29)
With Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Rākṣasas, Kinnaras, and humans dwelling within his belly;
with the earth as his waist, creation as his phallus, mountains as his thighs, and the ocean as his knees. || 30 ||
His shanks reach down to the netherworld (pātāla), his feet are like those of a sage, his big toes are black, and his body is the three Vedas;
his tail is a circle of light, and his heart is as steady as a brandished firebrand.
He dwells in the pericarp of the heart-lotus, serving as a pleasure-lake for the sky;
he is the fetter of meditation for true devotees and is warded off by the waters of worship.
The son of Kaśyapa, a leader of the Gaṇas, a lord of the world, powerful, illustrious, righteous, of noble birth, he is the foremost lord of the Pramathas.
He is the wish-fulfilling gem, the lord of the island, whose dwelling is the forest of the desire-granting trees;
he stands in the midst of a pavilion of jewels, taking his seat upon a throne of precious gems.
With his feet firmly placed upon the head of Tīvrā, he is caressed by the crown of Jvālinī;
the glory of his seat is gladdened by Nandā, and his throne is adorned by Bhogadā. || 35 ||
He is the seat that grants all desires, the refuge for the throbbing and fierce throne;
he is the crest-jewel of Tejovatī, adorned with Satya and Anityā as his ear-ornaments.

He is the sacred seat (pīṭha) that destroys all obstacles, the refuge of the lotus of all powers (sarvaśakti), the support for the lotus-throne of the letters (lipipadmāsana), and the abode of the three fires (vahnidhāmatraya). || 37 ||
He has elevated forefeet, hidden ankles, and well-rounded heels;
he has thick calves, joined knees, stout thighs, and a prominent waist. (38)
With a deep navel, a thick belly, a broad chest, and long arms;
with fleshy shoulders, a neck marked by three folds like a conch shell, protruding lips, and a long nose. (39)
With a broken chowrie and a tall tusk on the left side, possessing large jaws, three short eyes, ears like winnowing baskets, and a thick head; || 40 ||
His forehead is shaped like a cluster of blossoms, he wears a crest-jewel, and is unrestrained;
he has a serpent as a necklace, a serpent as a waist-thread, and a serpent as a sacred thread.
He has a crest-ornament of ten million serpents, with serpents as necklaces and armlets;
he has a girdle and waist-band of serpents, and the king of serpents as his upper garment.
He is red, wearing red garments, adorned with red garlands;
his eyes are red, his hands are red, and the sprouts of his palate and lips are red. || 43 ||
He was white, wearing white garments and adorned with white garlands;
he was radiant under a white parasol and fanned by white chowries.
Complete in all his limbs, marked by all the auspicious characteristics, enriched with the splendor of all ornaments, and endowed with every beauty. || 45 ||
The most auspicious of all that is auspicious, the cause of all causes;
he who acts alone at all times, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, the bearer of the Bījapūra fruit, and the holder of the mace.
He holds a sugarcane bow and a trident; he bears a discus and a lotus; he wields a noose and carries a blue lotus; he holds a cluster of śālī rice and bears his own teeth.
He wears the wish-fulfilling vine; he is the sole bestower of fearlessness to the universe and its master;
he holds a rosary, possesses the gesture of knowledge (*jñānamudrā*), and wields a mallet as his weapon.
He holds a full vessel, bears a conch shell, and carries a swarm of bees; he holds a citron fruit, possesses mango buds, and wields an axe.
He who rains down a shower of precious jewels from a golden pitcher situated upon a lotus;
the Lord of Bhāratī and Sundarī; he who is fond of Vināyaka and Rati. || 50 ||
The most beloved of Mahālakṣmī, charming with Siddhalakṣmī;
he whose eastern body is Ramā and Ramēśa, and whose southern [body] is Umā and Maheśvara. || 51 ||
He whose left side is the Earth-boar (Mahīvarāha), who is the western limit of Rati and Kandarpa;
he who generates fragrance and joy, and who is the delight of those full of joy. || 52 ||
He is the one who brings about prosperity, success, power, and accomplishment for those who have kindled the sacred fire;
he is the benevolent one who has granted his favor, and he is the abode from which the sprouts of splendor have blossomed.
With his feet resorted to by Madanāvatī, he made even the ill-natured face of Daurmukhya; like a tree that destroys the sprouts of calamities, he possessed a blossoming flow of compassion.
His feet crush those who create obstacles; he is honored by the power of Drāviṇī;
his eyes are intensely radiant; and his singular gaze is protected by Jvālinī.
The charmer of the charmers, adorned with the splendor that bestows enjoyment;
he whose earth was presided over by the beauty of the faces of beloved women. || 56 ||
The Lord is the master of the great treasure of the conch (mahāśaṅkha), which is as vast as the earth and filled with wealth;
he is the master of the great treasure of the lotus (mahāpadma), upon whose crown the prostrating earth rests.
He is to be served by all true gurus; he has the fire-crested one as his heart-abode;
he has Īśāna as his head; he has Indra as his crest; he is the son of the Wind-god.
He whose eyes are the foremost among all things new, who is skilled in the employment of divine weapons,
and who delights in the covering provided by all the elephants of the quarters, such as Airāvata and others.
He is surrounded by the Vajra and other weapons, taking refuge in the fierce Gaṇas;
he is encircled by Jaya and Ajaya, bringing about victory and non-victory.
He whose lotus feet are unconquered, who is adorned by the eternal and the non-eternal,
who takes delight in his playful consorts, and who is embellished by the beauty of his majesty.
Bestowing infinite and endless bliss, he is the most auspicious of the auspicious;
he is served by the powers of will (icchā-śakti), knowledge (jñāna-śakti), and action (kriyā-śakti).
His feet are resorted to by the fortunate; he is the refuge of the playful and the non-playful; he desires the beloved women; he is cherished in the amorous sports of Mālinī. (63)
He is the refuge of Sarasvatī, the delight of Gaurī, and the abode of Śrī;
his feet are protected by his teacher, he is perfected in speech, and he is the lord of Vāgīśvarī.
He is the lover of Nalinī, who delights in Vāmā, and who is charming through Jyeṣṭhā;
his lotus-feet are sealed by Raudrī, he has the seed-syllable HŪM, and his power (Śakti) is lofty. || 65 ||
The protector and progenitor of the universe, whose power is the sacrificial exclamation Svāhā, who possesses the *kīlaka*,
whose dwelling is made in the ocean of nectar, and whose eyes roll with intoxication.
He is the host of the remnants (ucchiṣṭagaṇa), the Lord of the hosts of remnants (ucchiṣṭagaṇeśa), and the leader of the Gaṇas;
he possesses eternal and perfect accomplishment, is a perpetual devotee of Śiva, and is clothed only by the directions (digambara).
He is without downfall, with vision that does not cease, immeasurable, ageless, and immortal;
he is untroubled, the matchless warrior, indeed the infallible, the deathless, and the imperishable.
He is beyond reasoning, imperishable, unconquerable, supportless, free from disease, and stainless;
he is the unfailing success, non-dual, non-terrible, and possesses immeasurable faces.
Formless, it overcomes the elements, the earth, fire, and strength; its characteristic is unmanifest.
It is the foundational seat, the support, and is devoid of both support and supported. || 70 ||
He whose banner is a rat, the fulfiller of hopes, the great chariot of the rat;
he who dwells in the midst of the ocean of sugarcane juice, and who is eager for the consumption of sugarcane.
He whose splendor exceeds that of the sugarcane-bow, and who is served by the Sugarcane-bow (Ikṣucāpa).
Possessing a splendor like that of the indragopa insect, with a luster equal to sapphire, dark as the petal of a blue lotus, and as pure as the orb of the moon. || 73 ||
He who loves the sacrificial fuel, the recipient of the *iḍā* portion, whose abode is the *iḍā*, and who is dear to Indrā;
he who destroys the obstacles of the Ikṣvākus and is desired as the one to be acted upon.
The Lord whose crown is Īśāna, the Sovereign, the son of Īśāna, the destroyer of calamities; he who brings about the end of the three types of craving, and who is devoid of even the slightest effort.
Upendra, the one whose crown bears the moon, who is fond of offerings of uṇḍeraka flowers, whose face is uplifted, who is exalted, and who is the noble leader of the gods. 76.
He is full of vigor, possessing the intoxication of heat; he is difficult to overcome through reasoning and refutation;
he is the source of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas; and he is the promoter of prosperity and spiritual accomplishments. || 77 ||
He is easily attained by those with upright minds; he is the liberator from the three debts;
he has destroyed the obstacles of his own devotees and has stripped the enemies of the gods of their power.
He whose glory has vanished due to worship performed with averted face; the destroyer of spider-webs and pustules;
seated in the center of the seat of the syllable *E*; having made his seat with a single foot. || 79 ||
He who has subdued the fortune of all the Daityas, who has caused all places of refuge to tremble,
who is a treasury of sovereignty, and who bestows worldly and otherworldly prosperity— (80).
He is the manifestation of the joy of the Nandana grove, his face resembling Airāvata;
he is denoted by the syllable Oṃ, he is the syllable Oṃ itself, the powerful lord of medicinal herbs.
A treasury of magnanimity, preeminent in the absence of arrogance, and devoid of the sound of pride;
he is the goad for the gods and nāgas, and the hook for the enemies of the gods. 82.
He is proclaimed in the verses as one whose emissions are not combined;
he holds a water-pot, he is the Ordainer, he has matted hair, and his face is like that of a young elephant. 83.
The witness of karma, the performer of karma, the bestower of the fruits of both action and inaction;
he who has the form of a kadamba bud and is the leader of the hosts of Kuṣmāṇḍas. || 84 ||
The compassionate deity Kapila, the expounder, the wearer of a waist-string;
the dwarf, the lover of the sword, he who dwells within the depths of the sword-fissure, and he who is as pure as the sky. || 85 ||

He whose abode is the horn of a bald man, who carries a skull-topped staff, who is difficult to approach, who is rich in virtues, who is profound, who dwells in the forest, and who is an ocean of the nectar of prose and verse. (86)
He who delights in prose-singing, the thundering one, the elder brother of the singing gods;
he who is devoted to secret conduct, the secret one, and he who is described as the arrival of the secret.
He whose intention is secret, who dwells in the ocean of the cave, who is accessible through the Guru and is the Guru of Gurus;
he who wears a garland of bells and small gongs, who is the water-pot and the jar, and whose belly is like a jar.
He is Caṇḍa, the friend of Caṇḍeśvara, the Lord Caṇḍeśa, and he of fierce valor.

The Lord of the moving and the unmoving, the wish-fulfilling gem, ever eager for the act of tasting; he who is the meter, whose body is the meter, the meter itself, and whose form as meter is difficult to perceive.
The source of the universe, the witness of the universe, the lord of the universe, and identical with the universe;
he is recitation, devoted to recitation, the object of recitation, and the Lord upon the lion-throne of the tongue.
It was filled with bees humming with the sound of "jhalajjhalla" from their joyful buzzing,
and its jeweled anklets resounded with the loud, ringing clatter of "ṭaṅkāra."
Situated within the sprouts of the two *ṭha*s, he is the sole bestower of perfection for all mantras;
he is Ḍiṇḍimuṇḍa, the lord of Ḍākinīs, the fierce one, and the lover of the ḍiṇḍima drum. || 93 ||
Delighted by the sound of the drum, the bull-mounted Vināyaka, Ḍhuṇḍhi, approaches. || 94 ||
He is the limit of the limits of the principles, defined as the state of reality;
he is situated within the other stars, the Savior, and the destroyer of the stars.
The Immovable One, beloved of the Immovable One, the Abider, the world of the stationary and the moving;
the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, the Giver, the deluder of the Dānavas. || 96 ||
Compassionate, possessing divine power, the wielder of the rod of punishment, the leader of the army;
he who shatters clouds with the luster of his tusks, the destroyer of the elephant-like Daityas. || 97 ||
He who has seized a multitude of elephants with his tusks, who takes the form of a divine elephant for the sake of the gods;
he is the lord of wealth and grain, the fortunate one, the giver of riches, and the upholder of the earth. (98)
He is the object of meditation, manifested solely through meditation, consisting of meditation, and devoted to meditation. || 99 ||
He is the source of joy, the beloved of joy, the primordial sound, established in the midst of sound;
he is partless, stainless, eternal, both eternal and non-eternal, and free from all ailment. || 100 ||
He is beyond the sky, the supreme abode, the Supreme Self, the highest state;
higher than the high, Paśupati, the liberator from the bonds of the individual souls (paśus). || 101 ||
He is the full bliss, the supreme bliss, the ancient Supreme Person;
his lotus-like eyes are serene, and he releases those who bow before him from ignorance.
He who transcends the cause of prostration; the remover of the suffering of those who bow down;
the one with fruit in his hand; the lord of serpents; the howler; the lover of molasses. 103.
He whose pair of feet is worshipped by Bāṇa; who delights in the playful sports of childhood;
whose feet are worshipped by Brahmā and Brahmā; who is a celibate student; and who is Bṛhaspati.
The greatest of the great, devoted to Brahman, a friend of those who know Brahman, dear to the knowers of Brahman;
possessing a vast resonance and the foremost of chants, he has the shell of the universe as his girdle.
Bharga, who bestows fortune with a mere glance of his eyebrows; Bhadra, the dispeller of fear;
the Blessed One, easily attained through devotion; the granter of prosperity, adorned with ashes. || 106 ||
He is the capable one, the abode of beings, the bestower of enjoyments, and he whose sphere of activity is between the eyebrows;
he is the minister, the lord of mantras, the counselor, and he who is as delightful as one intoxicated with passion.
Wearing a girdle, slow-moving, wise, with lotus-like eyes,
he possessed great strength, great heroism, great vital power, and a great mind.
He is the sacrifice, the lord of sacrifice, the protector of sacrifice, and the bestower of the fruit of sacrifice;
he is the maker of glory, attainable through yoga, the master of sacrifice, and beloved by the officiating priests. || 109 ||
He is the essence, the lover of essence, the one who is tasted, the delighter, and the one worshipped by Rāvaṇa;
he is the protector of the Rakṣasas, the womb of jewels, and the bestower of the happiness of sovereignty. || 110 ||
The bestower of the perceptible and the imperceptible, the one who is to be perceived, abiding in dissolution, fond of sweetmeat balls;
he who delights in bathing, devoted to the dance, the maker of gains, renowned throughout the world. || 111 ||
He is the most excellent, fire-faced, worthy of adoration, and the object of the Vedānta;
he is the transformer, with eyes on all sides, the ordainer, and with faces in every direction. || 112 ||
Vāmadeva, the leader of the universe, the wielder of the thunderbolt who wards off the thunderbolt;
the support that obstructs all bonds, the Lord of the Universe, the Sovereign. || 113 ||
He is the Brahman of Sound, attainable through tranquility; the Lord of the hosts of Śambhu’s powers;
the Teacher whose abode is the tip of the crest-lock; the Refuge, the Lord of the Mountain. || 114 ||
Wearing a garland of flowers from the six seasons, possessing the six supports, and consisting of six syllables;
he is the physician for cyclic existence, the omniscient one, and the medicine for all diseases. (115)
He who sports in the creation, maintenance, and dissolution [of the universe]; who pierces the elephants of the gods;
whose great frontal globes are crimsoned with vermilion; and who bestows the manifestation of both the existent and the non-existent. || 116 ||

The churner of the ocean with the witness as the churning-stick, he who is to be known by himself, whose sacrificial fee is his own self, independent, whose resolve is true, devoted to the singing of the Sāman hymns, and blissful. (117)

The swan, the lord of elephants and piśācas, the invocation, the consumer of oblations to gods and ancestors, the oblation dear to those who have sacrificed, joy, and he who dwells within the *hṛllekhā* mantra. (118)
Lord of the field, sustainer of the earth, devoted to supreme forbearance; the one who swiftly bestows well-being, the bliss of security, and the celestial tree for the world. || 119 ||
He is the bestower of the fruits of Dharma, the granter of desires, the increaser of good fortune;
he is the giver of knowledge, the giver of prosperity, and the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. || 120 ||
He who bestows beauty, the Hero, whose feet are auspicious, the giver of victory;
he who brings all under control, the remover of defects in the womb, and the bestower of sons and grandsons. || 121 ||
Bestower of intelligence, giver of fame, remover of sorrow, destroyer of misfortune;
remover of the grief of the illustrious, destroyer of misfortune, the bearer of all powers. 122.
It causes the mouths of opponents to become paralyzed, clarifies the joyful mind, pacifies the malevolent magic of others, and brings about the shattering of suffering. || 123 ||
A lava, truṭi, kalā, kāṣṭhā, nimeṣa, tatpara, and kṣaṇa;
then a ghaṭī, muhūrta, prahara, day and night (divānakta), and a full day-and-night (ahnar-niśam). || 124 ||
A fortnight, a month, a solstice, a year, a yuga, a kalpa, the great dissolution;
a zodiac sign, a star, a lunar day, a yoga, a weekday, a karaṇa, and a degree. || 125 ||
The Ascendant, the Hora, the Kālacakra, Meru, the Seven Sages, Dhruva, Rāhu, Saturn, Venus, Jupiter, Mercury, Mars, the Moon, and the Sun. (126)
The creation and maintenance of time, and the entire universe—both the stationary and the moving; earth, water, fire, wind, ether, ego-sense, primordial nature, and the individual soul. (127)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Rudra, Īśa, Śakti, and Sadāśiva;
the thirty gods, the ancestors, the Siddhas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Kinnaras. || 128 ||
The Sādhyas, Vidyādharas, spirits, humans, animals,
birds, oceans, rivers, and mountains— the source of all that has been, all that is to be, and all that exists.
Sāṅkhya, Pātañjala Yoga, the Purāṇas, Śruti, Smṛti, the Vedāṅgas, the conduct of the virtuous, Mīmāṃsā, and the extensive system of Nyāya; || 130 ||
Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, Gāndharva, poetry and drama, Vaikhānasa, Bhāgavata, Sāttvata, and Pāñcarātra. (131)
The Śaiva, Pāśupata, Kālamukha, and Bhairava scriptures; the Śākta, Vaināyaka, Saura, Jaina, and Ārhata compendiums. (132)
It is eternally manifest and unmanifest, conscious and unconscious;
it is bondage, liberation, happiness, enjoyment, non-yoga, truth, the subtle, and the great. (133)
Svasti, huṃphaṭ, svadhā, svāhā, śrauṣaṭ, vauṣaṭ, vaṣaṭ, namaḥ! Knowledge, realized wisdom, bliss, awakening, tranquility, and self-restraint—these are his. 134.
He is the support of the single syllable, devoted to the single syllable;
he possesses one-pointed intellect, he is the sole hero, and he assumes both singular and manifold forms.

He is of two forms, two-armed, and two-eyed; he is the elephant among men, the protector of the continents, the son of two mothers, two-faced, beyond dualities, and transcending the pairs of opposites. || 136 ||
He who has three abodes, who possesses three eyes, who is the triple age (tretā), and who bestows the fruits of the three aims of life;
whose nature consists of the three qualities (guṇas), who is the origin of the three worlds, who is the Lord of the three powers, and who is the three-eyed one. || 137 ||
He has four arms, four tusks, four natures, and four faces;
he consists of the fourfold means and is the refuge of the four castes and stages of life.
He who sets in motion the transformation of the fourfold activity of speech;
he who is pleased by the worship on the fourth lunar day; he who is born from the fourth lunar day. || 139 ||
He whose self consists of five syllables, who is fivefold in nature, who has five faces, and who performs the fivefold cosmic acts;
he who is the support of the five, who possesses five colors, and who is devoted to the five syllables. || 140 ||
He who is five palm trees high, who has five hands, who is permeated by the five *praṇavas*,
whose manifestation consists of the essence of the five *Brahmas*, and who is warded off by the five elephants.
He who delights in the five kinds of food, the one with five arrows, whose nature consists of the five Śivas;
whose seat is the six-cornered [triangle], whose abode is the six cakras, and who pierces the six knots. || 142 ||
He is the destroyer of the darkness of the six paths, the great lake of the six fingers, the six-faced one, the brother of the six-faced one, and he who is surrounded by the six powers. || 143 ||

He is the destroyer of the six classes of enemies, the shatterer of the fear of the six waves, far beyond the six systems of logic, devoted to the six duties, and the refuge of the six tastes. || 144 ||
He whose feet traverse the seven netherworlds, whose vast circle encompasses the seven continents, who is crowned by the seven worlds of sound, and who bestows the boons of the seven suns. || 145 ||

Bestowing the happiness of a kingdom with its seven constituents, adorned by the host of the seven sages, he is the treasury of the seven meters, the seven officiating priests, and the refuge of the seven musical notes. || 146 ||
The essence of the play of the seven oceans, served by the seven Mothers; he who brings joy and intoxication through the seven meters, the lord of the seven-meter sacrifices. (147)
He whose form is to be meditated upon as the eightfold form (Aṣṭamūrti), who is the cause of the eightfold primordial nature (Aṣṭaprakṛti),
who is the ground for the fruit of the eight-limbed yoga (Aṣṭāṅgayoga), and whose seat is the eight-petaled lotus.
He is the glorious one enriched by the eight powers, the bestower of the eight sovereign powers;
he possesses the glory of the eight sacred seats (pīṭhas) and secondary seats (upapīṭhas), and is surrounded by the eight Mothers. || 149 ||
He is served by the eight Bhairavas, worshipped by the eight Vasus, and assumes the eightfold form (aṣṭamūrti).
His form flashes with the eight wheels, and he is fond of the oblation of the eight substances.
He who occupies the throne of the nine Nāgas, who presides over the nine treasures, who is the support of the city of the nine gates, and whose abode is the nine gates. || 151 ||
He is worthy of praise by the nine Nārāyaṇas, served by the nine Durgās;
he is the great lord of the nine lords, adorned by the nine serpents.
His limbs are variegated with the nine gems, and he bears the nine Śaktis upon his head;
he consists of ten aspects, possesses ten arms, and is saluted by the lords of the ten directions. || 153 ||

He who consists of ten chapters, who possesses ten vital breaths, who is the restrainer of the ten sense organs, who is the great mantra of ten syllables, and whose body pervades the ten directions. || 154 ||
He is praised by the eleven Rudras and consists of eleven syllables;
he possesses twelve staff-like arms and his abode is at the end of the twelve.
He has the Viśvedevas, divided into thirteen classes, as his presiding deity;
he is the bestower of boons upon fourteen Indras and the lord of fourteen Manus. (156)
Rich in the fourteen and other sciences, he is the Lord of the fourteen worlds;
he is the fifteenth of the Sāmans, as pure as the moon of the fifteenth day.
He whose abode is the sixteen supports, whose matrix consists of the sixteen vowels, who dwells in the state beyond the sixteenth, and whose nature is the sixteen digits of the moon. || 158 ||
He is the seventeenth of the seventeen arts, possessing seventeen syllables;
he is the lord of the eighteen islands and the author of the eighteen Purāṇas. || 159 ||
The creation of the eighteen medicinal herbs is recorded as being of eighteen kinds;
he is skilled in the knowledge of the individual and collective aspects of the eighteen scripts.
The person is the twenty-first, possessing twenty-one sprout-like fingers;
he is the essence of the twenty-four principles (tattvas), known as the twenty-fifth puruṣa.
The lord of twenty-seven stars, the creator of twenty-seven yogas, the sovereign of thirty-two Bhairavas, and the great lake of thirty-four. || 162 ||
He is the source of the thirty-six principles, his body consists of the thirty-eight digits (kalās),
and he is unimpeded by the forty-nine classes of winds.
He is the array of fifty syllables, the embodiment of the fifty Rudras, the Lord of the fifty powers of Viṣṇu, and the abode of the fifty Mātṛkās. || 164 ||
He possesses a series of fifty-two forms, rests upon sixty-three syllables, is the determiner of sixty-four phonemes, and is the treasury of the sixty-four arts. || 165 ||
He is saluted by the host of Yoginīs who possess the sixty-four great siddhis;
he contemplates the sixty-eight great tīrthas, sacred fields, and Bhairavas. || 166 ||
The Lord consists of ninety-four mantras and exceeds [that] by ninety-six;
he is Śatānanda, Śatadhṛti, and he whose long eyes are like a hundred-petaled lotus. || 167 ||
Śatānīka, Śatamakhā, he whose excellent weapon has a hundred edges, whose abode is the thousand-petaled lotus, and who is adorned with a thousand hoods. || 168 ||
The Puruṣa with a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet;
he who is praised by a thousand names and who takes away the power of the thousand-eyed one. || 169 ||
Seated upon the throne provided by the king of serpents with ten thousand hoods,
he was attended by the hymns of a multitude of eighty-eight thousand great sages.
He is the support for the beloved of the lord of a hundred thousand; he consists of the mind of the lord of a hundred thousand;
he is pleased by four hundred thousand recitations; he is illuminated by four hundred thousand [recitations].
Abiding within the bodies of eighty-four million living beings,
he is resplendent like ten million suns and as pure as the rays of ten million moons.
He is the preeminent leader of seventy-five million Vināyakas,
his radiant limbs consecrated by seven crores of great mantras.
His feet are bowed to by the rows of thirty-three crores of gods;
he is indeed served by infinite deities and praised by infinite sages. (174)
"Of infinite names, of infinite glory, and the giver of infinite and boundless happiness"—thus has this thousand names of Vaināyaka been proclaimed. (175)
That man who recites this every day during the Brāhma-muhūrta has all happiness pertaining to this world and the next held within his hand. 176.
Longevity, health, sovereignty, virtue, heroism, strength, fame, intelligence, wisdom, fortitude, splendor, good fortune, and beauty. || 177 ||
Truthfulness, compassion, forbearance, tranquility, courtesy, virtuous conduct, self-restraint toward all beings, trustworthiness, and eloquence in speech; 178.
Assembly, scholarship, magnanimity, physical vigor, depth, spiritual luster, loftiness, lineage, character, majesty, heroism, and nobility. (179)
Through the single recitation of this, knowledge, discernment, faith, fortitude, superiority over all, and the increase of wealth and grain shall come to pass. (180)
Through the recitation of this [mantra], the fourfold subjugation of men arises:
[the subjugation] of a king, a king’s wife, a prince, and a minister. (181)
For one who recites this for the purpose of subjugation, that person becomes his servant;
it is the effortless means for accomplishing virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation. (182)
It removes the fear of *śākinīs*, *ḍākinīs*, *rākṣasas*, *yakṣas*, and diseases; it bestows the happiness of universal sovereignty and crushes all enemies. || 183 ||
It destroys all strife, causes the sprouting of burnt seeds, pacifies bad dreams, and gladdens the mind of an angry master. (184)
The accomplishment of the six rites, the eight great siddhis, and the knowledge of the three times; the pacification of the deeds of others and the crushing of enemy armies. || 185 ||
On the field of battle, this alone brings victory to all; it destroys the defect of barrenness and is the sole cause for the protection of the fetus. 186.
It is recited daily: "In whatever place this hymn to the Lord of the Gaṇas is [recited], in that region there shall be no famine, no calamities, and no misfortunes. (187)
Prosperity does not abandon that house where this hymn is recited;
[it wards off] consumption, leprosy, urinary disorders, hemorrhoids, fistula-in-ano, and cholera. (188)
It cures abdominal tumors, splenic enlargement, flatulence, diarrhea, and great abdominal distension;
it also cures cough, asthma, upward-moving wind (udāvarta), and colic arising from grief and other causes. (189)
Headache, vomiting, hiccup, scrofula, loss of appetite, and fever produced by wind, bile, phlegm, combinations of two, or all three humors; || 190 ||

Accidental diseases, irregular fevers, those that are cold or hot, those occurring every day (ekāhika) and so forth—these and others, whether mentioned or unmentioned, arise from the humors (doṣas) and other factors of disease. || 191 ||
By reciting this hymn even once, one quickly pacifies everything;
through a single reading, even women, Śūdras, and outcasts attain complete success. 192.
This mantra of the thousand names should be recited for the attainment of auspiciousness;
one who possesses desires, reciting this hymn of Mahāgaṇapati, [shall achieve their goal]. || 193 ||
Having enjoyed all earthly pleasures here according to his will,
he [travels] by means of delightful celestial aerial chariots that grant the fruits of one's desires.
Taking any form at will and moving according to his desire, he wanders here at will among the abodes of Candra, Indra, Bhāskara, Upendra, Brahmā, Rudra, and the others. (195)
Having enjoyed desired pleasures together with his beloved kinsmen,
he becomes an attendant of Gaṇeśa, dear to the Great Lord of the Gaṇas.
Filled with joy by Nandīśvara and others, he was gladdened by all the Gaṇas;
and by the grace of the two Śivas, he was cherished no differently than a son. || 197 ||

A devotee of Śiva whose desires are fulfilled, by virtue of a boon from Gaṇeśvara, is born again as one who remembers his past lives, is devoted to dharma, and becomes a sovereign ruler of the entire earth. (198)
But one who recites [the mantra] daily without desire, devoted with faith and intent upon Vighneśa, attains supreme perfection in yoga and remains established in knowledge and dispassion. || 199 ||
In that which is unceasingly arisen bliss, the state of supreme bliss, transcending the universe, the supreme beyond, free from returning again. || 200 ||
The man who offers oblations with these names, worships, and honors [the deity] shall delight, eternally blissful, merged in the abode of Vaināyaka.
Kings become submissive, enemies fall into servitude;
all mantras are perfected, and all accomplishments are easily attained by him. 202.
Even more dear to me than the root mantra is this hymn;
it was recited on the fourth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Nabhasya, on my birthday.
One should perform the worship and the libation (tarpaṇa) according to the rules with dūrvā grass and [the deities'] names;
specifically, one should offer oblations with the eight substances, endowed with devotion. || 204 ||
All his desires are accomplished here; of this there is no doubt.
This [mantra], when recited, read, caused to be read, heard, or taught, [yields these results]. || 205 ||
