It has been expounded, pondered, meditated upon, scrutinized, and rejoiced in;
it bestows universal sovereignty here and in the hereafter for all beings. || 206 ||
Even for one who wanders according to his own will, he by whom this praise is maintained is protected by crores upon crores of hosts born from Śiva. || 207 ||
One should worship the hymn written in a book, which has become a mantra;
therein, the most excellent Lakṣmīs are ever present. (208)

One does not obtain that fruit through all gifts without exception, nor through all vows, nor through all sacred fords, nor through all sacrifices, which is obtained immediately by the remembrance of the Thousand Names of Gaṇeśa.
That person who recites these thousand names every day when the sun is rising, or at midday, or in the evening— indeed, whether three times a day or continuously— [attains the supreme goal].

He shall become preeminent in sovereignty; he prevails through his speech, spreads high renown, destroys all obstacles, brings the entire world under his control, and flourishes for a very long time with sons and grandsons. || 210 ||
Possessing nothing, with a single-minded focus, disciplined and restricted in diet,
one should recite [the mantra] for four months, intent upon the worship of Gaṇeśa.
"Having utterly uprooted poverty, even that which has followed for seven lifetimes, one obtains great fortune; such is the command of the Supreme Lord. (212)
Longevity, a family free from disease and exceedingly pure, riches that grant relief from suffering, eternal and stainless fame, fresh splendor, and a truly auspicious beauty.
Virtuous sons, a wife esteemed for her virtues, whatever else is true and eternal—all this is in the hand of him who recites this hymn to Gaṇapati. || 213 ||
Oṃ, Gaṇañjaya, Gaṇapati, Heramba, Dharaṇīdhara, Mahāgaṇapati, Lakṣaprada, Kṣipraprasādana. || 214 ||

Amoghasiddhi is the immeasurable mantra, the wish-fulfilling gem, and the treasure-trove; he is the auspicious one, the seed-syllable, the fulfiller of hopes, the granter of boons, and the auspicious one. || 215 ||
Kāśyapa, Nandana, Vācasiddha, Ḍhuṇḍhi, and Vināyaka—by these twenty-one names, a man [is honored] here with these sweetmeats. (216)
He who praises me with his mind fixed on me and intent on my worship has, by that, praised me with the Thousand Names; of this there is no doubt. (217)
Homage, homage to you whose feet are worshipped by the best of gods; homage, homage to you whose self is incomparable auspiciousness!
Homage, homage to you who have achieved the one great power of vast hands; homage, homage to you whose face is as beautiful as a young elephant! 218.
May the one named Gaṇapati, whose feet resound with the tinkling of clusters of small bells, who has manifested a multitude of noble and great conducts,
and whose cheeks are touched by waves of rut-fluid, pacify all misfortune.
Thus ends the Śrī Gaṇeśa Sahasranāmastotra in its entirety.
Thus ends the Gaṇeśatantra.
Composed and compiled by the sovereign King Śrī Siṃha Bāhādura, the son of the illustrious Rājādeva and lord of the capital city of Śiva-Hara.
The sixteenth Sūryatantra, contained within the Śāktapramoda.
This has been edited by the learned Paṇḍita Śrī Raghurāja Dubejī, a descendant of the aforementioned royal preceptor.
Printed and published by Śrī Kṛṣṇadāsātmaja Khemarāja at his own Śrī Veṅkaṭeśvara Press.
Mumbai. Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. Now begins the Sūryatantra.

Now, the meditation on Śrī Sūrya: He whose crown is enriched with radiant jewels, whose beautiful hair is colored by the luster of his shimmering lips, who is resplendent with divine majesty, golden-hued, and endowed with rays of light, holds a lotus in his hand.

May He who provides space for the entire universe, who shines upon the mountain of sunrise accompanied by the planets, who bestows all bliss, and who is saluted by Hari and Hara—may that All-Seeing One protect me. 1.
Now, the extraction of the yantra: First, there is an eight-petalled lotus established with the Praṇava (Oṃ) and other syllables;
one should extract the yantra by placing the Māyā-bīja at the tip of each of the eight petals.
One should assign Āditya, Bhāskara, Bhānu, Ravi, Sūrya, Divākara, Mārtaṇḍa, and Tapana to the eight petals.
Dīptā, Sūkṣmā, Jayā, Bhadrā, Vibhūti, Vimalā, as well as Amoghā and Vidyutā— Śrī, facing in all directions, is in the center.
Now follows the extraction of the mantra:
Tāra (Oṃ), Ghṛṇi, Bhṛgu, followed by [the letter] adorned with the left ear (ū),
seated on fire (Ra), the remainder of Marut (Sa), with the eye (I), and finally Aditi (Ā).
The eight-syllabled mantra is declared to be the supreme favorite of the Sun.
Now the mantra: Oṃ Ghṛṇi Sūrya Āditya.
Now the procedure for worship.

Having performed the morning rites beginning with the preliminary duties and ending with *prāṇāyāma*, one should perform the *pīṭhanyāsa*. Regarding that, there is this specific procedure: having placed [the mantras] *prabhūta*, *vimala*, *sāra*, *samārādhya*, and *parasukha* in the directions starting from the east of the heart and in its center, one should then place the *ādhāraśakti* and the others.

One should perform the placement [of mantras] ending with: *oṃ asūryamaṇḍalāya daśakalātmane namaḥ*. Likewise, it is stated in the Nibandha: "Once the seat (pīṭha) has been prepared, one should first worship [the deities] in the cardinal directions and in the center. Immediately thereafter, one should worship Prabhūta, Vimala, Sāra, and Paramādisukha-pīṭha."
One should visualize [the deity] ending with one's own reflection. Then, upon the filaments and in the center: "Rāṃ, obeisance to Dīptā."
Thus: *rīṃ* to Sūkṣmā; *rūṃ* to Jayā; *raiṃ* to Bhadrā; *vaiṃ* to Vibhūti; *voṃ* to Vimalā; *vauṃ* to Amoghā; *raṃ* to Vidyutā; *raḥ* to Sarvatomukhī.
And so it is stated in the Nibandha: "Dīptā, Sūkṣmā, Jayā, Bhadrā, Vibhūti, and again Vimalā."
The seat-powers (pīṭhaśaktayaḥ) are the unfailing lightning that faces in all directions.
The wise know that the seed-syllables are to be deposited in sequence, having the form of the flame of a blazing lamp.

[One should write] the three vowels *a*, *li*, and *u* (forming *alī*), followed by *bha*, *ra*, and *sva* (forming *bharsva*), joined with the *bindu* and the fire (*ra*) and the bed (*sa*) [to form *hrīṃ*]. Above that, one should say:

*oṃ tadupari brahmaviṣṇuśivātmakāya saurāya yogapīṭhāya namaḥ*. And likewise in the Śāradā: "One should utter the word ending in the dative case, consisting of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, [as] *saurāya*."

"Salutation to the Yoga-pīṭha"—this is the mantra of the Sun, the Lord of the World, which is declared immediately following the [main] mantra. Then follows the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the seers and other elements: "Salutation to the seer Devabhāga on the head"; "Salutation to the Gāyatrī metre on the mouth"; "Salutation to the deity Āditya on the heart. And so it is stated in the Nibandha:

The sage is declared to be Devabhaga; the meter is said to be Gāyatrī; the deity is declared to be Āditya, who bestows both seen and unseen fruits. Then follow the ritual placements (nyāsa) on the hands and limbs: "To Satya, the jewel of blazing splendor, huṃ phaṭ svāhā—salutation to the two thumbs. Likewise: "To Brahmā, the jewel of blazing splendor... [and so forth].
To the two index fingers, svāhā! To Viṣṇu, te0! To the two middle fingers, vaṣaṭ!
To Rudra, you—ten [times] with the two ring fingers; *hum*. To Agni, you—ten [times] with the two little fingers; *vauṣaṭ*.

To Sarva, [the weapon-mantra] *phaṭ* with both palms and backs of the hands. Thus for the heart and the other limbs. And so it is stated in the Śāradā-tantra: "The heart is declared for Satya; the head is said for Brahmā; the crest (śikhā) belongs to Viṣṇu;
the armor (varman) is proclaimed for Rudra; the eye is named for Agni."
This is declared to be the weapon-mantra for all [deities]. "Tejojvālāmaṇe hūṃ phaṭ," ending with two *ṭhā*s (svāhā), is thus proclaimed.

p. 534) Then follows the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the forms (*mūrttinyāsa*). As follows: *Oṃ śirasi ādityāya namaḥ* (Oṃ, salutation to Āditya on the head); likewise, *e mukhe aravaye* (e, to Arava on the mouth), *u hṛdaye bhānave* (u, to Bhānu on the heart), *i guhye bhāskarāya* (i, to Bhāskara on the secret place), and *a caraṇayoḥ sūryāya* (a, to Sūrya on the two feet).
And likewise in the Nibandha: "One should place Āditya on the head, and one should place Ravi in the mouth."
One should place the heart-mantra named Bhānu upon the sun at the secret place.
Having placed the Sun upon the two feet with the five syllables beginning with *satya*, the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) follows:

*oṃ namaḥ* on the head; *oṃ ghrīṃ namaḥ* on the face; *oṃ ṇīṃ namaḥ* on the throat; *oṃ sūṃ namaḥ* on the heart; *oṃ ryyaṃ namaḥ* on the belly; *oṃ āṃ namaḥ* on the navel; *oṃ diṃ namaḥ* on the genitals; *oṃ tyaṃ namaḥ* on the two feet.
And likewise: Oṃ [is placed] upon the head, face, throat, heart, belly, navel, penis, and feet.
One should place the eight syllables of the mantra, each preceded by the Praṇava (Om). Then follows the meditation:
[the deity] whose hands grant the pair of red lotuses and the gesture of fearlessness, and who is adorned with armlets, necklaces, bracelets, and earrings.
I praise the Lord of Men, who wears a crown of rubies, whose splendor is like that of the Bandhūka flower, and whose three eyes shine with brilliance.
Having meditated thus and performed worship with mental offerings, one should perform the installation of the water-pot (*kumbha*).

Then, having performed the worship of the lineage of gurus (*gurupaṅkti*), one should perform the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭha*). Having conceived the form (*mūrti*) by means of the mantra "Oṃ Khaṃ, obeisance to Khakholka," [one should proceed].

Having meditated again and performed the rites from the invocation (āvāhana) up to the offering of five handfuls of flowers (pañcapuṣpāñjali), one should begin the worship of the enclosures (āvaraṇapūjā). And so it is stated in the Nibandha:

The visualization of the form is performed with the mantra *tārādikhaṃkhakholkāya*. Having invoked the Witness of all worlds (*sākṣin*) into that [form], one should worship him. In the filaments [of the lotus], in the corners starting from the southeast, in the center, and in the cardinal directions, [one worships] Satya, Tejas, Jvālāmaṇi, and Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā; likewise, *Hṛdayāya Namaḥ* [is recited]. Thus.

To Brahmā, ten [times], svāhā to the head. To Viṣṇu, ten [times], vaṣaṭ to the tuft of hair (śikhā). To Rudra, ten [times], huṃ to the armor (kavaca). To Agni, ten [times], vauṣaṭ to the three eyes. To Sarva, ten [times], phaṭ to the weapon (astra). In the directions and intermediate points, starting from the east: Oṃ, obeisance to Āditya; likewise to Aravī, to Bhānu.

*Īm* to Bhāskara; on the intermediate petals, starting from the southeast (*agni*) and so forth: *Ū* to Uṣā, likewise *Praṃ* to Prajñā, *Paṃ* to Prabhā, and *Saḥ* to Sandhyā. And thus it is said: "One should first worship the limbs (*aṅga*), then the forms of the Sun (*sūryamūrti*) on the cardinal petals, and the four powers (*śakti*) beginning with Ādityā, who reside on the corner petals."

The seed-syllables (*bīja*) of these [goddesses] are, in order, the initial letters of their respective names. Uṣā, Prajñā, Prabhā, and Sandhyā are proclaimed as the Śaktis. Then, on the petals, one should worship Brāhmī and the others, and in front, one should worship Aruṇa. And so it is stated in the *Śāradā*: "Situated at the tips of the petals..."

One should worship Brahmā and the others first, and then worship Aruṇa. Outside of that, one should worship the Moon and the others starting from the east: *Oṃ candrāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ maṅgalāya namaḥ*, and likewise for Budha, Bṛhaspati, Śukra, Śanaiścara, Rāhu, and Ketu.

And so it is stated in the *Śāradā*: "Having worshipped Candra and the others, as well as Vajra and the others, one should complete the ritual from the offering of incense (*dhūpa*) until the final dismissal (*visarjana*). The preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) for this consists of eight hundred thousand recitations (*japa*). And likewise: "One should recite the mantra eight hundred thousand times with clarified butter (*ājya*)."
Or, with self-controlled senses, one should offer oblations of sesame seeds sprinkled with honey, numbering ten parts. Thus is the worship.
Then Vasiṣṭha spoke a hymn of praise;
thereupon Sāmba, his body emaciated by the continuous practice of dharma, began to offer praise.
O King, [I praise] the thousand-rayed maker of day by means of a thousand names.
Then, seeing that son of Kṛṣṇa still present, Sūrya appeared to him in a dream and spoke these words again:
The illustrious Sūrya said:
"O Sāmba, Sāmba, O mighty-armed son of Jāmbavatī! Listen;
recite this auspicious hymn consisting of a thousand names."
I shall proclaim to you those names which are secret, purifying, and auspicious; having heard them, my child, attend closely.
Vikartana, Vivasvat, Mārtaṇḍa, Bhāskara, Ravi,
the Illuminator of the World, the Glorious One, the Eye of the World, and the Lord of the Planets.
The witness of the world, the lord of the three worlds, the creator and the destroyer, the dispeller of darkness;
the sun, the ascetic, the pure one, whose vehicle is drawn by seven horses.
Gabhastihasta and Brahmā, who is saluted by all the gods—
this hymn of twenty-one verses is always dear to me.
It bestows prosperity and health, increases wealth, and brings about fame;
it is known as the King of Hymns (Stavarāja), renowned throughout the three worlds.
O mighty-armed one, he who, having become humble, praises me with this at both twilights— at sunrise and at sunset— is liberated from all sins.
Whatever misdeed has been committed through body, speech, or mind—all that is destroyed by this recitation; of this there is no doubt.
This is the recitation, the fire-oblation, and the twilight worship;
likewise, the mantra for the bali offering, the mantra for the water-offering (arghya), and the mantra for incense.
When this auspicious great mantra— which removes all sins— is honored during the offering of food, bathing, prostration, or circumambulation, [it bestows its fruit].
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One Bhāskara, the Lord of the World,
took leave of Kṛṣṇa’s son and vanished right there.
Sāmbo also, having praised the seven-horsed charioteer with this king of hymns,
became purified in soul, free from disease, and glorious, being liberated from that affliction.
Thus ends the hymn to the Sun in the Sāmbapurāṇa.
Then the illustrious Sūrya spoke this armor:
"O Sāmba, O Sāmba, O mighty-armed one, listen to my auspicious armor."
The most wonderful armor named Trailokyamaṅgala.
Knowing which, the knower of mantras certainly attains the perfect fruit;
and by wearing which, Mahādeva became the lord of the Gaṇas.
Through recitation and retention, Viṣṇu is always the protector of all;
likewise, Indra and all the others shall attain every sovereignty.
The seer of the armor-mantra (kavaca) is Brahmā; its meter is declared to be Anuṣṭubh;
and the deity here is the glorious Sun, who is saluted by all the gods.
The application [of these mantras] is proclaimed for the sake of health, fame, and liberation.
May the Praṇava protect my head; may the syllable Ghṛṇi protect my forehead.
May Sūrya protect the pair of eyes, and Āditya the pair of ears;
may the eight-syllabled great mantra grant the fruit of all desired objects.
May the seed-syllable *hrīṃ* protect my mouth, and Bhuvaneśvarī protect my heart; may the moon-seed-syllable (*oṃ*) enriched with the visarga protect my private region.
This is the imperishable great mantra, hidden within all tantras;
it is Śiva conjoined with fire and adorned with the left eye and the bindu.
The single-syllable great mantra of the glorious Sun is proclaimed;
this mantra, more secret than the secret, is remembered as the wish-fulfilling gem of desires.
"May the supreme Manu protect [me] always from the head down to the feet.
Thus has been told to you that which is difficult to obtain even in the three divine worlds.
It bestows prosperity and beauty, grants peace eternally, increases wealth and health,
pacifies diseases such as leprosy, and destroys even the most formidable maladies.
Whoever recites this daily at the three junctions of the day shall become free from disease and endowed with strength.
What more need be said here? Whatever resides in one's mind [shall be attained].
p. 537) All these indeed come to pass through the wearing of this armor:
[the harm caused by] bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and rākṣasas.
Brahma-rākṣasas and vetālas are not even capable of looking [at him];
they flee from afar at the mere mention of his name.
Having inscribed it upon birch bark with yellow pigment, agallochum, and saffron, especially on a Sunday, at the sun's passage into a new sign (saṅkrānti), or on the seventh lunar day;
The best of practitioners should wear it; he shall become a conqueror of the three worlds.
Having placed it within three metals, he should wear it on his right arm.
Whether on the crest-lock or on the throat, he too is undoubtedly the Sun;
thus, O Samba, has been told to you that which is named the Auspiciousness of the Three Worlds.
This armor, difficult to obtain in the world, has been revealed out of affection for you.
Without knowing this divine armor, whoever should mutter the supreme Sūrya-mantra, [shall fail].
Success does not arise for him even in hundreds of millions of eons.
Thus ends the Śrī Sūrya-kavaca, named Trailokyamaṅgala, from the Brahmayāmala.
Then, his heart weary from the battle and remaining in the fray with anxious thought,
he beheld Rāvaṇa standing before him, having arrived for combat. || 1 ||
Then the venerable Agastya, having arrived together with the gods to witness the battle,
approached Rāma and spoke.
"O Rāma, Rāma, O mighty-armed one, hear this eternal secret by which, my child, you shall conquer all your enemies in battle. (3)
The *Ādityahṛdaya* is meritorious, the destroyer of all enemies;
by reciting it constantly, one attains victory, imperishability, and supreme auspiciousness.
It is the most auspicious of all auspicious things, the destroyer of all sins,
the pacifier of anxiety and grief, and the supreme increaser of longevity.
Worship Vivasvat, the radiant Bhāskara, the Lord of the World, who rises with his rays and is honored by gods and asuras alike.
For he is the essence of all the gods, radiant and the source of rays;
he protects the worlds, including the hosts of gods and asuras, with his beams of light.
He is indeed Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Skanda, Prajāpati,
Mahendra, Kubera, Kāla, Yama, Soma, and the Lord of Waters.
The Pitṛs, the Vasus, the Sādhyas, the two Aśvins, the Maruts, Manu, Vāyu, Agni, the progeny, Prāṇa, the performer of the seasons, and the maker of light. || 9 ||
Āditya, Savitṛ, Sūrya, Khaga, Pūṣan, Gabhastimān, Suvarṇasadṛśa, Bhānu, Hiraṇyaretas, and Divākara. || 10 ||
He who has bay horses, who possesses a thousand rays, whose chariot is drawn by seven horses, who is radiant with light;
he who is the destroyer of darkness, the source of well-being, the fashioner, the sun, and the possessor of beams. (11)
Hiraṇyagarbha, Śiśira, Tapana, Ahaskara, Ravi, Agnigarbha, Aditeḥputra, Śaṅkha, and Śiśiranāśana. (12)
Lord of the sky, destroyer of darkness, one who has reached the further shore of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas;
a rain of wealth, a friend of the waters, the path through the Vindhya mountains, and a leaping monkey. 13.
Ātapī, Maṇḍalī, Mṛtyu, Piṅgala, Sarvatāpana, Kavi, Viśva, Mahātejā, Rakta, and Sarvabhavodbhava. || 14 ||
O Creator of the universe, lord of the constellations, planets, and stars; O radiant one among all luminaries, twelve-fold self, homage be to you! 15.
Salutations to the eastern mountain and salutations to the western mountain;
salutations to the Lord of the hosts of luminaries, the Sovereign of the Day.
Salutations again and again to Jayāya, to Jaya, to Bhadrāya, and to Haryaśva;
salutations again and again to Sahasrāṃśu, to Āditya, salutations again and again. || 17 ||
Salutations to the fierce one, to the hero, salutations again and again to the Sāraṅga;
salutations to the awakener of the lotus, let there be salutations to you, the Pracaṇḍa.

Salutation to the Lord of Brahmā, the Lord of Īśāna, and the Lord of Acyuta; to the Hero, to him whose splendor is like the sun, to the Radiant One, to the All-devourer, and to the one of terrible form. || 19 ||
Salutation to the slayer of Namuci, the slayer of cold, the slayer of enemies, the immeasurable Self;
salutation to the God who destroys the ungrateful, the Lord of lights. || 20 ||
Salutations to Hari, the architect of the universe, who has the luster of molten gold;
salutations to the light that destroys darkness, the witness of the world.
This Lord indeed destroys and creates that very same world;
he purifies, he heats, and he rains by means of his rays.
He remains awake while all beings sleep; he is established within them all. He is both the Agnihotra sacrifice itself and the fruit of those who perform the Agnihotra.
The gods, the sacrifices, and the very fruits of those sacrifices—all the rites that exist in all the worlds—the Supreme Lord [is the source]. (24)
O Raghava, by chanting this in times of calamity, in hardships, in wildernesses, and in fears, no man ever comes to grief.
Worship this God of gods, the Lord of the world, with one-pointed concentration;
having recited this three times, you shall be victorious in battles. (26)
"O mighty-armed one, at this very moment you shall conquer Rāvaṇa.
Having spoken thus, Agastya then departed just as he had come.
Having heard this, the highly resplendent Rāghava, his grief then vanished, became well-pleased and, with a disciplined mind, held [the bow] fast.
Having looked at the sun and muttered this supreme mantra, he attained great joy;
then, having sipped water three times and become pure, the valiant one took up his bow.
Seeing Rāvaṇa approaching for the sake of victory with a joyful heart,
he became intent upon his slaughter with great and total effort.

Then Ravi, having gazed upon Rāma with a joyful mind and being greatly delighted, knowing that the destruction of the lord of the night-rangers was at hand, spoke these words while standing in the midst of the hosts of gods: "Hasten! (31)
Thus ends the Ādityahṛdaya Stotra in the glorious Rāmāyaṇa of Vālmīki.
Now, let the hymn "vibhrāḍ bṛhat" drink the Soma-mead; may it bestow unimpaired life upon the lord of the sacrifice.
He who, impelled by the wind, protects by his own self, has nourished all creatures and shines forth in many ways. (1)
The rays bear up that god Sūrya, the knower of all beings, so that everyone may behold him. 2.
With that purifying eye wherewith you, O Varuṇa, look upon the people as they stir about, [behold us]. 3.
O two divine Adhvaryu priests, come on your chariot with sun-bright skin;
anoint the sacrifice with honeyed mead. 4.
As of old, as before, as all along, and even so now, O you who sit upon the sacrificial grass, bestow the highest preeminence;
[bestow] the light-finding, the one who turns toward us, the roaring one, the swift winner, whom you strengthen in those [battles].
The unborn one impels the spotted-wombed ones, whose womb is light, in the measurement of the mid-air.
At the meeting of the waters and the sun, the wise lick him with their prayers like a young child. 6.
Wondrous is the vanguard of the gods; it has risen as the eye of Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni.
It has filled the heaven, the earth, and the mid-air. Sūrya is the soul of all that moves and stands still. 7.
May the all-encompassing god Savitṛ come to our sacrifice with nourishing gifts and fair praise.
And so that you, O youths, may exhilarate us, let every living world turn its mind toward us at the time of the pressing.
O Vṛtra-slayer, O Sūrya, whatever has risen today toward us—
All that, O Indra, is under your control. You are the one who carries us across, visible to all, the light-maker, O Sūrya.
You illuminate the entire radiant realm. || 10 ||
That divinity of the sun, its greatness, has gathered together what was spread out in the midst of creation.
When he has departed from his green dwelling, Night spreads her garment over all.
In the lap of heaven, Sūrya assumes the form of Mitra and Varuṇa for all to behold;
one part of his radiant power is endless, while the other is dark—the bay steeds bring them both together. 12.
Truly, O Sūrya, you are great; truly, O Āditya, you are great. The greatness of you who exist as the Great One is celebrated;
indeed, O God, you are great. Truly, O Sūrya, you are great in glory;
truly, O God, you are great. By your greatness, you are the divine Asura, the high priest of the gods, all-pervading.
The light that is invincible. || 14 ||
Turning toward him as if toward the sun, may all partake of Indra's bounty.
O you who are born and being born with vigor, bestow riches upon us as our portion. 15.
O gods, being praised today at the rising of the sun, deliver us from distress and from blame.
May Mitra, Varuṇa, Aditi, Sindhu, Earth, and Heaven grant us this. 16.
Turning through the dark space, establishing both the immortal and the mortal, the god Savitṛ comes on his golden chariot, beholding all beings. 17.
Thus it is well said.
Then Dhaumya, who possesses a hundred names, said: "You are Sūrya, Aryaman, Bhaga, Tvaṣṭṛ, Pūṣan, Arka, Savitṛ, and Ravi."
The Sun, the Unborn, Time, Death, the Ordainer, and the Maker of Light. || 1 ||
Earth, water, fire, ether, and wind are his ultimate refuge;
as are Soma, Bṛhaspati, Śukra, Budha, and Aṅgāraka. || 2 ||
Indra, Vivasvat, Dīptāṃśu, Śuci, Śauri, Śanaiścara; Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Skanda, Varuṇa, and Yama. || 3 ||
He is the fire of lightning and the digestive fire within the stomach; he is the lord of all luminous energies.
He is the banner of righteousness, the author of the Vedas, the embodiment of the Vedāṅgas, and the vehicle of the Vedas.
The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali ages—the latter being the locus of all impurities—as well as the divisions of time:
the kalā, kāṣṭhā, muhūrta, night, yāma, and likewise the kṣaṇa. (5)
The Ashvattha tree that bears the year, the wheel of time, the radiant one;
the eternal person, the yogi, both manifest and unmanifest, the ancient one. (6)
The overseer of time, the overseer of creatures, the architect of the universe, the dispeller of darkness;
Varuṇa, the ocean, the sun’s ray, the cloud, the giver of life, and the slayer of enemies.
He is the refuge of all beings, the Lord of beings, honored by all the worlds;
he is the creator, the destroyer, the fire, the origin of all, and free from greed.
Ananta, Kapila, Bhānu, Kāmada, Sarvatomukha, Jaya, Viśāla, Varada, and he who is served by all the elements. || 9 ||

He is the mind, the one with beautiful wings, the source of all beings, the swift-moving, the sustainer of life, Dhanvantari, the one whose banner is smoke-colored, the primordial god, and the son of Aditi.
The twelve-fold one, the lotus-eyed, the grandfather, the mother, and the great-grandfather;
he is the door to progeny, the door to creation, the door to liberation, and the triple heaven.
The burner, the one of tranquil soul, the soul of the universe, facing in all directions;
the soul of the moving and the unmoving, the subtle soul, Maitreya, endowed with compassion. 12.
This indeed is the hymn of one hundred and eight names of the Sun, of immeasurable splendor, which was proclaimed by the Self-born One.

I bow down for my own welfare to the Sun-god, who is served by the hosts of gods, the ancestors, and the yakṣas; who is venerated by asuras, night-stalkers, and siddhas; and who possesses the radiance of excellent gold and fire. 14.
He who, being well-composed, recites this at sunrise, shall obtain sons, wife, and accumulations of wealth and jewels;
furthermore, that man always attains the memory of his past lives, as well as steadfastness and intelligence. (15)

The man who, with a pure mind and concentrated attention, recites this hymn of praise to the best of gods, is liberated from the ocean of the forest-fire of sorrow and shall obtain the desires he wishes for in his heart. (16)
Thus ends the hymn of one hundred and eight names of the glorious Sun, from the dialogue between Dhaumya and Yudhiṣṭhira in the Vanaparvan of the glorious Mahābhārata.
Then, on the seventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha, O descendant of Kuru, Sumantu spoke the Thousand Names.
O King, fasting from food, one should worship the Sun with devotion according to the prescribed rite.
O King, standing before the deity with a mind that is pure, one-pointed, and with anger conquered and the senses subdued, one should perform the recitation as previously described.
Śatānīka said:
O observer of noble vows, tell me by which mantra, when recited, or by which hymn the Blessed Sun may come into my sight? (3)
Sumantu said: When I, full of devotion, had praised him with the Thousand Names,
the divine Sun himself appeared before my eyes.
Śatānīka said:
O twice-born one, I desire to hear from you the thousand names of Savitṛ,
by which the god Divākara himself appeared before your very eyes.
Sumantu said: It is the most auspicious of all auspicious things and the destroyer of all sins;
if there is no fear whatsoever, it is pacified by performing the sacrifice.
O King, when this hymn is recited, a person is liberated from fever;
other diseases as well are pacified for one who recites it or listens to it.
All enjoyments, exactly as desired and according to one's wish,
are attained by that man who, having heard this from the beginning, enters into battle.
Having conquered his enemies in battle, he returns home unhurt;
it is the birth of a son for the barren and the destruction of fear for the terrified.
It is a true benefactor for the poor and a supreme medicine for those afflicted by leprosy;
it wards off all planetary influences and malevolent spirits for children.
O King, whoever indeed recites this shall attain the highest welfare;
with all his desires fulfilled, he enjoys ultimate happiness.

This should be studied by those seeking the Dharma for the sake of attaining the Dharma and for happiness, by those seeking happiness, and by those desiring sovereignty for the sake of sovereignty. (12)
May they carry the knowledge of the Brahmins; may they bring victory to the Kṣatriyas;
may they carry livestock for the Vaiśyas; and may they increase the dharma of the Śūdras. (13)
There is no doubt that this occurs for those who read or hear it;
listen to that, O best of kings, for with a disciplined mind I shall speak to you. (14)
The Thousand Names of the Radiant God of Gods.

Oṃ. For this *Śrīsūryasahasranāman*, the venerable Parāśara is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the *anuṣṭubh* is the meter (*chandas*), and the venerable Sūrya is the deity (*devatā*). Its application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of attaining all desired goals during the recitation (*japa*).
Oṃ! He who knows all, the conqueror of all, the maker of all, the soul of all, whose face is turned in every direction;
the Lord of all, the source of all, whose self is restrained, and who has conquered his senses. (1)
He who has time as his support, the maker of time, the destroyer of time, the annihilator of time;
the great yogi, the one of great intellect, the great-souled one, and the one of very great strength. || 2 ||
The Lord, the all-pervading, the master of beings, the self of beings, the sovereign of the world;
he who exists in the past and the future, whose self is realized, the end of beings, the inner organ of beings—Śiva.
The refuge, the delight of Kamalā, the son, the increaser of joy, the most excellent, the giver of boons, the yogi, the one well-endowed with power, and the illuminator. || 4 ||
He is the primordial vital breath, the supreme life-force, the one whose soul is delighted, the beloved of the dear;
he is the leader, the thousand-footed, the virtuous one, adorned with divine earrings.

He who possesses unimpaired limbs, whose soul is steadfast, who is possessed of great wisdom, whose vehicle is the wind, whose mind is composed, the Ordainer, the Disposer, and he for whom auspicious rites have been performed.
Kapardin, the creator of the Kalpas, Rudra, the benevolent one who loves righteousness,
the one endowed with all attributes, the liberated soul, the perfected self, the accomplished one, the supreme.
He is of inconceivable form, the most excellent, the great yogin, the Great Lord;
he is the beloved, the source of desire and other qualities, the Sun, self-restrained, and undisturbed.
Kāma, the compassionate creator, the awakener of Kamalākara, the seven-horsed sun, the inconceivable self, the supreme among the greatly compassionate. || 9 ||
The one who brings back to life, the lord of life, the life of the world, the master of the world;
the unconquered, the abode of the universe, the indivisible one, whose banner bears the bull.

Vṛṣākapi, the creator of the eons, the sun that brings about the end of the eons, he whose chariot has a single wheel, the silent one, the possessor of a divine chariot, the foremost among charioteers. || 11 ||
He is free from anger, garlanded with rays, a mass of splendor, and the consumer of oblations;
he is the performer of divine acts, the maker of day, the god, the God of gods, and the Lord of the Day.
Lord of the distressed, the offerer of oblations, he of divine arms, the maker of day;
the sacrifice, the lord of sacrifice, Pūṣan, he whose seed is gold, the supreme bearer. || 13 ||
The knower of the higher and the lower, the sun, garlanded with rays, the captivating one;
the wise one, the lord of creatures, the sun, the progenitor, Viṣṇu, the radiant one. (14)
Sadāgati, Gandhabāhu, Vihita, Vidhi, Āśuga, Pataṅga, Pataga, Sthāṇu, Vihaṅga, Vihaga, and Vara. || 15 ||
Haryaśva, Haritāśva, Haridaśva, the beloved of the world, Tryambaka, Sarvadamana, Bhāvitātman, and the best of physicians. || 16 ||
The creator of light, the Lord of the World, honored by the world and its inhabitants;
he is Time, the fire at the end of the aeon, the burner, the one who causes intense heat. (17)
Virocana, Virūpākṣa, Sahasrākṣa, Purandara, the thousand-rayed Mihira, adorned with various garments and ornaments. (18)
Khaga, Pratardana, Dhanya, Hayaga, Vāgviśārada, Śrīmān, Śiśira, Vāggmī, Śrīpati, and Śrīniketana. || 19 ||
Śrīkaṇṭha, Śrīdhara, the illustrious Śrīmān, the abode of Śrī, the bestower of wealth;
he who moves at will, the great illusionist, the Great Lord whose intentions are known. || 20 ||

He is the performer of sacred rites, possessed of good conduct, all-pervading, affectionate toward his devotees, fame itself, the maker of renown, eternal, wearing earrings, clad in armor, and mounted on a chariot.
Hiraṇyaretas, Saptāśva, Prayatātman, Parantapa, Buddhimān, Amaraśreṣṭha, Rociṣṇu, and Pākaśāsana. || 22 ||
The ocean, the giver of wealth, the sustainer, Māndhātṛ, the remover of dejection;
the destroyer of darkness, the dispeller of gloom, the fire, the invoker, the inner organ, and Guha. || 23 ||
The Lord of Beings, possessed of cattle, endowed with supreme bliss, the most excellent among the illustrious, eternally risen, eternally charioted, the Lord of Gods, worshipped by the gods. || 24 ||
The unconquered, the victorious, the conqueror, consisting of both the moving and the stationary;
the bliss of life, the ever-moving, the subduer, and the bestower of victory. || 25 ||
Parjanya, Agnisthiti, Stheya, Sthavira, Aṇu, Nirañjana, Pradyotana, Rathārūḍha, and Sarvalokaprakāśaka. || 26 ||
He is the eternal, the sacrificial post, the one of great heroism, the swan who delivers one from saṃsāra;
he is the creator of the universe, the cause of action, the sun, and the lord of the Maruts. || 27 ||

Accompanied by the Maruts, the burner, Tvaṣṭṛ, Bhaga, the possessor of fortune, Aryaman, the lord, Varuṇa, Aṃśa, the Lord of the World, one who has accomplished all that was to be done, and the one with beautiful eyes. || 28 ||

Vivasvān, Bhānumān, the storehouse of splendor consisting of cause and effect, he who moves without attachment, Tigmāṃśu, the source of dharma and other virtues, and the one whose rays are radiant light. || 29 ||
He is the thousand-rayed, the ruddy one, the thousand-beamed, the maker of day;
he possesses rays and beams, he is adorned with garlands, the possessor of incomparable splendor.
Bhāskara, who knows the work of the gods, the omniscient one with piercing rays, the eldest of the gods, the lord of the gods, the knower of much, and the master of speech. || 31 ||
He is a treasury of splendor, possessed of vast brilliance, of great fame, and the teacher Bṛhaspati;
he is free from heat, powerful, wise, liberated, and the increaser of glory.
The great physician, Gaṇapati, Gaṇeśa, the leader of the hosts;
he of intense majesty, the scorcher, the burner, the one who torments the universe. (33)
Kārttasvara, Hṛṣīkeśa, Padmānanda, Abhinandita, Padmanābha, Amṛtāhāra, Sthitimān, Ketumān, and Nabha. || 34 ||
He is without beginning or end, the imperishable, the universe itself, the friend of all, the compassionate, the sovereign ruler;
he is the one from whom weapons are cast off, the wearer of armor, the eloquent speaker, the one clad in a mantle, and the creator of the universe.
He is the supreme one whose course is signless, the refuge for all, facing every direction;
he plunges forward, is endowed with a thousand rays, and is perfectly concentrated.

He whose banner is Dharma, who delights in Dharma, the destroyer, self-restraint personified, the restrainer, the remover of the suffering of those who bow before him, the speaker, he for whom all tasks are accomplished, and the Lord of Men.

He who traverses the sky, whose truth is established, who is free from darkness, and who is most enchanting; he who captivates, who is Hari, who is Hara, who is the wind, who is the season, and who possesses the splendor of the fire of time.
He who is to be served by the mouth, possessed of great splendor, the cause of the end of the worlds, the great Indra, praised with hymns, the motive for praise, and the maker of light. (39)

The thousand-rayed one, the venerable one, free from anger, the giver of happiness and happy himself; the destroyer of disease, the bestower of bliss, the auspiciousness of well-being, the most excellent of all that is conceived. 40.
The success of healthful actions, growth, prosperity, Bṛhaspati, the fire-god Hiraṇyaretas, health, the learned one, the kinsman, the wise one, and the great one. 41.
He is the Praṇava, the steadfast, Dharma, the performer of Dharma, the bestower of delight, dear to all, the endurer of all, and the warder-off of all enemies. || 42 ||
The lofty one, the illuminator, the light, the thousand-rayed one, the creator; resplendent with the ornament of armlets, the radiant one, the shining one, the fire-like one. || 43 ||
He is the protector who removes the suffering of those seeking refuge, the priest, the firefly, and the best of birds;
he is the light of all, the manifestation of existence, and the stainless one who creates all splendor.
He is auspicious, the performer of auspiciousness, the ritual, the creator of rituals, the seer;
he is the doer of good, the embodiment of the ritual, and the vessel of all that is auspicious.
He was fond of peace, serene in soul, tranquil, and devoted to tranquility;
his actions were noble, he was well-guided, radiant, and blazing with splendor.

He is radiant, the lord of splendors, the sovereign of the three worlds, and one who brings others under his control; he is majestic, possessed of excellent fame and complexion, the presiding authority over the social orders, and a lover of offerings.
He is renowned, the abode of the Vedas, radiant, established in his true nature;
he moves through space with swift motion, is the swift-arrowed one, possessed of sacred learning, and is the bird of the sky.
The lord of cattle, the sovereign of the planets and gods, the possessor of cows, the sole shatterer of obstacles;
the progenitor, the life-force that impels procreation, the lamp that illuminates everything. (49)
The witness of karma, eternally established in yoga, the wind, the destroyer of asuras;
the slayer of rākṣasas, the pacifier of obstacles, the wearer of the diadem, and the beloved of the virtuous.

He was garlanded with rays (Marīcimālī), possessed of excellent intellect (Sumati), a distinguished host who had performed hospitality (Kṛtātithyaviśeṣaka); he was one whose conduct was refined (Śiṣṭācāra) and auspicious (Śubhācāra), and was entirely devoted to the practice of his own proper conduct (Svācārācāratatpara).
Mandāra, Māṭhara, Reṇu, Kṣobhaṇa, Pakṣiṇāṅguru, Svaviśiṣṭa, Viśiṣṭātmā, Vidheya, and Jñānaśobhana. || 52 ||
He should be known as the beloved of Mahāśvetā, the singer of the Sāman hymns, the bestower of joy;
his self is sung by all the Vedas, he is the abode of all the Vedas, and he is the dissolution.
He is the embodiment of the Vedas, the knower of the four Vedas, the upholder of the Vedas, and one who has reached the further shore of the Vedas;
he is performative of rites, exceedingly radiant, most excellent, and the bestower of boons.
He was one who observed vows, a bearer of sacred observances, a kinsman of the world, and well-adorned;
he was adorned with the syllables of scripture, possessed of divine knowledge, and understood the intentions [of others]. (55)
He is the letter A, the ornament and that which is adorned, the one who prospers, honored by all beings;
he holds the discus in hand, wields the thunderbolt, is the lord of the gods, and is affectionate toward the world.

The lord of queens, the mighty-armed one, primordial nature, transformation, and the qualities; the dispeller of darkness, the most excellent, the turner of the ages, and the creator of the beginning of the ages. || 57 ||
He is immeasurable, ever-yoked in yoga, free from ego, and the Lord;
he is the bestower of auspiciousness, the auspicious one, splendor itself, the performer of auspicious deeds, and the abode of all that is auspicious.
He is truthful, steadfast, worthy of worship, the syllable 'A', the bestower of growth, and the fire;
he is the sustainer of strength, the giver of strength, the kinsman, the powerful one, and the sovereign of the strong.
He is the bodiless one, the king of serpents, the lord of the city, the lotus-born, the lord of the Gaṇas, the year, the sacrifice, the leader, and the setter-in-motion of the wheel of time. || 60 ||
The lotus-eyed one, the lotus-born, the source, possessing the luster of the rising sun, the one of beautiful form, the wise one, the moon, Govinda, the first-born of the universe.
Clad in yellow garments, clad in black, naked, beyond the senses, Hari;
beyond Indra, the soul of manifold forms, Skanda, the conqueror of the cities of enemies. 62.
He is the possessor of power, the wielder of the trident, the radiant one, the cause of liberation, and not born from a womb;
he is the all-seeing conqueror, the vision itself, and the destroyer of evil dreams and inauspiciousness.
The performer of auspiciousness, the savior, the swift, the remover of dejection;
the great mantra of distinct syllables, the branchless one, and the beloved of sacrifice. 64.
Viśvakarman, Mahāśakti, Jyotirīśa, Vihaga, Vicakṣaṇa, Dakṣa, Indra, Pratyūha, and Priyadarśana. || 65 ||
The Aśvins, whose abode is the Vedas, whose intentions are known by those who know the Vedas, the maker of light, the conqueror of enemies, and the one with a noble charioteer, Uruṇa. (66)
Skanda, the charioteer of Kubera, the honored preceptor, the king of planets, the subduer of planets, and the ornament of the lunar mansions; || 67 ||
Bhāskara, Satatānanda, Nandana, Nandivardhana; Maṅgala, Maṅgalavān, Māṅgalya, and Maṅgalāvaha. || 68 ||
He whose conduct is auspicious practice, who has worn away all vows yet remains a practitioner of vows,
who is four-faced, garlanded with lotuses, pure in soul, and the remover of the suffering of those who bow before him.
Possessing nothing yet true to his word, devoid of qualities yet endowed with virtues, he is the virtuous one;
he is complete, lotus-eyed, disciplined, and devoted to yoga.
He is the thousand-rayed one, the lord of sacrifices, the possessor of all wealth, the benevolent-minded, and the eloquent speaker.
He possesses excellent vehicles, wears garlands and wreaths, maintains his vows, and is dear to Hari. (71)
Brahmapracetas, the renowned, the one of realized self, the one of steadfast nature;
Śatabindu, Śatamakha, the most venerable, and the lord Anala. (72)
The wise man is the greatest, the fortunate one, the supreme among men;
for he stands as a possessor of knowledge, the sovereign king of the Vidyādharas, endowed with learning and the bestower of prosperity.
The glorious one of indescribable form, the soul of the universe, the source of manifold auspiciousness;
well-established, possessing a noble chariot, golden-hued, and the abode that is the foundation of liberation. (74)
Free from dualities, the destroyer of dualities, the creation, all-pervading, the illuminator;
compassionate, subtle-minded, peace itself, and one who loves security, well-being, and stability. (75)

The upholder of the earth, the lord of the earth, the speaker, the pure-souled one, the three-eyed one, the Great Boar, the doer of what is dear, the creator, the enjoyer, and the bestower of fear. (76)
He is the bearer of the four Vedas, eternal, sleepless, and a consumer of various foods;
he is the universal sovereign, the bestower of fortitude, the perfect one, and indeed Maheśvara. || 77 ||

He whose chariot is variegated, who is solitary, who possesses seven horses, who is higher than the highest; he who establishes the existence of all oceans, who is stability itself, who is to be steadfastly relied upon, and who is fond of stability.
He is partless, yet appearing as the fullness; he possesses all wealth and is dear to Indra;
he is the lord of Indra and the possessor of riches; he is the giver of wealth and the bestower of treasures.
The powerful and wise syllable Om is established in the three [worlds];
it is the source of all conceptualization, the maker of the day, the Blessed One who brings about the cause.
He is the blue-throated one, the lord of wealth, the speaker dear to the four Vedas;
he is the *vaṣaṭ* call, the oblation, the priest, the *svāhā* call, and the offered sacrifice. (81)
Janārdana, Janānanda, Nara, Nārāyaṇa, Ambuda, Svarṇāṅga, Kṣapaṇa, Vāyu, and he who is saluted by gods and demons. || 82 ||
The Embodied One, the Stainless, the Drop, the Griefless, the Pure Radiance, the Illuminated, the Illuminator, the Wise, the Sun, the Bestower of Boons, the Mighty. 83.
The source of dharma is Mahāmoha, the eternal brother of Viṣṇu;
the king is Sāvitrī-bhāvita, and the Virāṭ is Vighṛṇī.
Possessing seven flames, seven horses, and honored by the seven worlds, he is the perfected Lord of the Universe, benevolent-minded and fond of the auspicious.
The soul of all, the creator of all, possessing seven horses, beloved of the seventh;
the one of excellent intellect, Mādhava, the pure, the wise, the slayer of Madhu. || 86 ||
Aṅgiras, the knower of destinies and times, Dhūmaketu, Suketana, the happy one, the bestower of happiness, the seeker of bliss, the lover of splendor, and the sage. || 87 ||
The scorcher, the inflamer, the radiant one, the lord of austerities; Ugraśravas, Sahasrāsya, the doer of what is dear, and the bringer of joy.

The Lord of the worlds, the life-giver, the Father of the universe, whose mind is pleased, who is free from anger, who is like a rain-cloud, who is all things, and whose strength resides in the cave of the heart of all—He is delighted. (89)
All-pervading, the joy of the world, the leader of the world, the slayer of the enemies of the gods;
the auspicious one, the maker of auspiciousness, the eldest, the highest of the high, the supreme.
The supreme one, the great Meru, the sustainer, the upholder of the earth, the bearer of showers, the king of dharma, dharma itself, and the promoter of dharma. || 91 ||
The superintendent of chariots, the lord of chariots, the swift one, the measured fire, the northern one, the unsurpassed one, the Tāpī river, the lord of stars, and the lord of waters. 92.
He whose merit is proclaimed is meritorious; he is the cause and the refuge of the three worlds.
He is Svarbhānu, the enemy of birds (Garuda), and the performer of distinguished and supreme deeds.
The destroyer of disease, the secure one, the hero, the all-conqueror, the supreme, the sole lord, the master of the chariot, the father of Śanaiścara, and the white one. || 74 ||
The preceptor of Vaivasvata, Death, eternally devoted to dharma, observer of great vows, wearing long pendent necklaces, moving everywhere, radiant, and shining like fire. || 95 ||
He is the mantra that effects the continuity [of existence], whose form is the mantra, and who possesses great power;
he is the supreme self, most beloved, Śambhu, the Lord of the lords of the great. || 96 ||
The destroyer of the course of saṃsāra, the one who carries across the ocean of saṃsāra;
the seven-tongued one with a thousand rays, the invincible one whose womb is filled with jewels. || 97 ||

The banner of Dharma, immeasurable in essence, the bestower of the boons of dharma and adharma; the witness of the world, the teacher of the world, the lord of the world, whose vehicle is his own will. || 98 ||

He whose form is the Dharma, who is the subtle wind, who holds a bow in his hand, the wielder of the bow, the bearer of the Pināka, possessed of great energy, master of manifold illusions, and the great consumer. || 99 ||
The hero, the best among the powerful, the foremost of all wielders of weapons; he who is accessible through knowledge, difficult to propitiate, the red-limbed one, the crusher of enemies. 100.
Ananta, Dharmada, Nitya, Dharmakṛt, Cakravikrama;
Daivata, Tryakṣara, Madya, Nīlāṅga, and Nīlalohita. (101)
Ekonaika, Trayīvyāsa, Savitṛ, Samitiñjaya, Sārṅgadhanvan, Nala, Bhīma, and Sarvapraharaṇāyudha.
Parameṣṭhin, Parañjyotis, Nākapālin, Divaspati, Vadānya, Vāsuki, Vedyas, Ātreya, and Atiparākrama. || 103 ||
Dvāpara is supremely noble, a great observer of celibacy;
he wears radiant attire, a crown, and holds a lotus in his hand, bearing the cool-rayed moon.
Smiling with a serene countenance, his face resembling the interior of a lotus; possessing a divine body like that of the sun at twilight, he is the great chariot-warrior beyond description.

The great chariot-warrior, the great lord, Śeṣa, who consists of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas; he stands as a deliberation resembling a held parasol, established in discernment and final decision.
Non-violent, pure-minded, peerless, and the crusher of enemies;
the giver of all, the bestower of wealth, liberation, and pleasure; the one who grants many gifts. || 107 ||
Lord of the planets, master of the planets, ruler of the planets, dispeller of darkness;
he of the enchanting body, the pure one, the beautiful one, with a face of radiant luster. 108.
He is of beautiful radiance, the source of beautiful radiance, the one with excellent eyes, and the lord of the Nikṣubhā river.
He is dear to the queen, the maker of sound, the lord of the planets, and the dispeller of darkness.
The god who is the enemy of Siṃhikā’s son (Rāhu), the bestower of boons, the excellent leader, the four-armed one, the great yogin, and likewise the lord of the masters of yoga. || 110 ||
He is of beginningless form, born of Aditi, possessing the luster of jewels, consisting of light;
he is the lamp of the world, vast, with an exceedingly expansive mandala. || 111 ||
He possesses a chariot with a single wheel; he has a golden chariot and a golden body;
he is without support, moving through the sky, and he performs deeds that bring forth the power of Dharma.
The Supreme Lord is the soul of dharma, the witness of actions, and the direct perceiver;
he dwells upon Meru, is highly intelligent, and is the great protector of Meru. (113)
It is the foundation, full of delight, and likewise the provider of wealth and grain;
it is the destroyer of the torment of sin and the bestower of what the mind desires. || 114 ||
The remover of disease, the bestower of sovereignty, possessing delightful qualities and free from debt;
whose form is infinite throughout the three periods of time, he is saluted by the multitude of sages. (115)
He is the one who creates the glow of twilight, the perfected being (siddha) who is honored by the twilight salutations;
he is intent on bestowing imperial sovereignty and is pleased by complete propitiation.
The Lord, whose prowess is immeasurable, is the destroyer of his devotees' suffering, the savior from the ocean of worldly existence, and the remover of fear.
The lord of men, the protector of Manu, the venerable one, the sovereign of the Manvantara. || 117 ||
All this that you asked me has been told to you—
the thousand names of Savitṛ which Pārāśarya recited to me.
The chanting of the names of the Sun brings merit, fame, and long life; it destroys evil dreams and brings about liberation from bondage. (119)
But that man who, being self-restrained, should hear this daily after having recited it, for him there shall be imperishable happiness and food obtained at will. (120)
There shall be no fear from kings, fire, thieves, or diseases;
one shall be eternally victorious and attain the highest welfare. || 121 ||
He shall be famous, fortunate, learned, happy, and pleasing to behold;
he shall live for a hundred years, free from all diseases. || 122 ||
Whoever, being pure and observant of vows, recites this thousand names of Aṃśumat at dawn while endowed with perfect concentration—
diseases always avoid that person from afar, just as all the lords of serpents flee in fear from Garuḍa.
Thus ends the thousand names of the Blessed Lord Śrī Sūrya in the seventh section of the glorious Bhaviṣya Purāṇa.
Thus ends the Sūryatantra. Śrī. [Composed by] Siṃha, the son of the illustrious King Rājādeva, lord of the capital city of Śivahara.
The seventeenth [chapter] from within the Śāktapramoda, composed and compiled by the noble lord Bahādur.
The Viṣṇutantra,
edited by the scholar Śrī Raghurāja Dube, a descendant of the aforementioned royal preceptors.
This [work] was [published] by Khemarāja, son of Śrī Kṛṣṇadāsa,
at his own Śrī Veṅkaṭeśvara Press.
Having been printed and published in Mumbai;
salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
Now follows the Viṣṇu-tantra;
now the meditation on Śrī Viṣṇu:
O Lord of the gods, Padmanābha, whose form is peaceful and who reclines upon the serpent.
The support of all, resembling the sky, cloud-colored, and possessing auspicious limbs.

I salute Viṣṇu, the beloved of Lakṣmī, whose eyes are like lotuses, who is attainable through meditation by yogis, the remover of the fear of worldly existence, and the sole lord of all the worlds. || 1 ||
Now, regarding the extraction of the yantra: In a ritual procedure not previously mentioned, one should draw a yantra consisting of eight lotus petals,
a six-cornered [figure], and a pericarp, adorned with four gates.
(p. 554) Now follows the extraction of the mantra:
the wise one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) using the names ending in the dative case and followed by *namaḥ*.
One should utter the word *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*) and the word *namaḥ*, and the two letters *na* and *ra* joined with the long vowels [ā and ī].
The letter 'ya' is the beginning of this mantra; it is declared to be the supreme eight-syllabled one.
Now the mantra: Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya. Now the ritual procedure for worship (pūjā-prayoga).

Having performed the rites beginning with the morning duties (*prātaḥ-kṛtya*) up to the *mātṛkā-nyāsa*, one should perform the *keśava-kṛtya* and other *nyāsas*. Now follows the *ṛṣyādi-nyāsa*: "Salutation to Prajāpati, the seer (*ṛṣi*), on the head; salutation to the Gāyatrī metre (*chandas*), on the mouth; [salutation] to [the deity], on the heart."

Salutation to the deity Ardhalaṣmīhari. Then follow the Karanyāsa and Aṅganyāsa: "Śrī, salutation to the two thumbs," and so forth. And likewise in the Gautamīya: "The seer is Prajāpati, the meter is Gāyatrī, and the deity is declared to be Ardhalaṣmīhari."
The assignment of the limbs [of the deity] is performed with the seed-syllable *śrīṃ*. Then follows the meditation (*dhyāna*).

I worship Viṣṇu, who is as bright as gold refined by the light of a hundred rising suns, who is attended on both sides by the Daughter of the Ocean and the Mother of the Universe, who is adorned with various ornaments shining with diverse jewels, who wears yellow garments, and who holds the lotus, the Kaumodakī mace, and the discus in his hands. Having meditated thus, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*).

Having omitted the vowels, as indicated by the phrase "together with half-moons": *Aṃ* to Keśava, for Vitality (*sāra*), *namaḥ* on the forehead; *Āṃ* to Nārāyaṇa, for Radiance (*kānti*), *namaḥ* on the mouth; *Iṃ* to Mādhava, for Nourishment (*puṣṭi*), *namaḥ* on the right eye; *Īṃ* to Govinda, for Nourishment (*puṣṭi*), *namaḥ* on the left eye; *namaḥ* is used everywhere. *Uṃ*.
To Viṣṇu, for support (dhṛti), on the right ear. Ūṃ, to Madhusūdana, for peace (śānti), on the left ear.
Ṛṃ, to Trivikrama, for action (kriyā), on the right nostril. Ṝṃ, to Vāmana, for compassion (dayā), on the left nostril. Ḷṃ, to Śrīdhara, for intelligence (medhā), on the right cheek.
*Ḷṃ* to Hṛṣīkeśa and Durgā on the left cheek; *Eṃ* to Padmanābha and Śraddhā on the upper lip; *Aiṃ* to Dāmodara and Lajjā on the lower lip; *Oṃ* to Vāsudeva and Lakṣmī on the upper row of teeth.
Oṃ, to Saṅkarṣaṇa and Sarasvatī, [worship] on the lower row of teeth;
aṃ, to Pradyumna and Dhṛti, on the head; aḥ, to Aniruddha and Rati, on the mouth.
To Jayā for Kaṃcakrin; to Durgā for Khaṅgin; to Prabhā for Śārṅgin;
to Satyā for Khaḍgin; to Candrā for Śaṅkhin—at the base joints and the tips of the fingers of the right hand. To Vāṇī for Halin at [the base joint of] the left hand.
To Chaṃ, the wielder of the pestle, [namaskāra] to Vilāsinī; to Jaṃ, the wielder of the trident, [namaskāra] to Vijayā; to Jhaṃ, the wielder of the noose, [namaskāra] to Virajā;
to Ñaṃ, the wielder of the goad, [namaskāra] to Bimbā—at the base joints and the tips of the fingers of the left hand.
Ṭaṃ to Mukunda and Vinadā; Ṭhaṃ to Nandaja and Sunandā;
Ḍaṃ to Nandī and Smṛti; Ḍhaṃ to Nara and Ṛddhi; Ṇaṃ to Naraka-jit and Samṛddhi—at the root, joints, and tips of the right foot. Taṃ to Hari and Śuddhi.
*Thaṃ* to Kṛṣṇāyabṛddhi, *daṃ* to Daṃsatyāyabhūmi, *dhaṃ* to Sātvatāyamati, and *naṃ* to Saurāṣṭrāyakṣamā— at the root, joint, and tip of the left foot.
*Paṃ* to Paṃśurāya and Ramā, on the right side; *phaṃ* to Janārdana and Umā, on the left side; *baṃ* to Bhūdharāya and Kledinī, on the back; *bhaṃ* to Viśvamūrti and Klinnā, at the navel;
*maṃ* to Vaikuṇṭha and Vasudā, in the belly; *yaṃ* to the Self of the Skin (*tvagātman*).

To Puruṣottama, to Avasudhā—[salutation] in the heart; to Raṃ, the blood-self, to Bala, to Parā—on the right shoulder; to Laṃ, the flesh-self, to Vālānuja, to Parāyaṇā—on the crown of the head; to Vaṃ, the marrow-self, to Bala, to Sūkṣmā—on the left shoulder; to Śaṃ—
To the one whose self is bone, Vṛṣaghna, to Saṃghāyā—[assign] to the heart and so forth, and to the right hand.
To the one whose self is marrow, Vṛṣa, to Prajñāyā—[assign] to the heart and so forth, and to the left hand.

To *Haṃ* [the letter], the self of pure light (*saṃśuklātman*), to Varāha, and to Night (*niśā*), from the heart to the right foot; to *Haṃ*, the self of vital breath (*prāṇātman*), to Vimala, and to Amoghā, from the heart to the left foot; to *Laṃ*, the self of the individual soul (*jīvātman*), to Vimala, and to Amoghā, from the heart to the belly; to *Kṣaṃ*, the self of wrath (*krodhātman*).
To Nṛsiṃha, to Vidyutā, and so forth, [these are assigned] to the heart and the other limbs, as well as to the mouth; and likewise in the Gautamīya:
This installation (nyāsa) beginning with Keśava bestows the state of Acyuta upon embodied beings merely by its performance;

this is the truth, the truth—there is no doubt. Having uttered the phonemes of the Mātṛkā, one should recollect "To Keśava," and perform the installation beginning with "and for Kīrtti, joined with *namaḥ*," and so forth. Then, [to] Keśava...

This sequence is established by such statements from the Agastya-saṃhitā as "to Kīrtti, to Kānti, and to Nārāyaṇa," and not as "namas to Keśava and Kīrti," and so forth. Likewise, one who desires worldly enjoyment (bhukti) and liberation (mukti) should perform this nyāsa beginning with the Śrī-bīja.
p. 556) For example—
*Śrīṃ aṃ keśavāya kīrtyai namaḥ*, and so forth. Now follows the worship according to the sequence of the ritual services (*upacāra*).
Now, the invocation: He whose presence the gods desire for the sake of attaining their own cherished goals.

Out of compassion, O Lord of the gods of gods, be present before me! To you, O Supreme Lord, O Master, welcome, welcome! I am fulfilled and graced; my life has become fruitful, since you have come, O Lord of gods, O imperishable one consisting of consciousness and bliss—whether through ignorance or through negligence.
And because of the deficiency of the practitioner, even if that which is to be accomplished remains incomplete, nevertheless, manifest yourself!
Thus ends the invocation. Now follows the water for washing the feet (pādya).
"O Supreme Lord, to You who are pure and from whose contact with even a fragment of devotion the arising of supreme bliss occurs, I offer this water for the feet. Thus is the offering of the *pādya*.
Now, the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
"To the God of even the gods, the deity of the gods, O Lord, I offer water for sipping (ācamana) with the *svadhā* invocation for the sake of purification. Thus ends the water for sipping.
Now, the arghya offering.
It is divine, removing the threefold suffering, and characterized by supreme bliss.
"For the sake of liberation from the threefold suffering, I prepare this *arghya* for you. Thus, the *arghya*.
Now, the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
"O God, who art free from all impurity and whose nature is the fullness of nectar, I offer this *madhuparka* to you;
be gracious unto me. Thus [is the offering of] the *madhuparka*.
Then, furthermore, the water for sipping.
"Even one who is defiled by remnants or impure attains purity merely by the remembrance of you; for you, this is again the water for sipping. Thus is the water for sipping again.
Now, the anointing.
Having taken scented oil, one should recite: "O Great-souled Lord of the World, accept this oil with your own essence;
O Pure-souled One, I offer this supreme oil to all worlds. Thus is the anointing.
Now, the ritual bath: Oṃ. The Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet.
Having pervaded the earth on all sides, he transcended it by ten fingers' breadth. (1)
The Person alone is all this—whatever has been and whatever is to be;
he is the Lord of immortality, which he surpasses by means of food. 2.
Such is his greatness, and yet the Puruṣa is even greater than this. All beings constitute one quarter of him; his three quarters are the immortal in heaven. (3)
The Puruṣa rose up, three-quarters of him being above; one quarter of him came to be here again.
From there he strode out in all directions toward that which eats and that which does not eat.
From him Virāj was born; from Virāj, Puruṣa was born.
Once born, he extended beyond the earth, both behind and before. (5)
From that sacrifice in which everything was offered, the speckled butter was gathered;
he made those animals his own—the ones belonging to Vāyu, those of the forest, and those of the village.
From that sacrifice in which everything was offered, the Ṛg-verses and the Sāman-chants were born;
from it the meters were born, and from it the Yajus-formulas were produced. (7)
From him were born horses and whatever animals have two rows of teeth;
from him cows were born, and from him goats and sheep were produced. 8.
Upon the sacrificial grass at the sacrifice, they sprinkled the Puruṣa who was born in the beginning;
with him, the gods, the Sādhyas, and the Ṛṣis performed the sacrifice.
When they divided Puruṣa, into how many parts did they arrange him? What was his mouth, what were his arms, what were his thighs, and what are his feet called? 10.
The Brāhmaṇa was his mouth; the Rājanya (Kṣatriya) was made from his arms;
that which was his thighs became the Vaiśya; and from his feet the Śūdra was born. 11.
The moon was born from his mind; from his eye the sun was born; from his ear came the wind and the breath of life; and from his mouth fire was born. || 12 ||
From his navel arose the intermediate space; from his head the sky evolved; from his feet the earth, and from his hearing the quarters; thus the worlds were fashioned. 2 || 13 ||
When the gods performed the sacrifice with the Puruṣa as the oblation,
spring was its clarified butter, summer its fuel, and autumn its offering.
Seven were its enclosing sticks, thrice seven were the fuel-sticks prepared; when the gods were performing the sacrifice, they bound Puruṣa as the victim. 15.
By means of sacrifice the gods sacrificed to the sacrifice; these were the first ordinances.
They attained the heights of heaven where the ancient Sādhyas, the gods, abide. 16.
Now, the Tantric mantras:
"O Lord, I perform this bath for You, whose form is immersed in the ocean of the awakening of supreme bliss, together with all its limbs and sub-limbs. Thus ends the bath.
Now, the garment.
"Without Māyā, Your birth would not have been concealed due to Your own great splendor;
for You whose consciousness is unobscured, I prepare this dwelling. Thus ends the section on clothing.
O Supreme Lord, to You, depending upon whom that Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā) deludes the world,
I offer this upper garment.
(p. 558) Now, the sacrificial thread (yajñasūtra).

"To you, for whom this entire world is said to exist by means of the three powers, and who are the sacrificial thread (yajñasūtra), I offer this sacrificial thread. Thus ends the section on the sacrificial thread. Now, the ornaments.

"O you whose limbs are beautiful by their very nature, who are the refuge of both truth and untruth, and who are worshipped by the gods—I fashion various ornaments for you. Thus ends the section on ornaments.
Then, O Lord of all the lords of gods, water is the supreme means for the complete satisfaction of all.
"Accept this excellent water, which is filled with unbroken bliss. Thus [is the offering of] water.
Now, O Supreme Lord, out of compassion, please accept this supreme fragrance, whose scent fills the quarters of space with the aroma of supreme bliss. Thus, the offering of fragrance.
Now, for the flower:
"Please accept this supreme flower, endowed with the four qualities, captivating with its various virtues, and possessing the fragrance of bliss. Thus ends the flower.
Now for the incense:
"Born from the essence of the lord of the forest, rich in fragrance, the most excellent of scents—this incense, to be smelled by all the gods, is hereby accepted. Thus ends the incense.
Now, the lamp:
"May this lamp, well-illuminated, a great light that dispels darkness on all sides, a radiance both internal and external—may this lamp be accepted. Thus ends the lamp.
Now, for the food offering (naivedya):

"O Lord of Gods, I present this food offering—prepared in a worthy vessel, consisting of oblations and various many kinds of edibles—to You and Your attendants; please accept it. Thus ends the food offering.

"O Lord of all the lords of gods, accept this supreme water for the purpose of sipping (ācamana), which is the ultimate source of all knowledge and filled with unbroken bliss. Thus [is the offering of] the water.
Now, for the betel leaf:

"O Supreme Lord, please accept with devotion this excellent, divine betel leaf, well-scented with camphor and other ingredients, which has been offered by me. Thus ends the offering of the betel leaf.
Thus is the worship;
now, taking up the hymn of praise, having slain and churned the entire Vedas along with the oceans, he indeed [recovered] the exalted Madhu.
Worship that primordial Viṣṇu in the form of the Fish, by whom [the Vedas] were given to the Grandfather (Brahmā) in the past. || 1 ||

I bow to the Tortoise who became the supporting foundation for the earth as it was violently tossed about when the great ocean was churned by the gods and asuras using Vāsuki and Mandara for the sake of divine nectar.

I take refuge in that Primordial Boar, by whom the Earth—the one girdled by the oceans and clothed in rivers, bearing the weight of Meru as her crown—was lifted up when she had come within his tusk. || 3 ||

I do not forget the Lord Nṛsiṃha, who, out of compassion for the suffering of his devotees, arose from within a pillar; how he tore apart the enemy of the gods with the tips of his sharpened claws. (4)

I bow to that one who is omnipresent and possesses the three strides—not to any other—whose foot was not sufficient to encompass the earth adorned by the four oceans; I bow to him whose state is the triple-striding of the gods.
I bow to that Rāma, the foremost of heroes, who by the strength of his staff-like arms, having slain kings twenty-one times, properly offered a libation of blood to his ancestors.
I bow with devotion to that Lord of Sītā, who, having taken birth in the lineage of the Raghus and having constructed a bridge across the waters of the ocean, subdued the Lord of Laṅkā.
Having dragged all the asuras by his plow, he reduced them to powder with blows from his pestle;
I worship that Balabhadra Rāma, who, having encountered Kṛṣṇa, became even more powerful through devotion.

I bow to the Buddha, who in the past, desiring to help the gods conquer the asuras, assumed the guise and insignia of Śiva and composed that infallible manual which has become the very foundation [of all treatises].

At the end of the kalpa, he who was born from the lotus and is the soul of the universe— terrible with his own splendor— consumed everything in a mere twinkling of an eye, even as all the gods joined together against him.

I praise Viṣṇu in my heart—him who holds the conch, the beautiful discus, the mace, and the lotus in his four arms; who is mounted upon Garuḍa; who bears the Śrīvatsa mark; who is the primordial source of the universe; and who is dark blue like a Tamāla tree.

I repeatedly remember Him reclining upon the special couch of Śeṣa in the ocean of milk, His face beautified by an inner smile, His lotus-eyes fully blossomed, the primordial source of the waters of the clouds and of the Vedas.
One should please the Lord of the World, who consists of the world, the Supreme Person, for the attainment of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, with this hymn of praise. 13.
Thus ends the Śrī Viṣṇu-stotra.
Then the venerable Nārada spoke regarding the armor:
"O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, this armor has been revealed."
O Lord, please out of compassion tell me that which is named the "Auspiciousness of the Three Worlds."
Sanatkumāra said: Listen, O best of Brahmins, I shall declare the most wonderful armor (kavaca),
which was formerly told out of compassion by Nārāyaṇa to Brahmā.
(560) Brahmā said: Out of supreme affection, I shall tell you that which was told to me—the most secret reality, which is the embodiment of the multitude of Brahman-mantras.
By retaining and reciting which, Brahmā certainly expands the creation;
by retaining and reciting which, Mahālakṣmī protects the three worlds.
Through recitation and retention, Śambhu becomes the destroyer and knower of all mantras;
and Durgā, the mother of the three worlds, [destroys] the great asuras such as Mahiṣa.
Since he struck down those who were arrogant toward his boon merely by reciting and retaining it,
so may all [beings], beginning with Indra, attain complete sovereignty.
This armor must be kept strictly secret and never spoken of anywhere;
one should reveal it only to a devoted disciple or a spiritual practitioner (sādhaka).
By giving this armor of the *Trailokyamaṅgala* to a deceitful disciple of another, one shall meet with death; [it was revealed] by Prajāpati. (8)
The seer is [the same], the meter is Gāyatrī, and the deity is Nārāyaṇa himself;
its application is proclaimed to be for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. || 9 ||
May the Praṇava protect my head, and "Namaḥ Nārāyaṇāya" protect my forehead; may the eight-syllable mantra, which bestows devotion and liberation, protect the pair of my eyes.
With *klīṃ* one should worship the pair of ears, and with the single-syllable mantra *sarvamohana* (the all-enchanting);
with *klīṃ kṛṣṇāya* one should worship the nose, and with *sadā govindāya* the tongue.
To the beloved of the Gopījanapada, Svāhā; may it be mine. 11.
May the eighteen-syllable mantra protect the throat; may the ten-syllable one protect the neck.
To the Beloved of the Gopījanas, Svāhā—this for the two arms.
*Klīṃ glauṃ klīṃ śyāmalāṅgāya namaḥ*—the ten-syllable mantra for the shoulders. (13)
May *klīṃ kṛṣṇaḥ klīṃ* protect my two hands; may *klīṃ kṛṣṇāya klīṃ* protect my limbs. May Bhuvaneśānī protect my heart; may *klīṃ kṛṣṇāya klīṃ* protect my breasts.
May Gopāla, ending with the word Agnijāyā, always protect the pair of his belly;
may the most excellent Klīṃ-Kṛṣṇa always protect the pair of his sides. || 15 ||
The eight-syllable mantra "Kṛṣṇagovindau" (ending in the dative case) preceded by "Smara" protects the waist; may the two-syllable mantra "Kṛṣṇa" protect the navel.
May the back—*klīṃ kṛṣṇakaṅkālaṃ klīṃ kṛṣṇāya dviṭhāntakaḥ*—protect it;
may *śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ kṛṣṇa ṭha dvayam* protect the two thighs constantly.
May the seven-syllabled [mantra] protect the thighs; may the thirteen-syllabled one protect [the rest].
From the word "Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ" up to "Gopījanavallabha," may it protect the teeth. (18)
"Bhāya svāhā" protects the anus; indeed, "klīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ" is the ten-syllabled mantra.
And may "hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ," the ten-syllabled mantra, always protect the two knees. (19)
May the thirteen-syllable mantra protect the shanks;
[may] the eighteen-syllable mantra preceded by *hrīṃ* and *śrīṃ*, as well as the twenty-syllable one, [protect them]. (20)
May the powerful Lord of Dvārakā always protect all my limbs;
thereafter, obeisance to the Blessed One, Vāsudeva. (21)
May this twelve-syllable mantra beginning with "Tārā" always protect me in the east;
while "Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ" is ten syllables, and "Klīṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ" consists of sixteen syllables.
May Viṣṇu, armed with the mace and other weapons, protect me in the direction of Agni (the southeast).
May the ten-syllable mantra "hrīṃ śrīṃ" always protect me in the south.
*Tāro namo bhagavate rukmiṇīvallabhāya ca svāhā*—may this sixteen-syllable mantra protect [the practitioner] in the south-western direction. (24)
"Klīṃ hṛṣīkeśa-deśāya namaḥ"—may this protect me in the western direction. May the eighteen-syllable mantra ending with "kāma" always protect me in the northwestern direction. || 25 ||
The mantra "Śrīṃ Māyākāmakṛṣṇāya Hrīṃ Govindāya" consisting of twelve syllables, with 'dviṭha' (the letter ṭha preceded by two), may Viṣṇu always protect me in the north. (26)
Vāgbhava, Kāma, Kṛṣṇāya, Hrīṃ, Govindāya, followed by that;
Śrīṃ, Gopījanavallabha, then Bhāryai Svāhā, and thereafter Hsauḥ. (27)
May the twenty-two-syllable mantra always protect me in the northeast;
it shines and performs a divine dance within the midst of the hoods of Kāliya. || 28 ||
I bow to the son of Devakī, the King of Dance, the Infallible One;
may this thirty-two-syllable mantra also protect me at all times from below. (29)
We know Kāmadeva; we meditate upon him whose arrows are flowers;
may that bodiless one (Anaṅga) inspire us—may he protect me from above. || 30 ||
Thus, O Brahmin, I have told you this armor named *Trailokyamaṅgala*, which is the embodiment of the multitude of Brahma-mantras and possesses the very form of Brahman. (31)
This was previously spoken by Brahmā and emerged from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa;
out of affection for you, it has been told to me, but it must not be told to anyone else.
Having prostrated before the Guru according to the prescribed rite, one should then recite the armor-mantra (kavaca) once, twice, or as much as one knows; for he too consists of all austerity.
The teacher is indeed authoritative regarding all mantras; there is no doubt in this matter.
The prescribed rule for his preliminary ritual (puraścaryā) is one hundred and eight repetitions.
Having performed the oblations and other rites with a tenth part [of the total], one will certainly accomplish that;
if one possesses the perfected armor-mantra, one becomes Viṣṇu himself. (35)
Through the performance of the *puraścaryā* ritual, he shall attain mastery over mantras;
then, having overcome all rivalry, Lakṣmī and Vāṇī shall dwell with him forever.
Having offered eight handfuls of flowers, one should recite the root mantra once;
one shall obtain the fruit of ten thousand years of worship.
If one writes [this] on birch bark, makes it into a pill, and wears it placed in gold—either around the neck or on the right arm—he too is Viṣṇu, without a doubt. (38)
Thousands of horse sacrifices, hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices, the great gifts and so forth, as well as circumambulating the earth—[all these are equal to this]. (39)
Therefore, those [other mantras] do not equal even a sixteenth part of it from a single recitation;
by the grace of the Kavaca, a man becomes liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 40 ||
He truly agitates the three worlds and becomes a conqueror of the three worlds;
yet, he who worships Puruṣottama without knowing this armor-mantra [is otherwise].
Even if recited one hundred lakhs of times, the mantra does not succeed for him.
Thus ends the armor [mantra].
Then, having sipped water at the heart, performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), and recalled the place and time, for the sake of accomplishing my desired goal,
[I shall recite] the Nārāyaṇahṛdaya according to the method of encapsulation (saṅkalīkaraṇa) or the method of sandwiching (sampuṭīkaraṇa).
I shall perform the single return.

Of this Śrī Nārāyaṇa-hṛdaya-stotra-mantra: Bhārgava is the seer (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandas), Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa is the deity (devatā), Oṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja), Namaḥ is the power (śakti), and Nārāyaṇāya is the pin (kīlaka). Its application (viniyoga) is in the recitation for the purpose of pleasing Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
Oṃ, "Nārāyaṇa is the supreme light," with the two thumbs;
Oṃ, "Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Brahman," with the two index fingers;
Oṃ, "Nārāyaṇa is the supreme deity," with the two middle fingers.

Oṃ, "Nārāyaṇa is the supreme object of meditation," with the two ring fingers; Oṃ, "Nārāyaṇa is the supreme abode," with the two little fingers; Oṃ, "Nārāyaṇa is the supreme dharma," with the palms and backs of the hands. Thus [one performs the ritual] for the heart and other limbs. Now, the binding of the directions (digbandha): Oṃ, [the ten directions] beginning with the east.
"Oṃ, obeisance to the Sudarśana with its thousand spokes, hūṃ phaṭ! I bind [it]; obeisance to the Cakra, svāhā!"—this should be applied in each direction.

(p. 563) Now, meditation (*dhyāna*): One should meditate upon Hari, the Lord of Lakṣmī, who resembles the rising sun, who is clothed in yellow garments, who is Acyuta, and who holds a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands.
