The recitation (*japa*) is: "Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya. Now, the eight root verses (*mūlāṣṭaka*).
Oṃ, Nārāyaṇa is the supreme light, the Self; Nārāyaṇa is the highest.
Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman; O Nārāyaṇa, salutations be unto you! || 1 ||
Nārāyaṇa is the supreme deity; Nārāyaṇa is the supreme giver;
Nārāyaṇa is the supreme meditator; O Nārāyaṇa, salutations be unto you! || 2 ||
Nārāyaṇa is the supreme abode; Nārāyaṇa is the highest meditation;
Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Dharma; O Nārāyaṇa, salutations be unto You! || 3 ||
The Veda has Nārāyaṇa as its supreme goal; knowledge has Nārāyaṇa as its supreme goal;
the universe is directly Nārāyaṇa—O Nārāyaṇa, salutations be unto you! || 4 ||
From Nārāyaṇa Brahmā was born; from Nārāyaṇa Śiva was born;
from Nārāyaṇa Indra was born; O Nārāyaṇa, salutations be to you! || 5 ||
The sun is Nārāyaṇa’s splendor, the lunar light is Nārāyaṇa’s majesty, and fire is directly Nārāyaṇa;
O Nārāyaṇa, salutations be to you!
Nārāyaṇa is the one to be worshipped; the Guru is the supreme Nārāyaṇa.
Nārāyaṇa is the supreme awakening; O Nārāyaṇa, salutations be to You!
Nārāyaṇa is the primary fruit; Nārāyaṇa is accomplishment and bliss;
Nārāyaṇa is the pure one to be served; O Nārāyaṇa, salutations be unto you.
Thus ends the Root Octet. Now follows the Tenfold Prayer.
You alone are Nārāyaṇa, residing in the heart known as the *dahara*;
you are the impeller of those being impelled, for my mind has been set in motion by you.
Bearing your command upon my head, I shall mutter this purifier of people,
which awakens the heart's true disposition regarding the various paths of worship.
O Bhava, you who bring about the purpose of existence, you who have become existence itself, grant the happiness of existence!
The entire universe, deluded by your māyā, has been fashioned by you alone. (3)
By your mere presence, she is the accomplisher of all aims;
placing her at your side, grant me my desires.
There is no protector for me other than you; indeed, there is no deity other than you.
Truly, I know of no guardian in the form of merit other than you.
O Lord, as long as any worldly state remains situated in the mind and consists of mental cultivation, so long will the goal to be accomplished be attained in every way and at all times. (6)
I alone am the foremost among sinners, and you are the leader among the compassionate;
who else in these three worlds besides me is worthy of your mercy? (7)
If I had not been created by you, your compassion would not exist;
if disease were never created, the emergence of medicine would be in vain. (8)
Surrounded by a wicked assembly, evil-souled and assuming a sinful form—who else but you on this earth could be my protector from these evils? (9)
You alone are my mother and you alone are my father; you alone are my kinsman and you alone are my friend.
You alone are my knowledge and you alone are my teacher; you alone, O God of gods, are everything to me. 10.
The "Tenfold Prayer" and the "Eightfold Root" have been proclaimed;
for one who recites or hears them daily, prosperity shall become stable. (11)
The Heart of Nārāyaṇa bestows all desired fruits;
if this hymn, the Heart of Lakṣmī, is performed without it, [it is incomplete]. (12)
All that is declared to be fruitless, and Lakṣmī remains perpetually angry [with him]. This compiled hymn, however, bestows the fruits of all ritual actions. (13)
Whoever recites the *Lakṣmīhṛdaya* and likewise that which consists of Nārāyaṇa after performing the ritual of *saṅkalīkaraṇa*, shall obtain all their desired objects.
Having first recited the *Hṛdaya* of Nārāyaṇa, thereafter one should recite the hymn of the *Hṛdaya* of Lakṣmī, and then again the [Hṛdaya] of Nārāyaṇa. (15)
Having recited the Nārāyaṇa mantra again, one should then recite the Lakṣmī-mantra;
having recited the Nārāyaṇa mantra once more, the *saṅkalīkaraṇa* (the linking together) is accomplished. || 16 ||
Thus, one should recite it twice in the middle;
that is indeed the summarized Lakṣmīhṛdaya hymn, which reveals all desires. (17)

In that same way, one should perform recitation and other rites; this auspicious practice, when accumulated, brings about the attainment of all desires and removes the fear of mental anguish and physical disease.
One should always keep this secret and not reveal it everywhere;
thus was this most secret scripture obtained by Brahmā and the others in the past. (19)
Therefore, with every effort, the wise person should protect and accomplish [the practice] where this book, which consists of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, remains. 20.
Spirits, piśācas, and vetālas are never stable there;
therefore, the wise man should accomplish [the rite] according to the procedure taught in the *Lakṣmīhṛdaya*. 21.
On a Friday and at night, one should worship the two books;
the wise person should always protect all his possessions with truth and accomplish his goals.
By concealing [this] and practicing the means, one truly becomes blessed in the world. || 23 ||
Thus ends the Śrī Nārāyaṇahṛdaya in the latter part of the Atharvaṇarahasya.
Then Kaśyapa spoke this Upaniṣad:
"O one-horned bull, ocean, Vṛṣākapi, bull among gods, unborn origin, Rudra, Kapila!"

O Viṣvaksena, Lord of all beings, eternal Dharma, Vaikuṇṭha, Vṛṣāvarta, You who are without beginning, middle, or end, O Dhanañjaya, Śuciśravas, Pṛśnitejas, Nijajaya, Amṛtaśaya, Sanātana, Tridhāman, Tuṣita, Mahātattva, Lord of the worlds, Padmanābha!
Virañca, Bahurūpa, Akṣaya, Akṣara, Havyabhuk, Khaṇḍaparaśu, Śakra, Muñjakeśa, Haṃsa, Mahādakṣiṇa, Hṛṣīkeśa, Sūkṣma, Mahāniyamadhara,
Viraja, Lokapratiṣṭha, Arūpa, Agraja, Dharmaja, Dharmanābha, Havyabhuk.
Gabhastinātha, Śatakratu-nātha, Candraratha, Sūryatejas, Samudravāsa, Aja, Sahasraśiras, Sahasrapāda, Ayomukha, Mahāpuruṣa, Puruṣottama, Sahasrabāhu,
Sahasramūrti, Sahasrāsya, Sahasrasambhava— people call you Viśva.
O you whose smile is like a flower, you alone are Vauṣaṭ; they call you Vaṣaṭkāra, the one who consumes the offerings in the sacrifices.
It became possessed of a hundred streams and a thousand streams.

O you who are worthy of the world's praise, Lord of the Earth, son of Bhṛgu, known through the Vedas, resting in Brahman, beloved of the Brāhmaṇas— you alone are the sky, you are Mātariśvan, you are Dharma, the Hotṛ, the Potṛ, the slayer, the thinker, the leader,
and you alone are the cause of the oblation.

You alone are the foremost of all luminaries; you are the well-vessel to be worshipped with the Rig-verses; you are the wise one; you alone are the fuel, the intellect, and the goal; you are the giver, you are liberation, you are yoga; you create as the Ordainer; you are the supreme sacrifice; you are Soma; you are the consecrated initiate; you are the sacrificial fee; you are the universe.

O Elder Hiraṇyagarbha, Nārāyaṇa, Three-eyed One, Primordial Color, Splendor of the Sun, Great Person, Supreme Person, Primordial God, You who traverse the earth, You who stride the three worlds, Maker of Light, Śambhu, Self-born, You are the origin of beings and the Great Element; You are the Universal Being, the Universe itself.
You alone are the protector of the universe; you are the purifier, the source of all beings, O performer of lofty deeds, immortal Lord of Heaven!

O Lord of Speech, whose radiance is clarified butter, whose actions are infinite, and whose wisdom pervades the sacrificial hall and its fore-hall—you are the Horse Sacrifice itself; you are the bestower of boons upon those who seek them.
p. 566) "To the one who is offered oblations by four, by four, by two, and indeed by five, and again by two—to you, whose self is the Hotṛ-priest, obeisance! Thus ends the Upaniṣad.
Now, the one hundred and eight names by which [one praises] Viṣṇu of incomparable splendor:
by the mere hearing of which, a man becomes Nārāyaṇa. (1)
Viṣṇu, the Victorious, the Vaṣaṭ-call, the God of gods, Vṛṣākapi, Dāmodara, the Friend of the distressed, the Primordial God, and the Son of Diti. || 2 ||
Puṇḍarīka, supreme bliss, the Supreme Self, higher than the highest;
the wielder of the axe, the Soul of the Universe, Kṛṣṇa, who removes the impurity of Kālī. || 3 ||
Nara, Nārāyaṇa, Hari, whose chest is illuminated by the Kaustubha gem;
Hara, the beloved of Hara, the Lord Vaikuṇṭha, who faces in all directions. || 4 ||
Hṛṣīkeśa, the immeasurable Self, Varāha the upholder of the earth, Vāmana the speaker of the Vedas, and the eternal Vāsudeva. || 5 ||
Rāma, the cessation [of suffering], the stainless one, the enemy of Rāvaṇa, the Lord of Ramā;
the dweller in Vaikuṇṭha, the possessor of wealth, the giver of riches, and the upholder of the earth. || 6 ||
The Lord of Dharma, the protector of the earth, the one to be meditated upon, the foremost among those who uphold the Dharma;
he is the Puruṣa of a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet.
All-pervading, all-knowing, the All, the refuge, the beloved of the virtuous;
the delighter of Kausalyā, the glorious one, the destroyer of the Kṣatriya race.
The creator of the world, the sustainer of the world, the conqueror of the world, the remover of the suffering of people;
the Lord who is the beloved of Jānakī, the God whose form is victory, the Lord of the waters. || 9 ||
The dweller in the Ocean of Milk, the beloved of the daughter of the Ocean of Milk,
likewise the one who reclines upon Śeṣa, whose vehicle is the enemy of serpents, and Viṣṭaraśravas.
Mādhava, Lord of Mathurā, the giver of delusion, the destroyer of delusion, the enemy of the Daityas, the lotus-eyed one, the infallible Acyuta, and Madhusūdana. || 11 ||
Nṛsiṃha, whose eyes are the moon, the sun, and fire; who is affectionate toward his devotees;
eternal, free from disease, pure, a god among men, and the Lord of the universe. || 12 ||
Hayagrīva, the conqueror of enemies, the supreme lord of men, the husband of Rukmiṇī;
he who consists of all the gods, the Lord of Śrī, the support of all, the eternal one. 13.
He is gentle, the bestower of gentleness, the creator, Viṣvaksena, Janārdana;
he is the son of Yaśodā, the yogi devoted to the science of yoga.
Rāghava and Madhusūdana are identical with Rudra and are the very form of Rudra;
thus have these one hundred and eight divine names been recounted to you.
(567) This merit, which removes all sins, belongs to Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor;
it destroys suffering, poverty, and misfortune, and increases happiness. || 16 ||
O best of Brahmins, having risen in the morning, one should recite with a one-pointed mind this auspicious [hymn], which brings about all prosperity and destroys great sins. (17)
His heaps of calamities perish, and he shall attain perfection. || 17 ||
Thus ends the hymn of one hundred and eight names.
Then Śrī Mahādeva spoke the Thousand Names:
"In some way, the sin of thousands of killings of Brahmins may be pacified."
But when you are not recognized, even after hundreds of millions of eons.
"O Hari, since I have engaged in rivalry, how may it become pure?
O Lord of the Gods, tell me that by which all sins are destroyed. (2)
Then the divine Govinda spoke to me appropriately out of affection.
The Blessed Lord said:
O Śambhu, if you desire all sovereign powers, then be intent every day upon my thousand names, which are ever-purifying and lead to my state.
Śrī Mahādeva said:
"O Pārvatī, I constantly worship, praise, and meditate upon Him alone through austerity; by that, I possess matchless majesty and am worthy of worship by the world."
Śrī Pārvatī said:
O Lord of Gods, tell me that by which I may become, O Śaṅkara,
the peerless Mistress of All, equal to You, O Lord.
The illustrious Mahādeva said: "Excellent, excellent! O Śivā, you have asked well. I shall declare the thousand names of the Blessed Viṣṇu, which are preeminent and auspicious for the three worlds."
Salutation to Nārāyaṇa and Puruṣottama, the Great Soul;
we meditate upon the Great Swan who presides over the abode of purity. 8.

Oṃ. Of this mantra of the Thousand Names of the glorious Viṣṇu, Mahādeva is the seer (ṛṣi), the Supreme Self (Paramātman) is the deity (devatā), "resembling ten million suns" is the seed-syllable (bīja), "the supreme sacred ford of the Gaṅgā" is the power (śakti),
"the thunderbolt-cage for those who have surrendered" is the pin (kīlaka), and Vāsudeva is the Supreme Brahman.
Thus, *namaḥ* to both thumbs.
"To the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti), obeisance with the two index fingers."
Salutation with the middle two fingers to Bhūmahāvarāha.
Salutation with the two ring fingers to Rāma, the banner of the solar dynasty.
"Brahmā, Kamalā, Gada, Sūrya, and Keśava—[these are assigned] to the two little fingers; [the mantra] 'namaḥ' [is assigned to the palms]."
p. 568) For the remainder, [the mantra] is "namas" with both palms and backs of the hands joined.
"Divyāstra" refers to a divine weapon.
For the sake of the destruction of all evils, and for the sake of the accomplishment of all desired goals.
The application (viniyoga) is for the chanting of the Thousand Names of Śrī Viṣṇu.
Now, for the meditation: one should contemplate Viṣṇu,
adorned with a radiant crown, armlets, bracelets, various ornaments, necklaces, and decorations for his belly, feet, and hips.

I bow to Him whose shoulders are adorned with beautiful armlets, gems, and great makara-shaped earrings; who holds in His hands the discus, conch, lotus, and mace; who is clad in pure yellow silk garments; who possesses the brilliance of lightning; who resembles the rising sun; and who holds a lotus in His hand.
Oṃ! Vāsudeva is the supreme Brahman, the supreme Self, higher than the highest;
he is the supreme abode, the supreme light, the supreme reality, and the supreme goal. (10)
He is the supreme Śiva, the supreme object of meditation, supreme knowledge, the supreme goal;
he is the ultimate reality, the highest good, supreme bliss, and the supreme manifestation. || 11 ||
He is the supreme, the manifest, the beyond, the supreme ether, the half beyond the half, the Supreme Lord;
free from disease, changeless, free from conceptual construction, and without support. || 12 ||
He is unstained, without support, untainted, and unrestrained;
devoid of qualities, partless, infinite, inconceivable, immovable, and infallible.
Beyond the senses, immeasurable, unobstructed, desireless, without a superior lord, imperishable, undecaying, all-knowing, omnipresent, the All, the giver of all, and the creator of all beings. (14)
He is everything, the witness of all, the one to be worshipped by all, the seer of all;
he possesses all power, is the essence of all, the soul of all, and faces in every direction. || 15 ||
He is the abode of all, possessing all forms, the beginning of all, and the destroyer of all suffering;
he is the goal of all, auspicious in every way, and the cause of all causes. || 16 ||
He who transcends all, the supervisor of all, the Lord of all lords;
the twenty-sixth principle, the Great Viṣṇu, the Great Secret, the Great Hari. || 17 ||
Ever-arisen, ever-yoked, eternal bliss, and the ancient one;
the Lord of Māyā, the Lord of Yoga, the Lord of Kaivalya, the Self-born. || 18 ||
Transcending birth, death, and old age; beyond all parts (kalās); having passed over worldly existence;
full, true, and of the nature of pure awakening; eternally consisting of consciousness. || 19 ||
He is dear to yogis, composed of yoga, the sole liberator from the bonds of worldly existence;
he is the ancient Puruṣa, the inner consciousness, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama). || 20 ||
He is to be known through the Vedānta, difficult to comprehend, and free from the threefold afflictions;
he is the refuge of the knowledge of Brahman, unassailable, self-luminous, and self-effulgent. || 21 ||

The *praṇava* is indifferent toward all that is to be attained (*upeya*), equal in every respect, entirely irreproachable, difficult to reach, the fourth state (*turya*), and beyond darkness (*tamas*). (22)
Immovable, yet intimately connected with all, he transcends the range of speech and mind;
he is Saṅkarṣaṇa, the destroyer of all, Time itself, and the inspirer of fear in all beings.
The all-pervading Great Rudra is unassailable and difficult to approach;
he is the primordial nature, bliss, the knower of wisdom, and the deluder of the universe.
The great illusionist, the seed of the universe, who alone enjoys the bliss of supreme power; he who is desired by all, possessed of infinite virtue, and the subduer of all beings. || 25 ||
He is Aniruddha, the life-force of all, Hṛṣīkeśa, the lord of the mind; He is free from limiting adjuncts, the Beloved, the Swan, the Imperishable, and the ordainer of all. (26)
He is Brahmā, the Lord of Prāṇa, the sustainer of all beings, and the leader of the body;
he is the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña), the Master of Prakṛti, the Puruṣa, and the upholder of the thread of the universe. || 27 ||
The inner controller, the one with three abodes, the internal witness, the Lord of the three qualities;
He who is sought through yoga, the lotus-navelled one, who reclines upon Śeṣa, the Lord of Śrī. || 28 ||
Hari is the one whose lotus feet are worshipped by Śrī-Satya; he is Ananta, Śrī, and the abode of Śrī;
he is the eternal Śrī upon his chest, the treasure-house of Śrī, the bearer of Śrī, and Hari.
Viṣṇu possesses lovely splendor, bestows the glory of certainty, has his abode in the ocean of milk,
has his chest illuminated by the Kaustubha gem, is Mādhava, and is the remover of the world's affliction.
He whose chest bears the Śrīvatsa mark is boundless, a vessel of auspicious qualities;
he is the one clad in yellow garments, the Lord of the world, the sustainer of the world, and the father of the world.
The friend of the world, the creator of the world, the maker of the world, the treasure-house of the world;
he whose valor alone flashes throughout the world, who does not speak of "I" or "mine," and who is identical with the universe.

He consists of all wonders, he is the goal of all perfections, and he is the conqueror of all heroes; his exertion is never in vain, and his consciousness is superior to that of Brahmā, Rudra, and others. || 33 ||
The grandfather of Śambhu, the father of Brahmā, the sovereign lord of Śakra and the other gods;
beloved by all the deities, he whose conduct is that of all the gods, the unsurpassed one. (34)
The sole refuge of all gods, the sole deity of all gods;
the enjoyer of sacrifice, the giver of the fruit of sacrifice, the Lord of sacrifice, and the creator of sacrifice.

The protector of sacrifice, the personification of sacrifice, wearing a forest garland, beloved by the twice-born; the sole bestower of joy upon the twice-born, the non-violent, the family deity, and the destroyer of the asuras. || 36 ||
The ender of all the wicked, the protector of the joy of all the virtuous;
the single belly of all the worlds, the single mandala of all the worlds. || 37 ||
He who effects creation, preservation, and destruction; the wielder of the discus, the bearer of the Śārṅga bow, and the holder of the mace;
the possessor of the conch, the bearer of the sword Nandaka, with the lotus in his hand, whose vehicle is Garuḍa. || 38 ||
His form is indescribable; he is all things, the sole purifier of all the worlds;
his fame is infinite; he is the Lord beyond [worldly] glory; he is the Supreme Person, the source of all auspiciousness. (39)
He resembles ten million suns; he is the destroyer of ten million Yamas;
he is the creator of the world as ten million Brahmās; he possesses the great strength of ten million Vāyus. || 40 ||
He who brings joy to the world like ten million moons, the Great Lord who is the equal of ten million Śambhus;
he who possesses the fortune of ten million Kuberas, and who is the destroyer of ten million enemies. || 41 ||
Possessing the beauty of ten million Kandarpas, the subduer of ten million fortresses, as deep as ten million oceans, and bearing the names of ten million sacred fords (tīrthas). || 42 ||
Unshakable as ten million Himalayas, possessing a body of ten million universes,
he is the destroyer of the sins of ten million horse-sacrifices and is equal to the worship of ten million sacrifices.

He is the cause of well-being for millions of nectars, the fulfiller of desires for millions of wish-granting cows, the embodiment of millions of forms of the knowledge of Brahman, the one pervaded by rays (or entered by the rays), and he whose fame is pure.
The sustainer of the universe, whose feet are the sacred fords, whose hearing and chanting are meritorious,
the primordial god, the conqueror of the world, Mukunda, the slayer of Kālanemi.
Vaikuṇṭha, of infinite majesty, the Lord of the great lords of yogis,
eternally satisfied, the true essence of men, free from doubt, and the destroyer of hell.
The sole refuge for the poor and helpless, the remover of the world's singular misfortunes, eternally creating forbearance in the world, compassionate, and the shelter of the virtuous. (47)
The Lord of Yoga, eternally exalted, devoid of increase or decrease;
Adhokṣaja, the seed of the universe, the Lord of Prajāpati and of meditative absorption. || 48 ||
His feet are worshipped by Śakra and Brahmā; he has gone to the supreme abode of Śambhu and Brahmā;
his eyes are the sun and the moon; he is the enjoyer of the universe and the one who has reached the further shore of all things.
He is the bridge for the world, the bridge of dharma, the steadfast one who bears the burden of warding off misfortune;
he is free from possessiveness, the lord of all worlds, unattached, and the possessor of wondrous enjoyments.
Ramya, Māya, Viśvaviśva, Viṣvaksena, Nagottama, Sarva, and Śrīpati—the Lord of the Goddess—who is adorned with all ornaments. || 51 ||
He is endowed with all auspicious marks, the destroyer of the pride of all the lords of the Daityas, the omniscient among all gods, and the leader of all deities. || 52 ||
He is the fortress for all deities, a thunderbolt-cage for those who have sought refuge;
he is the armor for all gods and the crest-jewel of all deities.
The Lord Viṣṭaraśravas has shattered all worldly existence;
he is the pervasive one, the benefactor of all, the sun, the destroyer of enemies, and the bestower of supreme bliss.
The Lord of life for all the deities, the ordainer of the Brāhmaṇas and others; Brahmā, Śambhu, and those beyond the parārdha; the eldest of Brahmā, the Child, the self-sovereign.

Virāṭ is dependent upon his devotees, worthy of praise, the accomplisher of all goals, the creator of all things, the knower of what must be done, and eternally free from actions for his own sake. (56)
He who is eternally a giver, eternally auspicious, eternally peaceful, eternally propitious; who is eternally beloved, eternally contented, eternally nourished, and eternally worshipped. || 57 ||
Ever-pure, the foremost of purifiers, the secret of the Vedas, Vṛṣākapi;
he who has a thousand names, who exists in three ages, who possesses four forms, and who has four arms. || 58 ||
The Lord of the past, future, and present; preceded by the Great Puruṣa;
Nārāyaṇa; he of Muñja-like hair; he who has emerged from all yoga.
The essence of the Vedas, the essence of sacrifice, the essence of the Sāman chants, a treasury of austerity;
the foremost of the Sādhyas, an ancient seer, devoted to steadfastness and peace.
Śiva, the destroyer with his trident; Śrīkaṇṭha, the sole bestower of boons;
Nara, Kṛṣṇa, Hari; the son of Dharma; and the one whose life is Dharma. 61.
The first creator of all truth, the destroyer of the pride of all women-jewels, the conqueror of Kāma, he who eclipsed Urvashi’s gaze, the lord of sages. || 62 ||
Hayagrīva is the primordial poet, the Lord of all masters of speech,
composed of all the gods, the preceptor of Brahmā, and the husband of the Goddess of Eloquence.
He is the source of infinite knowledge, the destroyer of root-ignorance,
the one worthy of all worship, the annihilator of the world's dullness, and Madhusūdana.
Lord of infinite millions of mantras, the singular purifier of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman),
the primordial knower, the author of the Vedas, the soul of the Vedas, and the ocean of revelation.
He is the ornament of the Vedas and the meaning of Brahman, the birthplace of all higher knowledge;
he is the King of Sciences, the King of Wisdom, an ocean of gnosis, and possesses indivisible intellect.
Matsyadeva, possessing great horns, the creator and sustainer of the seed of the universe,
who pervaded the ocean with his sport, and the promulgator of the four Vedas.

The primordial tortoise, the support of all, who rendered the world's existence as insignificant as a blade of grass; he who immortalized the host of gods and was the cause of the production of the nectar of immortality.

The support of the self, the support of the earth, the limb of sacrifice, the upholder of the world; the slayer of Hiraṇyākṣa, the lord of the earth, and the ordainer of the ancestral rites (śrāddha) and other ceremonies. || 69 ||
He is the destroyer of all fear of the ancestors, the life-giver to all the ancestors,
the worthy recipient who alone partakes of the *havya* and *kavya* offerings, and the sole bestower of auspicious qualities.
The Great Boar, in whose body-hair the ocean was hidden and who agitated the entire sea; the destroyer of those who obstruct sacrifices and the refuge of the performers of sacrifice. 71.
Narasiṃha, the divine lion, the destroyer of all misfortunes, afflictions, and suffering;
the sole hero of wondrous power, the unique shatterer of yantras and mantras. (72)
His light was as unbearable as that of Brahmā and others, and he was more terrifying than the fire at the end of an eon;
his claws surpassed ten million thunderbolts in power, and he bore a form difficult even for an elephant to behold.
The crusher of the circle of Mothers, the Lord of the great host of Mothers;
inconceivable, rich in unfailing potency, and the devourer of all demons. (74)
The destroyer of Hiraṇyakaśipu, Time itself, Saṅkarṣaṇa, the Lord; he whose vehicle is the God of Death, the immediate destroyer of all fear.
The destroyer of all obstacles, the bestower of all accomplishments, the fulfiller of all [desires], the annihilator of all sins, and the one known as the authority over perfected mantras. || 76 ||
The Lord of Bhairava, the destroyer of Hara’s affliction, resembling Time itself, difficult to approach;
he whose name causes the embryos of the Daityas to fall away, and who is devoid of the manifest universe. 77.
The great Hari, whose form is the elements, is the protector of all through mere remembrance;
he has the skin of a Brahmin for his head-cloth, is adorned by the guardians of the quarters, and has half of his body as his ornament.

He whose abode is the twelve suns as his heads, who has Rudra’s head as his sole anklet, who delights in the Mountain-Daughter though she was seized by the Yoginīs, and who threatens Bhairava; || 79 ||
The Lord of the Heroic Circle (Vīracakreśvara), the exceedingly fierce Yamāri, the sovereign of Time (Kālasaṃvara),
the Lord of Wrath (Krodheśvara), the one who censures Rudra and Caṇḍī, and the possessor of great ferocity.
He possesses all eyes and is the death of all deaths; he is the death that turns back death itself.
He is incurable, the destroyer of all diseases, and the one who makes all malevolent planets auspicious.
The destroyer of the pride of ten million Gaṇeśas, the unbearable one who destroys all lineages, difficult to overcome by gods and demons, the father who bestows the world as food. 82.
The protector from all miserable states of existence, the devourer of the devourers of the world, the fierce lord, the cat to the demons, and the devourer of the mouse that is Time. || 83 ||
He whose staff-like arms bear infinite weapons; he who is the Man-lion (Nṛsiṃha) and the conqueror of Vīrabhadra;
the secret lord of the circle of Yoginīs; the enemy of Śakra (Indra); the consumer of animal flesh. 84.
Rudra is Nārāyaṇa, whose vehicle is Śaṅkara in the form of a ram;
he is the protector of Śiva in the form of a ram, the consumer of thousands of wicked powers.
The hero beloved of Tulasī, whose illusory power is inconceivable, the bestower of all desires;
the Great Auspicious One, Śiva, Rudra, and Bhairava who bears the single skull-cup. || 86 ||
The Bhilla, the Lord of the Discus, the Discus itself, assuming a divine and enchanting form;
the bestower of fortune upon Gaurī, the treasury of Māyā, and the remover of fear from Māyā. || 87 ||
Consisting of the splendor of Brahman, consisting of the glory of Brahman, and consisting of the three Vedas;
the one to whom the Subrahmaṇya hymn is addressed, the destroyer of Bali, the Dwarf, the remover of Aditi’s sorrow.

Upendra, the king, Viṣṇu, the ornament of Kaśyapa’s lineage, the bestower of sovereign kingship upon Bali, the imperishable soul of all gods and brahmins, and the one who is never shaken (Acyuta). (89)
Urukrama, Tīrthapāda, Tridaśa, Trivikrama, Vyomapāda, and he who has purified the three worlds with the water from his own feet. (90)
His feet are worshipped by Brahmā, Śiva, and others; he is the swift performer of actions and the sustainer of the mountains.
He possesses inconceivable and wondrous expansion; he is the cosmic tree and the one of great strength.
He who severed the heads of Bahu-mūrdhan and Parāṅga, who took the head of Bhṛgu’s wife,
who was a thief of sin yet ever meritorious, the lord of Daityas who was eternally broken.

He who has fulfilled all the lords of the gods, who acts as the sole incarnation for the sake of the universe, who is immortal, whose self is eternally protected, and who is always a wish-fulfilling gem for his devotees. 93.

The sinless Dattātreya, the lord of sages, is the bestower of boons and the grantor of royal sovereignty to Kārttavīrya and others; he is praised by the entire universe and follows immeasurable conduct.
United with his supreme Śakti, intoxicated by the pride of the bliss of yoga,
he is the tree of supreme bliss who robs the splendor of all the enemies of Indra.
The jewel born from Anasūyā’s womb, the bestower of the happiness of worldly enjoyment and liberation, the sun of Jamadagni’s lineage, who took away the wondrous power of Reṇukā. (96)
He is the one who completely wipes away the sin of matricide, the conqueror of Skanda, the bestower of sovereignty upon the Brahmins,
the end-maker of all Kṣatriyas, the destroyer of the pride of heroes, and the vanquisher of Kārtavīrya.
He is the yogi, the one who has entered yoga, the lord of yogis, and the one devoted to yoga;
he is the bestower of supreme bliss and the conferrer of glory upon the Śivācāryas. || 98 ||
Bhīma, Paraśurāma, Śivācārya, Ekaviśvabhū, Śivākhilajñānakośī, Bhīṣmācārya, and Agnidaivata—[these are the forms]. 99.
The teacher of Dronacharya, whose bow was victorious over the universe, the bringer of the end;
he was the embodiment of peerless darkness, whose only sacrificial fee was his lifelong celibacy.
The best of men, a bridge for the virtuous, most exalted, a bull among men, a sovereign, the first king, the father of the earth, and the one who caused all jewels to flow forth. (101)
Skilled in many births and other arts, he is Modesty, Fortune, Fame, and Self-Contentment;
he bestows the means of subsistence upon the world, is the most excellent of universal emperors, and wields formidable weapons.
He is the one who caused the sages beginning with Sanaka to attain an increase in devotion to the Lord;
he is the author, the expounder, and the promoter of the duties pertaining to the castes and stages of life.
Rāghava is the delight of the banner of the solar dynasty, an ocean of excellent virtues,
the dharma of the heroism of Kakutstha, and the bearer of the yoke of royal duty.
He whose intention is eternally well-established, who grasps all that is auspicious, whose vision is fixed solely on the pure;
he is the nine jewels, the treasure-store of gems, the presiding lord of all, and the great treasury. || 105 ||

The son of Daśaratha is the king who is the most excellent refuge for all, possessed of the power of every collection of weapons and missiles, the subduer of the world, and the repository of all jewels. (106)
Dharma abides in all dharmas; he is the seer of dharma and the remover of all suffering.
Transcending the senses, he has seen the further shore of both knowledge and realization; he is an ocean of forbearance. (107)
He was the most excellent of all, beloved by the learned, unperturbed by joy, grief, and other emotions;
he had renounced his empire at his father’s command and was free from fear regarding the rise of rivals.
Having bestowed his sovereignty upon the mountain cave, wearing matted hair in emulation of Śiva,
the Lord of the World who has acquired the jewel-mountain Citrakūṭa, he wanders through the battlefield.
He whose divine weapons and missiles were unfailing at will; the destroyer of the eyes of Indra’s son (Jayanta);
he who was bowed down to by Brahmā, Indra, and others; the one whose arrow was irresistible; the slayer of Mārīca; and the killer of Virādha.
He who purified the entire Daṇḍaka forest that had been struck by the curse of Brahmā,
and who alone wielded the single arrow that destroyed fourteen thousand rākṣasas.
The slayer of Khara, Ari, and Triśiras; the destroyer of Dūṣaṇa; Janārdana; the one who granted the state of Agni to Jaṭāyu; the giver of heaven to Kabandha. || 112 ||
With the tip of his play-lance, he cast down the great heap of Dundubhi’s bones;
by drawing back his bow, he caused the pain that felled the Dānavas of the netherworld from beneath the seven palm trees.
The wise bestower of Sugrīva’s kingdom, who grants fearlessness through his mere thought,
the lord of Hanumān, Rudra, and other chiefs, and the sustainer of the bodies of all the monkeys.
The ocean was utterly agitated by the single arrow whose deity is Agni;
the ocean was dried up and consumed by the single arrow of millions of Mlecchas. || 115 ||
He who agitated the ocean—the sole abode of the *nāgas* and *daityas*—and who, as a treasury of glory, constructed a bridge over it such as had never before been seen; (116)
The achiever of the impossible, skilled in uprooting the entire city of Laṅkā; the destroyer of the lineage of Paulastya, the arrogant inhabitants of Janasthāna who had received boons.
The slayer of Rāvaṇa; the destroyer of Prahasta, Chita, Kumbha, Karṇa, and Abhidrugha; the cutter of the single mouth of Rāvaṇa; the bestower of the unchallenged sovereignty of Indra alone. || 118 ||

He who cuts off the distinction between heaven and non-heaven; he who takes away the lordship from the king of gods; he who removes the divinity of the Rākṣasas; he who is the temple of dharma and adharma; he who is praised by many.
The enemy Rāvaṇa, whose ten faces were not excessively formidable, was terrified by Vibhīṣaṇa,
who alone brought back to life his entire slain army through the creation of nectar.
He who bears the names of the gods and Brahmā, the sole creator, worshipped by all the immortals;
he who is venerable to Brahmā, Sūrya, Indra, Rudra, and others, honored, and beloved by the virtuous. || 121 ||

Worthy of the entire kingdom of Ayodhyā, enchanting to all beings, he was granted by his lord out of incomparable compassion; he was the singular beloved friend of both the lowly and the exalted. (122)
He perceives the logic of his own side and others; though his purpose is humble, he accomplishes great things.
He assumes the guise of a hunter yet performs what is unbecoming to such a one, bringing satisfaction to all.
His soul was intensely united with Pārvatī; he was the conqueror of the enemies of the gods who had abandoned his beloved;
he was visibly like the abode of Kuśa and Lava; and he was unconquered by Indra, Agni, and Nārāyaṇa. || 124 ||
The lord of Kośala, Vīrabāhu, Satyārtha, he who abandoned his own brother, Yaśodānandana, Nandin, and the source of prosperity for the circle of the earth. 125.
He made the deities his own by bringing them under his control through the presence of Brahmā and others who desired him;
he was the leader of the entire caravan of living beings, from the outcaste to the highest, who had attained the world of Brahmā.
He alone brought about the long-term subjugation of the forces of Svarṇīta, Gardabha, Śva, and others;
he was peerless through Rāma, and by means of Lakṣmaṇa, the son of Sumitrā, he struck down Indrajit.
Devoted to Viṣṇu, a destroyer of the sins of Śiva, content with the sovereignty of sandals,
Bharata was the slayer of ten million unbearable Gandharvas and the ender of Lavaṇa.
Śatrughna is the king of physicians, the lord of medicinal herbs containing the essence of Āyurveda;
he is the source of the eternal and the non-eternal, Dhanvantari, the sacrifice, and the sustainer of the world.
He who is the obstacle to the sun, the one with excellent life, the lord of the south, the beloved of the twice-born;
he who possesses the instruction on the severed head and who has formed friendship with the son of the Sun (Yama). 130.
Kapila, the son of Kardama, established a man upon his remaining limb;
he was the one who reduced the sons of Sagara to ashes by interrupting their meditative absorption (*yogātman*).
Dharma is the lord of Viśveśvara and Surabhī, purified by his own essential nature; he is Śambhu, the sole source of stability in the burning of Tripura, and the one who raised the universal chariot.
The soul of the universe, whose form remained unimpaired even after the severing of the heads of all the Rudras for their sake;
he who is the fire known by names such as Vājapeya and others, and who is solely devoted to the dharma of the Vedas.

Lord of Śvetadvīpa, propounder of Sāṅkhya, sovereign of all supernatural powers, he who has illuminated the yoga of meditation for the entire world and who destroys the blinding darkness of delusion. (134)
Worshipped by Śambhu as his devotee, he performed all austerities at the Daityāmṛtavāpī;
he was the sole lord of all the Daityas, unique and without equal throughout the entire universe during the great dissolution.
The remaining deity is the thousand-eyed one, possessing a thousand feet, heads, and arms;
he supports the waters and the earth upon the tips of the hoods of his serpent-hood.
He is the progenitor of Kālāgnirudra, armed with a mace, and having a plow for his weapon;
he is clad in blue garments, the lord of Vāruṇī, and the destroyer of the defects of mind, speech, and body.
Content with his own satisfaction alone, he brought the ten-faced Rāvaṇa to his downfall; the terrible son of Rohiṇī bound Bali and slew Pralamba. (138)
The slayer of Muṣṭika, the destroyer of Dvivida, the divider of the Yamunā, Balarāma, the lover of Revatī, he whose devotion was formerly directed toward Viṣṇu, and the elder brother of Acyuta. (139)
Born of Devakī and Vasudeva, the joy of Aditi and Kaśyapa,
he is the descendant of Vṛṣṇi, the best of the Sātvatas, the son of Śūra, and the upholder of the Yadu lineage.
He who possesses a human form is the full Brahman, the ambidextrous archer, the scorcher of foes;
he is the eternal youth upon the mountain of the world, which is constantly subject to the desires of Brahmā and the other gods.
The slayer of Pūtanā, the breaker of the cart, the crusher of the twin Arjuna trees; the enemy of the demon Vatsāsura, the slayer of Keśin, the foe of Dhenuka, and the Lord of the cows. || 142 ||
Dāmodara, the god of the cowherds, who brings joy to Yaśodā;
the subduer of Kālīya, beloved by all the cowherds and cowherdesses. 143.
Govinda, who sportively held up Govardhana, the festival of Gokula, the slayer of Ariṣṭa, and the bestower of liberation upon the gopīs intoxicated by passion. || 144 ||
The immediate slayer of Kuvalayāpīḍa, the crusher of Cāṇūra, the enemy of Kaṃsa, the immortal who established Ugrasena and others in their kingdom, and the destroyer of enemies. 145.
He marked the world with the Sudharma hall, brought about the end of Jarāsandha, abandoned his devotion to Jarāsandha, and bestowed fame upon Bhīmasena. (146)
He who restored the dead son to Sāndīpani, the conqueror of Kāla, Antaka, and the rest;
the lover of Rukmiṇī, the subduer of Rukmin, and the destroyer of Naraka. 147.
The savior of all hell-beings, the conqueror of millions of all earthly kings, the beloved of all beautiful women, the enemy of the asuras, whose banner bears Garuḍa. || 148 ||
The sole conqueror of Rudra, Arka, Marut, and Āpa; the Lord of all;
the destroyer of the pride of the King of Gods; he who adorns the earth with the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣas). || 149 ||
He who conquered millions of mountain ranges with his arms severed by Bāṇa’s thousands of arrows;
he who effortlessly defeated Mahādeva and is worshipped solely by Mahādeva. 150.
He who reviled Arjuna for the sake of Indra, the bestower of victory, the sole supporter of the Pāṇḍavas;
he who severed the head of the King of Kāśī, and the sole crusher by Rudra’s power. || 151 ||
Richly endowed with the grace of Viśveśvara, he was the slayer of the daughter of the King of Kāśī;
he was the fulfiller of Śambhu’s vow and a worshiper of the self-manifested Gaṇa. || 152 ||
He multiplied the number of Gaṇas by ten million times a hundred thousand; he was the teacher of the world and the worshiper of the twice-born;
he was subdued by the intense penance of Śiva; and in former times, he was the bestower of boons upon Śiva.

He who upholds the vow of the demon Gaja, who worships Śaṅkara as his own partial incarnation, who is the lord of the vow of Śiva’s daughter, who possesses the form of Kṛṣṇa, and who is the slayer of Śiva’s enemies. 154.
He whose body is Mahālakṣmī, who is Gaurī’s protector, who is Devala, and who dispels the wind;
he who alone awakened the mucukunda tree, who is the Brahmāstra, and who carried away Yuvanāśva. 155.
Akrūra, the sole object of devotion for those headed by Akrūra, who grants liberation at his own will;
he who turned the ocean into an immortal pool for the water-sports of the children and women. 156.
The Lord of Yamunā, who brought and married the son of a twice-born;
Śrīdāma, Śaṅku, and Indrabhairava, who was brought from the land for the sake of his devotees. 157.
The Lord of Dvārakā, having liberated the ill-behaved Śiśupāla alone,
made Dvārakā a treasury for ten million people, reaching down even to the outcaste Cāṇḍālas.
He alone who restored to life Parīkṣit, whose embryo had been consumed by the Brahmāstra;
he who brought back the daughter of a twice-born man whom he had married; and he who removed the pride of Arjuna.
Having swallowed all the majesty of Bhīṣma and the others by means of his secret gestures (mudrās),
he shattered all the divine weapons for the sake of Pārtha and bore the delusion of Pārtha.
He who brought about the destruction of the Yādavas under the pretext of Brahmā’s curse; he who brings forth all prosperity;
he who is bodiless (Anaṅga); he who has conquered the Lord of Gaurī; he who is the beloved of Rati; he who is always desired. 161.

He whose arrow is the flower, the conqueror of the universe, Smara; the husband of Kāmeśvarī; the husband of Uṣā; the cause of the universe; he who is satisfied by the universe; the Supreme Person (Adhipuruṣa). || 162 ||
He is fourfold in nature, consisting of the four castes, and the ordainer of the four Vedas;
he is the soul of the twenty-four principles and the single universal soul among all millions of most excellent beings. 163.
The ancient seer Vyāsa, the author of a thousand scriptures, the creator of the Mahābhārata, and the lord of poets Bādarāyaṇa, is the very self of the substratum. || 164 ||
Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana is the teacher of the goal of all human beings, the author of the Vedānta, the revealer of Brahman alone, and the founder of the Pūru lineage. || 165 ||
The Buddha, who has conquered all the gods through meditation, is beloved by the world;
he is the unconquered victor over the universe, possessed of glorious wealth, and the deluder of the wicked. (166)

The expeller of Daityas and gods, the protector of the meaning and hearing of the Vedas, the pure one whose desires have perished, the bestower of happiness, and the Lord of both the existent and the non-existent. || 167 ||

Bestowing grace upon all according to their capacity, entirely empty yet the granter of all desires, he is the distinct reality beyond the four logical alternatives, the Lord of the Perfection of Wisdom. (168)
Following the path of heretical scriptures, Kalkī, the son of Viṣṇuyaśas and destroyer of the Kali age, will be a protector of the heretical scriptures. || 169 ||
He is the destroyer of all barbarians in hand-to-hand combat, the benefactor of all refined twice-born classes,
the promoter of truth, and the remover of the long-standing hunger of gods and brahmins.
Through the knowledge of the Aśvarāva and other [mantras], he destroys the miserable state of the earth;
he instantly bestows infinite prosperity upon the earth and restores all lost dharma in its entirety. (171)
He who has filled all the twice-born with gold through sacrifices for infinite heavens;
the sole ruler of the world who is difficult to overcome; he who is worshipped by the universe—the Banner of Victory. (172)
The Lord of the reality of the Self, the supreme creator, the Ordainer, the Lord of Umā;
the best of husbands, the foremost of the lords of creatures, and the leader of Marīci and Janaka.

Kaśyapa is the king of the gods, Indra; Prahlāda is the king of the Daityas, and the Moon is the lord of the constellations. The Sun is the most excellent of luminaries, and Śukra is the sovereign of poets. || 174 ||
Bhṛgu, the king of great sages; Viṣṇu, the lord of the Ādityas; Bali, the self-ruling sovereign; Vāyu; Agni; Śuci, the most excellent; Śaṅkara, the king of the Rudras; and Guru. || 175 ||
The most learned Citraratha, the foremost of the Gandharvas, the best of the Vasus, Varṇādya, the preeminent among women Gaurī, Śakti, the foremost of the Śrīs, and Nārada. (176)
The king of celestial sages, Arjuna the foremost of the Pāṇḍavas, the master of Nārada’s speech;
the wind, the lord of the winds, Varuṇa, the lord of aquatic creatures. || 177 ||
The excellent medicine is the preeminent *chatraka* extracted from the supreme *gaṅgātīrtha*;
food is the foremost *sudarśana* weapon, the best of armaments, the thunderbolt (*vajra*). || 178 ||
Uccaiḥśravas is the king of horses, Airāvata is the lord of elephants, Arundhatī is the sole mistress of her husband, and the Aśvattha tree is the sovereign of all trees. || 179 ||

He whose self is the knowledge of the inner science, who is the most excellent among the meters as the *praṇava*, the king of mountains as Meru, the path of the Sāma-veda collections, and the best of times. 180.
He whose self is the beginning of the day, the one established from of old, Kapila, the sovereign of the Sāmaveda;
Tārkṣya, the king of birds, the foremost of the seasons, the spring, and the wish-fulfilling tree. || 181 ||

He is the best of givers, the wish-fulfilling cow, the foremost destroyer of suffering, the supreme among gods, the thought-gem, the greatest of teachers, the most beneficial mother, and the father. 182.

Obeisance, obeisance to the lion, the king of beasts; to Vāsuki, the king of serpents; to the king who supports the earth; to the Brāhmaṇa, the lord of the castes; and to the foremost among those with internal organs. 183.
Thus ends this thousand names of Viṣṇu, known as Vāsudeva;
it pacifies all offenses and supremely increases devotion. (184)
It is the sole means for attaining all goals, beginning with the imperishable world of Brahmā;
it is the singular staircase to the realm of Viṣṇu and the destroyer of all suffering. (185)
It is truth that bestows all happiness, which grants supreme liberation, and which completely purifies the impurities of the mind, such as desire, anger, and the rest. || 186 ||
It bestows peace and purity even upon men who are great sinners;
it swiftly grants all desired fruits to all living beings. || 187 ||
It pacifies all obstacles, destroys all misfortunes, alleviates terrible suffering, and eradicates severe poverty. (188)
It removes the threefold suffering, it is secret, it bestows wealth, grain, and fame;
it grants all sovereignty, it bestows all perfections, and it yields [benefits] at all times. 189.
It bestows the fruit of millions of pilgrimages, sacrifices, austerities, gifts, and vows;
it pacifies the dullness of those lacking wisdom and sets all branches of knowledge in motion. || 190 ||
It bestows sovereignty upon those who desire a kingdom, removes all diseases from the sick,
grants sons quickly to barren women, and yields the fruit of all that is most excellent.
It destroys the poison of weapons, eliminates the affliction of planetary influences, and brings auspiciousness, merit, and long life through hearing, reciting, and chanting it. (192)
All the Vedas with their auxiliary limbs, millions of mantras, the Purāṇas, the Śāstras, and the Smṛtis were recited and likewise taught by him all at once. (193)
O Dear One, for one who recites even half a verse or a single quarter-verse of this [mantra] daily, everything is accomplished without delay; how much more so, then, the whole? 194.
O blessed lady, this which is equal to one's own life-breath must be recited by you every day in all activities;
it is to be kept secret for the sole purpose of achieving your own welfare. (195)

It must not be given to one who is not a Vaiṣṇava, to one whose self is afflicted by doubt, to one devoid of devotion and faith, or to one who views Viṣṇu as being on a par with ordinary beings. || 196 ||
This should be given to a son or to a pure disciple out of a desire for their welfare;
without my grace, those of small intelligence will not grasp this.
O Nārada, in the Kali age, Kalpagrāma will appear immediately,
by which the suffering of people who are devoid of fortune shall perish.
This shall indeed come to pass in the Vaiṣṇava fields within Āryāvarta.
There is no truth higher than Viṣṇu; there is no supreme state higher than Viṣṇu. (199)
There is no knowledge higher than Viṣṇu; indeed, there is no liberation for one who is not a Vaiṣṇava.
There is no mantra higher than Viṣṇu; there is no ascetic heat (tapa) higher than Viṣṇu.
There is no meditation higher than Viṣṇu, and indeed there is no mantra that is not Vaiṣṇava;
what is the use of his many mantras, or what is the use of extensive recitations? (201)
What is the use of thousands of Vājapeya sacrifices for one who possesses devotion to Janārdana?
Viṣṇu is the embodiment of all holy fords; the Lord is the embodiment of all scriptures.
Viṣṇu consists of all sacrifices; I speak the truth, the truth!
All this that has been declared by me is the very essence of everything up to the heart of Brahman. (203)
The illustrious Pārvatī said:
"O Teacher of the World, I am blessed, I am favored, and I have achieved my purpose, since I have heard this hymn, your secret which is very difficult to obtain. (204)
Alas! What great misery! Even while Hari, the Lord of all who bestows every happiness, exists, the deluded suffer in the cycle of worldly existence. 205.

It was for his sake that even the Lord Maheśa, clad in the directions, with matted hair, his limbs smeared with ashes, and appearing like an ascetic, was constantly looked upon with disdain by the people.
Therefore, there is no god superior to the beloved of Lakṣmī, the enemy of Madhu,
whose very essence is indeed constantly contemplated by you, the Lord of Yogins.
What higher state than this, beyond the glorious Puruṣottama, could there be?
Not knowing Him, those fools, who pride themselves on their knowledge, worship other things. 208.
I have been robbed by you, O Lord, since for so long this Sovereign has not been revealed to me, even though the divine powers were bestowed upon him today. (209)
"Aha! Viṣṇu, the Lord of all, the highest among the best of all gods, the primordial teacher of beings such as yourself, is perceived by the foolish as if he were an ordinary being. (210)
For when those of great majesty show favor even to their enemies, those abodes of forgiveness overlook the sins of even their detractors.
In my youth as well, my father’s subjects were once joyful yet hungry;
they were unable to support themselves due to suffering and were not formerly attended by prosperity. (212)
And by the subjects nurtured by you, the gods and others,
along with their friends, allies, and kinsmen, were served according to their respective capacities.
Without you, where is divinity, where is fortitude, and where is a wife?
All live on, yet the torments remain fixed upon their heads. (214)
Without that very nectar, dharma and artha are unattainable, and even kāma and mokṣa are difficult to obtain;
for those who are hungry and destitute, how can there be yoga and meditative absorption? (215)
O Śaṅkara, that Kamalā— who is the sole essence of saṃsāra and the unique protectress of all the worlds— is under his control, even though she has abandoned you as well.
Of that great-souled one, who was filled with glory, righteousness, heroism, beauty, and the perfection of uprightness, as well as with a prowess that surpassed all others.
Who can attain equality with Viṣṇu, the God of gods, by whose partial portion of a portion everything else dissolves? (218)
p. 581) Those who are deluded by this [ignorance] speak of this world as such for the sake of fault-finding;
yet for Him there is no birth, no old age, no death, nor even the failure to attain His own purpose. 219.
Nevertheless, he performs religious duties for the sake of protecting the virtuous;
therefore, having bowed down to the one Great Lord Maheśvara, make a request to Mahādeva.
Having understood it thus, O beloved, O eternal fulfiller of desires, O Lord of all, O Master, I [speak] because my mind is attached to desire and the like. (221)
O Bull-bannered Lord, if I am unable to recite this *Sahasranāma* of Viṣṇu every day— whether due to being absorbed in You or because of Your grace—
then tell me, O Master, which single name might yield that same fruit.
Śrī Mahādeva said:
"Rāma, Rāma, Rāma—O beautiful-faced one, I delight in the charming Rāma;
the name of Rāma is equal to a thousand names that are beyond compare. (223)
Therefore, all sacred fords and even the waters born of Prayāga do not equal even a sixteenth part of the thousand names of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the *Śrīviṣṇusahasranāma* as declared in the *Nāradapañcarātra*.
Thus ends the Viṣṇutantra;
thus ends the Śrī-Śāktapramoda. Herein is the table of contents of the work.

The meditation on Kālī has been described; here, moreover, her worship with painted limbs is written down. The extraction of the yantra, the mantra itself along with its extraction, and the method of worship—both concise and extensive—are given. Furthermore, the hymn that destroys all offenses has also been recounted.
A thousand names have been declared, and here one hundred [names] from the Upaniṣads are spoken as a protective armor for the heart. || 1 ||
Herein, indeed, the worship and hymn of Tārā have been declared, as well as her armor (varma);
thereafter, the excellent heart-mantra has been stated, followed by the supreme secret essence (upaniṣad) consisting of one hundred and eight names.
That hundred of his has been proclaimed here with effort as auspicious;
likewise, that thousand is delightful, the form of the Sun, the destroyer of darkness, and similarly the Ṣoḍaśī-yantra which brings swift results.

Chinnamastā is endowed with grace through Lakṣmī; likewise, she possesses all [auspicious things] such as pearls and the like, as well as smoke, and is joined with dharma and artha, bestowing devotion upon the worlds here.
p.

582) Herein, the worship, the praise, and the armor for the heart of Mātaṅgī—who possesses the intellect of Bagalāmukhī, who is endowed with the power that cuts down enemies, and who is the formidable Dambheśvarī—are proclaimed. || 3 ||

Herein, one hundred and eight names have been written; beyond that, a thousand [names] are prescribed for worship, and the hymn of Kumārī has also been told, as well as her armor (varma) and libation (tarpaṇa).
Indeed, when the *Śāktapramoda* has been obtained, the fire-oblation (homa), giving (dāna), and the practice with power (bala) are performed here in a beautiful manner.
But here, all of these rare opportunities, which are difficult to find elsewhere, are obtained together in one place. || 4 ||
That which was spoken is meditation (dhyāna), and the yantra and mantra are also proclaimed.
In this Śāktapramodaka, there is an extraction of the ten vidyās.

In this [work], there is the meditation on Viṣṇu with illustrations, the ritual for worship, a hymn of praise, and the armor-protecting mantra (varma-hṛt) which is declared to be appropriate; furthermore, the Upaniṣad, the one hundred and eight names,
the secret mantra of the gods, and the thousand names have all been written here.
The extraction of the yantras and mantras, the entire heart-mantra, and likewise that of the Goddess.
All this has been declared here as being devoid of the *Hṛdaya* of Gaṇeśeśvara;
likewise, even the *Mārttaṇḍa-sūkta* is complete in this regard, yet it is joined with a supreme *Hṛdaya*.
There is nothing else of its kind here, and this wonderful fact should be understood from what is known in the *Ugrā Upaniṣad*.
All that is appropriated therein has been presented by all learned people exactly as it was found in its respective place. || 7 ||

In the autumn year joined with six Vedas, digits, and the moon (1946), on a lunar day marked by the digit of the moon, during the sixth face [of the month], in the bright fortnight, in the auspicious month of Mādhava, which bestows victory, happiness, and welfare upon mankind— this entire work, the *Śāktapramoda*, having been fully instructed, reached its conclusion.
It was well-composed by the illustrious gods ending with Nandana, who were suns to the lotuses of the royal lineage. || 8 ||
Thus the subjects of the treatise are concluded.
